sources.correction_check: PubMed lists a published erratum for this article (PMID 27235404; BMJ 2016;353:i3041). Its text could not be opened (no abstract, no PMC copy; web search gave only the citation). The PubMed abstract gives trial registration NCT00350389 while the PMC text gives NCT00350855, which may be what was corrected. All falls figures used here are identical in the abstract and the full-text Table 2. Not retracted (PubMed retracted publication[pt] search). Scite unavailable (monthly usage limit reached), so no Scite editorial-notice check.

Subgroup findings are pre-planned with significant interaction (P<0.001) but rest on a median split of a self-reported outdoor-activity score. Single trial, not replicated; tinted lenses may have contributed; 357 people declined after initial interest (volunteer bias). Recommended by World Falls Guidelines 2022.

The 2023 notice (doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(23)00629-3) could not be opened (no readable text). No retraction. Median time to surgery in the standard-care group was already 24 h (IQR 10 to 42).

sources.quality_note: Small single-hospital QI report; measures documentation, not actual conversations (authors' stated limitation). Useful as the PubMed-indexed hip-fracture source that Consent Form Four is used when a patient lacks capacity and that clinicians must seek the views of those close to the patient as part of a best-interests decision under the MCA 2005.

sources.citation: Wade DT, Kitzinger C. Making healthcare decisions in a person's best interests when they lack capacity: clinical guidance based on a review of evidence. Clin Rehabil. 2019;33(10):1571-85.

sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices listed. PubMed: no retraction, erratum or expression of concern found (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Authoritative review by a rehabilitation physician and a medical law scholar; states who the legal decision-maker is under the MCA 2005.

sources.citation: Orr T, Baruah R. Consent in anaesthesia, critical care and pain medicine. BJA Educ. 2018;18(5):135-9.

sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices listed. PubMed: no retraction, erratum or expression of concern found (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Peer-reviewed educational article; describes the MCA 2005 best-interests process and consultation with family.

sources.citation: Edwardson S, Baruah R. Scots law and its relevance to anaesthesia, critical care, and pain medicine. BJA Educ. 2018;18(6):178-84.

sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices listed. PubMed: no retraction, erratum or expression of concern found (26 Sep 2026).

States the welfare-attorney consent requirement explicitly; it does NOT state in the opened text that a guardian with medical treatment powers must consent (it lists guardians among the persons to be consulted). The Act and its Part 5 code of practice were not opened.

sources.citation: Neuman MD, Feng R, Carson JL, Gaskins LJ, Dillane D, Sessler DI, et al. Spinal anesthesia or general anesthesia for hip surgery in older adults. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(22):2025-35.
sources.design: Pragmatic randomised superiority trial (REGAIN)

sources.tool_used: PubMed lookup_article_by_citation; get_article_metadata; Scite (editorial notices; full-text excerpts not returned)
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices listed. PubMed: PMID search with retracted publication[pt], retraction of publication[pt] or expression of concern[pt] returned no record (26 Sep 2026); published-erratum title search found no notice for this article.
sources.quality_note: Large pragmatic RCT. Primary outcome is a composite (death or inability to walk about 3 m at 60 days); 16% of the spinal group did not receive spinal as assigned. Full-text exclusion criteria were not accessible.

sources.citation: Vail EA, Feng R, Sieber F, Carson JL, Ellenberg SS, Magaziner J, et al. Long-term outcomes with spinal versus general anesthesia for hip fracture surgery: a randomized trial. Anesthesiology. 2024;140(3):375-86.

sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices listed. PubMed: no retraction or erratum found (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Vital status available for 89.2%; authors note one-year mortality lower than in unselected hip fracture populations and that subtle effects cannot be excluded.

sources.citation: Neuman MD, Feng R, Ellenberg SS, Sieber F, Sessler DI, Magaziner J, et al. Pain, analgesic use, and patient satisfaction with spinal versus general anesthesia for hip fracture surgery: a randomized clinical trial. Ann Intern Med. 2022;175(7):952-60.

sources.population_setting: REGAIN participants (1600), 46 US and Canadian hospitals
sources.tool_used: PubMed search_articles and get_article_metadata; Scite (editorial notices)
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices listed. PubMed: no retraction or erratum found (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Secondary outcomes with missing data and multiple comparisons (authors' limitation); gives the result that went the other way for spinal anaesthesia.

sources.citation: Magaziner J, Hawkes W, Hebel JR, Zimmerman SI, Fox KM, Dolan M, et al. Recovery from hip fracture in eight areas of function. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2000;55(9):M498-507.
sources.design: Prospective multicentre cohort, 2-year follow-up

sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. 3 contrasting citation statements in Scite tally (not reviewed individually).
sources.quality_note: Classic, well-cited cohort; old (1990-91) and US community-dwellers only; recovery times are group-level estimates of when the maximum is reached, not what each person reaches.

sources.citation: Dyer SM, Crotty M, Fairhall N, Magaziner J, Beaupre LA, Cameron ID, et al. A critical review of the long-term disability outcomes following hip fracture. BMC Geriatr. 2016;16(1):158.
sources.design: Critical (narrative-synthesis) review of 38 cohort studies
sources.population_setting: Hip fracture cohorts followed 3 months or longer, mainly Western countries
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Broad review with ranges rather than pooled estimates; describes outcomes under usual care of the time, not what better care can achieve.

sources.citation: Handoll HH, Cameron ID, Mak JC, Panagoda CE, Finnegan TP. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation for older people with hip fractures. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2021;11(11):CD007125.
sources.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 randomised and quasi-randomised trials (5351 participants)
sources.population_setting: People aged 65 and over after hip fracture surgery; inpatient and ambulatory multidisciplinary rehabilitation versus usual care
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Highest-level evidence; moderate certainty for the inpatient 'poor outcome' composite; heterogeneous interventions; home-based supported discharge evidence very low certainty.

sources.citation: Harrison JK, Garrido AG, Rhynas SJ, Logan G, MacLullich AM, MacArthur J, et al. New institutionalisation following acute hospital admission: a retrospective cohort study. Age Ageing. 2017;46(2):238-244.
sources.design: Retrospective case-note cohort (single centre)
sources.population_setting: 100 adults admitted from home to one Scottish teaching hospital (Nov 2013 to Feb 2015) and discharged to a care home; mostly medical admissions, 10% fractures
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Used only for its Background statement summarising NHS England and Scottish Government policy (secondary report of policy, 2017) and for context. Alasdair MacLullich is a co-author: the post must not present it as his own practice or opinion. Not hip-fracture specific.

sources.citation: Scottish Government. Choosing a care home on discharge from hospital: guidance. Edinburgh: Scottish Government [web page not opened].
sources.design: Government guidance (not opened)
sources.population_setting: Scotland, adults in hospital needing a care home place
sources.tool_used: WebSearch (official page could not be opened; also listed: publications.scot.nhs.uk/files/cel2013-32.pdf)
sources.correction_check: Not applicable (policy document); current version and wording not verified.
sources.quality_note: Search-engine summary only, not verbatim page text. Not sufficient for an essential claim; do not quote or paraphrase it as the guidance's wording.

sources.citation: Loggers SAI, Willems HC, Van Balen R, Gosens T, Polinder S, Ponsen KJ, et al. Evaluation of quality of life after nonoperative or operative management of proximal femoral fractures in frail institutionalized patients: the FRAIL-HIP study. JAMA Surg. 2022;157(5):424-434.
sources.design: Prospective multicentre cohort; treatment chosen through shared decision-making (not randomised); non-inferiority comparison of proxy-rated quality of life
sources.population_setting: 172 frail, institutionalised people aged 70 and over with limited life expectancy and a femoral neck or pertrochanteric fracture, 25 Dutch hospitals, 2018-2020; 6-month follow-up
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (abstract); Scite search_literature full-text excerpts (PMC full text not returned by PubMed tool)
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. PubMed author search for published errata/retractions (Ottesen, Kammerlander, Loggers): none linked to this article. The three Osteoporos Int corrections (PMIDs 36648543, 40387895, 40764419) concern the separate FRAIL-HIP cost-utility paper, not this article.
sources.quality_note: Only sizeable prospective study of this choice; selection by choice means mortality differences reflect who chose, not the effect of not operating (authors say so). Quality of life proxy-rated. Abstract week-1 confidence intervals look internally inconsistent (0.26 [0.11-0.23]); do not quote EQ-5D figures.

sources.citation: Kammerlander C, Pfeufer D, Lisitano LA, Mehaffey S, Böcker W, Neuerburg C. Inability of older adult patients with hip fracture to maintain postoperative weight-bearing restrictions. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2018;100(11):936-941.
sources.design: Prospective comparative gait study with insole force sensors
sources.population_setting: 16 patients aged 75 and over after hip fracture surgery versus 18 patients aged 18 to 40 after ankle fracture surgery, Munich, Germany; all told to keep to 20 kg or less
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. PubMed author search for published errata/retractions (Ottesen, Kammerlander, Loggers): none linked to this article.
sources.quality_note: Very small, single centre, one gait session after physiotherapy training; abstract's control-group figures are reported two ways (14 of 18 and 16 of 18).

sources.citation: Pfeufer D, Zeller A, Mehaffey S, Böcker W, Kammerlander C, Neuerburg C. Weight-bearing restrictions reduce postoperative mobility in elderly hip fracture patients. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg. 2019;139(9):1253-1259.
sources.design: Pre-post comparative study with insole force sensor gait analysis on day 5
sources.population_setting: 41 older patients with pertrochanteric fracture treated the same way, one German hospital; 19 told to partial weight-bear, 22 to full weight-bear
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Small, non-randomised (pre-post); same research group as Kammerlander 2018.

sources.citation: Ottesen TD, McLynn RP, Galivanche AR, Bagi PS, Zogg CK, Rubin LE, et al. Increased complications in geriatric patients with a fracture of the hip whose postoperative weight-bearing is restricted: an analysis of 4918 patients. Bone Joint J. 2018;100-B(10):1377-1384.
sources.design: Retrospective registry analysis with multivariable adjustment
sources.population_setting: 4918 patients over 60 having hip fracture surgery, 2016 US NSQIP hip fracture dataset; outcomes within 30 days
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. PubMed author search for published errata/retractions (Ottesen, Kammerlander, Loggers): none linked to this article.
sources.quality_note: Observational; confounding by indication likely (restriction is prescribed for harder fractures and fixations). Abstract arithmetic inconsistent: 3668 is given as 63.53% of 4918, but 3668/4918 is about 75%; do not quote the percentage.

sources.citation: Tarrant SM, Attia J, Balogh ZJ. The influence of weight-bearing status on post-operative mobility and outcomes in geriatric hip fracture. Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg. 2022;48(5):4093-4103.
sources.design: Prospective observational cohort with adjusted and mediation analyses
sources.population_setting: 1514 hip fracture patients aged 65 and over (1479 treated surgically), one Australian trauma centre, 4 years
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Conflicting evidence for the harm claim: only 58 had restricted weight-bearing, so estimates are imprecise.

sources.citation: Xu S, Gao F, Chen Y, Liu G, Peng K, Zhang J, et al. Impact of postoperative weight-bearing protocols on prognosis in geriatric hip fracture patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Clin Med. 2026;15(10):3912.
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO-registered), 10 studies (1 RCT, 9 cohorts), GRADE
sources.population_setting: 5806 patients aged 65 and over after hip fracture surgery, unrestricted versus restricted weight-bearing
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Most recent synthesis; low to very low certainty; abstract has garbled symbols and an implausible absolute risk difference (-0.10%), so quote only the direction and certainty.

sources.citation: Taraldsen K, Sletvold O, Thingstad P, Saltvedt I, Granat MH, Lydersen S, et al. Physical behavior and function early after hip fracture surgery in patients receiving comprehensive geriatric care or orthopedic care: a randomized controlled trial. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2014;69(3):338-45.
sources.design: Randomised controlled trial (part of the Trondheim Hip Fracture Trial)

sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (full text closed; Scite gave no excerpts)
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. 2 contrasting citation statements in Scite tally (not reviewed).
sources.quality_note: Randomised comparison of ward models; 80 of 397 did not wear the monitor; numbers of upright events not given in the abstract.

sources.citation: Zusman EZ, Dawes MG, Edwards N, Ashe MC. A systematic review of evidence for older adults' sedentary behavior and physical activity after hip fracture. Clin Rehabil. 2018;32(5):679-691.
sources.design: Systematic review of 14 studies (882 participants) measuring activity with monitors
sources.population_setting: Older adults with hip fracture in hospital, rehabilitation centres and the community
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Small, heterogeneous studies; gives ranges, not pooled estimates.

sources.citation: Love AL, Cornwell PL, Whitehouse SL. Oropharyngeal dysphagia in an elderly post-operative hip fracture population: a prospective cohort study. Age Ageing. 2013;42(6):782-5.
sources.design: Prospective cohort
sources.population_setting: 181 patients (mean age 83, range 65-103) in a specialised orthogeriatric unit, Brisbane, Australia, assessed after hip fracture surgery
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Single unit; assessment method and timing not given in abstract (authors are speech pathologists).

sources.citation: Suzuki M, Nagano A, Ueshima J, Saino Y, Kawase F, Kobayashi H, et al. Prevalence of dysphagia in patients after orthopedic surgery. Arch Gerontol Geriatr. 2024;119:105312.
sources.design: Scoping review with pooled prevalence (21 studies; 7 on hip fracture)
sources.population_setting: People aged 60 and over after orthopaedic surgery
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Wide confidence interval for hip fracture (15% to 54%) reflects different methods and timing.

sources.citation: Mateos-Nozal J, Sanchez Garcia E, Romero Rodríguez E, Cruz-Jentoft AJ. Oropharyngeal dysphagia in older patients with hip fracture. Age Ageing. 2021;50(4):1416-1421.
sources.design: Prospective cohort
sources.population_setting: 320 patients (mean age 86.2) in an orthogeriatric unit, Madrid, Spain; Volume-Viscosity Swallow Test within 72 hours of surgery
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Higher estimate than Love 2013, using a sensitive bedside test in an older group; shows how much prevalence depends on method.

sources.citation: Allen J, Greene M, Sabido I, Stretton M, Miles A. Economic costs of dysphagia among hospitalized patients. Laryngoscope. 2020;130(4):974-979.
sources.design: Retrospective parallel cohort using coded diagnoses
sources.population_setting: 2453 admissions with hip or femur fracture, Waitemata District Health Board, Auckland, New Zealand; 165 with a coded dysphagia diagnosis
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Observational and unadjusted in the abstract; the dysphagia group was older (mean 85 vs 78) and coded dysphagia captures more obvious cases.

sources.citation: Baijens LW, Clavé P, Cras P, Ekberg O, Forster A, Kolb GF, et al. European Society for Swallowing Disorders - European Union Geriatric Medicine Society white paper: oropharyngeal dysphagia as a geriatric syndrome. Clin Interv Aging. 2016;11:1403-1428.
sources.design: Consensus position paper (two European specialist societies)
sources.population_setting: Older people with oropharyngeal dysphagia, all settings
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed.
sources.quality_note: Consensus document rather than a trial; used for warning signs and the upright-posture advice. Not hip-fracture specific. An RCSLT or NICE source for the signs was not found.

sources.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Hip fracture: management. Clinical guideline CG124. Recommendations (web page). London: NICE; 2011, last updated 2023.
sources.design: National clinical guideline (current web version)
sources.population_setting: Adults with hip fracture, NHS England and Wales
sources.tool_used: WebSearch (nice.org.uk results; page not opened because WebFetch is blocked)
sources.correction_check: Not applicable; search extract only.
sources.quality_note: Used only to note that the imaging recommendation wording was amended in 2014 and that the recommendation still stands (MRI; CT if MRI not available within 24 hours or contraindicated). Not relied on for any essential claim; the opened full guideline (DRIVE source) carries the claim.

sources.citation: Haj-Mirzaian A, Eng J, Khorasani R, Raja AS, Levin AS, Smith SE, et al. Use of advanced imaging for radiographically occult hip fracture in elderly patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Radiology. 2020;296(3):521-531.
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 observational studies (2992 patients), MRI as reference standard
sources.population_setting: Older patients (mean age 76.8) clinically suspected of hip fracture with no definite fracture, or only an isolated greater trochanter fracture, on radiographs; studies published to September 2018
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; full text not in PMC and not retrievable via Scite (closed access) or Undermind (no PDF)
sources.correction_check: PubMed: no retracted publication or published erratum linked (searched PMID with retracted publication[pt] and published erratum[pt], and title with erratum/correction: none). Scite record shows no editorial notices.
sources.quality_note: Moderate strength of evidence per the authors for the pooled frequency. Patients are a selected group (doctors still suspected a fracture and MRI was done), so the 39% is not the chance for every older person with hip pain after a fall. Full-text definition of 'surgical hip fracture' not read; the abstract defines it as hip fractures not seen on radiographs 'but that require surgery'.

sources.citation: Sing CW, Lin TC, Bartholomew S, Bell JS, Bennett C, Beyene K, et al. Global epidemiology of hip fractures: secular trends in incidence rate, post-fracture treatment, and all-cause mortality. J Bone Miner Res. 2023;38(8):1064-1075.
sources.design: Multinational cohort study using 20 healthcare databases with a common data model; projection of numbers to 2050
sources.population_setting: People aged 50 and over hospitalised with hip fracture in 19 countries and regions, 2005 to 2018 (4,115,046 hip fractures); UK included
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; Scite search_literature and read_fulltext (full text denied, abstract only); Undermind read_pdfs (no PDF); publisher site blocked by proxy
sources.correction_check: PubMed: no retracted publication or published erratum linked (PMID and title searches). Scite record shows no editorial notices; 262 Smart Citations, 0 contrasting.
sources.quality_note: Large standardised multinational study. Only the abstract was read: the per-country trends (including the UK series), which countries did not decrease, and the projection method details were not verified. Several authors are Amgen employees (affiliations in PubMed record).

sources.citation: Webster J, Oguzman E, Morris EJA, Shepperd S, Griffin XL, Johansen A, et al. Trends and variation in the incidence of hip fracture in England before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic (2014-2024): a population-based observational study. Lancet Reg Health Eur. 2025;57:101427.
sources.design: Population-based observational study of national hospital data (HES-APC) with ONS population denominators; Poisson regression for pandemic effects
sources.population_setting: Adults aged 50 and over presenting to NHS hospitals in England with fragility hip fracture, January 2014 to October 2024 (704,762 hip fractures in 669,101 patients)
sources.correction_check: PubMed: no retracted publication or published erratum linked (PMID and title searches, 26 September 2026).
sources.quality_note: Near-complete national coverage for England; rates age-standardised to the 2013 European Standard Population. Counts by year are shown only in a supplementary figure (not read), so no count numbers are available. Internal inconsistency: the abstract gives 5595 excess hip fractures from August 2021 to October 2024, while one Discussion sentence gives 5955 from March 2021; use the abstract figure if any.

sources.citation: Veronese N, Kolk H, Maggi S. Epidemiology of fragility fractures and social impact. In: Falaschi P, Marsh D, editors. Orthogeriatrics: the management of older patients with fragility fractures. 2nd ed. Cham: Springer; 2021. p. 19-34.
sources.design: Open-access textbook chapter (narrative review)
sources.population_setting: Worldwide epidemiology of fragility and hip fractures
sources.tool_used: Google Drive read_file_content (open-access book PDF '2021_Book_Orthogeriatrics.pdf' saved in Alasdair's Drive); DOI taken from the book text
sources.correction_check: Book chapter; no retraction or correction mechanism found. Not PubMed-indexed as a journal article.
sources.quality_note: Expert narrative review, not primary data; used only for the explanation that population ageing drives the rising number of hip fractures. Chapter 1 of the same book (Marsh D et al.) makes the same point. Its 1.66 million (1990) to 6.26 million (2050) projection is an older estimate cited from another source and should not be used.

sources.citation: Deardorff WJ, Cenzer I, Nguyen B, Lee SJ. Time to benefit of bisphosphonate therapy for the prevention of fractures among postmenopausal women with osteoporosis: a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. JAMA Intern Med. 2022;182(1):33-41.
sources.design: Meta-analysis of 10 placebo-controlled RCTs (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid); Weibull survival curves and random-effects pooling of time to benefit
sources.population_setting: 23,384 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (vertebral fracture or T-score -2.5 or lower); trial mean ages 63 to 74; follow-up 12 to 48 months
sources.correction_check: Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: High-quality pooled trial data, but trial populations were younger and fitter than frail people near the end of life; time to benefit could be shorter in people at higher baseline fracture risk. Figures are for non-vertebral and hip fracture thresholds, not all fractures.

sources.citation: Lavan AH, Gallagher P, Parsons C, O'Mahony D. STOPPFrail (Screening Tool of Older Persons Prescriptions in Frail adults with limited life expectancy): consensus validation. Age Ageing. 2017;46(4):600-607.
sources.design: Delphi consensus validation of explicit deprescribing criteria (17-member expert panel, 3 rounds)
sources.population_setting: Criteria for frail older adults (65 and over) with limited life expectancy; Ireland
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (abstract); Scite search_literature full-text excerpts (verbatim criterion text G1 and G2); whole paper not read
sources.correction_check: Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: Expert consensus, not trial evidence. Version 1 criterion text verified; STOPPFrail version 2 (2021) replaced it and its criterion wording was not opened.

sources.citation: Curtin D, Gallagher P, O'Mahony D. Deprescribing in older people approaching end-of-life: development and validation of STOPPFrail version 2. Age Ageing. 2021;50(2):465-471.
sources.design: Literature review plus Delphi consensus (8-member panel)
sources.population_setting: Older people approaching end of life
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; Scite read_fulltext returned abstract only
sources.correction_check: Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: Current version of STOPPFrail. Abstract confirms 25 criteria and emphasis on shared decision-making; the text of the bone-medicine criteria in version 2 was not opened.

sources.citation: Gregson CL, Armstrong DJ, Bowden J, Cooper C, Edwards J, Gittoes NJL, et al. UK clinical guideline for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis. Arch Osteoporos. 2022;17(1):58.
sources.design: National clinical guideline (NOGG 2022), NICE-accredited, graded evidence review
sources.population_setting: Postmenopausal women and men aged 50 and over, UK
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_full_text_article (PMC8979902), searched for the relevant sections (bisphosphonate administration, denosumab, duration and monitoring, rare adverse effects, summary recommendations); the whole 126,000-character text was not read end to end
sources.correction_check: Correction published (PMID 35585444, Arch Osteoporos 2022;17:80), opened in PMC9117369: it adds a missing author affiliation only. Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite lists the same correction.
sources.quality_note: Main UK guideline. In the PMC text the bulleted criteria lists and the flowcharts (Figs 4 and 5) did not extract; continuation criteria were taken from the summary recommendations and body text instead. Product-information (SPC) statements are NOGG's report of the SPC, not the SPC itself.

sources.citation: Cummings SR, Ferrari S, Eastell R, Gilchrist N, Jensen JB, McClung M, et al. Vertebral fractures after discontinuation of denosumab: a post hoc analysis of the randomized placebo-controlled FREEDOM trial and its extension. J Bone Miner Res. 2018;33(2):190-198.
sources.design: Post hoc analysis of a randomised placebo-controlled trial and its open-label extension
sources.population_setting: Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis who received 2 or more 6-monthly doses of denosumab (n=1001) or placebo (n=470), stopped, and stayed in the study 7 months or more after the last dose
sources.correction_check: Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: Post hoc, non-randomised comparison of people who stopped; industry co-author (Amgen). Off-treatment follow-up length varied and is not given in the abstract. Consistent with ECTS systematic reviews and NOGG.

sources.citation: Greenspan SL, Perera S, Ferchak MA, Nace DA, Resnick NM. Efficacy and safety of single-dose zoledronic acid for osteoporosis in frail elderly women: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2015;175(6):913-21.
sources.design: 2-year randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial
sources.population_setting: 181 women aged 65 and over (mean 85.4) with osteoporosis in nursing homes and assisted living, including cognitive impairment and immobility; USA, 2007 to 2012
sources.correction_check: Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.

sources.citation: Lyu H, Yoshida K, Zhao SS, Wei J, Zeng C, Tedeschi SK, et al. Delayed denosumab injections and fracture risk among patients with osteoporosis: a population-based cohort study. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):516-526.

Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: Observational; dosing delay not randomised; wide confidence intervals; only the vertebral fracture association with delays over 16 weeks was statistically clear.

sources.citation: Tsourdi E, Zillikens MC, Meier C, Body JJ, Gonzalez Rodriguez E, Anastasilakis AD, et al. Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: Management advice is expert opinion based on limited evidence; efficacy of follow-on bisphosphonate is partial.

sources.citation: Tsourdi E, Langdahl B, Cohen-Solal M, Aubry-Rozier B, Eriksen EF, Guanabens N, et al. Discontinuation of denosumab therapy for osteoporosis: a systematic review and position statement by ECTS. Bone. 2017;105:11-17.

Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.

sources.citation: Black DM, Schwartz AV, Ensrud KE, Cauley JA, Levis S, Quandt SA, et al. Effects of continuing or stopping alendronate after 5 years of treatment: the Fracture Intervention Trial Long-term Extension (FLEX): a randomized trial. JAMA. 2006;296(24):2927-38.

Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.

sources.citation: Black DM, Reid IR, Boonen S, Bucci-Rechtweg C, Cauley JA, Cosman F, et al. The effect of 3 versus 6 years of zoledronic acid treatment of osteoporosis: a randomized extension to the HORIZON-Pivotal Fracture Trial (PFT). J Bone Miner Res. 2012;27(2):243-54.

Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Primary outcome bone density; fracture results secondary; confidence intervals for clinical fractures were wide (authors: some benefit cannot be excluded).

sources.citation: Adler RA, El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Bauer DC, Camacho PM, Clarke BL, Clines GA, et al. Managing osteoporosis in patients on long-term bisphosphonate treatment: report of a task force of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. J Bone Miner Res. 2016;31(1):16-35.

sources.population_setting: Mostly white postmenopausal women on long-term bisphosphonates

Passages used match both the PubMed and Scite versions of the abstract. Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Authors state the approach rests on limited evidence, only for vertebral fracture reduction.

sources.citation: Black DM, Geiger EJ, Eastell R, Vittinghoff E, Li BH, Ryan DS, et al. Atypical femur fracture risk versus fragility fracture prevention with bisphosphonates. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(8):743-753.
sources.design: Cohort study with radiographic adjudication and multivariable Cox models, plus a modelled risk-benefit comparison in a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 women
sources.population_setting: 196,129 women aged 50 or older who used bisphosphonates (mostly alendronate); Kaiser Permanente Southern California, 2007 to 2017
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; PubMed get_full_text_article (PMC9632334, author manuscript)
sources.correction_check: Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: Observational association. Benefit side is modelled from an untreated historical cohort (women 65 and over with T-score below -2.5 or prior hip or vertebral fracture) and meta-analysis effects, so the 149 versus 2 comparison is an estimate, not an observed count. Results mainly for alendronate; not applicable to denosumab.

sources.citation: Shane E, Burr D, Abrahamsen B, Adler RA, Brown TD, Cheung AM, et al. Atypical subtrochanteric and diaphyseal femoral fractures: second report of a task force of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. J Bone Miner Res. 2014;29(1):1-23.
sources.design: Expert task force review of studies published since 2010, with revised case definition
sources.population_setting: People with atypical femoral fractures, mainly on bisphosphonates; some on denosumab or on neither
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (abstract); Scite search_literature full-text excerpts and full-text citation snippets (verbatim passages); whole paper not read
sources.correction_check: Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: Review of case series and cohorts of varying quality. Proportions with warning pain and bilateral fractures differ between series. Published online 2013 (PubMed date 2013-10); print issue 2014.

sources.citation: Bird ST, Smith ER, Gelperin K, Jung TH, Thompson A, Kambhampati R, et al. Severe hypocalcemia with denosumab among older female dialysis-dependent patients. JAMA. 2024;331(6):491-499.
sources.design: Retrospective cohort study with inverse probability of treatment weighting
sources.population_setting: Female dialysis-dependent Medicare patients aged 65 and over starting denosumab (n=1523) or oral bisphosphonates (n=1281), USA, 2013 to 2020, with monthly dialysis-unit calcium results
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; PubMed get_full_text_article (PMC10799290 returned Key Points and abstract only, body empty)
sources.correction_check: Not retracted and no expression of concern (PubMed search of the PMID with retracted publication[pt] / retraction of publication[pt] / expression of concern[pt], 26 Sep 2026). Scite editorial-notice filters (has_retraction, has_correction, has_erratum) returned no notice for this DOI.
sources.quality_note: Observational (FDA investigators); outcome includes laboratory-defined hypocalcaemia measured monthly in dialysis units, so detection is high. Applies to dialysis-dependent older women only.

sources.citation: Bird ST, Gelperin K, Smith ER, Jung TH, Lyu H, Thompson A, et al. The effect of denosumab on risk for emergently treated hypocalcemia by stage of chronic kidney disease: a target trial emulation. Ann Intern Med. 178(1):29-38. Epub 2024 Nov 19.
sources.design: Target trial emulation using claims data
sources.population_setting: Female Medicare patients aged 65 and over starting denosumab (361,453), oral (829,044) or IV bisphosphonates (160,413), USA, 2012 to 2020
sources.correction_check: Not retracted (PubMed record shows no retraction or erratum link; Scite filters returned no notice).
sources.quality_note: Observational; outcome is only hospital or emergency care for hypocalcaemia (laboratory-only low calcium not counted), so absolute figures are much lower than Bird JAMA 2024 and must not be compared directly.

sources.citation: Lloret MJ, Jorgensen HS, Evenepoel P. Denosumab-induced hypocalcemia in patients treated with dialysis: an avoidable complication? Clin Kidney J. 2024;17(3):sfae048.
sources.design: Commentary (expert opinion) by nephrologists on Bird 2024
sources.population_setting: People on dialysis considered for denosumab
sources.correction_check: Not retracted (PubMed record; Scite filters returned no notice).
sources.quality_note: Expert opinion, not a guideline; also reports secondary figures from the Bird JAMA full text (5.4% life-threatening symptoms, 1.3% died) that were not verified in the primary paper.

sources.citation: North K, Dahl B, Dowling-McClay K, Highsmith M. Denosumab-bbdz: a review of the interchangeable biosimilar for the treatment of osteoporosis. Ann Pharmacother. 60(1):76-82. Epub 2025 Jun 12.
sources.design: Narrative drug review
sources.population_setting: US product labelling for a denosumab biosimilar
sources.correction_check: Not retracted (PubMed record; Scite filters returned no notice).
sources.quality_note: Secondary source used only to confirm that US denosumab labelling carries a boxed warning for severe hypocalcaemia in advanced chronic kidney disease.

sources.citation: US Food and Drug Administration. FDA adds Boxed Warning for increased risk of severe hypocalcemia in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease taking osteoporosis medicine Prolia (denosumab). Drug Safety Communication. 19 January 2024 (date from search-engine extract).
sources.design: Regulatory drug safety communication
sources.population_setting: US patients with advanced CKD taking Prolia
sources.correction_check: Not applicable (regulatory web page).
sources.quality_note: Search-engine extract only; not sufficient on its own. US regulatory action; UK product information wording differs and must not be merged with it.

sources.citation: Riggs BL, Hodgson SF, O'Fallon WM, Chao EY, Wahner HW, Muhs JM, et al. Effect of fluoride treatment on the fracture rate in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. N Engl J Med. 1990;322(12):802-9.
sources.design: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, 4 years
sources.population_setting: 202 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and vertebral fractures, Mayo Clinic, USA; sodium fluoride 75 mg/day versus placebo, all given calcium 1500 mg/day; 66 (fluoride) and 69 (placebo) completed
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; Scite search_literature (metadata and editorial notices; no full-text excerpt returned)
sources.correction_check: Scite (25 Sep 2026): no editorial notices listed. PubMed: PMID search with retracted publication[pt] returned no record.
sources.quality_note: Classic, well-cited RCT. Abstract reports fracture COUNTS (163 v 136 vertebral; 72 v 24 non-vertebral), not numbers of women, and does not give the size of each randomised group; completion was low (135 of 202). High-dose, plain (not slow-release) fluoride; a meta-analysis (Haguenauer 2000) links the excess non-vertebral fractures to high doses and non-slow-release forms.

sources.citation: Haguenauer D, Welch V, Shea B, Tugwell P, Adachi JD, Wells G. Fluoride for the treatment of postmenopausal osteoporotic fractures: a meta-analysis. Osteoporos Int. 2000;11(9):727-38.
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (1429 participants)
sources.population_setting: Postmenopausal women in randomised trials of fluoride
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices listed. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Older meta-analysis but the question (fluoride) is settled and not re-studied; confirms the Riggs finding is not a one-off. Abstract contains an apparent typographical error in one CI (GI side effects at 2 years); not used.

sources.citation: Black DM, Bauer DC, Vittinghoff E, Lui LY, Grauer A, Marin F, et al. Treatment-related changes in bone mineral density as a surrogate biomarker for fracture risk reduction: meta-regression analyses of individual patient data from multiple randomised controlled trials. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2020;8(8):672-82.
sources.design: Individual patient data meta-regression of 23 placebo-controlled RCTs (FNIH-ASBMR SABRE project)
sources.population_setting: 91,779 participants in 23 randomised placebo-controlled trials of osteoporosis drugs (bisphosphonates, denosumab, PTH receptor agonists, SERMs, hormone therapy, odanacatib); 1 to 9 years follow-up
sources.correction_check: Scite: 'has erratum' notice (10.1016/s2213-8587(20)30318-1, Oct 2020) plus published comments; erratum text not opened, so its content is unknown. PubMed abstract (current record) used. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Large IPD analysis; trial-level association supports BMD as a surrogate for future drug-registration trials. It does not validate a single person's repeat scan as a monitor. Several authors are industry employees.

sources.citation: Cummings SR, Karpf DB, Harris F, Genant HK, Ensrud K, LaCroix AZ, et al. Improvement in spine bone density and reduction in risk of vertebral fractures during treatment with antiresorptive drugs. Am J Med. 2002;112(4):281-9.
sources.design: Meta-analysis of 12 trials plus logistic modelling within the Fracture Intervention Trial
sources.population_setting: Postmenopausal women in 12 randomised trials of antiresorptive drugs; FIT alendronate data
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Older analysis limited to spine BMD and vertebral fractures with antiresorptives; the later Black 2020 IPD analysis found hip BMD explained a larger share (44-67%), so the 'small part' finding is site- and method-specific.

sources.citation: Bell KJ, Hayen A, Macaskill P, Irwig L, Craig JC, Ensrud K, et al. Value of routine monitoring of bone mineral density after starting bisphosphonate treatment: secondary analysis of trial data. BMJ. 2009;338:b2266.
sources.design: Secondary analysis of RCT data (Fracture Intervention Trial) using mixed models
sources.population_setting: 6459 postmenopausal women with low bone mineral density in FIT (alendronate v placebo), BMD at baseline and 1, 2 and 3 years
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Directly addresses individual monitoring; applies to the first 3 years of a potent bisphosphonate (alendronate) in postmenopausal women; does not address later reassessment or other drugs.

sources.citation: Buchbinder R, Johnston RV, Rischin KJ, Homik J, Jones CA, Golmohammadi K, et al. Percutaneous vertebroplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018;11(11):CD006349.
sources.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 RCTs (5 sham-controlled, 541 participants)
sources.population_setting: Adults with painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures; most female, mean age 62.6 to 81; symptom duration from a week to over 6 months; trials in hospitals in 15 countries
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; get_full_text_article (PMC returned abstract and plain-language summary only); Scite (editorial notices)
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none. Clark 2019 (PMID 30852489) states the April 2018 version was replaced in November 2018 'to address complaints of errors in analysis'; the version used here is the November 2018 replacement (pub4, 6 Nov 2018).
sources.quality_note: High- to moderate-certainty evidence for vertebroplasty v sham at one month. Search to November 2017. The VAPOUR authors dispute pooling VAPOUR with other sham trials (PMID 30852489).

sources.citation: Clark W, Bird P, Gonski P, Diamond TH, Smerdely P, McNeil HP, et al. Safety and efficacy of vertebroplasty for acute painful osteoporotic fractures (VAPOUR): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2016;388(10052):1408-16.
sources.design: Multicentre double-blind sham-controlled RCT, 6-month follow-up
sources.population_setting: 120 patients with one or two osteoporotic vertebral fractures under 6 weeks old and pain 7/10 or more, four hospitals in Sydney, Australia (2011 to 2014)
sources.correction_check: Scite: 'has erratum' (10.1016/s0140-6736(16)31468-4, Feb 2017) and three comments; erratum text not opened. PubMed abstract (current record) used. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Only sham trial restricted to very recent fractures with severe pain; single positive trial; primary outcome at 14 days; education grant from a device manufacturer (CareFusion). The abstract does not state the proportion who were inpatients, so 'inpatients' is not verified.

sources.citation: Buchbinder R, Osborne RH, Ebeling PR, Wark JD, Mitchell P, Wriedt C, et al. A randomized trial of vertebroplasty for painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures. N Engl J Med. 2009;361(6):557-68.
sources.design: Multicentre double-blind sham-controlled RCT, 6 months
sources.population_setting: 78 participants with one or two painful, unhealed osteoporotic vertebral fractures under 12 months old (MRI-confirmed), Australia
sources.correction_check: PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none. Scite not queried for this record.
sources.quality_note: Small but rigorous sham trial; used here for the observation that pain fell in both groups.

sources.citation: Kallmes DF, Comstock BA, Heagerty PJ, Turner JA, Wilson DJ, Diamond TH, et al. A randomized trial of vertebroplasty for osteoporotic spinal fractures. N Engl J Med. 2009;361(6):569-79.
sources.design: Multicentre sham-controlled RCT (INVEST), primary outcome at 1 month, crossover allowed after 1 month
sources.population_setting: 131 patients with one to three painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
sources.correction_check: PubMed abstract carries a '[corrected]' marker on the crossover-rate sentence (corrected text used). PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Trend toward more clinically meaningful pain improvement with vertebroplasty (64% v 48%, P=0.06); high crossover from control arm at 3 months.

sources.citation: Ebeling PR, Akesson K, Bauer DC, Buchbinder R, Eastell R, Fink HA, et al. The efficacy and safety of vertebral augmentation: a second ASBMR task force report. J Bone Miner Res. 2019;34(1):3-21.
sources.design: Specialist society task force report (systematic evidence review with recommendations)
sources.population_setting: Patients with painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures; international
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: American Society for Bone and Mineral Research task force; covers kyphoplasty separately from vertebroplasty.

sources.citation: [No authors listed]. Percutaneous vertebroplasty and balloon kyphoplasty for painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures: a health technology assessment. Ont Health Technol Assess Ser. 2025;25(4):1-253.
sources.design: Health technology assessment (systematic review, GRADE, economic evaluation)
sources.population_setting: People with painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures refractory to non-surgical treatment; Ontario, Canada
sources.correction_check: PubMed record: no linked correction seen; not in retracted publication[pt]. Scite not queried.
sources.quality_note: Recorded as conflicting/contextual evidence: found benefit against conservative care (low to very low certainty), i.e. open comparisons of the kind the Cochrane review judged likely to overestimate benefit.

sources.citation: Clark W, Bird P, Diamond T, Gonski P, Gebski V. Cochrane vertebroplasty review misrepresented evidence for vertebroplasty with early intervention in severely affected patients. BMJ Evid Based Med. 25(3):85-9 (PubMed publication date 2019 Mar 9).
sources.design: Critique (analysis/commentary) by the VAPOUR investigators
sources.population_setting: Not applicable
sources.correction_check: PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Recorded as dissent; authors are the VAPOUR trialists. Confirms VAPOUR was pooled in the November 2018 Cochrane update.

sources.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Percutaneous vertebroplasty and percutaneous balloon kyphoplasty for treating osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures. Technology appraisal guidance TA279. London: NICE; 2013.
sources.design: National technology appraisal guidance
sources.population_setting: England and Wales
sources.tool_used: WebSearch (nice.org.uk); page could not be opened (WebFetch blocked); not found in Drive
sources.correction_check: Not applicable; current status of TA279 not verified from the page.
sources.quality_note: Search-engine extract only. Not sufficient for an essential claim; use only as an optional, attributed clause, or replace with NOGG 2022 wording.

sources.citation: LeBoff MS, Chou SH, Ratliff KA, Cook NR, Khurana B, Kim E, et al. Supplemental vitamin D and incident fractures in midlife and older adults. N Engl J Med. 2022;387(4):299-309.
sources.design: Ancillary study of a 2x2 factorial double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (VITAL)
sources.population_setting: 25,871 US men aged 50+ and women aged 55+, not selected for vitamin D deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis; vitamin D3 2000 IU/day v placebo; median 5.3 years
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Large, well-conducted trial with adjudicated fractures; generally healthy, mostly vitamin D replete population (mean 25(OH)D 30.7 ng/mL); authors say it was not designed to test deficient people and may not generalise to people with osteoporosis or osteomalacia or older institutionalised people. Fractures were self-reported then confirmed; vertebral fractures not systematically imaged.

sources.citation: Waterhouse M, Ebeling PR, McLeod DSA, English D, Romero BD, Baxter C, et al. The effect of monthly vitamin D supplementation on fractures: a tertiary outcome from the population-based, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled D-Health trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2023;11(5):324-32.
sources.design: Population-based double-blind placebo-controlled RCT; fractures a tertiary outcome ascertained by record linkage
sources.population_setting: 21,315 adults aged 60 to 84 living in Australia; 60,000 IU vitamin D3 monthly for up to 5 years; 20,326 analysed
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Large trial but fractures were a tertiary outcome; monthly bolus dosing; baseline vitamin D status not given in the abstract.

sources.citation: Chapuy MC, Arlot ME, Duboeuf F, Brun J, Crouzet B, Arnaud S, et al. Vitamin D3 and calcium to prevent hip fractures in elderly women. N Engl J Med. 1992;327(23):1637-42.
sources.design: Placebo-controlled trial, 18 months
sources.population_setting: 3270 healthy ambulatory women, mean age 84, France (Lyon); vitamin D3 800 IU plus 1.2 g calcium daily v double placebo
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; Scite (metadata, editorial notices; no full-text excerpt returned); the 1994 BMJ follow-up (PMID 8173430) was tried but PMC returned no text
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Tested vitamin D and calcium together, so it cannot separate their effects. The residential setting (commonly described as nursing homes or apartment houses for older people) is NOT stated in the abstract and was not verified. Headline hip-fracture result is a relative reduction among completers.

sources.citation: Avenell A, Mak JC, O'Connell D. Vitamin D and vitamin D analogues for preventing fractures in post-menopausal women and older men. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2014;2014(4):CD000227.
sources.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (53 trials, 91,791 participants)
sources.population_setting: Post-menopausal women and older men in community, nursing home and hospital settings
sources.tool_used: PubMed search_articles; get_article_metadata; get_full_text_article (PMC returned abstract and plain-language summary only); Scite (editorial notices)
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none. No later version of CD000227 found in PubMed.
sources.quality_note: Search to December 2012, so it predates VITAL and D-Health. The per-1000 estimates for community and institutional residents are the pooled relative risk applied to assumed baseline risks, not separate results measured in each setting.

sources.citation: Bolland MJ, Grey A, Avenell A. Effects of vitamin D supplementation on musculoskeletal health: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2018;6(11):847-58.
sources.design: Systematic review, meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of 81 RCTs
sources.population_setting: Adults in RCTs comparing vitamin D with placebo, no treatment or lower dose (trials of co-administered calcium eligible only if arms differed by vitamin D alone)
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Tests vitamin D alone; abstract does not report results by baseline vitamin D status.

sources.citation: Yao P, Bennett D, Mafham M, Lin X, Chen Z, Armitage J, et al. Vitamin D and calcium for the prevention of fracture: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Netw Open. 2019;2(12):e1917789.
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies and RCTs (RCTs of 500+ participants and 10+ fractures)
sources.population_setting: 11 RCTs of vitamin D alone (34,243 participants); 6 RCTs of vitamin D with calcium (49,282 participants)
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Predates VITAL fracture results and D-Health. Combined vitamin D plus calcium effect is modest and CIs close to no effect.

sources.citation: Kendler DL, Marin F, Zerbini CAF, Russo LA, Greenspan SL, Zikan V, et al. Effects of teriparatide and risedronate on new fractures in post-menopausal women with severe osteoporosis (VERO): a multicentre, double-blind, double-dummy, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2018;391(10117):230-40.
sources.design: Double-blind double-dummy head-to-head RCT, 24 months
sources.population_setting: 1360 postmenopausal women with at least two moderate or one severe vertebral fracture and BMD T-score of -1.5 or lower; teriparatide 20 micrograms daily v risedronate 35 mg weekly
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; Scite (editorial notices; no full-text excerpt returned)
sources.correction_check: Scite: two 'has erratum' notices (10.1016/s0140-6736(17)33099-4, Jan 2018; 10.1016/s0140-6736(18)32944-1, Dec 2018) and comments; erratum texts not opened. PubMed abstract (current record) used. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Industry-funded (Lilly). Compared two drugs over 24 months; it did not test a sequence. Reported percentages (5.4%, 12.0%) do not equal 28/680 and 64/680, so the denominators appear to be women with evaluable follow-up X-rays; quote the percentages, do not recompute from 680.

sources.citation: Saag KG, Petersen J, Brandi ML, Karaplis AC, Lorentzon M, Thomas T, et al. Romosozumab or alendronate for fracture prevention in women with osteoporosis. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(15):1417-27.
sources.design: Double-blind head-to-head RCT (ARCH), 12 months blinded then open-label alendronate in both arms
sources.population_setting: 4093 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and a fragility fracture; romosozumab 210 mg monthly v alendronate 70 mg weekly for 12 months, then alendronate
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; Scite (editorial notices and citation statements)
sources.correction_check: Scite: no editorial notices listed. PubMed retracted publication[pt] check: none.
sources.quality_note: Industry-funded (Amgen and others). Serious cardiovascular adverse events more frequent with romosozumab in year 1; the paper says the imbalance was not seen in the larger placebo-controlled FRAME trial.

sources.citation: Leder BZ, Tsai JN, Uihlein AV, Wallace PM, Lee H, Neer RM, et al. Denosumab and teriparatide transitions in postmenopausal osteoporosis (the DATA-Switch study): extension of a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2015;386(9999):1147-55.
sources.design: Pre-planned extension of a small RCT; BMD outcomes

sources.citation: Szoszkiewicz M, Deskur-Smielecka E, Styszynski A, Urbanska Z, Neumann-Podczaska A, Wieczorowska-Tobis K. sources.citation: te Winkel MT, Damoiseaux-Volman BA, Abu-Hanna A, Lissenberg-Witte BI, van Marum RJ, Schers HJ, et al. Personal continuity and appropriate prescribing in primary care. Ann Fam Med. 2023;21(4):305-312.

sources.correction_check: PubMed: search of this PMID with retracted publication[pt] returned no record (checked in this session, 25-26 Sep 2026); search for published erratum[pt] records with matching title words found no notice for this article. Scite record returned no editorial notices.
sources.quality_note: Large routine-data study; automated criteria (100 of 108 programmed). Prevalence counts any PIM or PPO over 6 years, which inflates it relative to a single point in time.

sources.quality_note: Small, single-centre, older study; association only. Consistent with later larger data (te Winkel 2023; Szoszkiewicz 2025 found number of drugs associated with omissions in a Scite snippet, not relied on).

sources.citation: Savage RD, Visentin JD, Bronskill SE, Wang X, Gruneir A, Giannakeas V, et al. Evaluation of a common prescribing cascade of calcium channel blockers and diuretics in older adults with hypertension. JAMA Intern Med. 2020;180(5):643-651.
sources.design: Population-based cohort study using linked health administrative (dispensing) databases; Cox models
sources.population_setting: Community-dwelling adults aged 66 or over with hypertension and new prescription claims, Ontario, Canada, 2011 to 2016; 41,086 newly dispensed a CCB, 66,494 an ACE inhibitor or ARB, 231,439 an unrelated drug; mean age 74.5
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; get_full_text_article (PMC7042805 returned abstract and Key Points only, no body text)
sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Large population cohort with active comparators. Outcome is dispensing of a loop diuretic, not confirmed oedema or a documented cascade, so not every excess diuretic is a cascade. Relative rates (HR 1.68 to 3.89) sit on small absolute risks (1.4% vs 0.7% vs 0.5% at 90 days).

sources.citation: Rochon PA, Gurwitz JH. Optimising drug treatment for elderly people: the prescribing cascade. BMJ. 1997;315(7115):1096-9.
sources.design: Narrative review (education and debate)

sources.quality_note: Classic source for the term. Only the title and bibliographic record were read in this project; the definition quoted in claims comes from McCarthy 2022 and Savage 2020.

sources.citation: McCarthy LM, Savage R, Dalton K, Mason R, Li J, Lawson A, et al. ThinkCascades: a tool for identifying clinically important prescribing cascades affecting older people. Drugs Aging. 2022;39(10):829-840.

sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Consensus tool, not outcome evidence. The final nine-item table did not render, so which cascades are on the list (including CCB to loop diuretic) was not confirmed in this project.

sources.citation: Makani H, Bangalore S, Romero J, Htyte N, Berrios RS, Makwana H, et al. Peripheral edema associated with calcium channel blockers: incidence and withdrawal rate--a meta-analysis of randomized trials. J Hypertens. 2011;29(7):1270-80.

sources.quality_note: Large meta-analysis but trial populations were middle-aged (mean 56), so older people may have higher rates. Mechanism sentence in the abstract is background ('It has been thought to occur...'), not a finding.

sources.citation: Makani H, Bangalore S, Romero J, Wever-Pinzon O, Messerli FH. Effect of renin-angiotensin system blockade on calcium channel blocker-associated peripheral edema. Am J Med. 2011;124(2):128-35.

sources.quality_note: Short trials in middle-aged people; ACE inhibitor vs ARB comparison is indirect (authors say head-to-head studies are needed).

sources.citation: Woodford HJ. Calcium channel blockers co-prescribed with loop diuretics: a potential marker of poor prescribing? Drugs Aging. 2020;37(2):77-81.

sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Independent US replication of the CCB to loop diuretic signal; mostly younger insured adults, so not directly an older population.

sources.citation: Growdon ME, Tjota N, Campbell R, Gayda P, Jing B, Deardorff WJ, et al. Decision-making and downstream outcomes of the gabapentinoid-diuretic prescribing cascade. JAMA Netw Open. 2025;8(12):e2545274.

sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Small, mostly male sample; first drug is a gabapentinoid, not a CCB; events are 'potentially attributable' to the loop diuretic, with no comparison group. Useful for what happens after a loop diuretic is added, not for effect size.

sources.citation: Dreischulte T, Donnan P, Grant A, Hapca A, McCowan C, Guthrie B. Safer prescribing--a trial of education, informatics, and financial incentives. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(11):1053-64.
sources.design: Cluster-randomised stepped-wedge trial (DQIP), 48-week intervention; secondary admission outcomes compared intervention vs preintervention periods; post hoc post-incentive analysis
sources.population_setting: 34 general practices in Tayside, Scotland (33 completed); about 33,000 patients at risk of adverse drug events from NSAIDs or antiplatelet drugs
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (abstract); Scite search_literature full-text excerpts (open-access NEJM text) for methods, measures and post-incentive results
sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Strong design for the primary prescribing outcome. Admission outcomes were prespecified secondary outcomes and compared periods before and during the intervention; the authors say the intervention 'may have improved clinical outcomes'. Post-incentive result is a post hoc analysis.

sources.citation: Dreischulte T, Grant A, Hapca A, Guthrie B. Process evaluation of the Data-driven Quality Improvement in Primary Care (DQIP) trial: quantitative examination of variation between practices in recruitment, implementation and effectiveness. BMJ Open. 2018;8(1):e017133.

sources.citation: Grant A, Dreischulte T, Guthrie B. Process evaluation of the data-driven quality improvement in primary care (DQIP) trial: active and less active ingredients of a multi-component complex intervention to reduce high-risk primary care prescribing. Implement Sci. 2017;12(1):4.
sources.design: Qualitative process evaluation (in-depth interviews, framework analysis)

sources.citation: Payne RA, Blair PS, Caddick B, Chew-Graham CA, Dreischulte T, Duncan LJ, et al. Lancet Healthy Longev. 2025;6(10):100774.
sources.design: Pragmatic cluster-randomised trial

sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Well-conducted trial of a broad polypharmacy review model with informatics, training, feedback and incentives; null on its primary outcome. Different target (broad polypharmacy) from DQIP (nine named combinations), so it is a contrast, not a direct replication.

sources.citation: Lapi F, Azoulay L, Yin H, Nessim SJ, Suissa S. Concurrent use of diuretics, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and risk of acute kidney injury: nested case-control study. BMJ. 2013;346:e8525.
sources.design: Retrospective cohort with nested case-control analysis (UK CPRD linked to Hospital Episode Statistics)

sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Large, carefully adjusted study with active comparators. Outcome is hospital admission with AKI as primary diagnosis, which the 2015 Tayside study argues underestimates risk. Exposure is prescribed NSAIDs; over-the-counter use not captured.

sources.citation: Dreischulte T, Morales DR, Bell S, Guthrie B. Combined use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with diuretics and/or renin-angiotensin system inhibitors in the community increases the risk of acute kidney injury. Kidney Int. 2015;88(2):396-403.

sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Biochemical AKI definition catches milder, community events that hospital coding misses. Contradicts Lapi 2013 on double combinations. Observational.

sources.citation: Lipska KJ, Ross JS, Miao Y, Shah ND, Lee SJ, Steinman MA. Potential overtreatment of diabetes mellitus in older adults with tight glycemic control. JAMA Intern Med. 2015;175(3):356-62.
sources.design: Cross-sectional analysis of a nationally representative survey (NHANES)

sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt], expression of concern[pt] and published erratum[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record; title search for erratum/correction/corrigendum found no linked notice. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Nationally representative but US data from 2001 to 2010, before newer drug classes were common. Shows 'potential overtreatment' (low HbA1c on drugs that can cause hypoglycaemia); hypoglycaemia itself was not measured.

sources.citation: Hambling CE, Seidu SI, Davies MJ, Khunti K. Older people with type 2 diabetes, including those with chronic kidney disease or dementia, are commonly overtreated with sulfonylurea or insulin therapies. Diabet Med. 2017;34(9):1219-1227.

sources.quality_note: UK primary care data. 'Overtreatment' is defined by HbA1c below 53 mmol/mol on these drugs; hypoglycaemia was not measured. Percentages appear to use people with a recorded HbA1c as denominator (400 of 1,379 would be 29.0%, the abstract gives 29.9%).

sources.citation: Strain WD, Hope SV, Green A, Kar P, Valabhji J, Sinclair AJ. Type 2 diabetes mellitus in older people: a brief statement of key principles of modern day management including the assessment of frailty. A national collaborative stakeholder initiative. Diabet Med. 2018;35(7):838-845.

sources.quality_note: Consensus, not trial evidence. The frailty-specific HbA1c ranges in the body were not read, so only the abstract statement can be used.

sources.quality_note: Very small single-centre study; shows hypoglycaemia is common and mostly unrecognised even when HbA1c is high.

sources.citation: Howard R, McShane R, Lindesay J, Ritchie C, Baldwin A, Barber R, et al. Donepezil and memantine for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease. N Engl J Med. 2012;366(10):893-903.

sources.citation: Howard R, McShane R, Lindesay J, Ritchie C, Baldwin A, Barber R, et al. Nursing home placement in the Donepezil and Memantine in Moderate to Severe Alzheimer's Disease (DOMINO-AD) trial: secondary and post-hoc analyses. Lancet Neurol. 2015;14(12):1171-81.
sources.design: Secondary and post hoc analyses of the DOMINO-AD randomised trial, with 4-year follow-up of residence
sources.population_setting: Same 295 community-living participants as DOMINO-AD; place of residence recorded during 52 weeks and then every 26 weeks for 3 more years
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (published abstract); Scite search_literature full-text excerpts of the author accepted manuscript (LSE Research Online) for Kaplan-Meier probabilities and Table 3
sources.correction_check: PubMed: search of this PMID with retracted publication[pt] OR expression of concern[pt] returned no record (checked 26 Sep 2026); search of published erratum[pt] records with matching topic terms found no notice for this article. sources.quality_note: Nursing home placement was a secondary endpoint; the first-year analysis (piecewise model) was post hoc and not pre-specified. The authors note withdrawal from study drug was more common in the discontinuation groups, and that the later hazard ratio is subject to selection bias. Absolute first-year figures come from the accepted manuscript ('There may be differences between this version and the published version'); the hazard ratios match the published abstract. In this trial 'nursing home placement' was an irreversible move from independent accommodation to a residential caring facility (the CSRI coding also counted a few ward settings).

sources.citation: Parsons C, Lim WY, Loy C, McGuinness B, Passmore P, Ward SA, et al. Withdrawal or continuation of cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine or both, in people with dementia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2021;2(2):CD009081.

sources.quality_note: Best summary of the uncertainty. sources.population_setting: Adults prescribed long-term opioid therapy for chronic pain
sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] OR expression of concern[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: Overall evidence very low quality; 51 of 67 studies poor quality; many uncontrolled; interventions were often intensive (interdisciplinary programmes), so improvement may reflect the programme, not dose reduction alone.

sources.citation: Agnoli A, Xing G, Tancredi DJ, Magnan E, Jerant A, Fenton JJ. Association of dose tapering with overdose or mental health crisis among patients prescribed long-term opioids. JAMA. 2021;326(5):411-9. Corrected in: JAMA. 2022;327(7):687 (PMID 35166820).
sources.design: Retrospective cohort study of US commercial and Medicare Advantage claims (OptumLabs), 2008 to 2019
sources.population_setting: 113,618 US adults on stable higher-dose (mean 50 MME/day or more) long-term opioids for 12 months; mean age about 58
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (shows ORIGINAL uncorrected abstract); Scite search_literature (corrected abstract text and erratum letter 10.1001/jama.2022.0231); PubMed convert_article_ids and get_article_metadata for erratum PMID 35166820
sources.correction_check: CORRECTED ARTICLE. Scite editorialNotices list two errata (10.1001/jama.2022.0231 'Errors in Data Analysis and Outcomes Coding', PMID 35166820; notice 10.1001/jama.2021.22379 resolves to an unrelated item) and comments. The authors' letter states outcomes were miscounted and the aIRRs fell from 1.68 to 1.28 (overdose) and from 2.28 to 1.74 (mental health crisis); the article was corrected online. The PubMed abstract (26 Sep 2026) still shows the ORIGINAL figures (9.3 vs 5.5 and 7.6 vs 3.3 per 100 person-years); use only the corrected figures recorded here. Not retracted (PubMed retracted publication[pt] search: no record).
sources.quality_note: Large observational cohort; associations only; tapering was defined as any 15% or greater reduction and was not separated into voluntary and clinician-initiated; US population, mean age about 58. Outcome 1 is ED or hospital encounters for drug overdose OR withdrawal.

sources.citation: Krebs EE, Gravely A, Nugent S, Jensen AC, DeRonne B, Goldsmith ES, et al. Effect of opioid vs nonopioid medications on pain-related function in patients with chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain: the SPACE randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2018;319(9):872-82.
sources.design: Pragmatic randomised controlled trial, 12 months, masked outcome assessment
sources.population_setting: 240 US veterans in primary care (mean age 58.3; 13% women) with moderate to severe chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain, not on long-term opioids at entry
sources.correction_check: PubMed: PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] OR expression of concern[pt] (26 Sep 2026): no record. Scite editorialNotices: none listed (26 Sep 2026).
sources.quality_note: High-quality trial but of STARTING opioids, not reducing them; mostly middle-aged men; supports that opioids did not give better function than non-opioid medicines.

sources.citation: Suri P, Rainville J, Kalichman L, Katz JN. Does this older adult with lower extremity pain have the clinical syndrome of lumbar spinal stenosis? JAMA. 2010;304(23):2628-36.
sources.design: Systematic review of diagnostic accuracy of history and examination (JAMA Rational Clinical Examination series); likelihood ratios; no pooling
sources.population_setting: 4 studies, 741 patients with lower extremity pain (mostly specialist spine clinics; one sample about one-third from primary care, mean age 65); reference standard expert opinion plus imaging or anatomic confirmation; searches 1966 to Sept 2010
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Best available synthesis for this question but small (4 studies) and mainly specialty clinic populations, which the authors say may overestimate sensitivity and underestimate specificity in primary care. Several confidence intervals are wide (no pain when seated LR 1.9 to 30; wide-based gait 1.9 to 95). Incorporation bias unavoidable. Still the standard reference.

sources.citation: Nadeau M, Rosas-Arellano MP, Gurr KR, Bailey SI, Taylor DC, Grewal R, et al. The reliability of differentiating neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication based on symptomatic presentation. Can J Surg. 2013;56(6):372-7.
sources.design: Prospective observational diagnostic study (symptom questionnaire, likelihood ratios)
sources.population_setting: 53 patients with a diagnosis of lumbar spinal stenosis or peripheral vascular disease who reported claudication; London, Ontario, Canada
sources.tool_used: Found with Consensus search; confirmed and read on PubMed get_article_metadata
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Small single-centre study comparing the two diagnoses head to head, so it complements Suri 2010. Likelihood ratios from 53 patients are imprecise. Useful for the vascular side of the comparison.

sources.citation: Uesugi K, Sekiguchi M, Kikuchi S, Kanayama M, Takahashi K, Chiba K, et al. Lumbar spinal stenosis associated with peripheral arterial disease: a prospective multicenter observational study. J Orthop Sci. 2012;17(6):673-81.

sources.population_setting: 570 patients diagnosed with lumbar spinal stenosis (clinical diagnostic support tool plus MRI) at 64 facilities in Japan
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Orthopaedic LSS population in Japan; prevalence of coexisting PAD may differ elsewhere and in primary care. Shows that PAD coexists and can be undetected.

sources.citation: Katz JN, Zimmerman ZE, Mass H, Makhni MC. Diagnosis and management of lumbar spinal stenosis: a review. JAMA. 2022;327(17):1688-99.
