Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Recent authoritative review; used only for the diagnostic principle (history provoked by extension, relieved by flexion, confirmed with imaging). The abstract gives prevalence as about 11% of US adults in one place and 11% of older adults in another, so do not quote that figure.

sources.citation: Mathieson S, Maher CG, McLachlan AJ, Latimer J, Koes BW, Hancock MJ, et al. Trial of pregabalin for acute and chronic sciatica. N Engl J Med. 2017;376(12):1111-20.
sources.design: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (PRECISE)
sources.population_setting: 209 adults with sciatica (acute or chronic) randomised, 207 analysed; recruited through GPs and specialists in Sydney, Australia; pregabalin 150 to 600 mg/day for up to 8 weeks; follow-up to 52 weeks
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (no PMC full text); participant ages from Enke 2018 Table 1 read via Undermind
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached). Note: a NEJM correction notice exists for the published correspondence on this trial (PMID 29385374, doi 10.1056/NEJMx180002, 2018, titled 'Is Pregabalin Ineffective in Acute or Chronic Sciatica?'); it was not openable here and appears to concern the letters exchange, not the trial report. Figures used are those in the current PubMed abstract.
sources.quality_note: High-quality investigator-led RCT, but modest size and a working-age sample (mean ages 52 and 55); excluded people with creatinine clearance below 60 ml/min, so many older people were not eligible. Pregabalin had in-kind support from Pfizer.

sources.citation: Mathieson S, Maher CG, McLachlan AJ, Latimer J, Koes BW, Hancock MJ, et al. PRECISE - pregabalin in addition to usual care for sciatica: study protocol for a randomised controlled trial. Trials. 2013;14:213.
sources.design: Published trial protocol

sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Used only for eligibility criteria (age 18 or older; exclusion of creatinine clearance below 60 ml/min).

sources.citation: Enke O, New HA, New CH, Mathieson S, McLachlan AJ, Latimer J, et al. Anticonvulsants in the treatment of low back pain and lumbar radicular pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. CMAJ. 2018;190(26):E786-93.
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials (GRADE)
sources.population_setting: 9 trials, 859 participants with low back pain, sciatica or neurogenic claudication; topiramate, gabapentin or pregabalin versus placebo
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; PMC get_full_text_article returned abstract only; full text PDF read with Undermind read_pdfs (verbatim quotes, Table 1, Figure 3)
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Good-quality review; shares authors with PRECISE. Trials are mostly in working-age adults. Notes that the 2016 UK (NICE) guideline pointed to neuropathic pain guidance that endorses gabapentinoids; NICE changed this in a 2020 update (only a search extract available here).

sources.citation: Shanthanna H, Gilron I, Rajarathinam M, AlAmri R, Kamath S, Thabane L, et al. Benefits and safety of gabapentinoids in chronic low back pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. PLoS Med. 2017;14(8):e1002369.

sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Evidence quality very low to moderate; population is chronic low back pain, not sciatica specifically. Supports the adverse-effect profile (dizziness, fatigue, difficulty thinking, visual disturbance).

sources.citation: Khorami AK, Oliveira CB, Maher CG, Bindels PJE, Machado GC, Pinto RZ, et al. Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of lumbosacral radicular pain: a systematic review of clinical practice guidelines. J Clin Med. 2021;10(11):2482.
sources.design: Systematic review of clinical practice guidelines (AGREE II)
sources.population_setting: 23 international guidelines on lumbosacral radicular pain (sciatica), searches to August 2019
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; get_full_text_article (PMC8200038; recommendation tables not rendered)
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Search ended August 2019, before the 2020 NICE update on sciatica medicines, so it reports drug recommendations as inconsistent. Used for the consistent non-drug recommendations (education, physical activity).

sources.citation: Chaitoff A, Desai RJ, Choudhry NK, Jungo KT, Haff N, Lauffenburger JC. Assessing the risk for falls in older adults after initiating gabapentin versus duloxetine. Ann Intern Med. 2025;178(2):187-98.
sources.design: New-user active-comparator cohort (target trial emulation), US commercial claims 2014 to 2021
sources.population_setting: 57,086 adults aged 65 or over with diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia or fibromyalgia starting gabapentin (52,152) or duloxetine (4,934)
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Conflicting evidence for the falls claim: gabapentin starters had fewer fall-related visits than duloxetine starters and no difference in severe falls. Comparator is itself a falls-risk drug; claims data may under-represent frail adults and undercount falls; median follow-up 30 days.

sources.citation: Oh G, Moga DC, Fardo DW, Harp JP, Abner EL. The association of gabapentin initiation with cognitive and behavioral changes in older adults with cognitive impairment: a retrospective cohort study. Drugs Aging. 2024;41(7):623-32.
sources.design: Retrospective cohort (National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center data) with inverse probability weighting
sources.population_setting: Older adults with cognitive impairment (mean age about 79); 353 gabapentin initiators and 3,177 non-users in the motor analysis
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Observational; found higher odds of new falls about 2 years after starting gabapentin in people with cognitive impairment. Non-user comparator; residual confounding likely. Pulls the other way from Chaitoff 2025.

sources.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s: assessment and management. NICE guideline NG59. London: NICE; 2016 (updated 2020).
sources.design: National clinical guideline
sources.population_setting: People aged 16 and over with low back pain or sciatica, England

sources.correction_check: Not applicable (official guidance web page; not opened).

sources.citation: Beswick AD, Wylde V, Gooberman-Hill R, Blom A, Dieppe P. What proportion of patients report long-term pain after total hip or knee replacement for osteoarthritis? A systematic review of prospective studies in unselected patients. BMJ Open. 2012;2(1):e000435.
sources.design: Systematic review of prospective cohort studies (no pooled estimate)
sources.population_setting: 14 articles, 17 cohorts (6 hip, 11 knee) of consecutive unselected patients having primary hip or knee replacement for osteoarthritis; follow-up 3 months to 5 years; searches to January 2011
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; full text PDF read with Undermind read_pdfs (verbatim quotes on definitions, best-quality studies and limitations)
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Definitions of unfavourable pain varied across studies and the authors declined to pool. Superseded for current figures by the 2025 update (Cheng et al.), which gives lower long-term estimates for knee replacement.

sources.citation: Cheng HY, Beswick AD, Bertram W, Siddiqui MA, Gooberman-Hill R, Whitehouse MR, et al. What proportion of people have long-term pain after total hip or knee replacement? An update of a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. 2025;15(5):e088975.
sources.design: Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
sources.population_setting: Knee replacement: 68 studies, 89 time points, 598,498 patients, mean age 69.6 (SD 9.4), 63% women; hip replacement: 11 studies; searches 2011 to February 2024
sources.tool_used: PubMed search_articles; get_article_metadata; full text PDF read with Undermind read_pdfs (verbatim quotes on definitions, pooled estimates, certainty, age)
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Most recent and largest synthesis; authors state low confidence because of loss to follow-up and risk of bias, and that the rates are likely underestimates. Definitions of 'unfavourable pain' varied (study-specific cut-offs). Preferred source for current figures.

sources.citation: Bourne RB, Chesworth BM, Davis AM, Mahomed NN, Charron KD. Patient satisfaction after total knee arthroplasty: who is satisfied and who is not? Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2010;468(1):57-63.
sources.design: Cross-sectional survey of patients after primary knee replacement
sources.population_setting: 1,703 primary total knee replacements, Ontario, Canada
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Satisfaction is a different outcome from pain; single province, older implants. Useful for the 'most people are satisfied' counterweight and for unmet expectations as the strongest predictor of dissatisfaction.

sources.citation: Bedson J, Croft PR. The discordance between clinical and radiographic knee osteoarthritis: a systematic search and summary of the literature. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2008;9:116.
sources.design: Systematic literature search and narrative summary of population studies
sources.population_setting: Population studies combining knee X-rays with knee pain or clinical signs in adults
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Ranges are very wide and depend on X-ray views, pain definitions, grading and demographic factors; no pooled estimate. Older review but still the standard citation for discordance.

sources.citation: Neogi T, Felson D, Niu J, Nevitt M, Lewis CE, Aliabadi P, et al. Association between radiographic features of knee osteoarthritis and pain: results from two cohort studies. BMJ. 2009;339:b2844.
sources.design: Within-person, knee-matched case-control analysis of two cohorts (MOST and Framingham)
sources.population_setting: 696 people (MOST) and 336 people (Framingham) whose two knees differed in pain status; US
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Important counterweight to Bedson: comparing a person's two knees removes between-person differences and shows a strong link between X-ray severity and pain. Very large, imprecise odds ratios; must not be turned into 'times more likely'.

sources.citation: Sakellariou G, Conaghan PG, Zhang W, Bijlsma JWJ, Boyesen P, D'Agostino MA, et al. EULAR recommendations for the use of imaging in the clinical management of peripheral joint osteoarthritis. Ann Rheum Dis. 2017;76(9):1484-94.

sources.population_setting: Knee, hip, hand and foot osteoarthritis; task force from nine countries including rheumatologists, radiologists, primary care doctors and patients
sources.correction_check: PubMed (26 Sep 2026): PMID searched with retracted publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no record. Erratum screen: published erratum[pt] searches by title words and matching date window found no notice for this article. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached).
sources.quality_note: Official specialist-society guideline; the abstract summarises the seven recommendations but does not give their exact wording.

sources.citation: Bunzli S, O'Brien P, Ayton D, Dowsey M, Gunn J, Choong P, et al. Misconceptions and the acceptance of evidence-based nonsurgical interventions for knee osteoarthritis. A qualitative study. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2019;477(9):1975-83.

sources.quality_note: Small, single-site qualitative study of people already listed for surgery; describes beliefs, not how common they are. Authors call for larger studies.

sources.citation: Corbett DB, Simon CB, Manini TM, George SZ, Riley JL, Fillingim RB. Movement-evoked pain: transforming the way we understand and measure pain. Pain. 2019;160(4):757-61.

sources.quality_note: Expert narrative review; argues for measuring movement-evoked pain and notes that validation work linking it to function is still needed. Opinion, not a measured comparison.

sources.citation: Knox PJ, Simon CB, Pohlig RT, Pugliese JM, Coyle PC, Sions JM, et al. Construct validity of movement-evoked pain operational definitions in older adults with chronic low back pain. Pain Med. 2023;24(8):985-92.

sources.citation: El-Tawil S, Al Musa T, Valli H, Lunn MP, Brassington R, El-Tawil T, et al. Quinine for muscle cramps. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;2015(4):CD005044.
sources.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (23 trials, 1586 participants; 20 placebo-controlled trials, n = 1140)
sources.population_setting: People of any age with muscle cramps of any cause, mostly idiopathic night cramps; average age in individual trials 44 to 76 years (youngest 17, oldest 87); quinine 200 to 500 mg daily; trials up to 60 days

sources.correction_check: PubMed search of this PMID with retracted publication[pt], retraction of publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no match (control search returned the record). Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached), so Scite editorial notices were not checked. Checked 2026-09-25. No later version of this Cochrane review found in PubMed (searches in the 2015 update run to October 2014).
sources.quality_note: Highest-level source for quinine efficacy. GRADE low quality for cramp number and cramp days, moderate for intensity and adverse events; high heterogeneity (I2 71%) for cramp number; 58% of participants came from unpublished studies; searches are from 2014 but no newer review was found.

sources.citation: Man-Son-Hing M, Wells G, Lau A. Quinine for nocturnal leg cramps: a meta-analysis including unpublished data. J Gen Intern Med. 1998;13(9):600-6.

sources.correction_check: PubMed search of this PMID with retracted publication[pt], retraction of publication[pt] and expression of concern[pt]: no match (control search returned the record). PubMed erratum search (published erratum[pt] or correction/erratum in title, by first author and topic): none found. Scite not available (monthly usage limit reached), so Scite editorial notices were not checked. Checked 2026-09-25.
sources.quality_note: Older but useful: gives placebo baseline and absolute reduction per 4 weeks, and shows publication bias inflating published estimates. Consistent with the 2015 Cochrane review. Supporting source only.

sources.citation: Rabbitt L, Mulkerrin EC, O'Keeffe ST. A review of nocturnal leg cramps in older people. Age Ageing. 2016;45(6):776-82.

claims.claim: Robinovitch and colleagues analysed 227 falls from 130 residents, captured on video between 2007 and 2010 in two long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada.
claims.supporting_passage: We did this observational study between April 20, 2007, and June 23, 2010, in two long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada. Digital video cameras were installed in common areas (dining rooms, lounges, hallways). ... We captured 227 falls from 130 individuals (mean age 78 years, SD 10).
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents of two long-term care facilities / video-captured falls in common areas / no comparator / cause of imbalance and activity at time of fall / April 2007 to June 2010
claims.safe_wording: Researchers filmed 227 falls by 130 residents of two care homes in British Columbia, Canada, between 2007 and 2010.
claims.qualifications: Say 'care homes' (long-term care facilities); say cameras were in shared areas only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None for the descriptive facts.

numbers.meaning: all video-captured falls analysed, 2007 to 2010
people whose falls were captured; mean age 78
long-term care facilities in British Columbia, Canada

claims.claim: The commonest cause of falling was incorrect shifting of body weight (41%); trips or stumbles caused 21% and slips only 3%.
claims.supporting_passage: The most frequent cause of falling was incorrect weight shifting, which accounted for 41% (93 of 227) of falls, followed by trip or stumble (48, 21%), hit or bump (25, 11%), loss of support (25, 11%), and collapse (24, 11%). Slipping accounted for only 3% (six) of falls.
claims.pico_timeframe: 227 video-captured falls / cause of imbalance rated by a team with a validated questionnaire
claims.safe_wording: About 4 in 10 of the filmed falls (93 of 227) came from shifting body weight the wrong way during an ordinary movement. About 1 in 5 (48) came from a trip or stumble, and 6 from a slip.
claims.qualifications: These are shares of falls filmed in shared areas, not of all falls in the homes. Causes were judged by a research team watching the videos.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors note self-report studies found different patterns; they attribute part of the difference to location (their data exclude bedrooms and bathrooms). Do not say 'most falls did not involve an obstacle': hit or bump (11%) and loss of support from an object (11%) also involve external objects. It is accurate that trips and slips together were about 1 in 4 (54 of 227).

numbers.meaning: incorrect weight shifting, share of filmed falls
trip or stumble
hit or bump; loss of support; collapse
slip

claims.claim: Falls happened most often during forward walking, standing quietly and sitting down; about a fifth happened during transfers.
claims.supporting_passage: The three activities associated with the highest proportion of falls were forward walking (54 of 227 falls, 24%), standing quietly (29 falls, 13%), and sitting down (28 falls, 12%). Compared with previous reports from the long-term care setting, we identified a higher occurrence of falls during standing and transferring, a lower occurrence during walking ... 21% of falls occurred during transferring, suggesting the need for exercises to enhance muscle strength, and improved assistive devices that provide adequate body support (eg, locking of wheels) when moving to and from chairs. ... The activities associated with fewest falls were standing and reaching, standing and turning, and seated or wheeling in a wheelchair (table 4).
claims.pico_timeframe: 227 filmed falls / activity at time of fall
claims.safe_wording: The commonest moments were walking forward (54 falls), standing still (29) and sitting down (28). About 1 in 5 falls happened while moving to or from a chair or bed.
claims.qualifications: Do not list turning as a common moment: standing and turning was among the activities with the fewest falls. These are counts of falls, not risk per minute spent on each activity (the study did not measure time spent in each activity).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Proportions by activity partly reflect how often residents do each activity.

numbers.meaning: falls during forward walking
falls while standing quietly
falls while sitting down
falls during transferring (authors' Discussion)

claims.claim: Cameras were only in common areas, not bedrooms or bathrooms, so the findings describe falls in shared spaces.
claims.supporting_passage: Digital video cameras were installed in common areas (dining rooms, lounges, hallways); Delta View had a network of 216 cameras, and New Vista had 48. No cameras were located in bedrooms or bathrooms. ... In 2010, at Delta View, 45% of falls documented on incident report occurred in common areas, of which 65% were captured on video. At New Vista, 34% of documented falls occurred in common areas, of which 28% were captured on video. ... We did not measure (and were unable to incorporate in a risk analysis) the amount of time spent doing the various activities associated with falls. ... We stress that our results summarise the situational context of falls in common areas of the long-term care environment.
claims.pico_timeframe: Two facilities; 2010 incident-report comparison
claims.safe_wording: The cameras were in lounges, dining rooms and corridors only. Falls in bedrooms and bathrooms, where many care home falls happen, were not filmed.
claims.qualifications: Put this limitation on the chart itself. Do not state what share of all care home falls happen in bedrooms; the paper gives only that 45% and 34% of documented falls at the two sites were in common areas in 2010.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors report that people with filmed falls had similar demographics to those whose falls were not filmed (January to June 2010).

numbers.meaning: share of incident-reported falls in 2010 that occurred in common areas, at the two facilities
share of those common-area falls that were captured on video in 2010

claims.claim: Falls prevention in care homes should give as much attention to transfers and sitting down as to trip hazards.
claims.supporting_passage: Our findings emphasise the need to target each of these activities in fall risk assessment and prevention strategies. ... We showed that 25% of trips occurred due to the foot being caught on a chair or table leg, suggesting the need for improved staff awareness of this hazard, and improvements in environmental planning and furniture design. 21% of falls occurred during transferring, suggesting the need for exercises to enhance muscle strength, and improved assistive devices that provide adequate body support (eg, locking of wheels) when moving to and from chairs.
claims.pico_timeframe: Authors' interpretation; no intervention tested
claims.safe_wording: The authors suggested strength exercise and better support when moving to and from chairs, and noted that a quarter of trips were over chair or table legs. We should give sitting down, standing up and transfers the same attention as clearing trip hazards.
claims.qualifications: Mark the position as judgement drawn from the finding ('We should...'), not a tested intervention. Keep the furniture-leg point so the post does not dismiss trip hazards.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial in this study showed that focusing on transfers reduces falls.

numbers.meaning: trips where the foot caught on a chair or table leg (share of the 48 trips)

claims.claim: Repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years of onset are a core feature (P1, highest certainty level) in the MDS criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy; 'backward' falls are not part of the criterion wording.
claims.supporting_passage: Table 2, Postural instability, Level 1: "P1: Repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years". Table 4 definition: "Spontaneous loss of balance while standing, or history of more than one unprovoked fall, within 3 years after onset of PSP-related features." Discussion: "We are also aware of several other clinical signs that have been proposed to indicate the diagnosis of PSP, for example, retropulsion with spontaneous backward falls ... Whereas these signs may indeed be helpful to raise suspicion about PSP, we found no clear evidence suggesting that they would indeed contribute reliable information to substantiate the diagnosis of PSP." Table 5: Probable PSP = "(O1 or O2) + (P1 or P2)", "PSP with Richardson's syndrome".
claims.pico_timeframe: Diagnostic criteria; falls within 3 years after onset of PSP-related features
claims.safe_wording: In the Movement Disorder Society criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years of the first symptoms are a core feature. Combined with slowed or restricted up-and-down eye movements, they support a diagnosis of probable PSP.
claims.qualifications: Carousel label: 'Repeated falls without a clear cause in the first 3 years: think PSP'. Do not write 'early backward falls: think PSP' as if it were the criterion; backward falls are a traditional sign that the criteria authors found no clear evidence for.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Falls alone do not make the diagnosis; the criteria combine falls with eye-movement signs.

numbers.meaning: time window after onset of PSP-related features
unprovoked falls needed for P1 (or spontaneous loss of balance while standing)

claims.claim: Recurrent falls due to impaired balance within 3 years of onset are a red flag against Parkinson's disease in the 2015 MDS criteria, and in autopsy-confirmed cases they were documented far less often in PD than in atypical parkinsonism.
claims.supporting_passage: Red Flags were described as negative features which are potential signs of alternate pathology, but with lower or uncertain specificity. Red Flags rule out probable PD only when they cannot be counterbalanced by supportive criteria ... Table 1: "Recurrent falls (>1 per year) within first 3 years". Results: "'Recurrent falling because of impaired balance within 3 y' was reported in 3.8% of 124 PD cases and 28% in 19 DLB cases. In 274 MSA cases, these early falls were reported in 28.8%, in 33.6% of 28 PSP cases and in 22% of 27 CBD cases." Discussion: "Items with less clear discriminative value were 'rapid progression of gait impairment', 'recurrent falls', and 'bilateral symmetric Parkinsonism', as these features were reported in 3.8–17.6% of PD cases."
claims.location: Introduction; Table 1; Results, Red Flags; Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Autopsy-confirmed PD and atypical parkinsonism from 28 clinicopathological series, 1988 to 2024 / documented early recurrent falls
claims.safe_wording: Repeated falls from poor balance in the first 3 years of a Parkinson-like illness are a warning sign in the Movement Disorder Society criteria that the illness may be something other than Parkinson's disease. In people whose diagnosis was confirmed after death, such early falls were recorded in about 4 in 100 with Parkinson's disease and about 1 in 3 with PSP.
claims.qualifications: A red flag, not an exclusion: it can be outweighed by features supporting PD. Autopsy numbers are small for PSP (28 cases) and come from retrospective notes. The same review advises making sure dopamine treatment is adequate before relying on early falls as a red flag.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: About two thirds of the PSP cases in this dataset had no early recurrent falls documented, so absence of early falls does not rule PSP out. Postuma 2015 (the original criteria) could not be opened; the wording comes from this 2025 review.

numbers.meaning: autopsy-confirmed PD cases with documented recurrent falls within 3 years
autopsy-confirmed PSP cases with such falls
MSA cases
DLB and CBD cases

claims.claim: The gait of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is small-stepped, magnetic (feet barely lifted) and broad-based, and becomes unstable on turning.
claims.supporting_passage: Gait disturbance in iNPH has three characteristics: small-step gait, magnet gait, and broad-based gait. Walking becomes unstable and slow. ... When changing directions, steps are small and unstable. ... pathological gait features, such as small-step gait (short length of stride), broad-based gait (increasingly large step intervals), instability, difficulty in changing directions, frozen gait (no first step taken), and shuffle (dragging of feet and decreased elevation)
claims.location: Chapter 1, Characteristics and evaluation of gait disturbance; Chapter 3, CSF drainage test
claims.pico_timeframe: Guideline description of iNPH gait
claims.safe_wording: Normal pressure hydrocephalus typically causes short, wide-based steps with the feet barely lifted, which become more unsteady on turning.
claims.qualifications: Carousel label: 'Short, wide-based steps, feet barely lifted, unsteady on turning: think NPH'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The guideline notes some features overlap with Parkinson's disease (freezing), but external cues help less in NPH.

claims.claim: Gait disturbance is the commonest symptom of NPH; bladder symptoms and cognitive change are common but the full triad is often incomplete.
claims.supporting_passage: The percentage of gait disturbance is 94–100%, which is consistent in almost all studies and is seen in almost all iNPH cases. The rates reported for cognitive impairment and urinary dysfunction vary, being 78–98% and 60–92%, respectively. Consistently, gait disturbance is the most common symptom of iNPH, followed by cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence. Many reports state that the triad is complete in approximately 60% of cases. Meanwhile, a large-scale questionnaire survey conducted in Japan in 2012 revealed that the full triad was present in only 12.1% of 1524 patients. ... Urge incontinence associated with an overactive bladder is characteristic of dysuria in patients with iNPH.
claims.pico_timeframe: Mostly hospital-based series; one Japanese national survey (2012, 1524 patients)
claims.safe_wording: Almost everyone with NPH has the walking problem. Bladder urgency and slowed thinking are common too, but many people do not have all three.
claims.qualifications: Do not imply urgency and slowed thinking must be present before NPH is considered.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Triad completeness ranges from about 60% in hospital series to 12.1% in a national survey.

numbers.meaning: share of iNPH cases with gait disturbance (hospital-based studies)
cognitive impairment; urinary dysfunction
full triad in hospital reports; full triad in a Japanese national survey

claims.claim: Shunt surgery is effective for NPH and many people improve, with walking improving most.
claims.supporting_passage: CSF shunt intervention is effective for treating iNPH. Recommendation Grade 1, Level of Evidence B ... Symptoms usually improve after surgical intervention. ... The degree of improvement in gait disturbance is the highest, followed by cognitive impairment and urinary dysfunction. ... Based on evaluations such as mRS, improvement rate after shunt intervention is reported to be approximately 39–81% in 3–6 months, 63–84% in 1 year, 69% in 2 years, and approximately 60–74% in 3–6 years. ... gait disturbance showed the highest rate of improvement ... approximately 60–77%.
claims.location: Chapter 4, CQ-10; Chapter 5, CQ-14 and prognosis
claims.pico_timeframe: People with iNPH selected for shunt surgery / improvement on mRS and symptom scales / 3 months to 6 years
claims.safe_wording: Shunt surgery helps many people with NPH who are selected for it; in reported series, roughly 6 to 8 in 10 were better a year later, and walking improved most.
claims.qualifications: Applies to selected patients (usually after a positive tap test and typical imaging); outcomes depend on comorbidity, disease duration and complications.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Ranges come from varied series and measures; long-term benefit falls somewhat over years.

numbers.meaning: improvement rate on mRS-type measures at 1 year after shunt
improvement rate for gait disturbance
guideline recommendation strength for shunt surgery

claims.claim: Marked unsteadiness with eyes closed (a positive Romberg test) points to loss of position sense, for example from neuropathy, but also occurs with loss of inner-ear balance function; it is not a test of cerebellar function.
claims.supporting_passage: In clinical neurology, the Romberg test is traditionally used to assess postural stability by altering visual input, thereby unmasking disequilibrium in patients with sensory ataxia caused by proprioceptive deficits. ... The classic Romberg test primarily evaluates proprioceptive function, particularly the integrity of the posterior columns of the spinal cord. ... It is not a test of cerebellar function, as cerebellar dysfunction typically leads to balance impairment regardless of visual input. ... While the Romberg test is standard, it fails to clearly differentiate vestibular from sensory ataxia. (Anagnostou 2025) / ... sensory ataxia, as both conditions typically present with a positive classical Romberg test. (Anagnostou 2025 abstract) / We conclude that the Romberg test ... had an unsatisfactory classification value in terms of distinguishing patients from healthy controls. Instead, it should be interpreted within the comprehensive context of the broader neurological examination and the electrodiagnosis of peripheral nerve function. (Anagnostou 2024 abstract)
claims.location: Anagnostou 2025 Abstract and Introduction; Anagnostou 2024 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Bedside test physiology; small posturography studies
claims.safe_wording: If someone is much more unsteady standing with eyes closed than open, they are relying on vision to balance. Think of loss of position sense in the feet and legs (for example from neuropathy) or loss of inner-ear balance function.
claims.qualifications: Carousel label: 'Much worse with eyes closed: think loss of position sense (for example neuropathy) or inner-ear balance loss'. The test is a pointer, to be read with the rest of the examination.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Quantified Romberg testing separated neuropathy patients from controls only modestly (Anagnostou 2024).

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy and spinal cord degeneration, sometimes without anaemia, and damage can become permanent if untreated.
claims.supporting_passage: Table 2 Neurological: "Peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of the cord and autonomic eg bowel/urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction" ... "No particular correlation between haematological and neurological features has been demonstrated, such that those with neurological symptoms may have no haematological abnormalities, and vice-versa." ... "Sequelae of untreated vitamin B12 deficiency includes not only permanent neurological symptoms, but also osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease."
claims.location: Table 2; When should vitamin B12 deficiency be suspected?; Learning points
claims.pico_timeframe: Narrative review
claims.safe_wording: One treatable cause of neuropathy to check is vitamin B12 deficiency, which can damage nerves and the spinal cord even when the blood count is normal.
claims.qualifications: The source does not mention the Romberg sign; link B12 to neuropathy and spinal cord damage, not to the sign directly.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: Gait disorders in older people are not an unpreventable consequence of ageing but point to underlying diseases that need specific tests.
claims.supporting_passage: Another relevant message is that gait disorders are not an unpreventable consequence of ageing, but implicate the presence of underlying diseases that warrant specific diagnostic tests.
claims.pico_timeframe: Expert review
claims.safe_wording: A walking problem in later life usually has a cause that can be named. 'Old age' is not a diagnosis.
claims.qualifications: Expert review statement; frame the clinical instruction (watch every person who falls walk, turn and stand with eyes closed) as the post's recommendation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Gait disorders in older people are often multifactorial (same review), so one named cause may not explain everything.

claims.claim: In a 1997 study of 58 residents of sheltered accommodation in Umea, Sweden, 10 of the 12 who stopped walking when a conversation started fell within 6 months, compared with 11 of the 46 who kept walking.
claims.supporting_passage: 58 residents in sheltered accommodation in Umea, Sweden, were included. All were able to walk with or without aids and able to follow simple instructions (mean age [SD] 80·1 [6·1] years; 72% women). The most common diagnoses (some had more than one) were dementia (n=26), depression (25), and previous stroke (20). ... The staff registered falls indoors during a followup of 6 months. ... 12 people stopped walking when a conversation started and ten of them fell during the 6-month follow-up. 21 people fell at least once. ... claims.safe_wording: In the same study, people who regularly wore multifocal glasses had more falls over the following year, especially trips, falls outside the home and falls on stairs, even after allowing for other risk factors. This was an observational link in 156 people and does not prove the glasses caused the falls.
claims.qualifications: Association, not causation. Do not turn the odds ratio into 'twice as likely' (STYLE 9), even though the authors did. Small sample with wide confidence intervals.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The VISIBLE trial (C01-23-c) tested the change directly and did not show a clear overall reduction, so the cohort link should not be presented as proof that swapping glasses prevents falls.

numbers.meaning: adjusted odds ratio for any fall over 1 year, multifocal wearers vs non-wearers; practitioner use only, not for conversion

claims.claim: In the VISIBLE trial, giving regular multifocal wearers single-lens distance glasses for walking outdoors did not clearly reduce falls overall.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "606 regular wearers of multifocal glasses (mean age 80 (SD 7) years). Inclusion criteria included increased risk of falls (fall in previous year or timed up and go test >15 seconds) and outdoor use of multifocal glasses at least three times a week." ... "In the 299 intervention and 298 control participants available to follow-up, the intervention resulted in an 8% reduction in falls (incidence rate ratio 0.92, 95% confidence interval 0.73 to 1.16)." Results: "In the 597 participants who completed calendars, fall rates did not differ significantly between the groups." Table 2, All falls, Overall: intervention 299, fallers 170 (57), total falls 461, rate 1.54; control 298, fallers 175 (59), total falls 496, rate 1.66; IRR 0.92 (0.73 to 1.16).

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The trial was powered for total falls; the authors note that about half of all falls were indoors, where the intervention was not expected to help.

claims.claim: In a pre-planned subgroup of people who regularly took part in outdoor activities, distance glasses reduced falls, outdoor falls and injurious falls.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Pre-planned sub-group analyses showed that the intervention was effective in significantly reducing all falls (incidence rate ratio 0.60, 0.42 to 0.87), outside falls, and injurious falls in people who regularly took part in outside activities." Results: "Significant interactions were evident between the intervention and self reported baseline outdoor activity levels (assessed with the Adelaide activities profile) for the outcomes of all falls, falls outside the home, and injurious falls (P<0.001)." Table 2, All falls, High AAP level: intervention 148, fallers 77 (52), total falls 187, rate 1.26; control 113, fallers 68 (60), total falls 244, rate 2.16; IRR 0.60 (0.42 to 0.87).

Outdoor falls and falls causing injury were also lower. The researchers planned this comparison before the trial, but it is still a subgroup of one trial.

Table 2, Outside falls, Low AAP level: intervention 151, fallers 77 (51), falls 102, rate 0.92; control 185, fallers 66 (36), falls 76, rate 0.59; IRR 1.56 (1.11 to 2.19). All falls, Low AAP level: rate 1.81 vs 1.36; IRR 1.29 (0.95 to 1.75). Conclusions: "The intervention may be harmful, however, in multifocal glasses wearers with low levels of outdoor activity."

Their total falls also rose (from about 1.4 to 1.8 per person), but that difference could have been chance. The authors concluded the change may be harmful for people who wear multifocals and rarely go out.

claims.qualifications: Adherence self-reported.

claims.claim: The World Falls Guidelines 2022 support active older people avoiding multifocal glasses outdoors, and include checking multifocal use in a falls assessment.
claims.supporting_passage: Vision interventions: "Evidence from randomised controlled trials and prospective studies indicates cataract surgery for the first eye, [] and both eyes [] and achieving optimal safe functional vision by active older adults avoiding the wearing of multifocal glasses when outside [] are effective fall prevention strategies." ... "In fact, it is recommended that optometrists counsel their clients about likely short-term increased fall risk when dispensing new prescription glasses." Assessment table: "Objective assessment of visual problems and acuity and appropriate use of glasses (including check multi−/bifocal glasses)If indicated, refer to ophthalmologist or optometrist"

They also advise optometrists to warn people about a possible short-term rise in falls risk when new glasses are dispensed.
claims.qualifications: The guideline statement rests mainly on VISIBLE; the word 'active' carries the qualification.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.supporting_passage: Policy and practice implications: "Secondly, older people with considerable correctable distance refractive error who take part in frequent outdoor activities should use single lens distance glasses when outdoors and in other unfamiliar settings." ... "Thirdly, older regular wearers of multifocal glasses with considerable correctable distance refractive error who take part in little outdoor activity should use multifocal glasses for most activities (rather than using multiple pairs of glasses)." Conclusions: "clinicians should be conservative in eyewear prescription, particularly in frail older people who do not often leave their homes."
claims.location: Discussion, Policy and practice implications; Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: Authors' recommendations drawn from the trial and earlier work.
claims.safe_wording: The trial's authors suggest a separate pair of distance glasses for walking outside for people who are often out and about, and staying with one pair of multifocals for people who rarely go out. That makes it a conversation to have with your optometrist, not a change for everyone.
claims.qualifications: Authors' recommendations, not a formal guideline.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: In the 2019 Cochrane review of exercise for community-dwelling older people, exercise reduced the rate of falls by 23% and the number of people having one or more falls by 15%.
claims.supporting_passage: "Exercise reduces the rate of falls by 23% (rate ratio (RaR) 0.77, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.71 to 0.83; 12,981 participants, 59 studies; high-certainty evidence)." ... "Exercise also reduces the number of people experiencing one or more falls by 15% (risk ratio (RR) 0.85, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.89; 13,518 participants, 63 studies; high-certainty evidence)." Plain language summary: "Exercise reduces the number of falls over time by around one‐quarter (23% reduction)." ... "Exercise also reduces the number of people experiencing one or more falls (number of fallers) by around one‐sixth (15%) compared with control."
claims.location: Abstract, Main results (Exercise (all types) versus control); Plain language summary
claims.pico_timeframe: People aged 60+ living in the community (mean 76, 77% women); exercise (all types) vs control not thought to reduce falls; rate of falls and number of fallers over trial follow-up.
claims.safe_wording: In the 2019 Cochrane review of exercise for older people living at home, exercise cut the number of falls by about a quarter (23%) but cut the number of people who fell at least once by about a sixth (15%). Both results are high-certainty evidence from dozens of trials.
claims.qualifications: Relative effects; give the absolute figures (C01-02-b) first on the visual. The two outcomes come from overlapping but not identical sets of trials (59 and 63 studies).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Sherrington 2020 (PMID 33239019), an update for WHO, gives the same rate ratio (0.77). USPSTF 2024 (PMID 38833257) found smaller effects for exercise (IRR 0.85 for falls; RR 0.92 for people with 1 or more falls), same direction and same pattern.

numbers.meaning: rate ratio for falls; 23% relative reduction; 59 studies, 12,981 people
risk ratio for having 1 or more falls; 15% relative reduction; 63 studies, 13,518 people

claims.claim: The review's absolute illustration: 850 falls per 1000 people followed for a year becomes about 195 fewer falls with exercise; 480 fallers per 1000 people becomes about 72 fewer fallers.
claims.supporting_passage: "Based on an illustrative risk of 850 falls in 1000 people followed over one year (data based on control group risk data from the 59 studies), this equates to 195 (95% CI 144 to 246) fewer falls in the exercise group." ... "Based on an illustrative risk of 480 fallers in 1000 people followed over one year (data based on control group risk data from the 63 studies), this equates to 72 (95% CI 52 to 91) fewer fallers in the exercise group."
claims.pico_timeframe: Illustrative 1000 people followed for one year, baseline risks from control groups of the pooled trials.
claims.safe_wording: Picture 1000 people like those in the trials, followed for a year. Without exercise they would have about 850 falls between them; with exercise, about 195 fewer. Without exercise, about 480 of the 1000 would fall at least once; with exercise, about 72 fewer, so about 408. The first number counts falls; the second counts people.
claims.qualifications: The denominator is '1000 people followed over one year', not '1000 person-years' as the candidate wrote. These are illustrations built from average control-group risks, so label icon arrays 'illustration based on Cochrane 2019'. The 408 is simple subtraction (480 minus 72). The fallers figure is closer to the question 'will I fall this year?', but it is still an average across trial participants, not a prediction for one person (judge's concern).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Summary of findings table not opened (full text not returned); figures taken from the abstract.

fewer falls per 1000 people per year with exercise

claims.claim: Falls are recurrent events: some people fall more than once, so a count of falls and a count of people who fell measure different things.
claims.supporting_passage: Robertson 2005: "These techniques a) allow for the fact that falls are frequent, recurrent events with a non-normal distribution; b) adjust for the follow-up time of individual participants; and c) allow the addition of covariates." Fleming 2008 (Results): "There were 265 reported falls in total as most people fell at least twice." Cochrane 2019: "850 falls in 1000 people" versus "480 fallers in 1000 people followed over one year".
claims.location: Robertson 2005 Abstract; Fleming 2008 Results (Falling in different residential settings); Cochrane 2019 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Methods paper using two NZ exercise trials; Fleming: 66 fallers aged over 90 in Cambridge over one year.
claims.safe_wording: Falls repeat. A person who falls three times counts three times in the number of falls but once in the number of people who fell. So a programme can prevent some repeat falls without changing whether a person falls at all, and the two figures from the same trials will differ.
claims.qualifications: Do not claim that 'a minority of people have most falls': no opened source quantified this. The gap between a rate ratio and a risk ratio is partly a property of counting 'at least one fall' rather than every fall, not only of repeat fallers; keep the explanation to what each number counts.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: Fleming 2008, people over 90, one year (for practitioner illustration only)

claims.claim: Some falls interventions reduce the rate of falls without clearly reducing the number of people who fall; the 2026 Cochrane review of multifactorial interventions is the clearest example.
claims.supporting_passage: Swarnalatha 2026: "Multifactorial interventions may reduce falls rate (RaR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.87; I² = 92%; 29 trials, 9442 participants; low-certainty evidence) and the risk of recurrent falls (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.98; I² = 45%; 17 trials, 4826 participants; low-certainty evidence). They may have little or no effect on the risk of falling (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.01; I² = 55%; 38 trials, 12,774 participants; low-certainty evidence)." Guirguis-Blake 2024: "Multifactorial interventions were associated with a statistically significant reduction in falls (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 0.84 [95% CI, 0.74-0.95]) but not a statistically significant reduction in individual risk of 1 or more falls (relative risk [RR], 0.96 [95% CI, 0.91-1.02])"
claims.location: Swarnalatha 2026 Abstract, Main results; Guirguis-Blake 2024 Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling people aged 60+ (Cochrane) or 65+ (USPSTF); multifactorial interventions (assessment then tailored treatments) vs usual care or attention control; falls rate and risk of falling.
claims.safe_wording: The gap can be bigger. In the 2026 Cochrane review of multifactorial programmes (an individual falls assessment followed by treatments matched to each person's risks), compared with usual care the programmes may lower the rate of falls by about a quarter but may make little or no difference to the number of people who fall at all. The evidence is low certainty. A 2024 review for the US Preventive Services Task Force found the same pattern.
claims.qualifications: Low-certainty evidence, high heterogeneity. Keep 'may' wording. This is a sharper illustration of the post's point than exercise.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The same Cochrane review found multifactorial programmes may reduce recurrent falls (people with 2 or more falls), consistent with fewer repeat falls.

risk ratio for having 1 or more falls; 38 trials, 12,774 people; low certainty
risk ratio for recurrent falls (2 or more); 17 trials, 4826 people
USPSTF 2024, multifactorial: falls rate vs people with 1 or more falls

claims.claim: The same pattern appears in care homes: vitamin D probably reduces the rate of falls but not the number of residents who fall (in residents with low vitamin D).

The population in these trials had low vitamin D levels."
claims.pico_timeframe: Care-facility residents aged over 65 with low vitamin D levels; vitamin D vs control.
claims.safe_wording: The same split shows up elsewhere: in care homes, vitamin D for residents with low vitamin D levels probably lowers the rate of falls but probably makes little or no difference to how many residents fall (Cochrane 2025).
claims.qualifications: Optional supporting example; different population (care homes, low vitamin D). Not needed for the core post.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: care-facility vitamin D: rate of falls vs risk of falling; moderate certainty

claims.claim: Major falls reviews report the rate of falls and the number of people who fall as separate critical outcomes.
claims.supporting_passage: Swarnalatha 2026: "Our critical outcomes were falls rate (falls per person-year), risk of falling (number of people sustaining one or more falls), and risk of recurrent falls (number of people sustaining two or more falls)." McLennan 2026: "Critical outcomes were rate of falls (number of falls per unit time) and risk of falling (number of fallers)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Cochrane review methods.
claims.safe_wording: Cochrane falls reviews report the rate of falls and the number of people who fall as two separate main outcomes. Anyone quoting a falls result can say which one they mean (judgement).
claims.qualifications: The candidate's ProFaNE consensus claim (Lamb 2005) could not be verified: only the abstract was available and it does not state the reporting recommendation. Use Cochrane methods instead, or drop the ProFaNE reference.

claims.claim: About half of older people who fell without serious injury were unable to get up without help after at least one fall (Tinetti 1993).

"Inability to get up without help was reported after 220 of 596 non-injurious falls. Of 313 non-injured fallers, 148 (47%) reported inability to get up after at least one fall."

claims.safe_wording: In a US study that followed 1103 people aged 72 and over living at home, almost half of those who fell without serious injury (148 of 313) said that at least once they could not get up without help.
claims.qualifications: Old (1993), US, self-reported. Say 'a US study published in 1993' rather than implying current UK figures.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with later statements: Swancutt 2020 background ('approximately half of people who fall without injury are able to get themselves off the floor') and Fleming 2008 discussion ('between a third to a half could not when they fell in the community').

people aged 72+ in the cohort

Fallers who were unable to get up were more likely to die, to be hospitalized, and to suffer a decline in activities of daily living for at least 3 days, and were less likely to be placed in a nursing home than were fallers who were able to get up, but these trends were not statistically significant."

claims.safe_wording: In that study, people who could not get up were more likely to have a lasting decline in everyday activities afterwards (35 in 100, against 26 in 100 of those who could get up). Differences in hospital admission and death pointed the same way but could have been chance.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: lasting decline in activities of daily living, fallers unable vs able to get up

claims.claim: Among people over 90, most who fell could not get up after at least one fall, nearly a third lay on the floor for an hour or more, and long lies were linked with serious injury and hospital admission.

Of the 60% who fell, 80% (53/66) were unable to get up after at least one fall and 30% (20/66) had lain on the floor for an hour or more." ... "Lying on the floor for a long time was strongly associated with serious injuries, admission to hospital, and subsequent moves into long term care." Results: "giving a threefold increased odds of admission to a care home, though the risk estimate did not reach significance in this smaller sample (n=51 not living in care who fell) until the censoring, conducted when everyone had completed their year since interview (crude hazard ratio 3.4 (1.2 to 9.5), adjusted 2.3 (0.8 to 7.0))." Of those, 53 (80%) could not get up on their own after at least one fall and 20 (30%) lay on the floor for an hour or more. Most falls (82 in 100) happened when the person was alone. Lying on the floor for a long time was linked with serious injury and hospital admission; the link with later moving into a care home was uncertain once other factors were allowed for.

claims.supporting_passage: "An adult who sustains an injury requiring medical (including surgical) treatment, reports recurrent falls (≥2) in the previous 12 months, was laying on the floor unable to rise independently for at least one hour, is considered frail or is suspected to have experienced a transient loss of consciousness should be regarded as at high risk of future falls.." ... "(iv) inability to get up after the fall without help for at least an hour and (v) accompanied by (suspected) transient loss of consciousness. These high-risk older adults should be offered a multifactorial falls risk assessment."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults who have fallen; guideline risk stratification.
claims.safe_wording: The 2022 World Falls Guidelines count being unable to get up for an hour or more after a fall as a sign of high risk of further falls. People at high risk should be offered a full falls assessment.
claims.qualifications: The criterion is 'for at least one hour'; the candidate's wording ('lying on the floor and being unable to get up') must add the hour.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Long lies are linked with serious complications, and the skill of getting up is best relearnt by practising each movement (backward chaining).
claims.supporting_passage: "An important aspect to consider is avoiding 'long-lies' and harm from being unable to get up from the floor. One in 8 older adults who fall report lying on the floor for more than 1 hour [] and in those over the age of 90, up to 80% cannot rise from the floor after a fall []. Lying on the floor for more than an hour is associated with dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, renal failure, hypothermia, pneumonia and urinary tract infections, skin damage and pain [,], and declines in mobility and restrictions in activity, probably due to fear of a repeat fall." ... "Regaining the skill to rise from the floor is most successfully re-learnt through practice of each of the specific movements required (often called backward-chaining) where the last step in the chain is taught first []. Some falls prevention exercise programmes also have a specific focus on this skill and have shown success in regaining this function []." Also: "It may also be useful to assess rising from the floor and dual task activity performance."
claims.location: Full text, Exercise and physical activity interventions (Recommendation details and justification); Gait and balance assessment
claims.pico_timeframe: Guideline narrative for community-dwelling older adults.
claims.safe_wording: The World Falls Guidelines say lying on the floor for more than an hour is linked with dehydration, kidney problems, low body temperature, pneumonia, skin damage and pain. They say the skill of getting up is best relearnt by practising each movement in turn, often starting with the last step first (called backward chaining).
claims.qualifications: The 'one in 8' and 'up to 80%' figures are background citations within the guideline; if used, attribute them to the guideline citing other studies. The complications are associations.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: older adults who fall who report lying on the floor for more than 1 hour (guideline citing another study)
people over 90 who cannot rise after a fall (guideline citing Fleming 2008)

claims.claim: Getting up from the floor can be learnt: in a 2026 pilot trial, brief practice sessions improved older people's ability and speed at getting up.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Intervention: 5 weekly 20-minute FRT sessions utilising backward-chaining. Controls viewed a FRT demonstration video followed by discussion (20-minutes total), without physical practise." ... "Primary outcome (FES-I), FoF and activity avoidance showed no significant differences." Results: "At baseline, 77% of the FRT group could rise independently from supine, increasing to 100% post-intervention. In contrast, independent supine floor-rise in the control group remained unchanged at 63% (seefor more data on floor-rise ability). After adjusting for age, Otago duration and baseline ability, the intervention significantly increased the probability of rising from the supine position by 27% compared with controls (adjusted RD = 27%, 95% CI 7% to 47%,= .007)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 61 randomised, 49 analysed (22 training, 27 video) adults aged 65+ attending Otago classes in Scotland; 5 weekly 20-minute backward-chaining sessions vs instructional video; outcomes 1 week after.
claims.safe_wording: In a small Scottish pilot trial published in 2026, older people from community exercise classes practised getting up from the floor in five weekly 20-minute sessions. Afterwards, all of them could get up from lying on their back (77 in 100 could before). In the comparison group, who watched a video instead, it stayed at 63 in 100. Fear of falling did not change.
claims.qualifications: Pilot; only 49 analysed; unblinded assessor; fitter participants already in exercise classes (BMI under 30, no frame indoors); groups differed in age; outcomes measured one week after; falls and long lies not measured. Say practice builds the skill and confidence to get up; do not say it prevents long lies (judge's concern).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Earlier evidence is mixed (C01-03-g).

numbers.meaning: training dose
training group able to rise from lying on the back, before vs after
video group able to rise from lying on the back, unchanged
adjusted difference in probability of rising from supine, practitioner use
participants analysed (22 and 27)

claims.claim: Earlier evidence on floor-rise training is small and mixed, and no study has shown it prevents long lies.
claims.supporting_passage: Leonhardt 2020: "Seven studies with a total of 446 participants (mean age 82.4 ± 5.3 years) were identified. Emerging evidence shows that BCM significantly improves the ability to get up unassisted from the floor, as well as mobility with reduced fall incidence in older people. Furthermore, it can potentially reduce fear of falling. Reporting on feasibility and acceptance of BCM was limited. Study quality varied widely." Burton 2018: "meta-analyses of all RCT interventions indicated no significant change in time for older people to get up off the floor independently with intervention (MD: -0.43[-1.38, 0.51])." ... "Heterogeneity between studies was high, therefore results should be viewed with some caution." Swancutt 2020: "However, future research is required to establish whether undertaking 'getting up' training is effective and cost-effective at, for example, reducing the consequences of a long lie or ambulance callouts."
claims.location: Leonhardt 2020 Abstract; Burton 2018 Abstract; Swancutt 2020 Discussion (Implications)
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults 60+; floor-rise or backward-chaining training vs control; outcomes ability or time to rise.
claims.safe_wording: The earlier research is small and mixed. One review of 7 studies (446 people) found backward chaining improved people's ability to get up unaided; another review that pooled trials did not find a clear change in the time taken to get up. No study has yet shown that practising prevents long lies.
claims.qualifications: Evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Leonhardt's mention of 'reduced fall incidence' comes from few, variable-quality studies; do not repeat it as a finding.

numbers.meaning: Leonhardt 2020 review of backward chaining
Burton 2018 pooled change in time to rise; not significant

claims.claim: Getting-up techniques are rarely taught by therapists or ambulance staff.
claims.supporting_passage: Swancutt 2020: "Neither therapists nor ambulance service staff routinely teach strategies on how to get up, meaning that healthcare professionals largely have a reactive role in managing falls." Seeley 2026 (Introduction): "Floor-rise ability is an important functional skill, recognised in international guidelines [], which is rarely taught to fallers by physiotherapists or ambulance crews [] and is frequently omitted from fall prevention programmes []."
claims.pico_timeframe: Swancutt: 28 older people, spouses and staff in Devon; qualitative.
claims.safe_wording: It is often not taught. In a study in Devon, neither therapists nor ambulance staff routinely showed people how to get up after a fall. That is why it is worth asking.
claims.qualifications: Qualitative, one region; Seeley's statement is background citing other work.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: FaME (Falls Management Exercise) classes include practice at getting up from the floor.
claims.supporting_passage: "The Falls Management Exercise (FaME) programme is the only evidence-based exercise intervention for high-risk fallers that includes floor-rise training (FRT) [,] but usually only after 12 weeks of the 24-week programme."
claims.pico_timeframe: Background statement about a UK programme.
claims.safe_wording: Some falls prevention classes, such as FaME (Falls Management Exercise), include practice at getting up from the floor, usually from about halfway through the 24-week programme.
claims.qualifications: Background statement in a paper co-authored by FaME's developer (Skelton); the FaME trial (Skelton 2005, PMID 16267192) has no abstract in PubMed and was not opened. Do not quote the '31% fewer falls' figure from this background sentence.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Seeley calls FaME 'the only' such programme; the WFG says 'some' programmes include it. Use 'some'.

numbers.meaning: length of FaME programme; floor practice usually after week 12

claims.claim: NHS Inform in Scotland has a film ('Upwards and Onwards') on getting up after a fall.
claims.supporting_passage: Seeley 2026: "Controls viewed the NHS Inform video 'Upwards and Onwards' [], divided into segments over five 20-minute sessions including facilitated discussion." Swancutt 2020: "resources for older people and their families to enable them to practice getting up, such as the film produced by NHS Inform in Scotland [], could be a valuable supplement to face-to-face training or as a self-management resource." Seeley 2026 Discussion: "However, this did not translate to increased functional success (binary ability to rise), suggesting that while videos improve awareness, supervised practice is necessary for skill acquisition."
claims.location: Seeley 2026 Methods and Discussion; Swancutt 2020 Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Public resource named in two papers.
claims.safe_wording: NHS Inform in Scotland has a film called 'Upwards and Onwards' about getting up after a fall. In the 2026 trial, watching it without practising did not change whether people could get up, so use it alongside practice with a physiotherapist or trained instructor.
claims.qualifications: The NHS Inform page itself could not be opened; Alasdair must check the current link before it goes in source_reply.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: People who are hurt or in pain after a fall should not try to get up and should call for help (safety line the judge requires).
claims.supporting_passage: No supporting passage found in any opened source.
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Not verified. Until a source is opened, frame it as a question for the reader to ask: 'Ask the physiotherapist how to tell when to try to get up and when to stay put and call for help.'
claims.qualifications: The instruction is standard advice but no opened guideline or paper states it; NHS and CSP pages could not be opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: n/a

claims.claim: A step-by-step sequence for getting up (roll onto your side, hands and knees, crawl to a sturdy chair, stronger leg forward, push up, turn and sit) copied from a verified physiotherapy guide, for the carousel.
claims.supporting_passage: No step-by-step guide was opened. Nearest verified description, Seeley 2026: "Participants were instructed to rise from half-kneeling (one knee down), side-sitting (weight on one hip) and supine (lying flat on the back) positions using a sturdy chair for support".
claims.pico_timeframe: Assessment positions in the trial, not a public instruction sheet.
claims.safe_wording: Do not publish a step-by-step carousel from unverified steps. A visual may show the three positions practised in the trial (half-kneeling, side-sitting on one hip, lying on the back, each with a sturdy chair for support), labelled as positions practised in a 2026 trial, with 'Practise this with a physiotherapist first'.
claims.qualifications: A verified guide (for example the NHS Inform film or a CSP leaflet) must be opened before any step list is drawn.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: n/a

claims.claim: Exercise programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises reduce falls; programmes that are mainly strength training, dance or walking have uncertain effects.
claims.supporting_passage: "Compared with control, balance and functional exercises reduce the rate of falls by 24% (RaR 0.76, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.81; 7920 participants, 39 studies; high-certainty evidence) and the number of people experiencing one or more falls by 13% (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.91; 8288 participants, 37 studies; high-certainty evidence). Multiple types of exercise (most commonly balance and functional exercises plus resistance exercises) probably reduce the rate of falls by 34% (RaR 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88; 1374 participants, 11 studies; moderate-certainty evidence)" ... "Tai Chi may reduce the rate of falls by 19% (RaR 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.99; 2655 participants, 7 studies; low-certainty evidence)" ... "We are uncertain of the effects of programmes that are primarily resistance training, or dance or walking programmes on the rate of falls and the number of people who experience falls."
claims.location: Abstract, Main results (Different exercise types versus control)
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling people aged 60+; exercise type vs control; rate of falls and fallers.
claims.safe_wording: In the 2019 Cochrane review, programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises, such as standing up from a chair and stepping, cut falls by about a quarter. Programmes that mix several types, usually balance plus strength, probably cut falls too, and Tai Chi may. For programmes that are mainly strength training, dancing or walking, the effect on falls is uncertain.
claims.qualifications: 'Uncertain' is an evidence gap, not proof of no effect. Examples of functional exercise come from the World Falls Guidelines ('e.g. sit-to-stand, stepping').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: reduction in rate of falls with balance and functional exercise; 39 studies; high certainty
reduction in people with 1 or more falls, balance and functional exercise
multiple exercise types; moderate certainty
Tai Chi; low certainty

claims.claim: The balance exercises that prevented falls best were challenging exercises done standing.
claims.supporting_passage: "The greatest relative effects of exercise on fall rates (RR=0.58, 95% CI=0.48-0.69, 68% of between-study variability explained) were seen in programs that included a combination of a higher total dose of exercise (>50 hours over the trial period) and challenging balance exercises (exercises conducted while standing in which people aimed to stand with their feet closer together or on one leg, minimize use of their hands to assist, and practice controlled movements of the center of mass) and did not include a walking program."
claims.pico_timeframe: 44 trials, 9,603 older people in the community and residential care; meta-regression.
claims.safe_wording: In the trials, the balance exercises that challenged people most were done standing: feet closer together or on one leg, using the hands less for support, and practising controlled shifts of body weight.
claims.qualifications: The 'larger effects' part is a between-trial comparison (meta-regression). The definition is what the post needs.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: total exercise over the trial period in the most effective programmes (2008 meta-regression)

claims.claim: Programmes that challenged balance and involved more than about 3 hours a week had larger effects (between-trial comparison).
claims.supporting_passage: Sherrington 2017: "Overall, exercise reduced the rate of falls in community-dwelling older people by 21% (pooled rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.85, p<0.001, I47%, 69 comparisons) with greater effects seen from exercise programmes that challenged balance and involved more than 3 hours/week of exercise. These variables explained 76% of the between-trial heterogeneity and in combination led to a 39% reduction in falls (incident rate ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.72, p<0.001)." Sherrington 2020: "Interventions with a total weekly dose of 3+ h that included balance and functional exercises were particularly effective with a 42% reduction in rate of falls compared to control (Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR) 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.76)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling older people; between-trial meta-regression and subgroup analysis by weekly dose and balance challenge.
claims.safe_wording: Across trials, programmes that challenged balance and added up to 3 hours or more a week had the biggest effects. This comes from comparing different trials, not from a trial that tested different amounts, so treat 3 hours as a guide rather than a rule.
claims.qualifications: Meta-regression across trials, not a dose trial (judge's concern). Participants in higher-dose trials may differ in other ways.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: weekly exercise dose linked with larger effects
Sherrington 2017: reduction in falls rate for balance-challenging, >3 h/week programmes
Sherrington 2020: reduction for 3+ h/week programmes including balance and functional exercise

claims.claim: The World Falls Guidelines recommend balance-challenging and functional exercise, three or more times a week, individualised and progressed for at least 12 weeks and continued longer; benefits are lost when people stop.
claims.supporting_passage: "We recommend exercise programmes for fall prevention for community-dwelling older adults which include balance challenging and functional exercises (e.g. sit-to-stand, stepping), with sessions three times or more weekly which are individualised, progressed in intensity for at least 12 weeks and continued longer for greater effect." (1A) "We recommend inclusion, when feasible, of Tai Chi and/or additional individualised progressive resistance strength training." (1B) "Exercise needs to be progressive initially and maintained once a plateau is reached." "Benefits of exercise are lost on cessation so opportunities to continue with appropriate activity at the end of the programme are important."
claims.location: Full text, WG4 Exercise interventions table; Component interventions, Exercise and physical activity interventions
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling older adults; guideline recommendation with GRADE 1A.
claims.safe_wording: The 2022 World Falls Guidelines recommend exercise that challenges balance and practises everyday movements such as standing up from a chair and stepping, three or more times a week, tailored to the person and made harder over time, for at least 12 weeks and kept up for longer. Strength training or Tai Chi can be added where possible. The benefits are lost when people stop.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's wording 'with resistance training' should read 'with strength training added where feasible' (separate 1B recommendation).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: guideline frequency
minimum programme length, continued longer for greater effect
strength of recommendation

claims.claim: WHO 2020 guidelines advise older adults to do varied multicomponent activity emphasising balance and strength on 3 or more days a week to prevent falls (replaces the UK CMO claim, which could not be opened).
claims.supporting_passage: "As such it is recommended that as part of their weekly physical activity, older adults should do varied multicomponent physical activity at moderate or greater intensity on 3 or more days a week in order to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls." ... "Third, with respect to older adults, the recommendation regarding multicomponent physical activity that emphasises functional balance and strength training to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls now applies to all older adults rather than specifically those with poor mobility."
claims.location: Full text, Older adults section; Discussion (differences from 2010 guidelines)
claims.pico_timeframe: Global guideline for adults aged 65+.
claims.safe_wording: The World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines advise all older adults to do varied activity that focuses on balance and strength, at moderate effort or more, on 3 or more days a week, to keep up everyday abilities and prevent falls.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's UK Chief Medical Officers' claim (strength and balance on at least two days a week) was not verified: the CMO document was not in Drive and gov.uk could not be opened. Use WHO 2020 instead, or drop the CMO line.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The UK CMO figure (2 days) and WHO figure (3 days) differ; do not mix them.

numbers.meaning: WHO 2020 frequency for multicomponent balance and strength activity in older adults

claims.claim: Seated (chair-based) exercise has other benefits but has not been tested well as a way to prevent falls, and did not clearly improve balance.
