claims.safe_wording: International falls guidelines recommend that care home residents are assessed after every fall, to find any injury, work out why it happened, and avoid sending people to hospital when they don't need to go.
claims.qualifications: Grade E (expert opinion). The guideline does not specify what the on-the-floor assessment should contain, so it cannot supply the candidate's checklist.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Under the 2019 European definition (EWGSOP2), low muscle strength is the primary parameter: low strength means probable sarcopenia, low muscle quantity or quality confirms it, and low physical performance marks it as severe.
claims.supporting_passage: "In its 2018 definition, EWGSOP2 uses low muscle strength as the primary parameter of sarcopenia; muscle strength is presently the most reliable measure of muscle function (Table). Specifically, sarcopenia is probable when low muscle strength is detected. A sarcopenia diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of low muscle quantity or quality. When low muscle strength, low muscle quantity/quality and low physical performance are all detected, sarcopenia is considered severe." Also: "In these revised guidelines, muscle strength comes to the forefront, as it is recognised that strength is better than mass in predicting adverse outcomes"
claims.pico_timeframe: Consensus definition for older adults, European focus; published 2019 (online 2018)
claims.safe_wording: Since 2019, the main European definition puts muscle strength first. Low strength (weak grip or slow chair rises) means sarcopenia is 'probable'. A measure of muscle quantity confirms it, and slow walking or other poor performance marks it as severe.
claims.qualifications: European consensus; other regions (for example Asia) use their own criteria. Published in Age Ageing 2019 (the group met in 2018).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The 2024 global GLIS definition is conceptual only and has no operational cut-offs yet (see C02-18-f).

numbers.meaning: year the EWGSOP2 definition was published (Age Ageing 2019;48:16-31)

claims.claim: EWGSOP2 cut-offs: grip strength below 27 kg in men and 16 kg in women, or more than 15 seconds for five chair rises, indicate low strength; a usual gait speed of 0.8 m/s or less indicates severe sarcopenia.
claims.supporting_passage: EWGSOP2 Figure 2 caption: "Cut-off points based on T-score of ≤ -2.5 are shown for males and females (≤ 27 kg and 16 kg, respectively)." EWGSOP2 text: "The chair stand test measures the amount of time needed for a patient to rise five times from a seated position without using his or her arms" and "For simplicity, a single cut-off speed ≤0.8 m/s is advised by EWGSOP2 as an indicator of severe sarcopenia." Habboub 2026 abstract: "Sarcopenia was defined using EWGSOP2 criteria: probable sarcopenia as handgrip strength < 27 kg (men) or < 16 kg (women) and/or chair stand test > 15 s." Brennan-Olsen 2019: "the EWGSOP2 cut-points [11] of < 27 kg for men and < 16 kg for women as indicative of low grip strength"
claims.location: EWGSOP2 full text (Figure 2 caption; 'Muscle strength' and 'Physical performance' sections); Habboub 2026 Abstract, Methods; Brennan-Olsen 2019 full-text excerpt
claims.pico_timeframe: Cut-offs derived from UK normative grip data (Dodds 2014) at -2.5 SD; European populations
claims.safe_wording: In the European definition, grip strength below about 27 kg in men or 16 kg in women, or needing more than 15 seconds to stand up from a chair five times without using the arms, counts as low strength. A usual walking speed of 0.8 metres per second or slower marks severe sarcopenia.
claims.qualifications: The chair-stand cut-off (>15 s) was confirmed from secondary sources quoting EWGSOP2 because Table 3 of the consensus was not readable; the Figure 2 caption writes the grip cut-off as '<= 27 kg and 16 kg' whereas secondary sources quote '< 27 kg and < 16 kg'. Say 'below about 27 kg / 16 kg'. EWGSOP2 says its cut-offs focus on European populations and advises regional norms where available. Grip needs a calibrated dynamometer under standard conditions.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Huemer 2023 (German National Cohort) derived cut-offs of 29 kg and 18 kg, 2 kg higher than EWGSOP2, which would label more people as weak: "Cut-off points for low grip strength from German population-based data were 2 kg higher than the EWGSOP2 cut-off points." Asian criteria differ (numbers not checked here).

numbers.meaning: grip strength cut-off for men (below this = low strength), EWGSOP2
grip strength cut-off for women, EWGSOP2
time for five chair rises without arms; more than this = low strength (EWGSOP2, via secondary sources)
usual gait speed at or below which sarcopenia is classed as severe (EWGSOP2)
alternative German-derived grip cut-offs for men and women (Huemer 2023)

claims.claim: EWGSOP2 states that in clinical practice low muscle strength (probable sarcopenia) is enough to trigger assessment of causes and to start intervention, without waiting for a muscle-mass measurement.
claims.supporting_passage: Brennan-Olsen 2019 (full-text excerpt): "The revised EWGSOP2 consensus regarding sarcopenia identified that, in clinical practice, low grip strength is enough to trigger assessment of causes and start intervention for sarcopenia [11], which is indicative of an increasing focus on muscle strength rather than muscle mass as a key determinant of sarcopenia". EWGSOP2 Figure 1 note (PMC text): "Consider other reasons for low muscle strength (e.g. depression, sroke, balance disorders, peripheral vascular disorders)."
claims.location: Brennan-Olsen 2019 Discussion (Scite full-text excerpt); EWGSOP2 Figure 1 legend
claims.pico_timeframe: EWGSOP2 algorithm (Find-Assess-Confirm-Severity) for clinical practice
claims.safe_wording: In everyday practice, the European group says weak grip or slow chair rises are enough to start looking for causes and to start treatment. A scan to measure muscle can come later, if it will change what you do.
claims.qualifications: The exact EWGSOP2 wording sits in its algorithm figure, which could not be read directly; it is verified through a peer-reviewed paper quoting it (and a second, conference abstract found in Scite with the same wording). Low strength has other causes (EWGSOP2 lists depression, stroke, balance disorders, peripheral vascular disorders), so 'look for causes' must stay in the wording. Do not say imaging is unnecessary: EWGSOP2 still confirms sarcopenia with a muscle-quantity measure.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: SARC-F and grip measurement are not routine in many services: Sayer 2022 reports that 'In most settings, dynamometers are not widely available to measure muscle strength'.

claims.claim: The 2018 international (ICFSR) guideline strongly recommends resistance-based physical activity to treat sarcopenia, conditionally recommends protein supplementation or a protein-rich diet, and gives no recommendation for vitamin D or anabolic hormones.
claims.supporting_passage: Dent 2018: "To treat sarcopenia, we strongly recommend the prescription of resistance-based physical activity, and conditionally recommend protein supplementation/a protein-rich diet. No recommendation is given for Vitamin D supplementation or for anabolic hormone prescription. There is a lack of robust evidence to assess the strength of other treatment options." Sayer 2024: "Resistance exercise is currently the mainstay of treatment; however, it is not suitable for all."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with sarcopenia; GRADE-based guideline 2018; review 2024

Hospitalization led to an impairment in functional capacity (mean change from baseline to discharge in the Barthel Index of -5.0 points (95% CI, -6.8 to -3.2 points) in the usual-care group, whereas the exercise intervention reversed this trend (1.9 points; 95% CI, 0.2-3.7 points). claims.pico_timeframe: 4-m usual pace test
claims.safe_wording: A usual walking speed of 0.8 metres per second or slower is a common warning threshold; it is roughly the speed at which predicted survival matched the average for age and sex.
claims.qualifications: Thresholds are conventions; Studenski found the gait-survival relationship continuous.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: EWGSOP2 severity threshold; approx. median life expectancy point
speed above which survival was longer than expected for age and sex

claims.claim: Common causes of slow gait include joint pain, parkinsonism, neuropathy, heart and lung disease, low mood and medicines.
claims.supporting_passage: Studenski: "Walking requires energy, movement control, and support and places demands on multiple organ systems, including the heart, lungs, circulatory, nervous, and musculoskeletal systems. Slowing gait may reflect both damaged systems and a high-energy cost of walking." and "A recommended evaluation and management of slow walking includes cardiopulmonary, neurological and musculoskeletal systems." Snijders: "gait disorders are not an unpreventable consequence of ageing, but implicate the presence of underlying diseases that warrant specific diagnostic tests." EWGSOP2: "Consider other reasons for low muscle strength (e.g. depression, sroke, balance disorders, peripheral vascular disorders)."
claims.location: Studenski Comment; Snijders Abstract; EWGSOP2 Figure 1 legend
claims.pico_timeframe: Clinical reasoning statements
claims.safe_wording: Walking depends on the heart, lungs, circulation, nerves, muscles and joints, so slow walking can come from a problem in any of them. A slow walk is a reason to look for a cause, not a diagnosis of 'old age'.
claims.qualifications: The specific list (joint pain, parkinsonism, neuropathy, low mood, medicines) was not verified in an opened source; use the organ-system wording above. Depression is listed by EWGSOP2 as a cause of low muscle strength, not specifically of slow gait.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Gait disorders are often multifactorial (Snijders).

claims.claim: Gait speed is most useful when repeated: a small meaningful change is about 0.05 m/s and a substantial change about 0.10 m/s; a decline suggests a new problem to evaluate, and improvement over a year was linked with better survival.
claims.supporting_passage: Perera 2006: "Best initial estimates of small meaningful change are near 0.05 m/s for gait speed ... and of substantial change are near 0.10 m/s for gait speed" "For clinical use, substantial change in these measures and small change in gait speed and 6MWD, but not SPPB, are detectable." Studenski: "Fourth, gait speed might be monitored overtime, with a decline indicating a new health problem that requires evaluation." Hardy 2007: "Mortality after 8 years was 31.6%, 41.2%, and 49.3% for those with improved, transiently improved, and never improved gait speed, respectively. The survival benefit for improvement at 1 year persisted after adjustment for covariates (hazard ratio=0.42, 95% confidence interval=0.29-0.61, P<.001)" "Further research is needed to determine whether interventions to improve gait speed affect survival."
claims.location: Perera Abstract; Studenski Comment; Hardy Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Perera: older adults in trials and a cohort; Hardy: 439 primary care patients 65+, change over 1 year, 8-year mortality
claims.safe_wording: Measure usual walking speed the same way each time and repeat it. A drop of about 0.1 metres per second is a substantial change and a reason to look for a new problem. In one study, people whose walking speed improved over a year were less likely to die over the next 8 years, though that does not prove that speeding up caused it.
claims.qualifications: Hardy is observational; say 'linked with', not 'improving speed extends life'. Change thresholds are estimates.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Measurement error: staff in clinical settings may produce more variable results (Studenski).

numbers.meaning: small meaningful change
substantial change
8-year mortality, improved vs never-improved gait speed (Hardy)
adjusted hazard ratio for death with 1-year improvement, relative

claims.claim: UK pedestrian crossing timings assume a walking speed of 1.2 m/s.
claims.supporting_passage: Asher 2012 abstract: "to compare walking speed in the UK older population with the speed required to utilise pedestrian crossings (≥1.2 m/s)" and "An assumed normal walking speed for pedestrian crossings of 1.2 m/s is inappropriate for older adults and revision of these timings should be considered." Asher 2012 introduction (Scite excerpt): "UK pedestrian crossing timings assume a minimum walking speed of 1.2m/s (2.7miles/hr)." Webb 2017 introduction: "Pedestrian crossings in the UK and US require people to walk at 1.2 m/s to cross in time ( Pedestrian Facilities at Signal-Controlled Junctions, 2005 ; Fitzpatrick et al., 2006 )"
claims.location: Asher Abstract and Introduction; Webb Introduction
claims.pico_timeframe: UK signal-controlled crossings; guidance cited is DfT 2005
claims.safe_wording: UK researchers reported in 2012 and 2017 that pedestrian crossing times in the UK are based on an assumed walking speed of 1.2 metres per second (about 2.7 miles per hour).
claims.qualifications: Attribute it to the researchers and their cited guidance (DfT 2005). Current DfT guidance (Traffic Signs Manual Chapter 6, 2019) could not be opened, so do not say 'crossings are timed for 1.2 m/s today' as a bare fact. This figure is background in both papers' introductions.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether the 2019 guidance changed the assumption is unknown (C02-05-f). Some crossings can extend time (C02-05-g).

numbers.meaning: assumed walking speed for UK crossing timings, as reported by researchers
same speed in miles per hour

claims.claim: In Health Survey for England 2005 data on 3,145 adults aged 65+, mean usual walking speed was 0.9 m/s in men and 0.8 m/s in women; 84% of men and 93% of women either walked slower than 1.2 m/s or could not do the test.
claims.supporting_passage: "random population sample of 3,145 adults (1,444 men) aged ≥65 years." "walking speed was assessed by timing a walk of 8 feet at normal pace. Walking impairment was defined as walking speed <1.2 m/s or non-participation in the test due to being unsafe or unable." "the mean walking speed was 0.9 m/s in men and 0.8 m/s in women; 84% of men and 93% of women ≥65 years had walking impairment." Full-text excerpt: "76% men and 85% women had a walking speed <1.2m/s; 93% of woman and 84% of men had walking impairment" and "90% of men and 87% of women took the walking speed test; 5.7% of men and 7.2% of women were unable to walk short distances or felt unsafe"
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 65+ in private households in England (not care homes); 2005; 8-foot walk at normal pace; cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a 2005 national survey in England, older people's average walking speed was 0.9 metres per second for men and 0.8 for women. More than 8 in 10 women (85%) and about 3 in 4 men (76%) walked slower than 1.2 metres per second; counting those who could not safely do the walk, it was over 9 in 10 women (93%) and more than 8 in 10 men (84%).
claims.qualifications: Survey from 2005, private households only. Speed was timed over a short 8-foot (2.4 m) walk at normal pace, which may not match speed on a real crossing. Put the test method and year on the chart. The 84%/93% figures include people who could not do the test; the 76%/85% figures are walking speed alone.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Webb 2017 (ELSA 2002-2014) found an even lower share fast enough (10% of measurements). Asher notes non-response may have underestimated impairment; Webb notes participants carried nothing, whereas shopping would slow people further.

claims.safe_wording: Women, the oldest, the poorest and people in worse health were the most likely to walk too slowly to cross in time.
claims.qualifications: Associations; do not say poverty 'causes' slow walking.

claims.safe_wording: The researchers concluded that crossing times should be reconsidered to allow for older people's slower walking.
claims.qualifications: Report as the researchers' recommendation, not as Alasdair's policy position (values_concern).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: In the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2002-2014), only 10% of measured walking speeds among people aged 60+ were fast enough to cross in the allotted time.

"10% of measured walking speeds were fast enough to cross the road in time." Methods: "Participants walked eight feet (2.44 m) and back at their usual walking pace, using walking aids if required." claims.supporting_passage: Not verified: the DfT Traffic Signs Manual Chapter 6 (2019) was located by web search but could not be opened; no passage was read.
claims.pico_timeframe: Current UK guidance

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Unknown.

claims.claim: Some UK crossings (Puffin crossings) can extend the crossing time for people who take longer to cross.
claims.supporting_passage: "In the UK, the Puffin crossing has provision to extend pedestrian green time for those who take longer to cross."
claims.location: Abstract (first sentence; rest of abstract not available)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK Puffin crossings
claims.safe_wording: Some newer UK crossings, called Puffin crossings, can hold the traffic for longer when someone is still crossing.
claims.qualifications: Only the first sentence of a traffic-engineering abstract was read. How many crossings have this, and whether the extra time is enough, are unknown. Keep to 'some crossings'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The same abstract begins 'However, even...' and is truncated, suggesting limitations that could not be read.

claims.claim: About 3 in 10 older people admitted to an acute hospital leave less able to do basic daily activities (washing, dressing, using the toilet, eating, getting in and out of bed or a chair, walking) than they were before they became ill.
claims.supporting_passage: "Random effects meta-analysis showed the combined prevalence across studies was 30% (95% CI: 24%, 36%; p<0.001). Sensitivity analysis of only studies assessing ADL decline from 2 weeks prior to admission to discharge or within a month of discharge showed a combined prevalence of 33% (95% CI: 26%, 41%;)." ... "Prevalence among all hospital-based studies ranged from 17% to 61%" ... "The World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) describes functional impairments in activities as having a limitation in independent execution of daily tasks including self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)."
claims.location: Full text, Results (Prevalence of Hospital-Associated Disability) and Introduction; abstract Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 65+ in medical-surgical acute care (15 studies, n=7,375, 1983 to 2013, mostly US); exposure acute hospital stay; outcome loss of independence in basic ADL (modified Katz or Barthel) from before or at admission to discharge or shortly after; no comparator (prevalence).
claims.safe_wording: About 3 in 10 older people who go into an acute hospital come out less able to wash, dress, use the toilet, eat, or get in and out of bed or a chair than they were before they became ill. When only studies that asked about the person's abilities 2 weeks before admission were counted, the figure was about 1 in 3.
claims.qualifications: Pooled estimate from studies that varied widely (17% to 61%); mostly US; data from 1983 to 2013. Measures basic self-care, not tasks such as making tea or using a key. Some of the loss starts with the illness before admission, not only in hospital; do not say the hospital stay caused it. Quote the percentage, not the confidence interval (abstract and full text give different upper limits).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: High heterogeneity and possible publication bias among small studies (authors' funnel plots). Brown 2016 trial (cognitively intact veterans, median stay 3 days) found no significant ADL change after discharge in either arm, so the proportion is lower in fitter, shorter-stay groups.

numbers.meaning: pooled prevalence of hospital-associated disability, 15 studies, 7,375 people aged 65+, acute care
pooled prevalence when restricted to studies with a baseline 2 weeks before admission (8 studies)
range across individual hospital-based studies

claims.claim: Loss of daily abilities after a hospital stay is more common the older the person.
claims.supporting_passage: "Thirty-five percent of patients declined in ADL function between baseline and discharge." ... "The frequency of ADL decline between baseline and discharge varied markedly with age (23%, 28%, 38%, 50%, and 63% in patients aged 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, and > or =90, respectively, P <.001)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 2,293 medical inpatients aged 70+, two US hospitals (1990s); baseline 2 weeks before admission; outcome decline in any of five basic ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, transferring, toileting) at discharge; crude proportions by age band.
claims.safe_wording: In one large US study of people aged 70 and over admitted with a medical illness, about 1 in 4 of those aged 70 to 74 left hospital less able to manage basic self-care than 2 weeks before admission, rising to about 6 in 10 of those aged 90 or over.
claims.qualifications: One cohort, 1990s US data; crude age-band percentages; outcome measured at discharge only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; consistent with Loyd 2020.

numbers.meaning: all patients 70+, decline in basic ADL from 2 weeks before admission to discharge
aged 70 to 74
aged 90 or over

claims.claim: The first-hour tasks (door key, front step, toilet, chair, kettle, bed) make a practical pre-discharge check; the toilet, chair and bed are the kinds of task the hospital-disability studies measured, while the key, step and kettle go beyond them.
claims.supporting_passage: Loyd 2020: "self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)". Covinsky 2003: "interviewed about their independence in five ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, transferring, and toileting)".
claims.location: Loyd full text, Introduction; Covinsky abstract, Methods
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition of the basic ADL items used in the evidence.
claims.safe_wording: Present the six tasks as a practical checklist to ask about, not as a tested tool. Getting to and using the toilet, getting up from a chair and getting into bed are basic daily activities that studies of hospital-associated disability count; the key, the front step and the kettle are extra, everyday tasks the post suggests adding.
claims.qualifications: The first-hour framing and the checklist are judgement. No study tested this checklist. Do not claim that asking these questions prevents readmission or harm.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Occupational therapists can assess how a person manages at home, including by a home visit before discharge; families can ask whether this has happened.
claims.supporting_passage: "To determine the effectiveness of pre-discharge home assessment visits by occupational therapists in assisting hospitalized patients from a range of settings to return to community living." ... "There is low-to-moderate quality evidence that pre-discharge home assessment visits reduce patients' risk of falling and increase participation. The risk of readmission to hospital is also reduced, but not for patients following stroke." ... "There was no effect on activity or quality of life."
claims.pico_timeframe: Hospitalised patients (geriatric, mixed rehabilitation and stroke settings); pre-discharge OT home assessment visits versus none or usual care; falls, participation, readmission, activity, quality of life; 14 studies.
claims.safe_wording: Ask the ward therapist whether they have seen your relative do each of these tasks. If something has not been tried, ask whether it can be practised before discharge, whether equipment is needed, and whether an occupational therapist should look at the home.
claims.qualifications: A home visit is not needed or offered for everyone; do not say every hospital provides one or that NICE requires one (NICE NG27 could not be opened). If the evidence is mentioned, say 'low to moderate quality evidence' and that it did not improve daily activity or quality of life.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Evidence quality low to moderate; no effect on activity or quality of life; readmission benefit not seen after stroke.

numbers.meaning: studies in the review

claims.claim: Of older people who leave hospital after a medical illness less able to look after themselves than before, about 3 in 10 are back to their usual level a year later, about 3 in 10 are alive but have not recovered, and about 4 in 10 have died.
claims.supporting_passage: "By 12 months after discharge, among those discharged with new or additional ADL disability, 41.3% died, 28.6% were alive but had not recovered to baseline function, and 30.1% were at their baseline function. Among those discharged with baseline function, 17.8% died, 15.2% were alive but with worse than baseline function, and 67% were at their baseline function(p<.001)." Full text: "Out of 2,279 patients who were eligible for this analysis, 1,480 patients were discharged with similar or better functional status compared to 2 weeks prior to admission while 799 patients were discharged with worse functional status".
claims.location: Abstract, Results; full text, Methods (Setting and Participants)
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients 70+ admitted non-electively to general medical services, two Ohio hospitals, 1993 to 1998; exposure discharged with new or additional disability in 5 self-care ADLs versus discharged at baseline (2 weeks before admission); outcomes death, not recovered, recovered at 12 months; crude proportions.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of people aged 70 and over admitted in an emergency with a medical illness (1993 to 1998), 799 of 2,279 left hospital needing more help with washing, dressing, eating, the toilet or moving from bed to chair than 2 weeks before admission. A year later, about 30 in 100 of them were back to their usual level, about 29 in 100 were alive but still needed more help, and about 41 in 100 had died. Among people who left hospital at their usual level, 67 in 100 were still at that level a year later.
claims.qualifications: Old US data; lengths of stay have shortened since (authors' limitation). Deaths reflect how ill this group was; present them plainly and without drama, and say that for some people this decline marks the end of life (the authors recommend considering palliative care alongside rehabilitation).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Hardy and Gill 2004 found much higher recovery rates after disability episodes in the community (any cause), so figures depend on setting and cause.

claims.claim: Among people discharged with new loss of self-care, being back to their usual level one month after discharge is linked with a much better outlook at a year.
claims.supporting_passage: "Among patients discharged with a new or additional disability in self-care ADL, the presence or absence of recovery by one month was associated with long-term outcomes. Among those who had recovered by one month after discharge, 56.2% remained at baseline function 1 year after discharge, 20.7% died, and 23.1% declined again in self-care ADL function (). In contrast, among those who did not recover by one month after hospital discharge, only 17.1% recovered baseline function at 1 year after discharge, 44.4% died, and 38.4% were alive but not recovered (p<.001)."
claims.location: Full text, Results (Role of One-Month Outcomes in Predicting Long-term Outcomes); analysis sample n=651
claims.pico_timeframe: 651 of the 799 discharged with new disability who were alive with data at 1 month; exposure recovered to baseline self-care by 1 month versus not; outcomes at 12 months; crude proportions, prognostic association.
claims.safe_wording: In that study, people who were back to their usual self-care one month after leaving hospital did much better over the year: 56 in 100 were still at their usual level at 12 months. Of those not back to their usual level at one month, 17 in 100 had recovered by 12 months.
claims.qualifications: The study measured being back to the usual level by one month, not whether recovery had 'started'; do not say 'started to recover'. Prognostic association only; it does not show that a review at one month improves outcomes. Nearly a quarter of those recovered at one month later declined again.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial found showing that a scheduled one-month review changes outcomes (not specifically searched beyond this check).

claims.claim: Not being back to normal at one month does not rule out recovery: many recoveries happen later.
claims.supporting_passage: "Among those who had a new or additional disability in self-care ADL at hospital discharge, 30% recovered and were at their baseline level of functioning at 1 year. Of these patients, 62% recovered by 1 month with the remainder recovering over the next 11 months. Thus, most recovery, when it happens, occurs in the first month after hospitalization. However, 38% of patients who recovered in the year following discharge do so after the first month after hospitalization." Conclusion: "Since outcomes in the first month seem to predict long-term outcomes, particularly aggressive interventions may be indicated in the first month. However, as a large number of patients may recover after one month, and many who recover by one month decline again, there may also be a need for sustained long-term interventions."

claims.safe_wording: Of the people who were back to their usual level a year after discharge, about 6 in 10 had got there within the first month and about 4 in 10 got there later. So the one-month point is a useful time to check progress, not a final verdict.
claims.qualifications: Same cohort limitations (US, 1990s). The one-month review is the post's judgement, informed by the authors' conclusion; mark it as a suggestion.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Among community-living people aged 70 and over who became newly disabled (any cause), most regained independence within a year, but recovery was often short-lived; frail, cognitively impaired or severely disabled people recovered less often, although most still did.
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 420 participants (56%) experienced disability during a median follow-up of 51 months. Of these participants, 399 (81%) recovered (ie, regained independence in all 4 ADLs) within 12 months of their initial disability episode, and a majority (57%) of these maintained independence for at least 6 months. Among participants who experienced 3 or more consecutive months of disability, a majority (60%) recovered, but only a third of these maintained independence for at least 6 months. Persons who were cognitively impaired, physically frail, or severely disabled (ie, in 3-4 ADLs) at onset were less likely to recover than those who were cognitively intact, nonfrail, or mildly disabled, respectively. Nonetheless, a majority of participants within each subgroup recovered."
claims.pico_timeframe: 754 initially non-disabled community-living people 70+, New Haven, 1998 to 2003; exposure new disability (needing personal help with bathing, dressing, walking or transferring) from any cause; outcome regained independence within 12 months, and duration.
claims.safe_wording: In a US community study, 81 in 100 older people who became newly dependent (from any cause) regained independence within a year, but only 57 in 100 of those who recovered stayed independent for at least 6 months.
claims.qualifications: Not a post-hospital cohort; do not place its 81% beside Boyd's 30% as if they were the same group. If used at all, label it as disability arising in the community from any cause. Recommend leaving it out of a post about discharge.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Boyd 2008 discussion: post-hospital prognosis is 'substantially worse than that observed among community-dwelling elders with disability arising from a broad range of causes'.

claims.claim: Older people in hospital spend most of the day lying in bed, including many who can walk.
claims.supporting_passage: Brown 2009: "Forty-five male patients (mean age 74.2) with a mean length of stay of 5.1 days generated 2,592 one-hour periods of data. A baseline functional assessment indicated that 35 (77.8%) study patients were willing and able to walk a short distance independently. No patient remained in bed the entire measured hospital stay, but on average, 83% of the measured hospital stay was spent lying in bed. The average amount of time that any one individual spent standing or walking ranged from a low of 0.2% to a high of 21%, with a median of 3%, or 43 minutes per day." Pedersen 2013: "The ambulatory patients were lying median 17 hours, (interquartile range [IQR]: 14.4-19.1), sitting 5.1 hours (IQR: 2.9-7.1), and standing and/or walking 1.1 hours (IQR: 0.6-1.7) per day."
claims.location: Brown 2009 Abstract, Results; Pedersen 2013 Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Brown: 45 male medical inpatients 65+ able to walk before admission, one US VA hospital, first 7 days, accelerometers. Pedersen: 43 older medical patients able to walk independently, Copenhagen, accelerometers throughout stay.
claims.safe_wording: Older people in hospital spend most of the day in bed, even many who can walk. In a US veterans' hospital, 45 men aged 65 and over spent on average 83% of their measured time lying in bed; the typical time standing or walking was 43 minutes a day, although 35 of the 45 were able to walk a short distance on their own. In a Danish hospital, 43 older medical patients who could walk spent a typical 17 hours a day lying down and about 1 hour standing or walking.
claims.qualifications: Two small single-hospital studies; Brown 2009 is men only. Always name the setting with the figure. Pick one headline figure for the visual (judge's advice).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: C01-B2 notes other small accelerometer studies with lower lying times; figures vary by setting and method. The same Brown 2009 and Pedersen figures are used for C01-05 (falls rate angle); coordinate to avoid repeating the statistic as the lead in both posts.

claims.claim: Low mobility in hospital is linked with worse daily functioning at discharge and a month later.
claims.supporting_passage: "Low versus high in-hospital mobility was associated with worse basic functional status at discharge (adjusted odds ratio (AOR)=18.03, 95% confidence interval (CI)=7.68-42.28) and at follow-up (AOR=4.72, 95% CI=1.98-11.28) and worse IADLs at follow-up (AOR=2.00, 95% CI=1.05-3.78)." ... "Forty-six percent of participants had declined in ADLs at discharge and 49% at follow-up; 57% had declined in IADLs at follow-up."

claims.claim: In a randomised trial, a hospital walking programme helped older patients keep how far they got around their community a month after discharge, but made no difference to basic daily activities.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Patients in the MP group were assisted with ambulation up to twice daily, and a behavioral strategy was used to encourage mobility. Patients in the UC group received twice-daily visits." ... "For all periods, groups were similar in ability to perform ADL; however, at 1-month after hospitalization, the LSA score was significantly higher in the MP (LSA score, 52.5) compared with the UC group (LSA score, 41.6) (P = .02). For the MP group, the 1-month posthospitalization LSA score was similar to the LSA score measured at admission. For the UC group, the LSA score decreased by approximately 10 points." Full text: "Our initial trial registration described time out of bed using accelerometers as our primary outcome. However, technical failures in this measure precluded use of accelerometer data. Therefore, this report focuses on outcomes from other aims in the protocol." ... "The MP patients were seen up to twice a day for 15 to 20 minutes each session 7 days a week." ... "The MP group completed 122 of the potential 238 walks (51.3%)." ... "Although this is a small study that needs replication".
claims.location: Abstract, Interventions and Results; full text, Methods (Hospital Mobility Assessment, Hospital MP), Results and Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: 100 cognitively intact medical inpatients 65+ (97% men) able to walk before admission, one US VA hospital, 2010 to 2011; intervention assisted walking up to twice daily plus goal setting; comparator twice-daily attention visits; outcomes self-reported ADL and Life-Space Assessment 1 month after discharge.
claims.safe_wording: In one small US trial of 100 older veterans, helping people walk up to twice a day in hospital, with daily goals for time out of bed, did not change their basic daily activities. A month after going home, those who had the walking programme were getting about as far beyond their front door as before admission, while the usual-care group had lost about 10 points on a 120-point scale of how far and how often they went out.
claims.qualifications: 97% men, one veterans' hospital, cognitively intact, median stay 3 days; the originally registered main outcome (time out of bed) could not be measured, so these results come from other planned aims; only about half of offered walks happened; needs replication. Frame the family question around 'What is the walking plan for today?', not pressure to walk: some patients should not walk without help (the programme told patients not to walk without nursing help where needed).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Falls: 3 falls in 2 usual-care patients and none in the programme group; numbers too small to claim a safety benefit.

numbers.meaning: mean Life-Space Assessment score (0 to 120) 1 month after discharge, walking programme vs usual care
fall in life-space score in the usual-care group from admission to 1 month
patients randomised, 97% men
offered walks completed in the programme group

claims.claim: The Life-Space Assessment asks how far a person has moved from their bedroom out to beyond their town in the past 4 weeks, how often, and with what help.
claims.supporting_passage: Brown 2009 (Ann Intern Med) full text: "The LSA measures mobility during the four weeks preceding the assessment by asking about movement to specific life-space levels ranging from within one’s dwelling to beyond one’s town (–). Frequency of movement and use of assistance, either from equipment or another person, were assessed. Specifically, participants were asked: “During the past 4 weeks, have you: 1) been to other rooms in your home besides the room where you sleep; 2) been to an area outside your home such as your porch, deck, or patio, hallway of an apartment building, or garage; 3) been to places in your neighborhood other than your own yard or apartment building; 4) been to places outside your neighborhood, but within your town; and 5) been to places outside your town?”" ... "Life-Space composite scores ranged from 0 to 120 with higher scores representing greater mobility." Baker 2003: "The LSA assessed the range, independence, and frequency of movement over the 4 weeks preceding assessments." Brown 2016: "Life-space levels range from within one’s bedroom to beyond one’s town."
claims.location: Brown 2009 full text, Methods (Life-Space Mobility); Baker 2003 abstract, Measurements; Brown 2016 full text, Methods
claims.pico_timeframe: Measurement instrument; community-living older adults, Alabama.
claims.safe_wording: A life-space assessment asks about the past 4 weeks: have you been to other rooms of your home, outside your door (porch, garden, garage or landing), around your neighbourhood, elsewhere in your town, and beyond your town? It also asks how often and whether you needed a stick, frame or another person. Scores run from 0 to 120.
claims.qualifications: UK wording of the zones ('garden', 'landing') is a plain translation of the US questions; keep the five levels in the same order. Self-reported.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: life-space levels beyond the bedroom
recall period
composite score range

claims.claim: Standard daily-living scales count self-care tasks done in and around the home (washing, dressing, eating, toilet, getting in and out of bed or a chair, walking across a room).
claims.supporting_passage: Loyd 2020: "Included studies used the Katz Index of Independence in Activities of Daily Living or Barthel Index to measure ADL." ... "self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)." Brown 2016: "Participants were asked at baseline to rate their ability to perform basic ADLs (bathing, dressing, feeding, toileting, grooming, transferring, and walking)".
claims.location: Loyd full text, Methods and Introduction; Brown 2016 full text, Methods (Functional Outcome Assessment)
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition of basic ADL measures.
claims.safe_wording: The usual daily-living scores count whether you can wash, dress, eat, use the toilet, get in and out of bed or a chair, and walk across a room. They do not ask whether you get to the shop, the bus stop or a friend's house.
claims.qualifications: Some versions add walking or grooming; describe the items, not every version.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: In a small randomised trial, a hospital walking programme showed no difference on a daily-living scale but a difference in life-space a month after discharge.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "For all periods, groups were similar in ability to perform ADL; however, at 1-month after hospitalization, the LSA score was significantly higher in the MP (LSA score, 52.5) compared with the UC group (LSA score, 41.6) (P = .02). For the MP group, the 1-month posthospitalization LSA score was similar to the LSA score measured at admission. For the UC group, the LSA score decreased by approximately 10 points." Full text: "For all periods, groups were similar in their ability to perform ADL (= .62); furthermore, ability to perform ADL did not significantly change over time (= .77), and there were no significant group-time interactions (= .76)." ... "Our initial trial registration described time out of bed using accelerometers as our primary outcome. However, technical failures in this measure precluded use of accelerometer data. Therefore, this report focuses on outcomes from other aims in the protocol." ... "In addition, the study was not powered to see significant ADL changes." ... "An example of a 10-point decrease would be an older person who previously reported no assistance to go into town 1 to 3 times a week (LSA score, 64) but who now requires a cane to go into town and goes less than once a week (LSA score, 54)."
claims.location: Abstract, Results; full text, Methods (Hospital Mobility Assessment), Results and Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: 100 medical inpatients 65+ (97% men), one US VA hospital; walking programme vs attention control; Katz-type ADL and LSA 1 month after discharge.
claims.safe_wording: In a small US trial of 100 older veterans, a hospital walking programme made no difference to daily-living scores, which barely changed in either group. The life-space measure did pick up a difference: a month after discharge, people who had usual care had lost about 10 points, for example going from getting into town unaided 1 to 3 times a week to needing a stick and going less than once a week, while the walking group stayed close to where they started.
claims.qualifications: Do not say 'the choice of measure decided whether the programme looked useful' as a finding. Life-space was not the trial's registered primary outcome (time out of bed, which failed technically), so present this as one small trial that needs replication. The daily-living scale did not change in either group, so it could not show a difference; the trial was not powered for it. 97% men, cognitively intact, one veterans' hospital. For practitioner versions, name the registered-outcome issue.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Single small trial; 6 of 50 programme patients and 2 of 50 usual-care patients did not complete; imputation and complete-case analyses agreed.

numbers.meaning: mean LSA score (0 to 120) at 1 month, walking programme vs usual care
LSA fall in usual care, admission to 1 month after discharge; programme group similar to admission
authors' worked example of a 10-point fall

claims.claim: After an emergency medical admission, older people's life-space falls and, on average, does not recover over up to two years.
claims.supporting_passage: "Immediately after hospitalization, covariate-adjusted LSA scores decreased in non-surgical patients by 10.31 points (95% CI −14.30 to −6.32) and in surgical patients by 22.45 points (95% CI −29.91 to −14.99)." ... "Indeed, LSA score recovery after non-surgical hospitalizations was non-significantly different from the null (average recovery of 0.66 points [95% CI −0.60 to 1.91] per log week). For example, at 12 weeks post-discharge, life-space recovered by an average of 1.69 points in non-surgical patients and by 13.80 points in surgical patients. As illustrated in, on average, within up to two years of the incident non-surgical hospitalization, these patients did not recover to their pre-hospital levels of life-space."
claims.pico_timeframe: 687 community-living Medicare beneficiaries 65+, central Alabama; 167 non-surgical and 44 surgical hospitalisations; life-space before and after, modelled from 6-monthly interviews; adjusted for age, sex, race, rural status, comorbidity and baseline ADL problems.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study that followed older people living at home, those admitted to hospital for a medical (non-surgical) reason lost about 10 points of life-space on average and, as a group, had not got back to their earlier level up to two years later. People admitted for surgery lost more at first but recovered within about a year.
claims.qualifications: Observational; averages hide individual variation; life-space was reported every 6 months, so the before and after values are model estimates; 'non-surgical' was self-reported and broad. Not 'caused by' hospital: say 'after' or 'linked with'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Underlying illnesses such as heart failure may explain part of the lack of recovery (authors' discussion).

numbers.meaning: adjusted average life-space fall after a non-surgical admission (0 to 120 scale)
adjusted average fall after a surgical admission
average recovery by 12 weeks, non-surgical vs surgical
non-surgical admissions analysed

claims.claim: A smaller life-space is linked with a higher risk of death and of moving into a care home.
claims.supporting_passage: Boyle 2010: "In a proportional hazards model adjusted for age, sex, race, and education, a more-constricted life space was associated with a greater risk of death (hazard ratio=1.18, 95% confidence interval=1.09-1.27, P<.001)" ... "This association persisted after the addition of terms for several potential confounders, including physical activity, performance-based physical function, disability, depressive symptoms, social networks, body mass index, and number of chronic medical conditions." Mackey 2014: "In multivariable-adjusted models, there was a strong linear trend between decreasing life-space and increasing risk of noncancer mortality (P = .005)." Watanabe 2022: "We found a negative association between LSM score and overall mortality even after adjusting for confounders". Sheppard 2013: "Over 6 years, the odds of NH admission increased 2% for every one point lower baseline life-space score independent of previously recognized risk factors."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-living older adults: Chicago 1,445 without dementia (mean 4.1 years); 3,892 US men 71 to 98 (2.7 years); 10,014 Japanese adults 65+ (median 5.3 years); 1,000 Alabama Medicare beneficiaries (6 years, nursing home admission); all observational, adjusted.
claims.safe_wording: In studies in the US and Japan, older people whose life-space was smaller were more likely to die in the following years, and in an Alabama study more likely to move into a nursing home, even after allowing for other health problems. These links do not show that shrinking life-space itself causes these outcomes; it may be a sign of declining health.
claims.qualifications: Associations only. Do not convert the hazard or odds ratios into 'times more likely' or absolute risks. Do not use Mackey's crude 41.2% vs 2.4% (only 34 men in the lowest group).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Watanabe 2022 found an L-shaped relationship: little further difference in mortality above a score of about 60.

numbers.meaning: cohort sizes (Boyle, Mackey, Watanabe, Sheppard)

claims.claim: People with Alzheimer's disease can still improve a movement skill through repeated practice (implicit or procedural learning), even without being aware of learning it, though their performance stays below that of people without dementia.
claims.supporting_passage: "The present review discusses 23 experimental studies on implicit motor-skill learning in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD). All studies found intact implicit motor-learning capacities." (Abstract) ... "In implicit learning, skills are mastered without awareness, often simply by repeated exposure, and can be unconsciously revived from implicit memory" (Introduction) ... "All the studies found preserved motor-skill learning in AD patients although their overall performance levels in terms of reaction and movement time were always inferior to those of the controls." ... "Patients are capable of acquiring motor skills without awareness simply by repeated exposure, although their performances will not reach normal levels." (Conclusions)
claims.location: Abstract; full text Introduction, Performance and Amount of Learning, Conclusions and Recommendations
claims.pico_timeframe: People with clinically diagnosed Alzheimer's disease (mostly mild) versus healthy controls in 23 laboratory studies published 1985 to 2005; exposure repeated practice of procedural motor tasks (maze, rotor pursuit, serial reaction time, mirror tracing, puzzle assembly); outcome speed or error change within sessions.
claims.safe_wording: A person with Alzheimer's disease who does not remember yesterday's practice may still have learned from it. A 2007 review of 23 laboratory studies found that people with Alzheimer's disease still got better at movement tasks with repeated practice, even though they stayed slower than people without dementia.
claims.qualifications: Laboratory tasks, not real rehabilitation tasks; mainly mild Alzheimer's disease; people who could not do a task were removed from the analyses; learning did not reach normal levels and transferred little to other skills. Say 'often relatively preserved', not 'intact' or 'normal'. Do not extend to other dementias.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Palma 2023 scoping review (PMID:37337358): 7 of 15 studies reported that cognitive impairment impaired motor learning, though most were at high risk of bias. The 2007 review itself notes weaker learning on some tasks (maze without vision; spatial sequence tasks) and in 'mildly' versus 'very mildly' demented groups in one study.

numbers.meaning: experimental studies in the review, published 1985 to 2005

claims.claim: The review recommends frequent, consistent practice of the same movement, in a setting and with equipment like those the person uses in daily life, avoiding doing two things at once, and good vision; it found no Alzheimer's studies testing demonstration.
claims.supporting_passage: "The studies we reviewed showed that in (re)learning motor skills, constant, or rather frequent and consistent practice is important in AD patients. This way of learning draws less on episodic memory and other cognitive functions compromised in AD patients. These data also suggest that practice under dual-task conditions should also be avoided." ... "Because AD patients have difficulty in generalizing the motor skills learned during the sessions, training has to take place in an environment that closely resembles the one in which the skill is going to be used and presumably with tools used by the AD patient in his or her daily life." ... "Patients with AD appear to remain dependent upon visual feedback throughout training and performance. Screening and subsequent correction of visual problems or the use of visual aids can be effective in the training process in this group" ... On guidance, observation and mental practice: "Our automated computer search and an extra search combining the three keywords with Alzheimer dementia both failed to generate any relevant studies that employed one of these training methods." ... On verbal feedback: "it may be hypothesized that both forms of feedback knowledge probably place too much weight on the cognitive abilities in AD patients and therefore contribute little to successful performance."
claims.location: Full text: Conclusions and Recommendations; Practice; Feedback
claims.pico_timeframe: Recommendations inferred by the authors from laboratory studies in Alzheimer's disease (constant versus random practice; visual feedback).
claims.safe_wording: Practise the same movement the same way each time, in the place and with the chair, frame or bed the person will actually use, one task at a time, with glasses on. A review of the research recommends consistent practice of this kind for people with Alzheimer's disease because it relies less on remembering the session.
claims.qualifications: These are the review authors' recommendations drawn from laboratory studies, not tested rehabilitation trials. 'Show rather than tell' and 'use few words' were not tested in Alzheimer's disease (the review found no studies of demonstration and only hypothesised that verbal feedback helps little); present them as practical suggestions, not findings. The judge's 'same sit-to-stand sequence with one cue each time' fits the consistent-practice recommendation; 'one cue' is judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial in this batch compared consistent practice with other methods in real rehabilitation for people with dementia.

claims.claim: In a randomised trial, dementia-adapted strength and function training improved strength and chair-stand performance in people with mild to moderate dementia, and the degree of cognitive impairment did not predict who benefited.
claims.supporting_passage: "Individuals with confirmed mild to moderate dementia, no severe somatic or psychological disease, and ability to walk 10 m." ... "Supervised, progressive resistance and functional group training for 3 months specifically developed for people with dementia (intervention, n = 62) compared with a low-intensity motor placebo activity (control, n = 60)." ... "Training significantly improved both primary outcomes" ... "Training gains were partly sustained during follow-up. Low baseline performance on motor tasks but not cognitive impairment predicted positive training response." ... "The intensive, dementia-adjusted training was feasible and substantially improved motor performance in frail, older people with dementia"
claims.pico_timeframe: 122 people with mild to moderate dementia able to walk 10 m, outpatient geriatric rehabilitation, Germany, 2006 to 2009 / 3 months of supervised progressive resistance and functional group training adapted for dementia / low-intensity motor placebo activity / leg-press maximal strength and five-chair-stand time / 3 months, with 3-month follow-up.
claims.safe_wording: In a German trial of 122 people with mild to moderate dementia, 3 months of supervised strength and balance training designed for people with dementia made them stronger and quicker at standing up from a chair than gentle placebo exercise. How much their memory and thinking were affected did not predict who improved; people who started weakest gained most.
claims.qualifications: Participants could walk 10 m and had no severe illness; gains were only partly kept 3 months after training stopped. Do not quote the strength percentages (the abstract's units are inconsistent).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Single trial; the Cochrane review of rehabilitation after hip fracture for people with dementia (Smith 2020, PMID 32031676, abstract seen, not added as a source) rated most evidence very low certainty, so do not generalise to all rehabilitation settings.

numbers.meaning: people randomised (62 training, 60 placebo activity)
training period, followed by 3 months without training

claims.claim: Many people with dementia receive no rehabilitation after hip fracture surgery.
claims.supporting_passage: "Of 11,200 individuals with dementia who experienced a hip fracture during the study period, 4,494 (40.1%) received no rehabilitation, 2,474 (22.1%) were admitted to CCC, 1,157 (10.3%) received HCR, and 3,075 (27.4%) received IPR." ... "Postfracture rehabilitation for older adults with dementia is associated with lower risk of LTC placement and mortality. Improving access to rehabilitation services for this vulnerable population may improve postfracture outcomes."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling adults with dementia having hip fracture surgery, Ontario, Canada, 2003 to 2011 / type of post-fracture rehabilitation received / outcomes: care home placement, mortality, falls, repeat fracture.
claims.safe_wording: In Ontario, Canada, about 4 in 10 people with dementia living at home who had surgery for a hip fracture between 2003 and 2011 got no rehabilitation afterwards.
claims.qualifications: Canadian data from 2003 to 2011. The abstract gives no figure for people without dementia and no reasons, so do not say they were 'excluded because of dementia'. The lower care home placement and death rates with rehabilitation are associations; fitter people may have been chosen for rehabilitation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No UK access figure was verified in this batch (no National Audit of Intermediate Care report could be opened).

numbers.meaning: people with dementia receiving no rehabilitation after hip fracture surgery, Ontario 2003 to 2011; say 'about 4 in 10'

claims.claim: The evidence on preserved motor learning comes mainly from laboratory tasks in Alzheimer's disease; transfer to everyday tasks and to other dementias is less certain, and some studies find learning is impaired.
claims.supporting_passage: van Halteren 2007: "It should be noted that in all studies the patients that could not perform the task were eliminated from the analyses." ... "Clearly, AD patients show preserved implicit learning abilities that can be utilized in teaching (motor) skills, yet transfer to other skills is minimal." Palma 2023: "we selected 15 studies describing cognitive assessment tools, experimental designs, and the severity of cognitive impairment. Although seven studies reported that cognitive impairment impaired motor learning, most studies included a high risk of bias."
claims.location: van Halteren full text (Implicit Learning Ability; Conclusions); Palma abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment in motor learning experiments.
claims.safe_wording: Most of this research used laboratory tasks with people with Alzheimer's disease. Some studies find learning is weaker, and it is less clear for other types of dementia.
claims.qualifications: State the limitation once, plainly.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C02-21-a.

numbers.meaning: studies in the 2023 scoping review that reported impaired motor learning with cognitive impairment (most at high risk of bias)

claims.claim: Observational research by Baltes and colleagues described a pattern in which dependent behaviour of older people was met with help while independent behaviour was ignored or met with more help, in institutions and at home.
claims.supporting_passage: Baltes 1994: "Research has attested to the prevalence of a "dependency-support" and "independence-ignore" script characterizing the interactions between staff and elderly residents in long-term care institutions." Baltes and Wahl 1992: "This study tested the generalizability of the dependency-support script, a behavioral system describing and explaining dependent behaviors of the institutionalized elderly. A comparative study with 22 community-dwelling elderly was conducted, which identified typical interaction patterns between the elderly and family members or home health nurses. The dominant interaction pattern in the community setting, too, was the dependency-support script." ... "Independent behaviors were followed about twice as often by an incongruent (dependence-supportive) than by a congruent (independence-supportive) response."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people in German long-term care institutions and (1992) 22 older people at home with family or home nurses / observed sequences of behaviour and response / no outcome on long-term ability.
claims.safe_wording: Researchers in Berlin, publishing in the early 1990s, watched how staff responded to older people in long-term care. When a resident needed help, staff paid attention and helped. When a resident managed alone, it tended to go unnoticed. A 1992 study of 22 older people at home found the same: when they did something for themselves, family or nurses were about twice as likely to step in and help as to encourage them.
claims.qualifications: Small, old German studies; observational; describe responses, not long-term loss of ability. The 1994 abstract cites the institutional research without dates, so say 'published in the early 1990s' rather than naming a decade of fieldwork.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No modern UK observational replication was checked.

numbers.meaning: older people living at home in the 1992 study
independent actions followed by dependence-supportive rather than independence-supportive responses (1992 study, at home)

claims.claim: A staff training programme in 3 institutions reduced dependence-supportive staff behaviour, increased independence-supportive behaviour and increased residents' independent self-care behaviour.
claims.supporting_passage: "To examine whether the scripts could be modified, a staff training program (focusing on communication skills, knowledge about aging, and basic behavior principles) was implemented in 3 different institutions. Observational data on staff-resident interactions in the context of self-care were collected pre- and postintervention. Findings revealed significant changes for the experimental group. Specifically, a decrease in dependence-supportive behavior of staff and an increase in their independence-supportive behavior, an increase in independent behavior of residents, and an increase in independence-related interaction patterns were demonstrated."
claims.pico_timeframe: Staff and residents in 3 German long-term care institutions / staff training in communication, ageing and behaviour principles / comparison group (details not in abstract) / observed staff and resident behaviour during self-care, before and after training / follow-up length not stated.
claims.safe_wording: In a 1994 German study, staff in 3 care institutions were trained in communication, ageing and simple behaviour principles. Afterwards, staff did less for residents and encouraged them more, and residents did more of their own self-care.
claims.qualifications: Sample size, how groups were formed and how long the change lasted are not in the abstract; the outcome was observed behaviour during self-care, not a measured gain in function. Date and place the study.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A 2024 Dutch trial (C02-14-d) changed staff behaviour but did not show a significant change in residents' self-reliance.

numbers.meaning: institutions where the training was delivered

claims.claim: Function-focused (restorative) care has been tested in randomised trials in nursing homes; in a 12-home US trial it improved mobility, walking, bathing and stair climbing.
claims.supporting_passage: "A randomized controlled repeated-measure design was used, and generalized estimating equations were used to evaluate status at baseline and 4 and 12 months after initiation of the Res-Care intervention." ... "Twelve nursing homes in Maryland." ... "Four hundred eighty-seven residents consented and were eligible" ... "Res-Care was a two-tiered self-efficacy-based intervention focused on motivating nursing assistants and residents to engage in functional and physical activities." ... "Significant treatment-by-time interactions (P<.05) were found for the Tinetti Mobility Score and its gait and balance subscores and for walking, bathing, and stair climbing." ... "The findings provide some evidence for the utility and safety of a Res-Care intervention in terms of improving function in NH residents."
claims.pico_timeframe: 487 nursing home residents (mean age 83.8, mean MMSE 20.4), 12 Maryland nursing homes / programme motivating nursing assistants and residents to do functional and physical activity / control homes / Barthel items, Tinetti gait and balance, strength, quality of life / 4 and 12 months.
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial in 12 nursing homes, training care assistants to encourage residents to do what they could for themselves improved residents' walking, balance, bathing and stair climbing over a year, compared with homes without the programme.
claims.qualifications: The abstract gives no effect sizes; authors call it 'some evidence'. US nursing homes, 2009.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Vluggen 2024 (C02-14-d) did not show a significant resident benefit.

numbers.meaning: nursing homes in the trial
residents

claims.claim: A recent Dutch cluster-randomised trial of a staff programme improved nurses' encouragement of residents' independence but did not show a statistically significant change in residents' self-reliance.
claims.supporting_passage: "Twenty-eight nursing home wards, with 287 nurses and 241 residents participated in the study. A statistically significant treatment by time interaction effect was observed in nurses' activity encouragement behavior at three months (d = 0.53; p = .003; 95 % CI 1.88-8.02) and at nine months (d = 0.38; p = .02; 95 % CI 0.67-7.27). No statistically significant treatment by time interaction effects were observed in residents' self-reliance in activities of daily living. However, a trend was observed towards a less pronounced decrease in self-reliance in those residents allocated to wards that exposed nurses to the SELF-program"
claims.pico_timeframe: 28 Dutch nursing home wards, 287 nurses, 241 residents / SELF-program (7 interactive training sessions over 3 months, per conference abstract seen in Consensus) / care as usual / nurses' activity encouragement (MAINtAIN), residents' self-reliance in daily activities (GARS-4) / 6 months (residents), 9 months (nurses).
claims.safe_wording: In a Dutch trial in 28 nursing home wards, training helped nurses encourage residents to do more for themselves. Residents' independence in daily activities did not change clearly over 6 months, though it declined a little less on trained wards.
claims.qualifications: State both halves. 'Did not change clearly' is the correct reading of p = .07, not 'no effect'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Contrasts with Res-Care 2009 and Baltes 1994. The trial's own background notes that such programmes 'have demonstrated inconsistent effects'.

numbers.meaning: trial size, the Netherlands, recruitment from 2021

claims.claim: Time pressure and staff shortages are reasons staff give for still taking over tasks residents could do themselves.
claims.supporting_passage: "Still, time constraints, staffing shortages and lack of motivation were put forwards as factors leading some nurses to still take over tasks." ... "Contextual barriers to program implementation and outcomes included staffing shortages, low program attendance, time constraints, lack of manager support, and delivery of the program during the COVID-19 pandemic."
claims.pico_timeframe: Nurses and trainers on 28 Dutch nursing home wards during a 9-month trial; checklists, logbooks, questionnaires and focus groups.
claims.safe_wording: In the Dutch trial, nurses named time pressure and staff shortages among the reasons some of them still took over tasks that residents could do themselves.
claims.qualifications: Staff-reported barriers from one Dutch trial, not a measurement of how much extra time supported care takes. The position that time and training must be built into the rota is judgement and should be written as such ('Care homes should...').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No study in this batch measured the minutes needed for supported versus done-for care; do not put a time figure on a visual clock.

claims.claim: Reablement aims to maximise independence rather than doing tasks for people; trial evidence on its effects was very low certainty.
claims.supporting_passage: "Unlike traditional home-care services, reablement is frequently time-limited (usually six to 12 weeks) and aims to maximise independence by offering an intensive multidisciplinary, person-centred and goal-directed intervention." ... "We are very uncertain as to the effects of reablement compared with usual care as the evidence was of very low quality for all of the outcomes reported."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 65+ receiving home care in Western Australia and Norway / time-limited reablement up to 12 weeks / usual home care / function, mortality, admissions, quality of life / up to 24 months; searches to mid-2015.
claims.safe_wording: Home care 'reablement' services aim to help people do things for themselves again. A 2016 Cochrane review found only 2 trials and was very uncertain about their effects.
claims.qualifications: Optional context; home care, not care homes; searches from 2015 and no update checked.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Newer reablement trials were not reviewed in this batch.

numbers.meaning: evidence base of the 2016 Cochrane review

claims.claim: Doing a task for someone saves time today and can cost them ability later.
claims.supporting_passage: Vluggen 2024 (background, not a finding): "However, nurses often take over tasks unnecessarily, which can deprive resident's remaining abilities."
claims.pico_timeframe: No study in this batch measured long-term loss of ability caused by staff doing tasks for residents.
claims.safe_wording: Present as reasoning, not a finding: 'If staff always do it, residents get less practice. Trials that trained staff to encourage residents found gains in some homes and not in others.'
claims.qualifications: A background sentence in a paper's introduction is not that paper's finding. Do not say doing tasks for people 'causes' or 'leads to' loss of ability.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Mixed trial results (Res-Care versus SELF).

claims.claim: The top of a walking stick should be level with the crease of the wrist when the person stands upright with arms relaxed by their sides.
claims.supporting_passage: "The top of a cane or walker should be the same height as the wrist crease when the patient is standing upright with arms relaxed at his or her sides."
claims.pico_timeframe: Clinical advice for older adults fitting canes and walkers.
claims.safe_wording: Stand up straight in your usual shoes with your arms hanging loosely. The top of the stick should be level with the crease on the inside of your wrist.
claims.qualifications: Professional advice from a clinical review, not a trial. 'In your usual shoes' is a practical addition, not from the source; keep or drop.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Camara 2019 (PMID 31322813, abstract seen, not added as a source) found sticks set longer than wrist height increased postural sway in 18 older women, consistent with the advice.

claims.claim: A stick is held in the hand opposite the weak or painful leg and moved forward at the same time as that leg.
claims.supporting_passage: "A cane should be held contralateral to a weak or painful lower extremity and advanced simultaneously with the contralateral leg."
claims.pico_timeframe: Clinical advice for one-sided leg weakness or pain.
claims.safe_wording: Hold the stick in the hand on the opposite side to the painful or weak leg, and move the stick forward at the same time as that leg.
claims.qualifications: Applies to pain or weakness on one side. Someone with problems in both legs or poor balance may need a different aid (see C02-01-e).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: Among people who use walking sticks, wrong height, poor condition, use in the wrong hand and lack of professional advice are common.
claims.supporting_passage: Sheehan 2008: "Fifty randomly selected patients attending a rheumatology department were surveyed to determine whether their stick was appropriate to their needs and whether they were using it correctly." ... "Of the 50 patients, 38% used their stick incorrectly, usually in the wrong hand. Forty-four per cent of sticks were of the wrong length and 54% were in imperfect condition, the main defect being a worn ferrule." Liu 2011: "Five major problems from data analysis were identified: lack of medical consultation for device selection/use, incorrect cane height/maintenance, placement of cane in improper hand, inability to maintain the proper reciprocal gait pattern, and improper posture during ambulation." Bradley 2011: "Most patients with assistive devices have never been instructed on the proper use and often have devices that are inappropriate, damaged, or are of the incorrect height." George 1988: "Many of the aids that the elderly had were faulty, including half of the walking aids and 15% of hearing aids, reading spectacles, and dentures"
claims.pico_timeframe: Sheehan: 50 stick users with arthritis, rheumatology department, England, 2008 (adults, not only older people). Liu: 93 cane users aged 65+, US senior living communities. George: 140 people over 75, one English general practice, 1988.
claims.safe_wording: In a survey of 50 stick users at an English hospital arthritis clinic, 44 in 100 sticks were the wrong length and 54 in 100 were in poor condition, most often because the rubber tip was worn. About 4 in 10 people were using their stick wrongly, usually in the wrong hand. A US study of 93 stick users aged over 65 found the same problems, and many had never had professional advice when choosing the stick.
claims.qualifications: Small surveys; Sheehan's clinic patients were not all older people. Liu gives no percentages in the abstract, so quote only Sheehan's figures. George 1988 ('half of the walking aids' faulty, 140 people over 75) is dated and 'walking aids' includes frames; use only with the year.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No recent UK survey of stick fit was found.

numbers.meaning: sticks of the wrong length, 50 stick users, rheumatology department, England, 2008
sticks in imperfect condition, main defect a worn ferrule (same survey)
people using the stick incorrectly, usually in the wrong hand (same survey)
people who had been taught who used their stick correctly (same survey); do not compare with the 50% figure for the untrained, which measured correct hand only
cane users aged 65+ in the US study (no percentages in abstract)
walking aids found faulty among 140 people over 75 in one English practice, 1988

claims.claim: A worn rubber tip (ferrule) is a common defect and should be checked and replaced.
claims.supporting_passage: "Walking sticks are used widely by people with arthritis, principally to reduce pain and improve stability and balance. However, they are frequently used incorrectly and can be dangerous if not properly maintained." ... "54% were in imperfect condition, the main defect being a worn ferrule." ... "These findings highlight the importance of educating patients on how to obtain greatest benefit from their walking stick and of the necessity to check it regularly for defects to ensure safe usage."
claims.pico_timeframe: 50 stick users with arthritis, rheumatology department, England, 2008.
claims.safe_wording: Turn the stick over and look at the rubber tip. A worn tip was the most common defect in one English clinic survey, and the authors advise checking sticks regularly for faults. If the tread is worn smooth, replace the tip.
claims.qualifications: The source says poorly maintained sticks 'can be dangerous' and names the worn ferrule as the main defect; it does not measure grip. Do not claim a worn tip 'grips less well' as a finding. 'Replace it' is practical advice.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No NHS or physiotherapy leaflet could be opened (web pages blocked; Drive search found none).

claims.claim: The right aid depends on strength, balance and cognition; people with weakness or poor balance may need a frame rather than a stick, and clinicians should check height, fit and maintenance.
claims.supporting_passage: "Selection of a suitable device depends on the patient's strength, endurance, balance, cognitive function, and environmental demands." ... "Walkers improve stability in those with lower extremity weakness or poor balance and facilitate improved mobility by increasing the patient's base of support and supporting the patient's weight. Walkers require greater attentional demands than canes and make using stairs difficult." ... "Clinicians should routinely evaluate their patients' assistive devices to ensure proper height, fit, and maintenance, and also counsel patients on correct use of the device."
claims.pico_timeframe: Clinical advice for older adults choosing assistive devices.
claims.safe_wording: A stick is the wrong aid for some people. If both legs are weak or balance is poor, a walking frame may be safer; ask a physiotherapist or GP to check which aid suits you and that it fits.
claims.qualifications: Clinical review advice. Frames have downsides too (more attention needed, harder on stairs).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: In a randomised trial of 110 frail patients aged 65+ (mean 78) having colorectal cancer surgery within an enhanced recovery pathway, a multimodal programme started before surgery did not reduce 30-day complications compared with the same programme started after surgery.
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 418 patients 65 years or older were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 298 patients were excluded (not frail [n = 290], unable to exercise [n = 3], and planned neoadjuvant treatment [n = 5]), and 120 frail patients (Fried Frailty Index,≥2) were randomized." ... "Hence, 110 patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (55 in the prehabilitation [Prehab] and 55 in the rehabilitation [Rehab] groups)." ... "Multimodal program involving exercise, nutritional, and psychological interventions initiated before (Prehab group) or after (Rehab group) surgery. All patients were treated within a standardized enhanced recovery pathway." ... "Of 110 patients randomized, mean (SD) age was 78 (7) years" ...
