claims.claim: FRAIL-HIP studied 172 very frail care home residents aged 70 and over with limited life expectancy who broke a hip; after shared decision-making, 88 chose care without an operation and 84 chose an operation. It was not randomised.
claims.supporting_passage: Eligible patients were aged 70 years or older, frail, and institutionalized and sustained a femoral neck or pertrochanteric fracture. The term frail implied at least 1 of the following characteristics was present: malnutrition (body mass index ... <18.5) or cachexia, severe comorbidities (American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status class of IV or V), or severe mobility issues (Functional Ambulation Category ≤2). ... Of the 172 enrolled patients with proximal femoral fractures (median [25th and 75th percentile] age, 88 [85-92] years; 135 women [78%]), 88 opted for nonoperative management and 84 opted for operative management.
claims.location: Abstract, Design/Setting/Participants and Results; full-text excerpt: 'Only a randomized clinical trial would have avoided selection bias through the SDM process but was considered unfeasible and unethical.'

claims.safe_wording: A Dutch study followed 172 very frail care home residents (median age 88) who broke a hip and whose life expectancy was already short. After talking it through, 88 chose care without an operation and 84 chose an operation. People chose; they were not allocated at random.
claims.qualifications: Say near the top that it was a small, selected, non-randomised group who chose. Very frail and institutionalised; not applicable to most people with hip fracture.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the description.

chose non-operative / operative management

claims.claim: In the weeks after the fracture, quality of life (rated by relatives and carers) in people who chose no operation was not worse than in those who had an operation, within the study's preset margin.
claims.supporting_passage: The EQ-5D utility scores by proxies and caregivers in the nonoperative management group remained within the set 0.15 noninferiority limit of the operative management group (week 1 ... week 2 ... and week 4 ...). ... Although the short-term mortality in the nonoperative management group was higher than in the operative management group, there was no loss of QOL and HRQoL, and there was high treatment satisfaction and humane quality of dying.

claims.qualifications: Proxy-rated, not self-rated. Non-inferiority within a 0.15 margin, not 'the same'. Comparisons after about 30 days are unreliable because most of the non-operative group had died (authors' own limitation). Do not quote EQ-5D numbers (abstract confidence intervals look inconsistent).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors: 'given the even-higher-than-expected mortality rate in the nonoperative management group, the validity of the results comparing nonoperative management with operative management was reduced 30 days after the injury.'

claims.claim: UK guidance treats surgery as the best pain relief for a broken hip and says surgery should still be considered even when the fracture comes with a terminal illness, as part of palliative care.
claims.supporting_passage: It is recognized surgery is the best form of analgesia and as over 30% present with cognitive impairment, it can be otherwise difficult to assess patients suffering. ... If a hip fracture complicates or precipitates a terminal illness, the multidisciplinary team should still consider the role of surgery, as part of a palliative care approach that: • minimises pain and other symptoms and • establishes patients' own priorities for rehabilitation and • considers patients' wishes about their end-of-life care.
claims.location: NICE CG124 full guideline 2011: Timing of surgery, guideline group discussion (page 65); Guideline summary recommendations (page 38)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with hip fracture, NHS England and Wales
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance (NICE) describes surgery as the best form of pain relief for a broken hip, and says that even when a hip fracture comes with a terminal illness, the team should still consider surgery as part of palliative care that eases pain and respects the person's wishes.
claims.qualifications: 'Best form of analgesia' is from the guideline group's discussion, not a numbered recommendation; attribute it as 'NICE's guideline group'. NICE does not set out when non-operative care is appropriate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: FRAIL-HIP authors note guidelines give no clear advice on non-operative treatment for frail people with limited life expectancy.

claims.claim: Scottish hip fracture standards allow for a decision not to operate, provided a management or palliative care plan is recorded and the decision is reviewed if the person improves.
claims.supporting_passage: Should conservative treatment be agreed, the management plan or palliative care plan, should be clearly recorded in the patient records. Best practice is to evaluate this decision should the patient's medical condition improve.
claims.pico_timeframe: Hip fracture care in Scotland
claims.safe_wording: Scotland's hip fracture standards expect that, if a decision not to operate is agreed, a clear care or palliative care plan is written down and the decision is looked at again if the person gets better.
claims.qualifications: Quote the standard only; do not state or imply Scottish Hip Fracture Audit results or Alasdair's role.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: In a gait study with pressure-sensing insoles, none of 16 people aged 75 and over after hip fracture surgery kept to a partial weight-bearing limit of 20 kg; 11 of 16 put more than twice that weight through the leg.
claims.supporting_passage: Both groups were instructed to maintain partial weight-bearing on the affected limb (≤20 kg) postoperatively. Following standardized physiotherapy training, gait analysis was performed. None of the patients in the elderly test group were able to comply with the weight-bearing restriction as recommended. We found that 69% (11 of 16) of the patients exceeded the specified load by more than twofold, whereas significantly more patients in the younger control group (>75% [14 of 18]) achieved almost the entire weight-bearing restriction (p < 0.001). Only 1 of the elderly patients was able to comply with the predetermined weight-bearing restriction, and only for a short period of time.
claims.pico_timeframe: 16 patients 75+ after hip fracture surgery vs 18 patients 18-40 after ankle fracture surgery / instruction to bear 20 kg or less after physiotherapy training / younger group / measured load during gait analysis / single session after surgery
claims.safe_wording: In a German study using pressure-sensing insoles, none of 16 older people after hip fracture surgery kept to a 'partial weight-bearing' limit when they walked (one managed it briefly); 11 of the 16 put more than twice the permitted weight through the leg. Most young adults with ankle fractures could keep to it.
claims.qualifications: Very small single-centre study, one walking session. Say 'none kept to it throughout; one managed briefly'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Abstract gives the young group's compliance two ways (14 of 18 'almost the entire restriction'; 16 of 18 'maintained the partial load for nearly the entire time'); use '14 of 18' or say 'most'.

numbers.meaning: older hip fracture patients (aged 75+) tested
kept to the 20 kg limit as instructed (1 managed briefly)
exceeded the limit by more than twofold
prescribed partial weight-bearing limit
young ankle fracture patients who achieved almost the whole restriction

claims.claim: Told to partial weight-bear, older people after hip fracture walked less well and more slowly, yet put the same load through the leg as those allowed full weight-bearing.
claims.supporting_passage: The postoperative Parker Mobility Score in the PWB group compared to the FWB group was significantly reduced (3.21 vs. 4.73, p < 0.001). Accordingly, a significantly lower gait speed in the PWB group of 0.16 m/s vs. 0.28 m/s was seen (p = 0.003). No difference in weight bearing was observed in between the groups (average peak force 350.25 N vs. 353.08 N, p = 0.918), nor any differences in the demographic characteristics, ASA Score, Barthel Index or EQ5D.
claims.pico_timeframe: 41 older patients with pertrochanteric fracture, one German hospital / partial weight-bearing instruction (19) / full weight-bearing (22) / mobility score, gait speed, peak load / day 5 after surgery
claims.safe_wording: In a second small German study, older people told to limit weight on the leg after hip fracture surgery walked more slowly and had lower mobility scores on day 5 than those allowed full weight, but pressed just as hard through the leg.
claims.qualifications: Small, non-randomised (before-and-after groups), same research group as C03-19-a.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found that contradicts the mobility finding.

numbers.meaning: patients told partial vs full weight-bearing
gait speed on day 5, partial vs full weight-bearing

claims.claim: NICE recommends that hip fracture surgery should aim to let the person bear full weight without restriction straight after the operation.
claims.supporting_passage: 4.2.6 Surgical procedures ➢ Operate on patients with the aim to allow them to fully weight bear (without restriction) in the immediate postoperative period.
claims.location: NICE CG124 full guideline 2011, Guideline summary, section 4.2.6 Surgical procedures
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults having hip fracture surgery, NHS England and Wales
claims.safe_wording: NICE guidance says surgeons should operate with the aim of letting the person put full weight on the leg, without restriction, straight after surgery.
claims.qualifications: Wording verified in the 2011 full guideline (not among the 2017 replaced recommendations); the current web version was not opened. BOAST wording not checked; do not cite BOAST.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Clinicians still restrict weight-bearing for some fractures and fixations (implant concerns); the guideline states an aim, not a ban.

claims.claim: Restricted weight-bearing after hip fracture surgery is linked with more complications and deaths.
claims.supporting_passage: Ottesen 2018: 'Controlling for patient and procedural factors, multivariate odds of any adverse event, major adverse event, delirium, infection, transfusion, length of stay ≥ 75th percentile (six days) and mortality within 30 days were all higher in patients with weight-bearing restrictions.' Tarrant 2022: 'In adjusted analysis, RWB did not influence 30-day mortality (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.15-01.13, p = 0.293) ... RWB was significantly related to increased DVT (OR 7.81, 95% CI: 1.81-33.71 p = 0.002) but no other secondary outcomes.' Xu 2026: 'Unrestricted weight-bearing was significantly associated with lower long-term mortality compared with restricted weight-bearing (RR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.51-0.88 ...). Short-term mortality did not differ significantly in the primary analysis ... No significant differences were observed for short-term complications, long-term complications, reoperation risk, or LOS between the two groups (all> 0.05). GRADE assessment showed low certainty of evidence for long-term mortality and short-term complications, and very low certainty of evidence for the remaining outcomes.'
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults after hip fracture surgery / restricted weight-bearing / weight-bearing as tolerated / complications, mortality, reoperation / 30 days to long term
claims.safe_wording: Studies disagree about harm. A large US database study linked restrictions with more complications and deaths within 30 days; an Australian study did not find more deaths; a 2026 review found restriction was linked with more deaths in the longer term, but the evidence was weak, and found no clear difference in complications or repeat operations.
claims.qualifications: Observational only: 'linked with', never 'causes'. Restriction is usually prescribed for harder fractures or fixations, so these links may reflect the injury, not the instruction. Do not give the Ottesen percentages (arithmetic inconsistency in abstract). Better to rest the post on the compliance and mobility findings plus NICE, and mention harm evidence as mixed.

Optimal strategy for patient selection and timing of secondary imaging strategies to ensure early diagnosis of occult hip fractures, while avoiding over investigation of patients with soft tissue injury only, is yet to be determined. Being able to stand does not rule one out.

claims.qualifications: The candidate's 'X-ray both femurs' for every new thigh ache goes slightly beyond the NOGG wording, which says image the femur and then the other femur if an atypical fracture is found. claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: MHRA 2011 advice was not opened, so it is not cited.

claims.claim: In older women on dialysis, severe low calcium within 12 weeks of starting denosumab was far more common than with oral bisphosphonates (41.1% vs 2.0%).

In patients predisposed to hypocalcaemia (e.g., patients with a creatinine clearance < 35 ml/min), serum calcium levels should also be checked within 2 weeks after the initial dose []."

Patients should know to report symptoms of low calcium.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Bird JAMA 2024 and Lloret 2024 suggest a single check at 2 weeks may be too little in dialysis patients ('frequent monitoring', 'close monitoring').

claims.claim: In advanced CKD, especially on dialysis, bone fragility may be CKD mineral and bone disorder; high bone turnover raises hypocalcaemia risk; planning with the kidney team is advised.
claims.supporting_passage: Bird JAMA 2024 (Abstract, Importance): "Chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder is nearly universal in dialysis-dependent patients, complicating diagnosis and treatment of skeletal fragility." Lloret 2024: "Management of osteoporosis for patients on dialysis should be centred in the dialysis unit because it needs to be integrated in the overall treatment of CKD-MBD []. Knowledge of bone turnover determines therapy choices in this patient population []. A high bone turnover calls for parathyroid hormone (PTH) suppressive therapy, particularly if the plan is to initiate (potent) antiresorptive therapy. High turnover bone disease is a robust risk factor for iatrogenic hypocalcemia ... Coordination of care in the dialysis unit should also include a post-denosumab hypocalcemia prevention regimen, which may involve (transient) increase of the calcium supply via diet, supplements or dialysate, ensuring adequate intake of vitamin D and close monitoring of serum calcium levels."

claims.safe_wording: In people on dialysis, weak bones are often part of a kidney-related bone disorder, and the kidney team should be part of the decision and the calcium plan.
claims.qualifications: The 'nearly universal' sentence is background in Bird, not its finding. The management advice is expert commentary, not a guideline. Checking phosphate specifically was not verified; PTH and bone turnover are named by Lloret. Applies to dialysis; for CKD stage 4 to 5 not on dialysis, rely on C04-24-b and C04-24-c.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: KDIGO 2017 was not opened.

Lloret 2024: "denosumab rapidly gaining interest in the nephrology community because of its potency and non-renal clearance."

claims.claim: In a 4-year trial in 202 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and spinal fractures, sodium fluoride raised spine bone density by about a third compared with placebo, but spinal fractures were not reduced and fractures away from the spine were about three times as common.
claims.supporting_passage: "we conducted a four-year prospective clinical trial in 202 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and vertebral fractures who were randomly assigned to receive sodium fluoride (75 mg per day) or placebo. All received a calcium supplement (1500 mg per day). Sixty-six women in the fluoride group and 69 women in the placebo group completed the trial. As compared with the placebo group, the treatment group had increases in median bone mineral density of 35 percent (P less than 0.0001) in the lumbar spine ... The number of new vertebral fractures was similar in the treatment and placebo groups (163 and 136, respectively; P not significant), but the number of nonvertebral fractures was higher in the treatment group (72 vs. 24; P less than 0.01)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 202 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and vertebral fractures (USA) / sodium fluoride 75 mg daily plus calcium 1500 mg / placebo plus calcium / lumbar spine BMD, new vertebral and non-vertebral fractures / 4 years
claims.safe_wording: In a trial published in 1990, 202 women with osteoporosis and spinal fractures took sodium fluoride or a dummy tablet for four years. Spine bone density rose by about a third (35%) more with fluoride. Spinal fractures were not reduced (163 new spinal fractures with fluoride, 136 with placebo, not a clear difference). There were 72 fractures away from the spine with fluoride against 24 with placebo, about three times as many.
claims.qualifications: The fracture figures are counts of fractures, not numbers of women. Only 66 and 69 women completed the trial. It tested a high dose of plain (fast-release) fluoride; fluoride is not a current treatment. Do not say 'spinal fractures went up' (163 v 136 was not significant).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Later work suggested lower-dose slow-release fluoride behaved differently; the meta-analysis (C04-29-b) links the excess non-spinal fractures to high doses and non-slow-release forms.

claims.claim: For the osteoporosis drugs tested in placebo-controlled trials, larger average bone density gains go with larger fracture reductions across trials.

Hip BMD changes explained substantial proportions (44-67%) of treatment-related fracture risk reduction." These analyses support BMD as a surrogate outcome for fracture outcomes in future randomised trials of new osteoporosis therapies"

claims.safe_wording: For the drugs in current use, density is a reasonable guide at the level of whole trials: across 23 trials with over 90,000 people, drugs that raised hip density more cut fractures more. That is why density is used to judge new drugs.

There was some between-person variation in the effects of alendronate, but this was small in size compared with within-person variation. Alendronate treatment is estimated to result in increases in hip bone density >or=0.019 g/cm(2) in 97.5% of patients." Conclusion: "Monitoring bone mineral density in postmenopausal women in the first three years after starting treatment with a potent bisphosphonate is unnecessary and may be misleading. Routine monitoring should be avoided in this early period after bisphosphonate treatment is commenced."
claims.pico_timeframe: 6459 postmenopausal women with low BMD in FIT / alendronate / placebo / between-person v within-person variation in hip and spine BMD / 3 years
claims.safe_wording: In the alendronate trial data, nearly everyone who took the drug gained hip density, but the scan's own variation from one measurement to the next was larger than the differences between people. The authors concluded that routine repeat scans in the first three years are unnecessary and can mislead.
claims.qualifications: Postmenopausal women, alendronate, first 3 years, trial adherence. Does not address later reassessment (NOGG uses BMD with FRAX at 3 to 5 years to decide on continuing) or other drugs.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Some guidelines support selective repeat DXA; the ISCD 'least significant change' claim in the candidate was not verified and should be dropped.

numbers.meaning: women in the FIT analysis
period in which routine monitoring was judged unnecessary
estimated proportion of treated women with hip BMD gain of at least 0.019 g/cm2

claims.claim: UK guidance says that if someone has a fragility fracture while on treatment, check whether the treatment has been taken correctly and look for secondary causes; fracture risk is reassessed after about 5 years of oral or 3 years of intravenous bisphosphonate.
claims.supporting_passage: "Review treatment adherence in men and women who sustain a fragility fracture whilst on drug treatment, (poor adherence is when less than 80% of treatment has been taken correctly) and investigate for secondary causes of osteoporosis" ... "Plan to prescribe oral bisphosphonates (alendronate, ibandronate and risedronate) for at least 5 years and then re-assess fracture risk." ... "Plan to prescribe intravenous bisphosphonate (zoledronate) for at least 3 years and then re-assess fracture risk." ... "Fracture risk assessment in patients receiving drug treatment should be performed using FRAX with BMD"

claims.pico_timeframe: UK postmenopausal women and men 50+ on osteoporosis drugs / guideline recommendation
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance: if someone breaks a bone while on a bone medicine, first check whether it has been taken correctly (less than 80% of doses taken correctly counts as poor adherence) and look for other causes of bone loss. Density is used, with a risk calculator, when deciding after 3 to 5 years whether to continue.
claims.qualifications: Guideline recommendation (NOGG 2022, NICE-accredited).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

planned minimum duration of oral / intravenous bisphosphonate before reassessment

claims.claim: A Cochrane review found high- to moderate-certainty evidence from five sham-controlled trials that vertebroplasty gives no clinically important benefit for pain, disability, quality of life or treatment success at one month, whatever the duration of pain.
claims.supporting_passage: "Twenty-one trials were included: five compared vertebroplasty with placebo (541 randomised participants), eight with usual care (1136 randomised participants), seven with kyphoplasty (968 randomised participants)..." ... "Compared with placebo, high- to moderate-quality evidence from five trials indicates that vertebroplasty provides no clinically important benefits with respect to pain, disability, disease-specific or overall quality of life or treatment success at one month." ... "Mean pain (on a scale zero to 10, higher scores indicate more pain) was five points with placebo and 0.7 points better (0.3 better to 1.2 better) with vertebroplasty, an absolute pain reduction of 7% (3% better to 12% better, minimal clinical important difference is 15%)" ... "Our subgroup analyses indicate that the effects did not differ according to duration of pain (acute versus subacute)." Plain language summary: "People who had vertebroplasty rated their pain as 4.3 points." "People who had placebo rated their pain as 5 points."
claims.location: Abstract (Main results; Authors' conclusions) and plain language summary
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures, mostly women, mean age 62.6-81 / vertebroplasty / sham procedure / pain (0-10), disability, QoL, treatment success / 1 month
claims.safe_wording: When vertebroplasty (injecting cement into a broken spinal bone) was compared with a sham procedure in five trials, pain at one month averaged 4.3 out of 10 after cement and 5 out of 10 after the sham. That gap is smaller than the difference patients notice. Disability and quality of life were also much the same.
claims.qualifications: One-month outcome; five trials, 541 people; review search to November 2017.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The VAPOUR investigators argue their trial of very recent fractures should not have been pooled with the others (PMID 30852489).

numbers.meaning: review scope
mean pain at one month, vertebroplasty v sham
mean pain difference on 0-10 scale
absolute pain reduction observed v minimal clinically important difference

claims.claim: Open trials comparing vertebroplasty with usual care probably overestimated its benefit.
claims.supporting_passage: "Sensitivity analyses confirmed that open trials comparing vertebroplasty with usual care are likely to have overestimated any benefit of vertebroplasty. Correcting for these biases would likely drive any benefits observed with vertebroplasty towards the null, in keeping with findings from the placebo-controlled trials."
claims.pico_timeframe: 8 open trials v usual care (1136 participants) compared with 5 sham trials
claims.safe_wording: In trials where people knew they had had the procedure and were compared with usual care, it looked better. The review judged those open trials likely to have overestimated the benefit.
claims.qualifications: Judgement of the review authors based on sensitivity analyses.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Ontario HTA 2025 (PMID 40950842) found short-term pain benefit against conservative care (low to very low certainty), from the kind of open comparison the Cochrane review considers biased.

numbers.meaning: open trials v usual care

claims.claim: Serious adverse events reported after vertebroplasty include bone infection, spinal cord compression, damage to the spinal cord covering and respiratory failure; whether overall risk is increased is uncertain.
claims.supporting_passage: "Notably, serious adverse events reported with vertebroplasty included osteomyelitis, cord compression, thecal sac injury and respiratory failure." ... "Numerous serious adverse events have been observed following vertebroplasty. However due to the small number of events, we cannot be certain about whether or not vertebroplasty results in a clinically important increased risk of new symptomatic vertebral fractures and/or other serious adverse events."
claims.pico_timeframe: Trials of vertebroplasty v control; harms
claims.safe_wording: Serious complications have been reported, including bone infection and pressure on the spinal cord, but they are uncommon and the trials were too small to say whether the overall risk is higher than without the procedure.
claims.qualifications: Low-certainty harm estimates; do not imply the procedure is known to be more dangerous overall.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Other serious adverse events: 16/408 v 23/413 (RR 0.61, 0.33 to 1.10), so no clear excess in pooled trials.

claims.claim: One sham-controlled trial (VAPOUR) in people with severe pain from fractures under 6 weeks old found more people reached low pain at 14 days with vertebroplasty.
claims.supporting_passage: "This was a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of vertebroplasty in four hospitals in Sydney, Australia. We recruited patients with one or two osteoporotic vertebral fractures of less than 6 weeks' duration and Numeric Rated Scale (NRS) back pain greater than or equal to 7 out of 10." ... "120 patients were enrolled. 61 patients were randomly assigned to vertebroplasty and 59 to placebo. 24 (44%) patients in the vertebroplasty group and 12 (21%) in the control group had an NRS pain score below 4 out of 10 at 14 days (between-group difference 23 percentage points, 95% CI 6-39; p=0·011)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 120 patients, fractures under 6 weeks, pain 7/10 or more, four Sydney hospitals / vertebroplasty / sham / pain below 4/10 / 14 days (follow-up 6 months)
claims.safe_wording: One sham-controlled trial went the other way. In 120 people with severe pain (7 out of 10 or more) from spinal fractures less than 6 weeks old, treated in four Sydney hospitals, 44 in 100 had low pain at two weeks after cement against 21 in 100 after the sham.
claims.qualifications: Single trial; 14-day primary outcome; industry education grant; erratum listed (content not checked). Do not call the participants 'inpatients' (not verified).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: When pooled with the other sham trials in the Cochrane review, results did not differ by pain duration; the VAPOUR authors dispute the pooling.

numbers.meaning: patients randomised (61 v 59)
proportion with pain below 4/10 at 14 days, vertebroplasty v sham
absolute difference
fracture age and minimum pain score for entry

claims.claim: In sham-controlled trials, pain improved substantially in both groups, including those who had the sham procedure.
claims.supporting_passage: Buchbinder 2009: "Vertebroplasty did not result in a significant advantage in any measured outcome at any time point. There were significant reductions in overall pain in both study groups at each follow-up assessment. At 3 months, the mean (+/-SD) reductions in the score for pain in the vertebroplasty and control groups were 2.6+/-2.9 and 1.9+/-3.3, respectively". Kallmes 2009: "Both groups had immediate improvement in disability and pain scores after the intervention."
claims.pico_timeframe: 78 and 131 patients with painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures / vertebroplasty / sham / pain / 1 week to 6 months
claims.safe_wording: In the sham trials, people's pain eased in both groups, including those who had no cement. Improvement after a procedure does not by itself show the procedure caused it.
claims.qualifications: Improvement in the sham arm reflects natural recovery, expectation and regression to the mean together; the trials do not separate these.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Kallmes: trend toward more clinically meaningful pain improvement with vertebroplasty (64% v 48%, P=0.06).

numbers.meaning: mean pain reduction at 3 months (0-10), vertebroplasty v sham, Buchbinder 2009

claims.claim: The sham-controlled evidence is for vertebroplasty; for balloon kyphoplasty there is insufficient evidence of benefit over non-surgical care, and routine use of either is not supported by current specialist and UK guidance.
claims.supporting_passage: ASBMR: "For patients with acutely painful VF, percutaneous vertebroplasty provides no demonstrable clinically significant benefit over placebo. Results did not differ according to duration of pain. There is also insufficient evidence to support kyphoplasty over nonsurgical management, percutaneous vertebroplasty, vertebral body stenting, or KIVA®." ... "Routine use of vertebral augmentation is not supported by current evidence. When it is offered, patients should be fully informed about the evidence." NOGG: "The current evidence does not support the routine use of percutaneous vertebroplasty or balloon kyphoplasty for the treatment of painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures, as these procedures do not show consistent patient benefit"
claims.location: ASBMR abstract; NOGG full text, 'Management of symptomatic osteoporotic vertebral fractures'
claims.pico_timeframe: People with painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures / vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty / guideline position
claims.safe_wording: The sham comparisons were of vertebroplasty. Balloon kyphoplasty (a balloon is inflated before the cement goes in) has not been tested against a sham, and there is not enough evidence that it beats non-surgical care. The UK osteoporosis guideline and a US specialist task force both say the evidence does not support routine use of either procedure; if it is offered, people should be told what the evidence shows.
claims.qualifications: Say 'not routine', not 'never': NICE TA279 (search extract only) still lists both as options for a narrow group with severe ongoing pain after a recent unhealed fracture despite optimal pain relief.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: NICE TA279 narrow indication (see C04-17-h); Ontario HTA 2025.

claims.claim: Recommended care after a painful spinal fracture includes safe pain relief to restore mobility, physiotherapist-supervised exercise, and prompt treatment to prevent further fractures.
claims.supporting_passage: NOGG: "Analgesia for acute pain is important to allow restoration of function and mobility but must be used safely" ... "Physiotherapist supervised exercise following vertebral fracture improves pain and physical performance" ... "Ensure prompt secondary fracture prevention is started following a fracture, with follow-up through fracture liaison services for all postmenopausal women, and men aged 50 years and older, with a newly diagnosed vertebral fracture" ... "Patients with a recent vertebral fracture have a high imminent risk of further fragility fracture". ASBMR: "Anti-osteoporotic medications reduce the risk of subsequent vertebral fractures by 40-70%."
claims.location: NOGG full text, 'Management of symptomatic osteoporotic vertebral fractures'; ASBMR abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: People with painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures / guideline recommendations
claims.safe_wording: What helps meanwhile: pain relief used safely so you can keep moving, physiotherapy-guided exercise, and starting bone treatment, because a recent spinal fracture raises the risk of another one soon.
claims.qualifications: Exercise evidence is modest; NOGG notes urgent spinal surgical referral if there are neurological signs.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: relative reduction in subsequent vertebral fractures with osteoporosis drugs (ASBMR)

claims.claim: NICE TA279 recommends vertebroplasty and balloon kyphoplasty (without stenting) only for people with severe ongoing pain after a recent, unhealed vertebral fracture despite optimal pain management.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine extract (nice.org.uk, not opened): "Percutaneous vertebroplasty and percutaneous balloon kyphoplasty without stenting are recommended as options for treating osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures only in people who have severe ongoing pain after a recent, unhealed vertebral fracture despite optimal pain management"
claims.location: NICE TA279 recommendations page (search extract only)
claims.pico_timeframe: England and Wales; 2013 appraisal
claims.safe_wording: Optional, non-essential clause only: 'NICE guidance from 2013 reserves these procedures for a narrow group with severe ongoing pain from a recent fracture despite good pain relief.' Better: rely on NOGG 2022 (C04-17-f).
claims.qualifications: Search extract only; the page could not be opened and current status was not verified. The candidate's wording about confirmation by examination and imaging was not found in the extract.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: NOGG 2022 (opened) does not support routine use.

claims.claim: VITAL: in 25,871 US adults not selected for vitamin D deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis, 2000 IU vitamin D a day for a median 5.3 years did not reduce total, non-spinal or hip fractures.
claims.supporting_passage: "Participants were not recruited on the basis of vitamin D deficiency, low bone mass, or osteoporosis." ... "Among 25,871 participants ... we confirmed 1991 incident fractures in 1551 participants over a median follow-up of 5.3 years. Supplemental vitamin D, as compared with placebo, did not have a significant effect on total fractures (which occurred in 769 of 12,927 participants in the vitamin D group and in 782 of 12,944 participants in the placebo group; hazard ratio, 0.98; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.89 to 1.08; P = 0.70), nonvertebral fractures (hazard ratio, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.07; P = 0.50), or hip fractures (hazard ratio, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.70 to 1.47; P = 0.96)."
claims.pico_timeframe: US men 50+ and women 55+, generally healthy / vitamin D3 2000 IU daily / placebo / adjudicated total, non-vertebral, hip fractures / median 5.3 years
claims.safe_wording: In VITAL, nearly 26,000 generally healthy Americans aged 50 and over took 2000 units of vitamin D a day or a dummy pill for about 5 years. About 6 in 100 in each group broke a bone (769 of 12,927 v 782 of 12,944). Hip fractures were no different either.
claims.qualifications: Generally healthy, mostly replete population; vitamin D without calcium.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None within the trial; see C04-20-b for subgroups.

numbers.meaning: participants
vitamin D3 dose
median follow-up
people with at least one fracture, vitamin D v placebo (about 5.9% v 6.0%)

claims.claim: Few VITAL participants were deficient; the trial was not designed to test deficient people, and the small group with very low levels showed no benefit either; results may not apply to people with osteoporosis or osteomalacia or to older people in institutions.
claims.supporting_passage: "The mean baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D level (16,757 participants) was 30.7±10.0 ng per milliliter. At baseline, 401 (2.4%) had 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of less than 12 ng per milliliter and 2161 (12.9%) had levels of less than 20 ng per milliliter." ... "In post hoc analyses, we found no benefit for supplementation in the relatively small number of participants with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of less than 12 ng per milliliter (401 participants)." ... "We evaluated only one vitamin D dose, and the trial was not designed to test the effects of vitamin D supplementation in those who are vitamin D deficient. Only a small percentage of participants (2.4%) had vitamin D levels of less than 12 ng per milliliter." ... "In addition, results may not be generalizable to adults with osteoporosis or osteomalacia or older institutionalized persons."
claims.location: Full text: Results (Trial participants; Fracture incidence); Discussion (limitations)
claims.pico_timeframe: VITAL participants with baseline blood samples (16,757) / subgroups by 25(OH)D / fractures / median 5.3 years
claims.safe_wording: Most VITAL volunteers already had normal vitamin D levels; only about 2 in 100 were very low. The trial was not designed to test people who are deficient, and in that small very-low group there was no sign of benefit either. The authors say the results may not apply to people with osteoporosis or to older people living in care homes. So the evidence for deficient people is thin, not absent.
claims.qualifications: The very-low subgroup (401) is post hoc and small; 'no benefit found' in it is weak evidence, but it must be stated. Do not say deficient people were 'untested'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No large trial has tested vitamin D alone in people selected for deficiency; the authors say such a placebo trial would not be feasible or ethical.

numbers.meaning: mean baseline 25(OH)D (about 77 nmol/L)
participants below 12 ng/mL (about 30 nmol/L)

claims.claim: D-Health: in 21,315 Australians aged 60 to 84, 60,000 IU vitamin D monthly for up to 5 years did not reduce fractures.
claims.supporting_passage: "We did a population-based, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of oral vitamin D supplementation (60 000 IU per month) for up to 5 years in adults aged 60-84 years living in Australia." ... "Over a median follow-up of 5·1 years (IQR 5·1-5·1), 568 (5·6%) participants in the vitamin D group and 603 (5·9%) in the placebo group had one or more fractures. There was no effect on fracture risk overall (HR 0·94 [95% CI 0·84-1·06]), and the interaction between randomisation group and time was not significant (p=0·14). However, the HR for total fractures appeared to decrease with increasing follow-up time."
claims.pico_timeframe: 20,326 analysed adults aged 60-84, Australia / vitamin D3 60,000 IU monthly / placebo / any fracture (linked records) / median 5.1 years
claims.safe_wording: In D-Health, over 20,000 Australians aged 60 to 84 took a monthly dose of vitamin D or a dummy for about 5 years. 5.6 in 100 broke a bone with vitamin D and 5.9 in 100 with the dummy, not a clear difference.
claims.qualifications: Fractures were a tertiary outcome; monthly bolus dosing; baseline vitamin D status not in abstract, so do not describe D-Health participants as 'having enough' without qualification.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors note the effect estimate appeared to strengthen with longer follow-up (interaction not significant).

claims.claim: An older French trial in 3,270 ambulatory women with an average age of 84 found that vitamin D3 plus calcium reduced hip and other non-spinal fractures over 18 months.
claims.supporting_passage: "We studied the effects of supplementation with vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) and calcium on the frequency of hip fractures and other nonvertebral fractures, identified radiologically, in 3270 healthy ambulatory women (mean [+/- SD] age, 84 +/- 6 years). Each day for 18 months, 1634 women received tricalcium phosphate (containing 1.2 g of elemental calcium) and 20 micrograms (800 IU) of vitamin D3, and 1636 women received a double placebo." ... "Among the women who completed the 18-month study, the number of hip fractures was 43 percent lower (P = 0.043) and the total number of nonvertebral fractures was 32 percent lower (P = 0.015) among the women treated with vitamin D3 and calcium than among those who received placebo. The results of analyses according to active treatment and according to intention to treat were similar."
claims.pico_timeframe: 3270 ambulatory women, mean age 84, France / vitamin D3 800 IU + calcium 1.2 g daily / double placebo / hip and non-vertebral fractures / 18 months
claims.safe_wording: An older French trial in women with an average age of 84 found fewer hip fractures (43% fewer) with daily vitamin D and calcium together over 18 months. It tested the two together, so it cannot show vitamin D alone works.
claims.qualifications: Care home or sheltered-housing setting NOT verified from the opened abstract: do not describe the participants as care home residents on the strength of this source. Relative reduction only (absolute numbers not in abstract); completers analysis headline; published 1992.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Later large trials of calcium plus vitamin D in community-dwelling people found smaller effects (Cochrane pooled RR 0.84 for hip fracture).

numbers.meaning: women randomised
mean age in years
daily vitamin D3 and elemental calcium
relative reduction in hip / non-vertebral fractures among completers, 18 months

claims.claim: Meta-analyses find vitamin D alone does not prevent fractures, while vitamin D with calcium gives a small reduction in hip fractures, larger in absolute terms for people living in institutions.
claims.supporting_passage: Bolland 2018: "In pooled analyses, vitamin D had no effect on total fracture (36 trials; n=44 790, relative risk 1·00, 95% CI 0·93-1·07), hip fracture (20 trials; n=36 655, 1·11, 0·97-1·26), or falls". Avenell 2014: "There is high quality evidence that vitamin D alone, in the formats and doses tested, is unlikely to be effective in preventing hip fracture" ... "There is high quality evidence that vitamin D plus calcium results in a small reduction in hip fracture risk (nine trials, 49,853 participants; RR 0.84, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.74 to 0.96; P value 0.01). In low-risk populations (residents in the community: with an estimated eight hip fractures per 1000 per year), this equates to one fewer hip fracture per 1000 older adults per year (95% CI 0 to 2). In high risk populations (residents in institutions: with an estimated 54 hip fractures per 1000 per year), this equates to nine fewer hip fractures per 1000 older adults per year (95% CI 2 to 14)." Yao 2019: "a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (49 282 participants, 5449 fractures, 730 hip fractures) of combined supplementation with vitamin D ... and calcium ... found a 6% reduced risk of any fracture (RR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89-0.99) and a 16% reduced risk of hip fracture (RR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.72-0.97)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults in RCTs / vitamin D alone or with calcium / placebo or control / fractures / trial durations
claims.safe_wording: Reviews of many trials agree that vitamin D on its own does not prevent fractures. Vitamin D with calcium cut hip fractures slightly: about 1 fewer per 1000 older people a year living at home, and about 9 fewer per 1000 a year in care homes, where hip fractures are far more common.
claims.qualifications: The per-1000 figures apply the pooled relative risk to assumed baseline risks (8 and 54 per 1000 per year); they are estimates, not separate results in each setting. Reviews predate VITAL and D-Health.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Calcium supplements have their own harms (the Cochrane review notes more gastrointestinal symptoms and renal disease with vitamin D plus calcium).

numbers.meaning: vitamin D alone, total fracture, 36 trials (Bolland)
vitamin D plus calcium, hip fracture (Avenell; Yao)
estimated hip fractures prevented, community residents
estimated hip fractures prevented, institution residents

In clinical practice, dietary sources of calcium are the preferred option and calcium (combined with vitamin D) supplementation should be targeted to those who do not get sufficient calcium from their diet and who are at risk of osteoporosis and/"

claims.supporting_passage: "we enrolled post-menopausal women with at least two moderate or one severe vertebral fracture and a bone mineral density T score of less than or equal to -1·50. "At 24 months, new vertebral fractures occurred in 28 (5·4%) of 680 patients in the teriparatide group and 64 (12·0%) of 680 patients in the risedronate group (risk ratio 0·44, 95% CI 0·29-0·68; p<0·0001). Clinical fractures occurred in 30 (4·8%) of 680 patients in the teriparatide group compared with 61 (9·8%) of 680 in the risedronate group (hazard ratio 0·48, 95% CI 0·32-0·74; p=0·0009). Non-vertebral fragility fractures occurred in 25 (4·0%) patients in the teriparatide group and 38 (6·1%) in the risedronate group (hazard ratio 0·66; 95% CI 0·39-1·10; p=0·10)."

New spinal fractures on X-ray: about 5 in 100 with teriparatide, 12 in 100 with risedronate. Fractures that caused symptoms: about 5 in 100 against 10 in 100. Fractures away from the spine did not clearly differ.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Non-vertebral fractures not significantly different (4.0% v 6.1%, HR 0.66, 0.39 to 1.10).

new radiographic vertebral fractures at 24 months, teriparatide v risedronate

non-vertebral fragility fractures, not significant

"Over a period of 24 months, a 48% lower risk of new vertebral fractures was observed in the romosozumab-to-alendronate group (6.2% [127 of 2046 patients]) than in the alendronate-to-alendronate group (11.9% [243 of 2047 patients]) (P<0.001). "the risk of hip fracture was lower by 38% (41 of 2046 patients [2.0%] vs. 66 of 2047 patients [3.2%]; P=0.02)." ... "During year 1, positively adjudicated serious cardiovascular adverse events were observed more often with romosozumab than with alendronate (50 of 2040 patients [2.5%] vs. 38 of 2014 patients [1.9%])."

claims.claim: UK guidance defines very high fracture risk (for example a spinal fracture in the last 2 years, two or more spinal fractures, T-score -3.5 or lower, or high-dose steroids) and advises considering specialist referral and a bone-building drug first, particularly with spinal fractures.

"Consider teriparatide as a first-line treatment option in men age 50 years and older who are at very high fracture risk, particularly in those with vertebral fractures" ... "very high risk is identified as a FRAX-based fracture probability that exceeds the intervention threshold by 60%"

For these people it says consider referral to a specialist and consider a bone-building drug first, especially after spinal fractures.

"is approved for the treatment of severe osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at very high risk of fracture. It is currently not approved for use in men." ... claims.claim: In FIT (2,027 women with existing spinal fractures, 36 months), alendronate cut spinal fractures found on scheduled X-rays from 15.0% to 8.0%, spinal fractures that came to clinical attention from 5.0% to 2.3%, and any clinical fracture from 18.2% to 13.6%.

"New vertebral fractures, the primary endpoint, were defined by morphometry as a decrease of 20% (and at least 4 mm) in at least one vertebral height between the baseline and latest follow-up radiograph." ... "New symptomatic vertebral fractures were based on self-report and confirmed by radiography." ... "78 (8.0%) of women in the alendronate group had one or more new morphometric vertebral fractures compared with 145 (15.0%) in the placebo group (relative risk 0.53 [95% Cl 0.41-0.68]). For clinically apparent vertebral fractures, the corresponding numbers were 23 (2.3%) alendronate and 50 (5.0%) placebo (relative hazard 0.45 [0.27-0.72]). The risk of any clinical fracture, the main secondary endpoint, was lower in the alendronate than in the placebo group (139 [13.6%] vs 183 [18.2%]; relative hazard 0.72 [0.58-0.90]). The relative hazards for hip fracture and wrist fracture for alendronate versus placebo were 0.49 (0.23-0.99) and 0.52 (0.31-0.87)."

claims.qualifications: Women with existing spinal fractures and low hip density; absolute hip-fracture numbers are not in the abstract (only relative hazard 0.49), so do not chart hip bars from this source.

"As compared with placebo, denosumab reduced the risk of new radiographic vertebral fracture, with a cumulative incidence of 2.3% in the denosumab group, versus 7.2% in the placebo group (risk ratio, 0.32 ...)--a relative decrease of 68%. Denosumab reduced the risk of hip fracture, with a cumulative incidence of 0.7% in the denosumab group, versus 1.2% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.60 ...)--a relative decrease of 40%. Denosumab also reduced the risk of nonvertebral fracture, with a cumulative incidence of 6.5% in the denosumab group, versus 8.0% in the placebo group"

hip fractures, 3 years
non-vertebral fractures
relative reductions (vertebral / hip)

claims.claim: UK guidance says to take alendronic acid after an overnight fast, swallowed whole with a glass of plain water (about 200 mL) while sitting or standing, at least 30 minutes before the first food or drink (other than water), other medicines or supplements including calcium, and not to lie down for 30 minutes afterwards.

Tablets should be swallowed whole with a glass of plain water (~ 200 ml) whilst the patient is sitting or standing in an upright position. Patients should not lie down for 30 min after taking the tablet."

claims.claim: Even when taken correctly, less than 1 in 100 of the alendronate dose is absorbed (0.76% in women, 0.59% in men, fasting with water and food 2 hours later).

Bioavailability was similar in men [0.59%, (0.43, 0.81)]."

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; this is the standard reference for alendronate absorption.

same measure in men

claims.claim: In volunteer absorption studies, black coffee or orange juice taken with the tablet cut absorption by about 60%, and taking it with or up to 2 hours after breakfast cut absorption by more than 85%.

claims.qualifications: Relative reductions of an already tiny absorbed amount; measured in volunteers, not in fracture trials. Say it is an absorption finding. Do not claim a specific loss of fracture protection.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No opened source links these absorption reductions to fracture outcomes; the effect on fracture protection is unmeasured (an evidence gap, not evidence of no effect).

numbers.meaning: relative reduction in absorption with black coffee or orange juice versus water
relative reduction when taken with breakfast or 2 hours after breakfast

claims.claim: Waiting 30 or 60 minutes before breakfast gave about 40% less absorption than waiting 2 hours; the authors set at least 30 minutes as a practical minimum for long-term use.

"A practical dosing recommendation, derived from these findings and reflective of the long-term nature of therapy for a disease such as osteoporosis, is that patients take the drug with water after an overnight fast and at least 30 minutes before any other food or beverage."
claims.pico_timeframe: Volunteers / alendronate 30 or 60 min before breakfast / 2-hour wait / fraction absorbed / single doses
claims.safe_wording: Thirty minutes is the minimum wait, set as a practical compromise; in the absorption studies, waiting 2 hours let more of the tablet be absorbed than waiting 30 minutes.
claims.qualifications: Optional nuance; do not advise a 2-hour wait, since guidance says at least 30 minutes.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: lower absorption with a 30 or 60 minute wait than with a 2-hour wait (relative)

claims.claim: Alendronate can irritate the gullet (oesophagus); reported cases were linked with taking it with little or no water, lying down during or after the dose, or carrying on after symptoms began.

"Recommendations to reduce the risk of esophagitis include swallowing alendronate with 180 to 240 ml (6 to 8 oz) of water on arising in the morning, remaining upright for at least 30 minutes after swallowing the tablet and until the first food of the day has been ingested, and discontinuing the drug promptly if esophageal symptoms develop." NOGG: "Oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated in people with abnormalities of the oesophagus that delay oesophageal emptying such as stricture or achalasia, and inability to stand or sit upright for at least 30–60 min."

claims.safe_wording: The full glass of water and staying upright help the tablet pass quickly into the stomach. Reports of gullet irritation from alendronic acid were mostly linked with taking it with little water or lying down afterwards. If swallowing becomes painful or you get new heartburn, stop taking it and ask your doctor or pharmacist.
claims.qualifications: Case reports and spontaneous reports only; gives no rate. Do not state how common oesophagitis is. The 'stop if symptoms' advice comes from de Groen's recommendations ('discontinuing the drug promptly if esophageal symptoms develop'); 'painful swallowing' and 'new heartburn' are a plain-English gloss of 'esophageal symptoms', not quoted examples.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Frequency is uncertain; the 199 oesophageal reports among about 475,000 estimated users are voluntary reports and must not be used as a risk figure.

claims.claim: UK guidance says a fracture risk assessment (FRAX) should be done for any postmenopausal woman or man aged 50 or over who has a clinical risk factor for fracture; people found to be at low risk without a previous fracture are reassured and given lifestyle advice rather than drug treatment.

"Men and women with, without a prior fragility fracture, can be reassured that their fracture risk is low and offered lifestyle advice as appropriate" ... "An initial FRAX assessment, which provides the ten-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture (MOF; clinical spine, hip, forearm or humerus) and/or hip fracture, can be used to identify patients at low, intermediate, high or very high risk of fracture"
claims.location: NOGG full text, 'Fracture risk assessment and case finding' and 'Intervention thresholds and strategy' recommendations (the risk category after 'Men and women with' is missing from the PMC text extraction)

No opened source sets a routine recheck date for untreated people at low risk (searches of the NOGG text found set intervals only for people near the treatment threshold who are on steroids or cancer hormone treatment, and after pausing treatment). Do not claim anything about GP recall systems.

age from which the recommendation applies to men

claims.claim: A new broken bone after a minor fall or strain is a risk factor for further fractures: in pooled data from 11 cohorts, a previous fracture was linked with nearly twice the risk of another fracture, and UK guidance says the risk is highest just after the fracture, falls over the next 2 years, and stays above average after that.
claims.supporting_passage: Kanis: "A previous fracture history was associated with a significantly increased risk of any fracture compared with individuals without a prior fracture (RR = 1.86; 95% CI = 1.75-1.98). The risk ratio was similar for the outcome of osteoporotic fracture or for hip fracture. There was no significant difference in risk ratio between men and women." NOGG: "Prior fragility fracture is a well-established risk factor for a future fracture. This risk of subsequent osteoporotic fracture is particularly acute immediately after an index fracture and wanes progressively over the next 2 years, but thereafter remains higher than that of the general population"

claims.pico_timeframe: Men and women in 11 population cohorts / prior fracture / no prior fracture / any subsequent fracture / 250,000 person-years of follow-up
claims.safe_wording: A broken bone after a minor fall or bump is the clearest reason to have your fracture risk looked at again. People who have had one fracture have nearly twice the risk of another. The risk is highest soon after the fracture, eases over the next 2 years, and stays above average after that.
claims.qualifications: Relative risk from observational cohorts (association). 'Nearly twice' is the plain reading of RR 1.86; do not convert to an absolute number. 'Fragility fracture' means a fracture from a fall from standing height or less.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

numbers.meaning: relative risk of any fracture after a previous fracture versus none, pooled across 11 cohorts; plain reading 'nearly twice the risk'
period after a fracture over which the raised risk of another fracture gradually eases (it stays above average afterwards)

claims.claim: Steroid tablets taken for 3 months or more (any dose) count as a fracture risk factor; bone loss starts early after they begin, and UK guidance says some people should start bone protection at the same time as the steroids.

"Because bone loss and increased fracture risk occur early after initiation of oral glucocorticoids, bone-protective treatment should be started in the following people, at the same time as glucocorticoid therapy without waiting for bone density assessment, which should follow later" ... "Bone loss and increased fracture risk occur rapidly after initiation of oral glucocorticoid therapy and increase with the dose of glucocorticoids"

prednisolone dose above which NOGG counts steroids as high dose (optional, practitioner version only)

claims.claim: Losing 4 cm or more in height, or a new stoop (kyphosis), is a reason for spine imaging to look for spinal fractures and for fracture risk assessment.

"There are many clinical risk factors for fracture in addition to those included in FRAX which can be used to trigger fracture risk assessment (Table), including thoracic kyphosis and height loss (> 4 cm), either in comparison with recalled young adult height or a documented loss on serial measurements"

"Vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) is indicated ... in cases of acute onset back pain with risk factors for osteoporosis"

"The majority of non-vertebral fractures are preceded by a fall."

claims.claim: In US registry and Medicare records of 50,613 men with prostate cancer, among men who survived at least 5 years, 19.4% of those given androgen deprivation therapy had a fracture compared with 12.6% of those not given it; the study is observational.
claims.supporting_passage: "We studied the records of 50,613 men who were listed in the linked database of the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results program and Medicare as having received a diagnosis of prostate cancer in the period from 1992 through 1997." ... "Of men surviving at least five years after diagnosis, 19.4 percent of those who received androgen-deprivation therapy had a fracture, as compared with 12.6 percent of those not receiving androgen-deprivation therapy (P<0.001). In the Cox proportional-hazards analyses, adjusted for characteristics of the patient and the tumor, there was a statistically significant relation between the number of doses of gonadotropin-releasing hormone received during the 12 months after diagnosis and the subsequent risk of fracture."
claims.pico_timeframe: US men with prostate cancer diagnosed 1992 to 1997 (Medicare) / androgen deprivation therapy / no androgen deprivation therapy / any fracture / at least 5 years after diagnosis
claims.safe_wording: In US records of men with prostate cancer, among men who lived at least 5 years after diagnosis, about 19 in 100 who had hormone treatment had broken a bone, compared with about 13 in 100 who did not. The study was observational, so it shows a link; men who had more doses of treatment had more fractures.
claims.qualifications: Crude percentages in the subgroup who survived at least 5 years; difference is about 7 percentage points. Say 'linked with', not 'causes', despite the paper's own wording. Treatments and bone care have changed since the 1990s.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Men given ADT may differ from others (age, cancer stage); adjusted models still showed a dose-response. Consistent with the 2021 meta-analysis (C04-22-b).

ADT use is associated with increasing fracture risk (OR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.26-1.52) and fracture requiring hospitalization (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.29-1.88)." ... "The GRADE level of evidence was moderate for any fracture and low for fracture requiring hospitalization."

claims.qualifications: Odds ratio from observational studies; do not turn it into 'X times more likely' or an absolute figure. Use for consistency, not for a number in public posts.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: High heterogeneity (I2 83%).

numbers.meaning: odds of any fracture with ADT versus none, pooled; practitioner version only
men across 16 cohort studies

There is a significant increase in fracture risk in men with prostate cancer in the 5 years following the initiation of ADT when compared to those not receiving ADT" ... "In addition to glucocorticoids, several medications are known to increase hip fracture risk including thyroid hormone excess, aromatase inhibitors for the treatment of breast cancer and androgen deprivation for the treatment of prostate cancer"

claims.claim: Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) speed up bone loss (on average 1 to 3% a year in postmenopausal women) and are linked with more fractures; the excess risk is seen mainly during treatment.
claims.supporting_passage: NOGG: "The use of aromatase inhibitors (AI) in postmenopausal women induces bone loss at an average rate of 1–3% per year at sites rich in trabecular bone." Hadji 2025: "AI, which are now more commonly prescribed due to improved anticancer efficacy, are associated with a higher fracture risk than tamoxifen due to their ability to almost completely suppress circulating and tissue estrogen levels, and are known to accelerate bone loss and increase fracture risk in this population beyond that seen with natural menopause" ... "A meta-analysis of 30 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) including 117,974 breast cancer patients found a significantly higher incidence of osteoporotic fractures, in AI users versus those not treated with AI (controls), particularly for vertebral fractures []. The relative risk (RR) for hip fractures and non-vertebral fractures was 1.18 (p < 0.001 in each case) versus controls, while the RR for vertebral fractures was 1.84 (p < 0.001)." Tseng: "Compared with the tamoxifen group, aromatase inhibitor-associated fracture risk increased by 33% (pooled RR 1.33; 95% CI 1.21-1.47) during the tamoxifen/aromatase inhibitor treatment period, but did not increase (pooled RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.72-1.37) during the post-tamoxifen/aromatase inhibitor treatment period."
claims.location: NOGG full text, 'Women receiving aromatase inhibitor therapy'; Hadji 2025 full text section 3.1; Tseng abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Postmenopausal women with hormone-sensitive breast cancer / aromatase inhibitor / no AI or tamoxifen / bone density and fractures / during 5 to 10 years of treatment
claims.safe_wording: Aromatase inhibitors for breast cancer (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) work by removing almost all oestrogen, and they speed up bone loss. Women taking them lose on average 1 to 3 per cent of bone density a year and have more fractures than women not taking them.
claims.qualifications: Relative risks quoted by Hadji 2025 come from a meta-analysis not opened here; keep them out of public posts. Tseng is limited to women aged 65 and under. Longer (extended) AI treatment adds to the risk (Hadji 2025).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Individual placebo-controlled trials have not all shown a clear fracture difference, but pooled evidence and position statements agree on raised risk.

numbers.meaning: average bone loss at trabecular sites in postmenopausal women on AIs (NOGG)
relative risk of hip/non-vertebral and vertebral fractures with AI versus controls, second-hand from Hadji 2025; practitioner use only with attribution

claims.claim: Tamoxifen, the other common hormone tablet for breast cancer, has not been found to harm bone or raise fracture risk in postmenopausal women.
claims.supporting_passage: Hadji 2025: "In contrast to the case in premenopausal women, tamoxifen has not been found to have a negative impact on BMD or fracture risk in postmenopausal women []. Indeed, results of a systematic review and meta-analysis suggest it may potentially preserve bone mass in postmenopausal women" Tseng: "Similar fracture risk was observed in women treated and not treated with tamoxifen [pooled risk ratio (RR) 0.95; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.84-1.07]."
claims.location: Hadji 2025 full text section 3.1; Tseng abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Postmenopausal women with breast cancer / tamoxifen / no tamoxifen / bone density and fracture / treatment period
claims.safe_wording: The bone warning applies to aromatase inhibitors; tamoxifen has not been found to thin bone after the menopause.
claims.qualifications: Tamoxifen can reduce bone density in premenopausal women; keep the statement to women after the menopause.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: UK guidance says all women starting an aromatase inhibitor should have their fracture risk assessed (FRAX, counting the AI as a cause of osteoporosis, with a bone density scan where practical), and international position statements say every woman starting or on an AI should be told of the risk and have it assessed.

Hadji 2025: "All women receiving AI treatment should be informed of this significantly increased risk and its consequences and have their individual fracture risk evaluated to determine an appropriate management strategy."
claims.location: NOGG full text, recommendation 24; Hadji 2017 abstract (Conclusions); Hadji 2025 full text, Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: Women starting aromatase inhibitors / fracture risk assessment at start / not applicable / fracture risk / start of treatment, reassess 12 to 24 months if near threshold
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance says every woman starting an aromatase inhibitor should have her fracture risk checked, with a bone density scan where practical. If you are starting one and nobody has mentioned your bones, ask.
claims.qualifications: NOGG also advises a repeat assessment after 12 to 24 months for women near the treatment threshold or starting other treatments such as steroids.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Hadji 2025 notes FRAX without bone density can overestimate risk in women on AIs; a scan improves the estimate.

claims.supporting_passage: Brown 2020: "All men starting or continuing long-term ADT should receive lifestyle advice regarding bone health. Calcium/vitamin D supplementation should be offered if required. Fracture risk should be calculated (using the FRAX® tool), with BMD assessment included where feasible." ... "Those near to, but below an intervention threshold, and patients going on to additional systemic therapies (particularly those requiring glucocorticoids), should have FRAX® (including BMD) repeated after 12-18 months." NOGG: "The NOGG supports the recent guideline published by Brown et al. 2020" ... "A recent UK consensus statement on prostate cancer treatment-induced bone loss concluded that fracture risk should be calculated using FRAX, considering ADT use as a secondary cause of osteoporosis, and including BMD where available and practical."

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.supporting_passage: "In this context, careful consideration of skeletal health is required to reduce the risk of treatment-related fragility fractures and their associated morbidity and mortality. This risk is currently not well-managed." ... "Current PC guidelines lack specific recommendations for optimising bone health."
claims.pico_timeframe: UK men with prostate cancer on ADT / current practice / not applicable / bone health management / as of 2020
claims.safe_wording: UK specialists writing in 2020 said bone health was often not well managed in men on hormone treatment for prostate cancer.
claims.qualifications: Expert judgement from 2020, not an audit figure; do not state how often assessment is missed today.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No opened audit data on current UK assessment rates.

claims.claim: If fracture risk is high, treatment helps: bisphosphonates and denosumab prevent bone loss in men on androgen deprivation therapy (fracture reduction shown for denosumab in one trial, not clearly for bisphosphonates), and in women on aromatase inhibitors denosumab and risedronate have been shown to reduce fracture risk.

"Denosumab and zoledronate both lead to significant gains in BMD at the spine and hip in postmenopausal women with breast cancer receiving AI, and both denosumab and risedronate have been shown to reduce fracture risk" Bassatne 2026: "Oral bisphosphonates had no effect on fracture incidence at 12-months (RR = 0.57; 95%CI[0.10, 3.23]; very low certainty). Intravenous bisphosphonates had no effect on the risk of morphometric vertebral fractures at 36-months (RR = 1.06; 95%CI[0.57,1.98]; very low certainty). One trial showed that denosumab probably results in a large reduction in new morphometric vertebral fracture risk at 12 (RR = 0.15), 24 (RR = 0.31) and 36-months (RR = 0.38; 95%CI[0.19-0.78]). Treatment with bisphosphonates or denosumab for 12-months increased BMD at the hip (+1.5 to +3.9%) and lumbar spine (+4.0 to +6.8%)"

Common symptoms in mild dementia include forgetting the details of a recent event, though still remembering the event itself, repeating the same question/story and social withdrawal. In moderate dementia, recent memory is very impaired, even though they seemingly can remember their past life events well. They can do personal care with prompting. In severe dementia, they cannot do personal care without help. In very severe dementia they are often bedfast. Many are virtually mute." Body text: "The degree of dementia generally corresponds to the degree of frailty."

Often at this level minimal assistance with personal care might be needed. Moderate dementia is the case when people who are dependent in their performance of instrumental ADLs can still do their basic or personal ADLs with prompting. This can also be the case in people who are cognitively intact, but whose disability obliges them to have someone nearby (so-called 'standby assistance' or 'set-up')." Also for level 7: "Still, people living with severe frailty can be mobile."

The number alone does not tell you which.

'Walks well' for the dementia example is consistent with the guidance (people with severe frailty 'can be mobile'), but the scale does not say mobility is normal in moderate dementia; keep it as an illustration.

claims.claim: The CFS is a judgement-based summary that requires clinical judgement; prognosis needs both baseline frailty and the severity of the acute illness; the score is no substitute for a patient-centred care plan.
claims.supporting_passage: "It is not a questionnaire. Grading the degree of frailty requires clinical judgement that is based in part on screening criteria..." ... "Still, as discussed below, their prognosis requires information about both their baseline degree of frailty, and the severity of their acute illness." ... "In geriatric medicine, the goal of grading the degree of frailty is both to ease communication through a shared language, and also as the foundation for a care plan. The care plan needs to address the gap between the current level of function, cognition, mobility, and social relationships (especially with the primary carer) and how those have changed with the acute illness (when present)." ... "It should not be confused with the more instrumental purpose to which the Clinical Frailty Scale is now being put, which is no substitute for a patient-centred care plan."
claims.location: Body text: 'What is the Clinical Frailty Scale?'; 'Summary'

claims.safe_wording: The developers describe the score as a clinical judgement that summarises function, cognition and mobility; they say predicting outcome also needs the severity of the current illness, and that the score is the start of a care plan, not a substitute for one.
claims.qualifications: This is developer guidance, not a trial result.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: In routine practice, both dementia and mobility independently relate to the CFS score given.
claims.supporting_passage: "The CFS was scored on 658 (89%) (median 4, range 1-8; mean age 81 years, 61% women). Independent predictors of higher CFS were older age (p<0.001), history of dementia (p<0.001), mobility (p≤0.007), disability (p<0.001), and higher acuity of illness (p=0.009). Disability and mobility were the main classifiers in the CRT."

claims.safe_wording: In one Dublin emergency department, higher CFS scores were linked with a history of dementia and, separately, with poorer mobility and more disability.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Note that 'acuity of illness' also predicted a higher CFS, which suggests some scores were influenced by the acute illness rather than baseline.

claims.claim: Position: record what drove the CFS score (physical, cognitive or both) beside the number, and do not use the number alone to judge how someone will tolerate surgery, rehabilitation or exercise.
claims.supporting_passage: See C05-16-d and C05-16-e: "This can also be the case in people who are cognitively intact, but whose disability obliges them to have someone nearby"; "requires clinical judgement"; "no substitute for a patient-centred care plan".

claims.safe_wording: Mark this as a practice suggestion: 'Write the reason next to the number', for example 'CFS 6 (moderate dementia; walks independently)'. It follows from how the scale is built; it is not a published recommendation and no outcome study of this habit was found.

Do not claim that people with a cognitive route to CFS 6 do better or worse after surgery or rehabilitation: no study comparing outcomes by route was found in this batch's searches (searching was limited).

While not dependent on others for daily help, often symptoms limit activities. A common complaint is being 'slowed up' and/or being tired during the day. 5 | LIVING WITH MILD FRAILTY People who often have more evident slowing, and need help with high order instrumental activities of daily living (finances, transportation, heavy housework)... 6 | ... claims.claim: The CFS is meant to describe the person's usual (baseline) state, for example how they were about two weeks before an acute illness, not how they seem while ill.

This is especially needed in clinical settings where health can change quickly. For example, many older patients in the Emergency Department who were fit two weeks ago (their baseline state), may appear to be frail while ill; a prospect that becomes more likely the longer they wait there." ... "We then ask about four features: how the person moved, functioned, thought, and felt about their health over the last two weeks." Abstract: "the Clinical Frailty Scale assays the baseline state".

claims.claim: Level 9 (terminally ill) applies to people with a life expectancy under about 6 months who are not otherwise living with severe frailty, and is the one level scored on the current rather than baseline state.
claims.supporting_passage: Figure 1: "9 | TERMINALLY ILL Approaching the end of life. This category applies to people with a life expectancy <6 months, who are not otherwise living with severe frailty. (Many terminally ill people can still exercise until very close to death.)" Body text: "[Level 9] is notable for being the only level in which the current state trumps the baseline state, in that the terminally ill person might have been operating at any frailty level at baseline." ... "Even so, if a terminally ill person was completely dependent for personal care at baseline, they would be scored as Level 8."
claims.location: Figure 1; body text, 'Using the Clinical Frailty Scale in People Towards the End of Life'
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition.
claims.safe_wording: Level 9 is used for people expected to live less than about 6 months who are not otherwise severely frail; many are still active. It is the one level based on the current illness rather than the usual state.
claims.qualifications: None beyond paraphrase.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: What the score is used for and its limits: prognosis and setting care goals (and, during COVID-19, triage for scarce resources); it requires clinical judgement; it is not widely validated in younger people or people with stable single-system disabilities.
claims.supporting_passage: "In ordinary time (i.e., with no pandemic), the Clinical Frailty Scale is used both in prognosis and to set care goals." Abstract: "The key points discussed are that the Clinical Frailty Scale assays the baseline state, it is not widely validated in younger people or those with stable single-system disabilities, and it requires clinical judgement. The Clinical Frailty Scale is now commonly used as a triage tool to make important clinical decisions such as allocating scarce health care resources for COVID-19 management". Body text: "In geriatric medicine, the goal of grading the degree of frailty is both to ease communication through a shared language, and also as the foundation for a care plan."
claims.pico_timeframe: Developers' guidance (2020).
claims.safe_wording: Doctors use the score to help judge how someone may cope with illness and treatment and to plan care. It depends on a clinician's judgement, so you can ask what it was based on. It was designed for older people and is not well tested in younger people or in people with a long-standing single disability.
claims.qualifications: Do not imply that the score alone decides treatment; describe it as one input.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: In pooled community studies (average follow-up about 4 years), about 14 in 100 older people became less frail, about 29 in 100 became more frail and about 57 in 100 stayed the same.
claims.supporting_passage: "Among 42,775 community-dwelling older people from 16 studies with a mean follow-up of 3.9 years (range: 1-10 years), 13.7% (95%CI = 11.7-15.8%) improved, 29.1% (95%CI = 25.9-32.5%) worsened and 56.5% (95%CI = 54.2-58.8%) maintained the same frailty status."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling older people (mean age over 60); frailty phenotype (robust/prefrail/frail); change between first and last assessment; mean 3.9 years (1 to 10).
claims.safe_wording: In 16 studies of 42,775 older people living at home, followed for about 4 years on average, about 14 in 100 became less frail. About twice as many, 29 in 100, became more frail, and 57 in 100 stayed the same.
claims.qualifications: Worsening must appear next to improvement, in the first two lines. Figures use one definition (the frailty phenotype) and people living at home; follow-up ranged from 1 to 10 years. Describe as 'of people reassessed' (handling of deaths not stated in the abstract).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Transition rates varied with age, sex and follow-up length (stratified analyses).
