claims.claim: More recent pooled evidence shows about 30% of older adults lose independence in basic daily activities after an acute hospital stay, with little change by study start year.
claims.supporting_passage: Random effects meta-analysis across included studies identified combined prevalence of HAD as 30% (95% CI 24%, 33%; P < .001). The effect of study initiation year on the prevalence rate was minimal. A large amount of heterogeneity was observed between studies, which may be due in part to nonstandardized measurement of ADL impairment or other methodological differences.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults aged 65 and over in acute medical-surgical care; 7,375 participants across studies; ADL (Katz or Barthel) measured at 2 or more time points before or during and after hospitalisation.
claims.safe_wording: A 2019 review that pooled studies of 7,375 older adults found that about 3 in 10 lost independence in basic daily activities after an acute hospital stay, and the figure had changed little over the years the studies were done.
claims.qualifications: Studies measured function in different ways and results varied widely between studies. Definitions of the starting point differ (some before admission, some on admission).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneity is large; the pooled figure is an average across different populations.

numbers.meaning: pooled prevalence of hospital-associated disability, adults 65+
total participants across included studies

claims.claim: The Covinsky cohort dates from the 1990s (published 2003).
claims.supporting_passage: Counsell 2000 abstract: "A total of 1,531 community-dwelling patients, aged 70 or older, admitted for an acute medical illness between November 1994 and May 1997." Scite Smart Citations for Covinsky 2003 list this trial (10.1111/j.1532-5415.2000.tb03866.x) as cited in the Methods section.
claims.location: Counsell 2000 abstract (Participants); Scite citation record for Covinsky 2003 (Methods)
claims.pico_timeframe: Era of data collection for Covinsky 2003.
claims.safe_wording: The study was published in 2003, so its data are more than 20 years old.
claims.qualifications: The exact enrolment years were not read in the Covinsky 2003 full text (closed access); 'more than 20 years old' is certain from the publication date; 'the 1990s' is strongly indicated by the cited parent trial but not directly read.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Pair with C05-01-d to show the pattern persists in later studies.

numbers.meaning: publication year of Covinsky cohort
enrolment period of the Akron ACE trial cited in Covinsky 2003 Methods

claims.claim: Function before admission is often not documented in hospital notes, and when it is, it misses impairment.
claims.supporting_passage: Bogardus 2001: "Subjects were 525 medical patients, aged 70 years or older, hospitalized at an academic medical center. Patient interviews determined status for 7 basic activities of daily living (BADLs) and 7 instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). Medical records were reviewed to assess documentation of BADLs and IADLs. Most medical records contained no documentation of individual BADLs and IADLs (61% to 98% of records lacking documentation), with the exception of walking (24% of medical records lacking documentation). Impairment prevalence was lower in medical records than at interview for all BADLs and IADLs, and agreement between interview and medical record was poor (kappa < 0.40 for individual BADLs and IADLs)." ... "assuming that nondocumentation of functional status is equivalent to independence may be unwarranted." Scite Methods snippet: "The patient provided information on sociodemographics ... and preadmission BADLs and IADLs". Covinsky 2011 abstract: "Since recognition of functional status problems is an essential prerequisite to preventing and managing disability, we also describe a pragmatic approach toward functional status assessment in the hospital focused on evaluation of ADLs, mobility, and cognition."
claims.location: Bogardus 2001 Abstract (Methods, Results, Conclusions) and Methods snippet via Scite; Covinsky 2011 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: 525 medical inpatients aged 70+, one US academic centre; interview about preadmission ADLs (reference) versus medical record documentation; cross-sectional, published 2001.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of 525 medical patients aged 70 and over, most hospital records did not record whether the person could manage individual daily tasks before admission; walking was the exception. Where records did say something, they found less impairment than the patients themselves reported.
claims.qualifications: One centre, published 2001, paper records; electronic records may differ. Do not say 'most notes never mention function'; say individual daily tasks were usually not recorded.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No recent documentation audit was checked in this batch.

numbers.meaning: medical inpatients aged 70+
proportion of records lacking documentation of individual basic and instrumental ADLs
records lacking documentation of walking

claims.claim: Position: hospital teams should record function from about two weeks before the illness and state at discharge how far the person is from that level.
claims.supporting_passage: Covinsky 2003: "patients or their surrogates were interviewed about their independence in five ADLs ... 2 weeks before admission (baseline) and at admission." Conclusion: "Many hospitalized older people are discharged with ADL function that is worse than their baseline function." Covinsky 2011: "we also describe a pragmatic approach toward functional status assessment in the hospital focused on evaluation of ADLs, mobility, and cognition."
claims.pico_timeframe: Practice recommendation derived from cohort method and expert review; not tested in a trial.
claims.safe_wording: Present as judgement: 'We should record what the person could do two weeks before they became ill, and say at discharge how far they are from that level.' The evidence shows this baseline can be obtained at admission by asking the person or a relative, and that measuring only from admission misses loss that happened before arrival.
claims.qualifications: No trial shows that recording a pre-illness baseline improves outcomes; mark as the author's position. The discharge-letter line (two weeks before: X; now: Y) is a suggested format, not a published standard.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: Older women who had changed how or how often they did a mobility task, without reporting difficulty, had walking speed, balance and strength between those of women with no change and women with difficulty.
claims.supporting_passage: The Women's Health and Aging Study II, an observational study of 436 women 70-80 years of age who were among the two-thirds least disabled living in the community. ... (3) no difficulty but reported modification and/or change in frequency of task performance (a self-report measure of preclinical disability predictive of incident difficulty). ... Physical performance decreased, and disease frequency increased, in association with decreasing self-reported mobility function (in walking one-half mile and climbing 10 steps), across three self-report categories: High Function, Preclinical Disability (Task Modification but No Difficulty) and Disability (Difficulty). These findings pertained for measures of walking speed, balance, strength, and knee and hip osteoarthritis.
claims.pico_timeframe: 436 higher-functioning community-dwelling women aged 70 to 80, Baltimore; cross-sectional at the 18-month visit; self-report category versus measured walking speed, balance, strength and joint disease.
claims.safe_wording: In a Baltimore study of 436 women aged 70 to 80, those who said they had changed how or how often they walked half a mile or climbed 10 steps, but had no difficulty, were measured as slower, weaker and less steady than women with no change, though not as affected as women who reported difficulty.
claims.qualifications: Cross-sectional (one time point). Women only, the more able two thirds of the age group, one US city, data from the 1990s.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with Mänty 2007 in Finnish men and women (C05-02-d).

numbers.meaning: women aged 70 to 80, Women's Health and Aging Study II

claims.claim: In the same cohort, women without mobility difficulty who reported changing how they did a task had 3 to 4 times the odds of developing walking or stair difficulty over 18 months.
claims.supporting_passage: At baseline, 69.3% of the cohort reported no difficulty with mobility. After 18 months, 16.0 and 11.7% of this group reported incident difficulty walking 1/2 mile or climbing up 10 steps, respectively. Those reporting baseline task modification due to underlying health problems, our measure of preclinical disability, were at three- to fourfold higher odds of progressing to difficulty than were those without such modification. In multivariate logistic regression analyses, this self-report measure, task modification without difficulty, and objective measures of performance were independently and jointly predictive of incident mobility difficulty. Specifically, for incident difficulty walking 1/2 mile, self-reported task modification odds ratio (OR) = 3.67 ... for incident difficulty climbing up 10 stairs, OR for task modification = 3.84
claims.pico_timeframe: Women aged 70 to 80 without mobility difficulty at baseline (69.3% of 436); exposure: self-reported task modification without difficulty; comparator: no modification; outcome: self-reported incident difficulty walking half a mile or climbing 10 steps; 18 months; adjusted odds ratios.
claims.safe_wording: Over the next 18 months, women who had already changed how they walked or climbed stairs were more likely to develop difficulty with those tasks than women who had not changed anything, even after taking their measured walking speed into account. Overall, about 1 in 6 (16 in 100) of the women with no difficulty at the start developed difficulty walking half a mile.
claims.qualifications: Effect sizes are odds ratios; for practitioners write 'about 3 to 4 times the odds', never 'times more likely'. Absolute risks by group were not available. The 16.0% and 11.7% are for all women without mobility difficulty at baseline, not by modification group.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: of 436 women reported no mobility difficulty at baseline
of those without difficulty, new difficulty walking half a mile at 18 months (whole group)
of those without difficulty, new difficulty climbing 10 steps at 18 months (whole group)
task modification and incident difficulty walking half a mile, adjusted
task modification and incident difficulty climbing 10 steps, adjusted

claims.claim: Women who newly reported changing how or how often they walked were more likely 1.5 years later to report new walking difficulty and to have stopped walking 8 blocks outdoors; the question used was 'Have you changed the way you walk 1/2 mile, or how often you do this, due to a health or physical condition?'
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Data are from a prospective study of 436 community-dwelling women age 70-79 years. Outcome measures include subjective and objective measures of walking ability at 3 years. ... Compared to women without, women with incident PCMD at 1.5 years after baseline were 2.7 (95%CI 1.4-7.2) times more likely to report that they no longer walk outdoors at least 8 blocks and 4.9 (1.9-13.1) times more likely to report new difficulty walking." Methods (full text): "The main variable of interest, reported PCMD, was obtained as part of a series of task-specific questions about changing the frequency or method of performing daily activities: 'Have you changed the way you walk 1/2 mile (about 5–6 city blocks), or how often you do this, due to a health or physical condition?'" Table 2 heading: "Modeled Risk Ratios (PCMD+/PCMD−)"; footnote: "RR and change in mean are from propensity-adjusted marginal structural models estimating causal association with PCMD− as the reference group". Methods: "Participants were recruited from a sample representing the higher functioning two-thirds of women age 70–79 in eastern Baltimore City and Baltimore County, Maryland and were enrolled in 1994 and 1995."
claims.location: Abstract; Methods sections 2.1 to 2.5; Table 2 (via Undermind PDF read and Scite Smart Citation snippet)
claims.pico_timeframe: Women aged 70 to 79, higher-functioning, Baltimore, enrolled 1994 to 1995; exposure: new report of changed method or frequency of walking half a mile at 1.5 years (women with PCMD at baseline excluded); outcome at 3 years; adjusted risk ratios.
claims.safe_wording: In the same Baltimore study, women who began to report changing how or how often they walked were, a year and a half later, more likely to say walking had become difficult and more likely to have stopped walking 8 blocks outdoors. The question they were asked was: 'Have you changed the way you walk half a mile, or how often you do this, because of a health or physical condition?'
claims.qualifications: Adjusted risk ratios with wide confidence intervals; if a number is used, say 'about 5 times as likely to report new walking difficulty (wide uncertainty)'. Do not use the abstract's 2.7 for stopping walking 8 blocks: Table 2 gives 3.1 (1.35 to 7.23). Raw proportions not reported. Cite the paper as 2012.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Abstract and Table 2 disagree for one outcome (2.7 vs 3.1).

numbers.meaning: women aged 70 to 79
new walking difficulty at 3 years, incident PCMD vs none, adjusted risk ratio
no longer walking 8 blocks outdoors at 3 years; avoid or use table value
PCMD measured at 1.5 years; outcomes at 3 years

claims.claim: The finding was replicated in Finnish men and women aged 75 to 81: preclinical mobility limitation predicted progression to major mobility limitation over 2 years.
claims.supporting_passage: A total of 632 community-living (age range, 75-81 y) women and men took part in the baseline assessments and 302 persons in the semi-annual interviews on mobility limitation over 2 years. ... Preclinical mobility limitation was defined as self-reported tiredness or modification of task performance without task difficulty. ... At baseline, participants with preclinical mobility limitation showed intermediate levels of walking speed and muscle power, compared with those with no limitation or manifest mobility limitation. Participants reporting baseline preclinical mobility limitation had 3- to 6-fold higher age- and sex-adjusted risk of progressing to major manifest mobility limitation during the 2-year follow-up compared with participants with no limitation at baseline
claims.pico_timeframe: 632 community-living women and men aged 75 to 81, Finland (302 followed); exposure: tiredness or modified task performance without difficulty; outcome: major manifest mobility limitation; 2 years; age- and sex-adjusted.
claims.safe_wording: A Finnish study of women and men aged 75 to 81 found the same pattern: people who had changed how they walked or climbed stairs, without difficulty, were slower and weaker than those with no change, and more likely to develop serious walking limitation over 2 years.
claims.qualifications: Definition includes tiredness as well as changed method. Only 302 followed up. Multiplier not needed; if used, '3 to 6 times the risk' in practitioner versions only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: baseline participants / followed up over 2 years
age- and sex-adjusted risk of progressing to major mobility limitation, preclinical vs no limitation

claims.claim: Limitation: the US studies were in initially high-functioning women aged 70 to 79 in Baltimore, enrolled in 1994 and 1995.
claims.supporting_passage: Weiss (Methods): "Participants were recruited from a sample representing the higher functioning two-thirds of women age 70–79 in eastern Baltimore City and Baltimore County, Maryland and were enrolled in 1994 and 1995." Fried 2000: "The participants were 436 community-dwelling women, 70-80 years of age at baseline, not cognitively impaired, and reporting difficulty in no areas, or only one area, of physical function".
claims.location: Weiss 2012 Methods (Scite Smart Citation snippet); Fried 2000 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Population description.
claims.safe_wording: The main studies were of women aged 70 to 79 in Baltimore who were among the more able two thirds of their age group when recruited in the mid-1990s; a smaller Finnish study found the same in men and women.
claims.qualifications: State in every version.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: enrolment years, Women's Health and Aging Study II

claims.claim: Finding people at the preclinical stage gives strength and balance work 'more to work with' (earlier intervention prevents disability).
claims.pico_timeframe: No intervention trial targeting people identified by preclinical disability was found or checked in this batch. The cohort authors suggest screening and targeting as a 'potential basis' (Fried 2000) and Weiss 2012 says PCMD 'appears to be a target for programs', which are hypotheses, not tested effects.
claims.safe_wording: Do not claim that acting at this stage prevents disability. Permissible: 'The researchers suggested this stage could be a point to offer help; that has not been tested in these studies.'
claims.qualifications: Drop the inference, as the judge advised.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit.

claims.claim: In 29 trials (13,766 people), CGA for older people admitted to hospital increased the chance of being alive and at home at 3 to 12 months and reduced nursing home admission (high certainty), with little or no difference in death or dependence.
claims.supporting_passage: We included 29 trials recruiting 13,766 participants across nine, mostly high-income countries. CGA increases the likelihood that patients will be alive and in their own homes at 3 to 12 months' follow-up (risk ratio (RR) 1.06, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.01 to 1.10; 16 trials, 6799 participants; high-certainty evidence), results in little or no difference in mortality at 3 to 12 months' follow-up (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.07; 21 trials, 10,023 participants; high-certainty evidence), decreases the likelihood that patients will be admitted to a nursing home at 3 to 12 months follow-up (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.89; 14 trials, 6285 participants; high-certainty evidence) and results in little or no difference in dependence (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.04; 14 trials, 6551 participants; high-certainty evidence).
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults admitted to hospital (acute care or inpatient rehabilitation after acute admission); CGA on geriatric wards or by mobile teams vs usual care; outcomes at 3 to 12 months; randomised trials to October 2016.
claims.safe_wording: A Cochrane review of 29 trials with 13,766 older people found that full specialist assessment and care in hospital meant more people were alive and living in their own home 3 to 12 months later, and fewer moved into a care home. It made little or no difference to the number who died or to how much help people needed with daily tasks.
claims.qualifications: Effects are modest (see C05-08-b for absolute numbers). Trials were mostly in high-income countries and span several decades. 'Dependence' showed little or no difference, so do not claim CGA improves day-to-day function.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Cost-effectiveness is low certainty (abstract).

numbers.meaning: trials and participants
alive and in own home at 3 to 12 months, high certainty
nursing home admission at 3 to 12 months, high certainty
mortality, high certainty
dependence, high certainty

claims.claim: Absolute effects of hospital CGA per 1,000 people (Cochrane summary of findings).
claims.supporting_passage: Summary of findings for the main comparison: Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) versus admission to hospital without CGA. Anticipated absolute effects (95% CI), Risk with usual care / Risk with CGA: Living at home (end of follow-up 3 to 12 months): Study population 561 per 1000 / 595 per 1000 (567 to 617). Mortality (end of follow-up 3 to 12 months): Study population 230 per 1000 / 230 per 1000 (214 to 247). Admission to a nursing home (end of follow-up 3 to 12 months): Study population 186 per 1000 / 151 per 1000 (136 to 169). Dependence: Study population 291 per 1000 / 282 per 1000 (259 to 302). Footnote: "*The risk in the intervention group (and its 95% confidence interval) is based on assumed risk in the comparison group and the relative effect of the intervention (and its 95% CI)."
claims.location: Summary of findings table for the main comparison, PDF page 6 (transcribed by Undermind read_pdfs reading agent)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C05-08-a; assumed control risks are the study-population risks.
claims.safe_wording: For every 100 older people admitted to hospital, about 3 more were alive and living at home 3 to 12 months later with specialist geriatric assessment and care (about 60 in 100 compared with 56 in 100), and about 3 to 4 fewer had moved into a care home (about 15 in 100 compared with 19 in 100). Deaths were the same: 23 in 100 in both groups.
claims.qualifications: Numbers were transcribed from the PDF by a reading agent; the nursing home figure implies a ratio of about 0.81 against the abstract's 0.80, so keep the rounded 'about 3 to 4 fewer in 100'. Absolute differences are percentage points of the study population.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small absolute gain; worth stating plainly alongside the high certainty.

numbers.meaning: alive and at home, usual care vs CGA, 3 to 12 months (about 3 more per 100)
nursing home admission, usual care vs CGA, 3 to 12 months (about 3 to 4 fewer per 100)
mortality, 3 to 12 months (no difference)
dependence (little or no difference)

claims.claim: In 21 studies (7,893 people), CGA for frail older people living in the community probably made little or no difference to death, made little or no difference to nursing home admission (high certainty), and may reduce unplanned hospital admission (low certainty).
claims.supporting_passage: We included 21 studies involving 7893 participants across 10 countries and four continents. ... CGA probably leads to little or no difference in mortality during a median follow-up of 12 months (risk ratio (RR) 0.88, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.76 to 1.02; 18 studies, 7151 participants (adjusted for clustering); moderate-certainty evidence). CGA results in little or no difference in nursing home admissions during a median follow-up of 12 months (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.14; 13 studies, 4206 participants (adjusted for clustering); high-certainty evidence). CGA may decrease the risk of unplanned hospital admissions during a median follow-up of 14 months (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.99; 6 studies, 1716 participants (adjusted for clustering); low-certainty evidence). The effect of CGA on emergency department visits is uncertain and evidence was very low certainty
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling frail or at-risk older people; CGA at home or in general practice or community clinic vs usual care; median follow-up 12 to 14 months; randomised trials to April 2020.
claims.safe_wording: For frail older people living at home, a Cochrane review of 21 studies found that the same kind of assessment made little or no difference to deaths or to care home moves over about a year. It may reduce unplanned hospital admissions, but that evidence is weak.
claims.qualifications: 'Probably' for mortality (moderate certainty); 'may' for unplanned admissions (low certainty, only 6 studies). Absolute effects not available (see C05-08-d).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Mortality confidence interval (0.76 to 1.02) includes a possible benefit; 'little or no difference' is the review's wording.

numbers.meaning: studies and participants
mortality, median 12 months, moderate certainty
nursing home admission, median 12 months, high certainty
unplanned hospital admission, median 14 months, low certainty, 6 studies

claims.claim: Absolute effects per 100 for community CGA.
claims.location: Not found: the summary of findings table could not be opened (PubMed full text returned abstract only; Scite and Undermind had no full text).
claims.safe_wording: Give no absolute numbers for the community row. Describe it in words: little or no difference in deaths or care home moves; may reduce unplanned admissions, low-certainty evidence.
claims.qualifications: Do not compute absolute numbers from the relative risks without the control-group risk.

claims.claim: CGA is defined as a multidimensional, multidisciplinary diagnostic and therapeutic process that leads to a coordinated plan for treatment and follow-up, not only an assessment.
claims.supporting_passage: Ellis 2017: "Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) is a multi-dimensional, multi-disciplinary diagnostic and therapeutic process conducted to determine the medical, mental, and functional problems of older people with frailty so that a co-ordinated and integrated plan for treatment and follow-up can be developed." Briggs 2022: "CGA is not limited simply to assessment, but also directs a holistic management plan for older people, which leads to tangible interventions."
claims.location: Ellis 2017 Abstract, Background; Briggs 2022 Abstract, Background
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition.
claims.safe_wording: In the Cochrane reviews, comprehensive geriatric assessment means a team assessing a frail older person's medical, mental and functional problems, then making and following up a coordinated plan of treatment. A form or a one-off assessment on its own is not what was tested.
claims.qualifications: The last sentence is an interpretation of the definition; keep it as such.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: The 2011 meta-analysis suggested larger benefit from designated wards than visiting teams; the 2017 update judged this comparison underpowered and uncertain.
claims.supporting_passage: Ellis 2011 BMJ: "Subgroup interaction suggested differences between the subgroups 'wards' and 'teams' in favour of wards." Ellis 2017: "We are uncertain whether data show a difference in effect between wards and teams, as this analysis was underpowered."
claims.location: Ellis 2011 Abstract, Results; Ellis 2017 Abstract, Authors' conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: Subgroup comparison of CGA delivery model within hospital trials.
claims.safe_wording: An earlier 2011 analysis suggested dedicated geriatric wards did better than visiting teams, but the 2017 update said the data were too few to tell.
claims.qualifications: Subgroup analysis; do not state that wards are better.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Genuine uncertainty.

claims.claim: Position: services that call themselves CGA should be judged on whether they deliver and follow up a plan; claims for community services should match the more modest evidence.
claims.supporting_passage: See C05-08-c and C05-08-e.
claims.pico_timeframe: Editorial judgement based on definition and effect estimates.
claims.safe_wording: Mark as judgement: 'A service using the name should be able to show the plan and the follow-up, not only the assessment.' The reviews did not test services that assess without acting.
claims.qualifications: Judgement, not a finding. Avoid implying community CGA is useless: the evidence shows no clear effect on deaths or care home moves and a possible reduction in admissions.

claims.claim: CAPABLE trial design: 300 low-income adults aged 65 and over in Baltimore with difficulty in daily tasks; up to 10 home visits over 5 months from an occupational therapist, a nurse and a home repair worker, working on goals the person chose; controls had 10 social visits.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "In this randomized clinical trial of 300 low-income community-dwelling adults with a disability in Baltimore, Maryland, between March 18, 2012, and April 29, 2016, 65 years or older, cognitively intact, and with self-reported difficulty with 1 or more activities of daily living (ADLs) or 2 or more instrumental ADLs (IADLs) ... The CAPABLE group received up to 10 home visits over 5 months by occupational therapists, registered nurses, and home modifiers to address self-identified functional goals by enhancing individual capacity and the home environment. The control group received 10 social home visits by a research assistant." Full text: "For 5 months, CAPABLE participants receive up to 6 one-hour home sessions with the OT; up to 4 one-hour home sessions with the RN; and up to $1300 worth of home repairs, modifications, and assistive devices. The cost of delivering CAPABLE services in this trial was $2825 per person" ... "In consultation with the team, the home modifier stabilizes stairs, levels flooring, and repairs floors".
claims.pico_timeframe: 300 low-income, cognitively intact adults 65+, Baltimore, 2012 to 2016; CAPABLE vs attention control (social visits); outcomes at 5 and 12 months.
claims.safe_wording: A US trial offered 300 older people on low incomes in Baltimore, who had difficulty with everyday tasks, up to 10 home visits over 5 months: up to 6 from an occupational therapist, up to 4 from a nurse, and repairs or equipment from a handyperson, all aimed at goals each person chose. The comparison group had 10 friendly social visits.
claims.qualifications: Repairs were capped at 1,300 US dollars per person; total programme cost 2,825 US dollars per person in the trial.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: participants randomised (152 CAPABLE, 148 control)
up to 6 OT, up to 4 nurse sessions
cap on home repairs, modifications and devices per person
cost of delivering CAPABLE per person in the trial

claims.claim: At 5 months, difficulty scores for basic daily activities were about 30% lower in the CAPABLE group than in the control group.
claims.supporting_passage: In unadjusted analyses, participants in the intervention group reported a 26% reduction (relative risk [RR], 0.74; 95% CI, 0.57-0.97; P = .03) in ADL disability scores compared with participants in the control group. ... In adjusted analyses, the CAPABLE treatment effect on ADL disability scores remained statistically significant (30% reduction; RR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.54-0.93; P = .01) ... a The effect-size estimates are presented as the ratio of means between the intervention group (CAPABLE) and the attention control group after accounting for study attrition. ... Activities of daily living refer to self-reported difficulty or need for help when performing 8 essential ADLs: walking across a small room, bathing, upper-body dressing, lower-body dressing, eating, using the toilet, transferring in and out of bed, and grooming.
claims.location: Full text Results (5-month outcomes), Table 2 footnote a, Methods (Outcomes)
claims.pico_timeframe: CAPABLE vs attention control; outcome: self-reported ADL disability score (8 tasks, 0 to 16); 5 months (end of programme); ratio of mean scores.
claims.safe_wording: After 5 months, people who had the programme reported less difficulty with basic tasks such as washing, dressing, using the toilet and getting in and out of bed than people who had social visits. On average their difficulty scores were about 30% lower (a relative comparison).
claims.qualifications: Relative effect only: a ratio of average scores, not a proportion of people. Absolute scores were not available (C05-19-f). Self-reported outcome in an unblinded intervention, though interviewers were masked. The control group also improved.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Benefit faded by 12 months (C05-19-d); a 2025 trial after hospital discharge did not improve ADLs (C05-19-h).

numbers.meaning: adjusted ADL disability score, CAPABLE vs control, 5 months (about 30% lower, relative)
unadjusted, 5 months (26% lower, relative)
ADL score range, 8 tasks scored 0 to 2; 1 point considered clinically meaningful

claims.claim: The 17% reduction in difficulty with household tasks (IADLs) was not statistically clear.
claims.supporting_passage: In adjusted analyses ... the effect on IADL scores was still not statistically significant (17% reduction; RR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.65-1.06; P = .13) (Table 2). ... Instrumental activities of daily living refer to self-reported difficulty or need for help when performing 8 tasks: using the phone, shopping, preparing food, light housekeeping, washing laundry, traveling independently, taking medications, and managing finances independently.
claims.pico_timeframe: Same trial; IADL score at 5 months.
claims.safe_wording: The trial did not show a clear difference for household tasks such as shopping, cooking and laundry.
claims.qualifications: Not 'no effect': the result was uncertain.

numbers.meaning: adjusted IADL score, 5 months; not statistically clear

claims.claim: By 12 months (7 months after visits ended), the difference in basic daily activities was no longer statistically clear.
claims.supporting_passage: Unadjusted analyses showed that participants in the intervention group reported a statistically nonsignificant 7% improvement in ADL disability scores (RR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.72-1.21; P = .60) from baseline to 12-month measurement (7 months after the conclusion of CAPABLE visits), compared with the control participants. ... In adjusted analyses, the effect on ADL (RR, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.68- 1.18; P = .44) and IADL (RR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.81-1.31; P = .80) scores remained statistically nonsignificant (Table 2). ... The effect of the CAPABLE intervention diminished between 5 and 12 months, which may suggest that a booster visit or call could be useful.
claims.pico_timeframe: Same trial; 12-month follow-up.
claims.safe_wording: Seven months after the visits stopped, the difference between the groups had faded and was no longer clear.
claims.qualifications: State as plainly as the 5-month result (house style: the result that went the other way).

numbers.meaning: adjusted ADL score at 12 months; not statistically clear

claims.claim: More CAPABLE participants said the programme made their life easier (82% vs 43%).
claims.supporting_passage: The intervention group participants (n=119), compared with controls (n=123), responded with a great deal to the following survey items: overall benefit (91.6% [109] vs 63.4% [78]; P < .001); the CAPABLE program made their life easier (82.3% [98] vs 43.1% [53]; P < .001), made their home safer (82.3% [98] vs 28.5% [35]; P < .001), kept them living at home (79.8% [95] vs 43.4% [53]; P < .001)
claims.pico_timeframe: Participants who completed the end-of-programme survey (119 CAPABLE, 123 control) at 5 months; response 'a great deal'.
claims.safe_wording: About 8 in 10 people who had the programme said it made their life easier 'a great deal', compared with about 4 in 10 of those who had social visits.
claims.qualifications: Survey of those who answered, not all randomised; self-report; participants knew which programme they had.

numbers.meaning: 'made life easier' a great deal, CAPABLE vs control, survey respondents at 5 months
'made home safer' a great deal

claims.claim: Absolute ADL disability scores in each group.
claims.location: Not found: Table 1 and Table 2 values were not rendered by PubMed full text, Scite read_fulltext or search excerpts; Undermind could not retrieve the PDF; Europe PMC blocked by network policy.
claims.safe_wording: Do not give absolute scores. Label the 30% as a relative difference in average difficulty scores, and lead with the plain description and the 8 in 10 vs 4 in 10 survey result.
claims.qualifications: The judge asked for absolute scores; they remain unverified.

claims.claim: Population limits: 87% women, most self-identified as Black, low income, one US city.
claims.supporting_passage: Of the 152 participants in the intervention group, 133 (87.5%) were women and 19 (12.5%) were men, with a mean (SD) age of 75.7 (7.6) years, and 126 (82.9%) self-identified as black. Of the 148 participants in the control group, 129 (87.2%) were women ... and 133 (89.9%) self-identified as black. ... In addition, this study was limited to low-income older adults in Baltimore, Maryland, and the sample was predominantly black women, which may limit generalizability.
claims.pico_timeframe: Population description.
claims.safe_wording: Most participants were Black women with low incomes in one US city, so the results may not carry over to everyone.

numbers.meaning: women, CAPABLE / control
self-identified as Black, CAPABLE / control
mean age, CAPABLE / control

claims.claim: Conflicting evidence: in a 2025 trial of 268 low-income people recently discharged from hospital, CAPABLE did not improve basic daily activities compared with no further care, though it improved a mobility measure.
claims.supporting_passage: This randomized clinical trial enrolled 268 low-income community-dwelling adults who had been discharged to home from the hospital 60 days prior, had a home health episode, yet had remaining difficulties in at least one activity of daily living. Participants were randomized to no further care or to CAPABLE ... The CAPABLE group decreased their ADL difficulty by -1.76 (CI -2.98, -0.54) and the control group decreased (-0.63: CI -1.86, 0.60) over 5 months, which was not statistically or clinically significant. However, the CAPABLE treatment group demonstrated greater improvement in a composite mobility measure than control participants (-0.52 and -0.02, respectively, p = 0.028). ... Among recently hospitalized persons receiving skilled home health care, CAPABLE did not improve ADLs.
claims.pico_timeframe: 268 low-income adults about 60 days after hospital discharge with remaining ADL difficulty; CAPABLE vs no further care; 5 months.
claims.safe_wording: A second trial, published in 2025, tried the same programme with 268 people on low incomes who had recently left hospital. It did not clearly improve basic daily tasks, although walking and stairs improved more than in the comparison group.
claims.qualifications: Different population (post-hospital, already had home health care) and comparator (no further care). The benefit in people with 4 or more conditions is a subgroup finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: This is the main reason to present CAPABLE as promising rather than established.

numbers.meaning: participants, post-hospital trial
change in ADL difficulty score (range 10 to 50) over 5 months, CAPABLE vs control; difference not statistically or clinically significant

claims.claim: UK action: an occupational therapy assessment of the person and the home can be requested from the GP or local council.
claims.location: Not found: no UK guideline or official document on access to occupational therapy home assessment was found in Drive (search returned only unrelated or confidential files, which were not opened); official web pages cannot be opened here.
claims.safe_wording: Phrase the action as a question without naming who provides it or how: 'If daily tasks at home are getting harder, ask whether an occupational therapist can look at both how you do things and your home.' Do not say CAPABLE or a combined OT, nurse and repair service is available in the UK.
claims.qualifications: Service fact unverified; keep out of captions unless a source is added.

claims.claim: In a UK interview study, 22 people aged 71 to 98 with Clinical Frailty Scale 5 to 8 (mild to very severe frailty), a quarter of them living with dementia, were interviewed in their first 72 hours in hospital about what they wanted from acute care.
claims.supporting_passage: "Participants aged over 65 with Clinical Frailty Score 5-8 (mild to very severe frailty) were recruited during their first 72 hours in a UK hospital." ... "The 22 participants were aged 71 to 98 and had mild to very severe frailty. One quarter were living with dementia. Most participants had reflected on their situation and considered their outcome goals."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people living with frailty (CFS 5 to 8) in emergency or acute hospital care, one UK hospital; semi-structured interviews within the first 72 hours; outcome goals for acute care; no comparator.
claims.safe_wording: Researchers interviewed 22 people aged 71 to 98 living with frailty, a quarter of them with dementia, in their first three days in a UK hospital, and asked what they wanted from their care.
claims.qualifications: One hospital, 22 people, qualitative. Say 'a small interview study' and give the number. The paper calls the scale the 'Clinical Frailty Score'; the scale's usual name is Clinical Frailty Scale.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found that contradicts the themes; Phelps 2022 (C05-13-j) reports similar goals in a different sample.

numbers.meaning: people interviewed (whole sample)
age range of participants in years
inclusion range, described as mild to very severe frailty
timing of recruitment after arrival in hospital
proportion of the 22 living with dementia

claims.claim: The outcome goals grouped into 'Autonomy' (information, control, security) and 'Functioning' (physical, psychosocial, relief); 'relief' meant relief from distressing symptoms.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Theme categories (and corresponding sub-categories) were 'Autonomy' (information, control, and security) and 'Functioning' (physical, psychosocial, and relief)." Full text: "In choosing to attend for acute healthcare, participants sought relief from distressing symptoms and support to overcome limitations in physical and psychosocial function."
claims.location: Abstract, Results; Results (full-text excerpt via Scite)
claims.safe_wording: What they wanted fell into two groups. One was having some control: understanding what was happening, having a say, and feeling safe. The other was being able to function: to move and do things, to keep up their relationships and activities, and to get relief from distressing symptoms.
claims.qualifications: These are themes, not frequencies; do not say 'most people wanted X' except for security (see C05-13-c). For the visual, 'to have a say' should be qualified by C05-13-e (to be asked how much say they want).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors note the boundaries between categories were indistinct.

claims.claim: A theme new to the literature was security: participants wanted to feel safe in their usual living place and with their health problems; this was common to most participants.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "A novel 'security' theme was identified, whereby participants sought to feel safe in their usual living place and with their health problems." Full text (Conclusions): "The novel sub-theme 'security', comprising feeling safe in living place, routine, and health, was common to most interview participants."
claims.location: Abstract, Results; Conclusions (full-text excerpt via Scite)
claims.safe_wording: A goal the researchers had not seen described before was security: wanting to feel safe at home, in their routine and with their health problems. Most of the 22 people raised it.
claims.qualifications: 'Novel' is the authors' description relative to earlier studies of older people in general.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: participants for whom the security theme was common (not quantified further)

claims.claim: People with milder frailty were concerned to keep supporting loved ones; those with the most severe frailty were concerned about being a burden on others.
claims.supporting_passage: "Those living with milder frailty were concerned to maintain ability to support loved ones, while those living with most severe frailty were concerned about burdening others."
claims.location: Abstract, Results (complete in the PubMed record)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C05-13-a; comparison across frailty severity within the 22 participants.
claims.safe_wording: People with milder frailty wanted to keep being able to help the people they love. People with the most severe frailty worried about being a burden on others.
claims.qualifications: Pattern within a small qualitative sample; not a measured difference. The word 'burden' here is the participants' concern, which STYLE.md allows; do not describe older people as a burden.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found. The candidate's note that the severe-frailty finding was cut off is resolved: the full abstract is in PubMed.

claims.claim: Not all participants wanted to be active decision-makers; participants with frailty wished first to be asked how involved they wanted to be.
claims.supporting_passage: Full text (Results): "Participants preferred varying degrees of active involvement in healthcare decision-making personally or with relatives and wished to be consulted on this." Full text (Discussion): "Older people in general wished to be active decision-makers, whereas that was not always the case among these participants with frailty, who first wished to be asked about their preferred degree of involvement."
claims.location: Results and Discussion (full-text excerpts via Scite)
claims.safe_wording: Not everyone wanted to make the decisions themselves. Some wanted relatives involved. What they wanted was to be asked how involved they wished to be.
claims.qualifications: Supports a closing question for staff, such as 'How much do you want to be involved in decisions about your care today, and who else should be part of them?' Present the question as a suggestion drawn from the study, not as a tested intervention.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: Acute care for older people is usually judged by service measures such as waiting times and time targets, length of stay, readmission and deaths, which the researchers argue may not capture what older people living with frailty consider meaningful.
claims.supporting_passage: van Oppen 2022, Introduction (Scite citation-context excerpt): "As emergency departments (ED) worldwide become crowded increasingly frequently, poorer attainment of time targets can be expected" ... "Older people living with frailty are at particular risk of prolonged length of stay, as well as other adverse outcomes including mortality and functional decline. These outcomes are service metrics and, while useful for managers, may not capture what older people consider meaningful." van Oppen 2024, Abstract (Background): "Current acute healthcare service metrics are not meaningful for older people living with frailty. Healthcare knowledge, situational security, and physical and psychosocial function are important outcomes typically not collected." Phelps 2022, Discussion (Scite citation-context excerpt): "Emergency care research and quality improvement usually focuses upon service metrics such as length of stay and readmission rates, which do not necessarily align with patient perspectives."
claims.pico_timeframe: Authors' description of current emergency and acute care quality measures; not a survey or audit of what services record.
claims.safe_wording: Emergency care is usually judged on things like waiting times, length of stay and readmissions. The research team behind this study argue that these measures miss much of what people living with frailty want from their care, such as understanding what is happening and feeling safe.
claims.qualifications: These are the authors' statements in introductions and discussions, not measured findings. Do not say services 'never' or 'do not' record these outcomes as a fact; say they are 'usually judged on' service measures and attribute the argument. The visual's left column ('time in the department, admitted or not, length of stay') is fair as a description of common service measures.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Some services do use patient-reported experience measures; no audit of UK acute care measures was opened in this batch.

claims.claim: A systematic review found no patient-reported outcome measure designed for older people with frailty in emergency care; the existing measures mainly assessed functioning, with limited coverage of autonomy.
claims.supporting_passage: "There is no person-reported outcome measure (PROM) for older people with frailty and emergency care needs." ... "Of 9392 unique citations screened, we appraised the full texts of 158 studies. Nine studies were identified, evaluating nine PROMs." ... "PROMs mainly assessed 'Functioning' constructs, with limited coverage of 'Autonomy'."
claims.pico_timeframe: PROMs used 2010 to 2021 by older people living with frailty in acute hospital care; mapping of instrument content against the Autonomy and Functioning framework.
claims.safe_wording: When the same team reviewed existing questionnaires in 2022, the ones used with older people in acute care mostly asked about physical and daily functioning. Few asked about understanding, control or feeling safe.
claims.qualifications: Situation up to 2021; PROM-OPAC has since been developed (C05-13-h). Optional claim.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The mapping uses the authors' own framework.

numbers.meaning: PROMs identified in 9 studies (from 9392 citations screened)

claims.claim: A patient-reported outcome measure built on these goals (PROM-OPAC) was field-tested with 241 people living with frailty within 72 hours of an emergency attendance and had acceptable reliability; further evaluation is needed.
claims.supporting_passage: "People aged 65+ with Clinical Frailty Scale 5-8 were recruited within seventy-two hours of an emergency attendance." ... "241 people participated." ... "The final eight-item draft had acceptable reliability (Cronbach's alpha: 0.71), structure (two factors for self-determination and security; RMSEA: 0.065; TLI: 0.917; CFI: 0.944), and construct validity (lower scores from respondents waiting longer and requiring admission). Feasibility was promising (response rate 39%; 98% responses complete; median completion time 11 (IQR: 12) minutes)." ... "Administration of the PROM-OPAC appeared feasible and the instrument had acceptable psychometric properties. Further evaluation is required to assess generalisability."
claims.pico_timeframe: People aged 65 and over, CFS 5 to 8, within 72 hours of emergency attendance; three-stage field-testing; cross-sectional.
claims.safe_wording: The team has since built an eight-question measure from these goals, covering self-determination and security. In testing with 241 people living with frailty in emergency care, it worked acceptably, and the authors say it needs further evaluation.
claims.qualifications: Say 'eight-question' and '241 people'. Do not quote Cronbach's alpha or fit indices for the public. The link between lower scores and longer waits or admission is a cross-sectional validity check, not evidence that waiting causes lower scores; if mentioned, say 'people who waited longer or were admitted tended to score lower'. The response rate was 39%.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Development by the same group; generalisability not yet shown.

numbers.meaning: participants across the three field-testing stages
items in the final draft measure
response rate among those approached
responses that were complete
median completion time
Cronbach's alpha (internal consistency); practitioner use only

claims.claim: In a 2026 study, 60 older people living with frailty and significant cognitive impairment completed PROM-OPAC during emergency care; 92% of responses were complete, with a median time of 8 minutes.
claims.supporting_passage: "PROM-OPAC is currently the only PROM for Older People living with frailty receiving Acute Care. However, there is limited evidence for its feasibility among the 40% of that cohort who have cognitive impairment." ... "60 people (63% (95% CI 53% to 73%) of 95 approached) with significant cognitive impairment participated (median 6CIT 21/28; IQR 16-25). 92% responses were complete, with median time 8 (IQR 5-11) min. Internal consistency was acceptable (Cronbach's alpha, 0.70) but the observed response distribution (SD <1 in two items) and end effects suggested interpretability issues." ... "Older people living with frailty and cognitive impairment can complete PROMs during emergency care."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people living with frailty and significant cognitive impairment, one UK emergency setting; feasibility and reliability; cross-sectional.
claims.safe_wording: A 2026 study found that people living with frailty and significant memory and thinking problems could answer these questions in the emergency department: 60 of 95 people approached took part, and most completed it in about 8 minutes.
claims.qualifications: Single site; some items had interpretability issues. The '40% of that cohort' figure is background from the introduction, not a finding of this study; do not present it as one. Optional claim.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Interpretability issues noted by the authors.

numbers.meaning: people with significant cognitive impairment approached who took part
responses complete
median completion time

claims.claim: A second interview study (24 patients and 16 carers, three English hospitals) found similar goals (diagnosis and resolution of the problem, information for them and relatives, a well-planned discharge home, keeping mobility and function) and participants felt many goals were not attained.
claims.supporting_passage: "Forty participants were interviewed either alone or jointly (24 patients and 16 carers), describing episodes of urgent care which started in ED for 28 patients. The goals of care for participants accessing emergency care were that their medical problem be diagnosed and resolved; information about tests and treatment be given to them and their relatives; they receive an appropriate well-planned discharge to their own home with support where needed and without readmission or re-attendance at ED; and that they retain mobility, function and normal activities. Participants perceived that many of these goals of care were not attained." ... "Older people living with frailty have heterogeneous urgent care goals which require individual ascertainment."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people living with frailty and carers, three hospitals in England, interviewed after an urgent care episode in 2019.
claims.safe_wording: A separate study of 24 patients and 16 carers in three English hospitals heard similar aims: find and treat the problem, explain it to us and our family, plan a safe discharge home, and help me keep moving. Many felt these aims were not met.
claims.qualifications: 'Not attained' is participants' perception, not a measured rate. Optional corroborating claim; it shows the goals are not unique to one hospital.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: participants (24 patients, 16 carers)
hospitals in England
patients whose care episode started in the emergency department

claims.claim: A 2024 systematic review of 19 studies of older people's experiences of frailty found resistance to the medical use of the term frail.
claims.supporting_passage: "Thirty-four studies were subsequently excluded as they did not address the systematic review question, leaving 17 included in the final review. An additional two studies were identified via grey literature sources. Older persons' experiences of frailty were synthesised with reference to three themes: (i) living with frailty: a multidimensional experience; (ii) living with frailty: acceptability and associations; and (iii) living with frailty: resisting and adapting and losing control." ... "Older persons' experiences of frailty revealed a resistance to the biomedical use of the term generally used in clinical practice."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older persons living with frailty; qualitative meta-synthesis; literature to January 2024.
claims.safe_wording: A 2024 review brought together 19 studies of older people's own accounts of frailty. Many resisted the medical label 'frail' being applied to them, and described frailty in broader terms than clinicians usually do.
claims.qualifications: Qualitative synthesis; 'many' rather than a proportion. Abstract only. Use this review, not a single study, for the general statement that many older people dislike or resist the word.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Schoenborn 2018 (C05-10-d) found people who were frail were more open to discussing frailty than those who were not, so resistance to the word is not the same as not wanting the information.

numbers.meaning: studies included (17 from databases plus 2 from grey literature)

claims.claim: In a 2024 interview study within a home rehabilitation trial, older people saw the frail label as negative and something to avoid, and the authors concluded the term needs to be used cautiously; some participants saw frailty as temporary and reducible with exercise and activity.
claims.supporting_passage: "Ninety three HERO trial participants were sampled for the process evaluation with a total of 60 observational home visits and 35 interviews were undertaken. There was a wide range in perceptions about what it meant to be classified as frail with no clear understanding from our participants. However, there was a negative attitude towards frailty with it being considered something that needed to be avoided where possible. Frailty was seen as part of a negative decline that people struggled to associate with. There was discussion about frailty being temporary and that it could be reduced or avoided with sufficient physical exercise and activity." ... "Having a label of being "frail" was deemed to be negative and something to be avoided, suggesting the term needs to be used cautiously."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people taking part in a home-based rehabilitation trial (HERO); secondary qualitative analysis of interviews and observed visits.
claims.safe_wording: In a 2024 study of 35 interviews with older people in a home rehabilitation trial, being labelled frail was seen as negative and something to avoid. The researchers concluded the word needs to be used with care. Some participants saw frailty as something exercise and activity could reduce.
claims.qualifications: Do not name the country in the post unless checked (author affiliations are UK; abstract does not say). Participants were in a rehabilitation trial.

numbers.meaning: interviews
observed home visits
trial participants sampled for the process evaluation

claims.claim: In US focus groups with 29 community-dwelling older adults, participants wanted to know how to treat or prevent frailty and the risks it carries, and many felt this information could be given without the word 'frail', which they saw as negative.
claims.supporting_passage: "The participants' mean age was 76.3. Of the 29 participants, 21 (72%) were female, and 21 (72%) were white." ... "3) Participants wanted know about how to treat or prevent frailty and the risks associated with being frail. Many participants felt that these information can be conveyed without necessarily using the specific term "frail", which they perceived to have a negative connotation." ... Conclusions: "Further research is needed to understand acceptable ways for communicating about frailty in clinical practice." Full text (Discussion): "Furthermore, given the negative reactions to the term "frailty" and that the interventions are not exclusive to frailty, it is conceivable that clinicians may make the appropriate recommendations without having to explicitly discuss frailty."
claims.location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions; Discussion (Scite excerpt)
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling older adults in the USA, focus groups stratified by frailty status (Fried criteria); perceptions and informational needs; no comparator intervention.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study, 29 older people in focus groups said they wanted to know their risks and how to prevent or treat frailty. Many felt this could be explained without the word 'frail', which they heard as negative.
claims.qualifications: One small US study; name the size (29 people). The authors call for research on acceptable ways to communicate about frailty: no study has tested which wording works better, so present the 'translate the assessment' approach as a suggestion, not a proven method.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C05-10-d: people who were frail were more willing to hear the word.

numbers.meaning: focus group participants
mean age in years
female participants

claims.claim: In the same study, participants who were frail were more receptive to discussing their frailty status with clinicians than those who were non-frail or pre-frail.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "2) Compared to participants who were non-frail or pre-frail, participants who were frail were more receptive to discussing their frailty status with clinicians". Full text (Results): "On the contrary, both of the focus groups consisting of frail participants were much more amenable to discussing frailty status with clinicians than the non-frail and the pre-frail participants. “We want to know what’s going on and how to treat it and we are not afraid to hear these words, we get more upset that you didn’t tell us.”" Full text (Discussion): "We were surprised to find that the more frail participants were more receptive to discussing frailty, as compared to the non-frail and pre-frail participants." Limitation: "Lastly, for most of the frail participants, several years have lapsed since their frailty assessment and their frailty status may have changed."
claims.location: Abstract, Results; Results and Discussion (Scite full-text excerpts)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C05-10-c; comparison between focus groups by frailty status (two frail groups).
claims.safe_wording: In that study, the people who were frail were more willing to talk about frailty with their doctors than those who were not. One participant said: "We want to know what's going on and how to treat it and we are not afraid to hear these words, we get more upset that you didn't tell us."
claims.qualifications: Two focus groups of frail participants in one US study; frailty status had been assessed years earlier for most. The quotation is a participant's words from the published paper and may be quoted with attribution ('a participant in a US study'); do not present it as said to Alasdair or as a UK patient. This finding means the post must not suggest avoiding frank discussion of risk.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Other studies (C05-10-a, C05-10-b, C05-10-e) report resistance to the label among people classed as frail; the difference may reflect willingness to discuss information versus acceptance of the label as an identity.

numbers.meaning: focus groups of frail participants

claims.claim: In an interview study of 29 people aged 66 to 98 in the South West of England, participants described being labelled 'old and frail' by others as encouraging a frailty identity, including loss of interest in social and physical activities; most resisted identifying as frail.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Twenty-nine participants aged 66–98 with varying degrees of frailty, residing either in their homes or institutional settings, participated in semi-structured interviews." ... "Being labelled by others as 'old and frail' contributed to the development of a frailty identity by encouraging attitudinal and behavioural confirmation of it, including a loss of interest in participating in social and physical activities, poor physical health and increased stigmatisation." Full text (Methods): "All participants lived in the South West of England and the sample included both community dwellers and care home residents." Full text (Results): "Most participants actively resisted the identity, even those who could be classified as frail using objective criteria." Full text (Discussion): "As participants in this study expressed, being labelled as frail – particularly against one’s will – was seen as damaging to health, because it may lead to behavioural confirmation of the label." and "The current participants described the readiness of others to label them as frail, often on the basis of isolated events or temporary impairments."
claims.location: Abstract; Methods, Results and Discussion (Scite full-text excerpts)
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with varying frailty in the South West of England (home and care home); grounded theory interviews; perceptions only, no measured outcome.
claims.safe_wording: In an English study of 29 people aged 66 to 98, participants described how being called 'old and frail' by others could lead people to see themselves that way and give up activities. Most resisted the label, including some who met frailty criteria.
claims.qualifications: This is what participants described and how the researchers interpreted it; the study did not measure whether labelling reduces activity. Do not write that the word 'causes' people to stop exercising. Say 'may' and attribute it: 'older people in one study described...'. If a direct quotation is used in a post, quote the abstract sentence, since the full-text sentence contains dashes that the house style does not allow.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Schoenborn 2018 (C05-10-d) found frail participants more willing to discuss frailty. The authors of this study also note that identifying as frail can sometimes help people get support.

numbers.meaning: participants interviewed
age range in years

claims.claim: International frailty guidelines recommend, as first-line treatment, a physical activity programme with a resistance (strength) training component, with protein or calorie supplements when weight loss or undernutrition is present, and a fuller assessment for people who screen positive.
claims.supporting_passage: "For individuals screened as positive for frailty, a more comprehensive clinical assessment should be performed to identify signs and underlying mechanisms of frailty (strong recommendation)." ... "First-line therapy for the management of frailty should include a multi-component physical activity programme with a resistance-based training component (strong recommendation). Protein/caloric supplementation is recommended when weight loss or undernutrition are present (conditional recommendation)."
claims.location: Abstract, Recommendations for Screening and Assessment; Recommendations for Management
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with physical frailty; ICFSR guideline 2019, GRADE.
claims.safe_wording: International frailty guidelines recommend an exercise programme that includes strength training as the first step, with extra protein or calories for people who are losing weight or undernourished.
claims.qualifications: The visual's 'strength exercise with enough protein' should become 'exercise that builds strength; extra protein or calories if you are losing weight'. Protein supplements are a conditional recommendation for people losing weight or undernourished, not for everyone.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No recommendation for vitamin D, hormones or cognitive therapy; drug treatment not recommended.

claims.claim: Strength training with protein supplementation has the most consistent evidence for delaying or reversing frailty (candidate's wording).
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 925 studies satisfied search criteria and 46 were included. There were 15 690 participants (median study size was 160 participants). Studies reflected a broad heterogeneity." ... "Interventions with both muscle strength training and protein supplementation were consistently placed highest for effectiveness and ease of implementation."
claims.pico_timeframe: Primary care frailty interventions, RCTs and controlled cohorts to May 2017; relative ranking map, no pooled effect.
claims.safe_wording: Use the guideline wording in C05-10-f instead. If this review is cited, say: 'A review of 46 studies in general practice ranked strength training combined with protein supplements highest among the approaches studied.'
claims.qualifications: 'Most consistent evidence' overstates a relative ranking of heterogeneous studies with no pooled effect. Not essential to this post.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneous evidence; only a minority of studies measured change in frailty status (see C05-B1, claim C05-07-e).

numbers.meaning: included in the review

claims.claim: In a UK study of 73 older migrants from six racialised minority groups, many had not heard the term frailty and did not know what it meant.
claims.supporting_passage: "Photovoice and biographical interviews were used to explore the experience of getting older among 73 participants of 6 different racialised groups living in a UK city." ... "Many of the participants hadn't heard the term frailty and had no understanding of what it might mean." ... "The first theme was more likely to be the case for participants who spoke little English and for those who hadn't been living in the UK for long." ... "Healthcare professionals must consider that older, racially minoritised patients may have never encountered the term frailty before in any type of setting."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older racialised minority migrants in one UK city; qualitative.
claims.safe_wording: In a 2026 UK study of 73 older migrants from six ethnic minority groups, many had never heard the word frailty, especially those who spoke little English or had arrived recently.
claims.qualifications: Optional supporting point for 'ask what the word means to the person'. Qualitative; 'many' is not quantified.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: participants
racialised minority groups represented

claims.claim: OPERAM enrolled 2,008 adults aged 70 or over with multimorbidity and polypharmacy admitted to university hospitals in four European countries; a doctor and pharmacist used STOPP/START software to review medicines; the main outcome was a first drug-related readmission within 12 months.
claims.supporting_passage: "110 clusters of inpatient wards within university based hospitals in four European countries (Switzerland, Netherlands, Belgium, and Republic of Ireland) defined by attending hospital doctors." "2008 older adults (≥70 years) with multimorbidity (≥3 chronic conditions) and polypharmacy (≥5 drugs used long term)." "Clinical staff clusters were randomised to usual care or a structured pharmacotherapy optimisation intervention performed at the individual level jointly by a doctor and a pharmacist, with the support of a clinical decision software system deploying the screening tool of older person's prescriptions and screening tool to alert to the right treatment (STOPP/START) criteria to identify potentially inappropriate prescribing." "Primary outcome was first drug related hospital admission within 12 months."
claims.location: Abstract (Setting, Participants, Interventions, Main outcome measures)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 70+, 3+ chronic conditions, 5+ long-term drugs, hospital inpatients (medical and surgical), Switzerland/Netherlands/Belgium/Ireland; single in-hospital structured review with STOPP/START software plus GP letter vs usual care; first adjudicated drug-related readmission; 12 months
claims.safe_wording: A European trial of 2,008 people aged 70 or over, each with at least 3 long-term conditions and at least 5 regular medicines, tested a structured medicines review in hospital, done by a doctor and a pharmacist with the help of checklist software (STOPP/START). The main question was whether it reduced readmissions caused by medicines over the next year.
claims.qualifications: Hospital inpatients in university hospitals; the review happened once, during the admission, with recommendations also sent to the GP.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None for the design description.

numbers.meaning: participants randomised (963 intervention, 1045 control)
clusters (attending hospital doctors' wards)
age criterion
countries

claims.claim: Step 1-2 of the chain: of 916 people who received the review, 789 (86.1%) had at least one STOPP/START recommendation, a mean of 2.75 each; 2,331 recommendations in all, two thirds to stop or change and one third to start a medicine.
claims.supporting_passage: "Of 916 patients who received the intervention (), 789 (86.1%) had at least one STOPP/START recommendation provided to their attending hospital doctor, with a mean of 2.75 (SD 2.24) recommendations for each participant ()." "In total, 2331 recommendations were made, of which 1524 (65.4%) were STOPP recommendations and 807 (34.6%) were START recommendations."
claims.pico_timeframe: Intervention arm only; recommendations made to attending hospital doctors during the index admission
claims.safe_wording: The review found something to recommend for 86 in 100 people who received it, on average almost 3 recommendations each. About two thirds of the recommendations were to stop a medicine and one third to start one.
claims.qualifications: 86 in 100 is the proportion with at least one flagged prescribing problem in the intervention arm, NOT a reduction and not a between-group result (judge's concern confirmed). The denominator is 916 who received the intervention, not all 963 randomised.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The STOPP/START version 3 paper reports that a later analysis of OPERAM found over half of software-generated recommendations were not considered clinically relevant in individual cases (see C06-04-h), so 'problems found' overstates clinically important problems.

numbers.meaning: intervention patients with at least one STOPP/START recommendation, at the index admission
mean recommendations per participant
total recommendations
share of recommendations that were STOPP (stop or change) / START (start)

claims.claim: Step 3: by 2 months, at least one recommendation had been carried out for 491 people, 62.2% of those with a recommendation, mostly stopping a medicine.
claims.supporting_passage: "After two months, at least one of these recommendations was successfully implemented in 491 participants (62.2% of all participants in the intervention group with ≥1 recommendation), with a mean of 1.16 (SD 1.48) implemented recommendations for each participant, primarily discontinuation of potentially inappropriate drugs ()."
claims.pico_timeframe: Intervention arm, people with at least one recommendation (n=789); implementation assessed at 2 months
claims.safe_wording: By 2 months, at least one recommendation had been acted on for about 6 in 10 of the people who had one (491 of 789). On average, just over 1 recommendation per person was carried out out of almost 3 made.
claims.qualifications: The candidate wording '62.2% of intervention participants' is slightly wrong: the denominator is the 789 with at least one recommendation (the paper's Discussion loosely says 'of participants in the intervention group'). About 4 in 10 had none acted on.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: people with at least one recommendation who had at least one implemented, at 2 months
mean implemented recommendations per participant, vs 2.75 made

claims.claim: Step 4: at 2 months, the proportion of people with an overused, underused or misused medicine, and the number of long-term medicines, were about the same in the intervention and control groups.
claims.supporting_passage: Methods: "Secondary outcomes within two months after enrolment included the presence of drug overuse and misuse (based on STOPP criteria), drug underuse (defined by START criteria), and clinically significant drug-drug interactions". Table 5 (Control n, events (%); Intervention n, events (%); odds ratio (95% CI); P): "Drug misuse§:  2  893  378 (42.3)  832  355 (42.7)  0.99 (0.81 to 1.20)  0.92  Drug overuse§:  2  893  376 (42.1)  832  348 (41.8)  0.99 (0.82 to 1.20)  0.91  Drug underuse§:  2  893  638 (71.4)  832  583 (70.1)  0.91 (0.70 to 1.17)  0.45  Mean (SD) No of long term drugs¶:  2  893  11.0 (4.27)  833  11.2 (4.54)  −0.13 (−0.49 to 0.22)  0.47". Abstract conclusion (for contrast): "Inappropriate prescribing was common in older adults with multimorbidity and polypharmacy admitted to hospital and was reduced through an intervention to optimise pharmacotherapy, but without effect on drug related hospital admissions."

claims.safe_wording: At 2 months, about 42 in 100 people in each group were still on at least one medicine judged to be overused, and about 70 in 100 in each group were missing at least one medicine judged to be indicated. The trial did not show a clear difference between the groups on these measures, or in the number of long-term medicines (about 11 in both).
claims.qualifications: The authors' own conclusion says inappropriate prescribing 'was reduced'; that refers to recommendations implemented within the intervention arm, not to the randomised comparison at 2 months. The post must not say the trial 'cut' or 'reduced' inappropriate prescribing. 'Did not show a clear difference' is the right phrase (non-significant, not proof of no effect).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Why implemented changes did not produce a between-group difference is not explained in the paper; possible reasons (usual-care changes, new prescriptions, measurement) are speculation and must not be stated as findings.
