claims.claim: Step 5: within 12 months, 21.9% of the intervention group and 22.4% of the control group had a first drug-related readmission (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17); falls and deaths also did not clearly differ; quality of life at 12 months was slightly better with the intervention.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "In the intervention group, 211 participants (21.9%) experienced a first drug related hospital admission compared with 234 (22.4%) in the control group. In the intention-to-treat analysis censored for death as competing event (n=375, 18.7%), the hazard ratio for first drug related hospital admission was 0.95 (95% confidence interval 0.77 to 1.17)." Results: "Drug related outcomes, pain, activities of daily living status, and drug adherence did not differ significantly between the groups, except for quality of life at 12 months, which was better in the intervention group (between group adjusted mean difference 2.29, 95% confidence interval 0.31 to 4.26,)." Table 4: "First drug related hospital admission in patients with ≥1 STOPP recommendation implemented after two months*  156/875 (17.8)  64/398 (16.1)  0.88 (0.65 to 1.19)  0.41" (* Post hoc analysis).
claims.location: Abstract (Results); full text Results (Secondary outcomes) and Table 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Randomised comparison; first adjudicated drug-related readmission within 12 months; secondary outcomes falls, death, EQ-VAS quality of life (0 to 100)
claims.safe_wording: Over the following year, about 22 in 100 people in each group were readmitted to hospital because of a medicine. The trial did not show a clear difference. Quality of life scores at 12 months were slightly higher with the review, by about 2 points on a 100-point scale.
claims.qualifications: Say 'did not show a clear difference', not 'no effect'; the confidence interval runs from a 23% relative reduction to a 17% relative increase. The quality-of-life difference is small and was one of many secondary outcomes. The post hoc per-protocol comparison (16.1% vs 17.8%) also did not show a clear difference and is exploratory.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Cochrane 2023 (C06-04-g) finds medication-review interventions may make little or no difference to admissions (low certainty), consistent with OPERAM. A single-centre trial with face-to-face physician delivery (reported in STOPP/START v3 paper) had high implementation and fewer in-hospital ADRs; different outcome and setting.

numbers.meaning: first drug-related readmission within 12 months, intervention vs control
hazard ratio, intention to treat with death as competing event
adjusted difference in EQ-VAS quality of life at 12 months, 0 to 100 scale
deaths during follow-up, both arms

claims.claim: The OPERAM authors suggest the effect of a single review may not persist over a year of contacts with other doctors, and that high mortality may have diluted benefit.
claims.supporting_passage: "Firstly, the impact of a single time point pharmacotherapy optimisation might not persist over a one year follow-up, during which multiple contacts with doctors might occur. Although we provided evidence based recommendations on inappropriate prescribing to patients’ GPs, including reasons for stopping or starting drugs, the contacts with other doctors (eg, specialists) over one year might have resulted in new potentially inappropriate drugs or discontinuation of appropriate drugs, which could have negated an intervention effect." "Secondly, the high mortality rate of the population, approaching 20% at 12 months,"
claims.location: Full text, Discussion (Potential explanations for lack of effect)
claims.pico_timeframe: Authors' interpretation
claims.safe_wording: The trial team suggested that one review in hospital may not last through a year of appointments with other doctors, who may start or stop medicines again.
claims.qualifications: These are the authors' possible explanations, not findings. Label them as such.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: 12-month mortality in the trial population

claims.claim: Across 38 randomised trials, it is uncertain whether medication review and similar pharmaceutical care reduce inappropriate medicines, and they may make little or no difference to hospital admissions or quality of life.
claims.supporting_passage: "We identified 38 studies, which includes an additional 10 in this update." "It is uncertain whether pharmaceutical care reduces the proportion of patients with one or more PIM (risk ratio (RR) 0.81, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.98; I= 84%; 13 studies, 4534 participants; very low-certainty evidence)." "Pharmaceutical care may make little or no difference to hospital admissions (data not pooled; 14 studies, 4797 participants; low-certainty evidence). Pharmaceutical care may make little or no difference to quality of life (data not pooled; 16 studies, 7458 participants; low-certainty evidence)." "It is unclear whether interventions to improve appropriate polypharmacy resulted in clinically significant improvement."
claims.pico_timeframe: People 65+ with 4+ medicines; pharmaceutical care interventions vs usual care; appropriateness measures, admissions, quality of life; trials to January 2021
claims.safe_wording: A Cochrane review of 38 trials found it uncertain whether medicines reviews reduce inappropriate prescribing, and they may make little or no difference to hospital admissions or quality of life. The certainty of this evidence is low or very low.
claims.qualifications: Low and very low certainty: this is an evidence gap as much as evidence of no benefit. Do not say reviews 'do not work'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Individual trials vary; heterogeneity high (I-squared 84% for the proportion with a PIM).

numbers.meaning: randomised trials in the review
risk ratio for proportion with 1 or more PIM, 13 studies, very low certainty
hospital admissions outcome, not pooled, low certainty

claims.claim: In SENATOR, a software-guided STOPP/START review given once to hospital clinicians had about 15% of its advice implemented and did not reduce adverse drug reactions within 14 days; a later OPERAM analysis found over half of software recommendations were not clinically relevant in individual cases.
claims.supporting_passage: SENATOR abstract: "For the primary endpoint, there was no difference between the intervention and control groups (24.5 vs. 24.8%; OR 0.98; 95% CI 0.77-1.24; P = 0.88)." "Among attending clinicians in the intervention group, implementation of SENATOR software-generated medication advice points was poor (~15%)." STOPP/START v3 Discussion: "Recent analysis of the specific STOPP and START criteria elicited in the OPERAM trial shows that over half of all the STOPP and START recommendations generated by the software tool were not  considered clinically relevant in individual cases []."
claims.location: SENATOR Abstract (Results); STOPP/START v3 full text, Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: SENATOR: 1537 older inpatients, six European centres, ADRs within 14 days of randomisation. OPERAM relevance analysis: reported second-hand in the v3 paper
claims.safe_wording: In a second European trial (SENATOR), hospital doctors acted on only about 15 in 100 of the software's suggestions, and side effects in hospital were no less common (about 25 in 100 in both groups).
claims.qualifications: The OPERAM relevance finding is reported second-hand in the STOPP/START v3 paper; the original analysis was not opened, so quote it only as 'a later analysis reported'. SENATOR has a corrigendum whose content was not opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The v3 paper also describes an earlier single-centre trial where a physician explained criteria face to face: implementation 81% (STOPP) and 87% (START), with fewer hospital-acquired ADRs. That trial was not opened; it suggests how the advice is delivered may matter.

numbers.meaning: probable or certain ADRs within 14 days, SENATOR intervention vs control; OR 0.98 (0.77 to 1.24)
SENATOR advice implemented by attending clinicians
OPERAM software recommendations judged not clinically relevant (second-hand report)

claims.claim: In an English cohort, being prescribed a Beers-listed medicine at discharge was not significantly associated with overall medication-related harm, readmission or death at one year, though multiple listed medicines were associated with adverse drug reactions.
claims.supporting_passage: "Two hundred and seventy-six patients (22%) were prescribed one or more PIMs at hospital discharge." "There was no significant relationship between patients prescribed PIMs and overall MRH, hospital readmission or all-cause one-year mortality. Multiple PIMs at discharge was independently associated with an increased risk of ADR (OR 2.32, 95% CI 1.03-5.23)." "The 2015 Beers criteria have a limited clinical value to predict adverse outcomes following hospital discharge in this setting."
claims.pico_timeframe: 1280 people 65+ discharged from English hospitals (2013 to 2015); exposure Beers 2015 PIM at discharge; outcome MRH over 8 weeks, readmission, 1-year mortality
claims.safe_wording: In an English study of older people leaving hospital, being on a medicine from one well-known 'avoid' list (Beers) was not clearly linked with later harm from medicines overall. People on several listed medicines did have more side effects.
claims.qualifications: Observational association; one list (Beers, a US list), not STOPP/START. Must state the multiple-PIM result that went the other way. Optional claim.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Supports the general point that list-based counts are imperfect stand-ins for harm, but it is not evidence about STOPP/START or about OPERAM.

numbers.meaning: prescribed 1 or more Beers PIM at discharge
multiple PIMs vs fewer, adjusted odds of an ADR; do not convert to 'times more likely'

claims.claim: In the PRIME cohort (five English teaching hospitals, 2013 to 2015), 413 of 1,116 people aged 65 or over followed for 8 weeks after discharge (37%) had medication-related harm.
claims.supporting_passage: "Between September 2013 and November 2015, research nurses invited patients to participate from medical wards in five NHS teaching hospitals in Southern England, near to the time of hospital discharge." "Senior, trained research pharmacists followed discharged participants for 8 weeks to determine if they experienced MRH." "Therefore, our final cohort included 1116 (87.2%) participants" "Overall, 413 participants [37.0% (95% CI 34.2–39.9%)] experienced MRH in the 8‐week follow‐up period, with 856 medicines implicated in 621 events."
claims.location: Full text, Methods (Design, setting and participants) and Results (Incidence of MRH)
claims.pico_timeframe: People 65+ (median 82) discharged from medical wards, five teaching hospitals, Southern England, 2013 to 2015; medication-related harm over 8 weeks after discharge; pharmacist follow-up via interview, GP records and readmission review

claims.qualifications: Southern England teaching hospitals, 2013 to 2015. 'Harm' includes side effects, harm from not taking medicines, and a few medication errors; 40% of cases were rated only 'possible' (see C06-13-b).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Record-only studies report lower rates; the authors attribute their higher figure to prospective interviews and inclusion of non-adherence.

numbers.meaning: people with medication-related harm within 8 weeks of discharge
recruited; 1,116 completed follow-up
median age

claims.claim: What counted as harm: an adverse drug reaction, harm from not taking a medicine, or harm from a medication error; most cases were side effects alone; 40% of cases were rated only 'possible'.
claims.supporting_passage: "We defined MRH as an ADR or harm arising from a failure to receive medication owing to non‐adherence. Harm arising from medication error was included where reported. Intentional overdose was excluded." "ADRs were solely responsible for MRH in 301 out of 413 cases (72.9%), non‐adherence in 45 cases (10.9%) and a medication error in 14 cases (3.4%). In five cases (1.2%), the patient experienced harm from both an ADR and a medication error." "In 48 cases (11.6%), harm was due to both an ADR and non‐adherence." "Of the 413 participants whom we classified as having MRH, 246 (60%) experienced at least one MRH event considered ‘probable’ (= 110) or ‘definite’ (= 136). "However, MRH risk (incidence per 1000 prescriptions) was greatest for opiates (399), followed by antibiotics (189)."

claims.claim: Most harm led to healthcare use: 328 of the 413 people with harm (79%) used an NHS service because of it, and 87 were readmitted to hospital because of it; 81% of cases met the study's definition of serious (needing a change of treatment or treatment by a health professional) or worse.

"Four participants (1.0%) experienced a fatal event associated with the MRH" "Nine participants (2.2%) had a life‐threatening event, and MRH was serious in a further 323 participants (78.2%)." Patients were followed up by senior pharmacists to determine MRH occurrence." "Data of 1066 patients (83%) with completed predictions and follow‐up, out of 1280 recruited patients, were analysed." "There was no relationship between doctors' predictions and patient MRH (OR 1.10, 95% CI 0.82–1.46,= 0.53), irrespective of years of clinical experience." claims.claim: In 2017 interviews, 13 GPs and 10 pharmacists in England and Scotland said that, because of workload, most medication reviews were done remotely without involving the patient; several called them a 'tick box' exercise.

Interviews took place between January and October 2017." "Due to high workload pressures and time constraints, interviewees reported that most medication reviews were conducted remotely, without involving the patient. Several GPs and pharmacists described the medication reviews as a ‘tick box’ exercise, which they did in the quickest way possible without involving the patient. Two GPs and most pharmacists argued that a ‘proper’ medication review required patient involvement and could not be done remotely"

claims.claim: NICE guidance emphasises involving the person in medication review; NICE defines a medication review as a structured examination of a person's medicines aiming to reach agreement with the person about treatment.
claims.supporting_passage: Duncan 2019 (peer-reviewed description of NICE): "The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends that patients with frailty, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy should undergo regular medication review, and emphasises the importance of involving them in this process." "This does not align with NICE guidance, which puts a strong emphasis on involving patients and their families in decisions about their medicines, and on reducing medicine waste." NICE NG5 (search-engine extract only, page not opened): Medication review is defined as "a structured, critical examination of a person's medicines with the objective of reaching an agreement with the person about treatment, optimising the impact of medicines, minimising the number of medication‑related problems and reducing waste". Search summary also states: "During a structured medication review, healthcare professionals should take into account the person's, and their family members or carers where appropriate, views and understanding about their medicines, as well as their concerns, questions or problems with the medicines."

claims.qualifications: NG5 itself could not be opened; rely on Duncan's peer-reviewed description and phrase generally ('national guidance in England says reviews should involve the person'). Do not quote NICE wording verbatim in the post or give a recommendation number.

claims.claim: Since September 2020 England has had structured medication reviews (SMRs), distinct from re-authorising repeat prescriptions; in a survey of 120 clinical pharmacists doing them, most were by telephone, and only 26% said they gave patients information in advance.
claims.supporting_passage: Introduction: "SMRs were formally introduced via NHS England (NHSE) in September 2020,8 as distinct from the act of re-authorising repeat prescriptions or a review of specific medicines during a long-term condition review. However, full implementation was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic 9". Abstract: "Patient selection was largely driven by the primary care contract specification: care home residents, patients with polypharmacy, patients on medicines commonly associated with medication errors, patients with severe frailty and/or patients using potentially addictive pain management medication. Only 26% (n=36) of respondents reported providing patients with information in advance. The majority of SMRs were undertaken remotely by telephone and were 21–30 min in length." Introduction: "A qualitative interview study with clinical pharmacists delivering SMRs remotely in primary care in England between 2020–2022 reported that early implementation, without the opportunity for adequate clinical knowledge development, consultation training provision and skills acquisition, fell short of policy aspirations for holistic, personalised reviews."
claims.pico_timeframe: 120 self-selected clinical pharmacists conducting SMRs in primary care, England, surveyed about 3 years after SMRs began
claims.safe_wording: Since 2020, practices in England have offered a longer 'structured medication review' for some people, such as care home residents and people on many medicines. In a survey of pharmacists who do them, most were by phone, and only about 1 in 4 pharmacists said they sent people information beforehand.
claims.qualifications: The 2020 start date is background from the paper's introduction (citing NHS England). Survey of pharmacists who chose to reply; no response rate. England only; Scotland's arrangements not checked. '26% (n=36)' as printed (denominator unclear).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: An earlier interview study (2020 to 2022, cited in the introduction, not opened) reported early SMRs fell short of holistic, personalised reviews.

numbers.meaning: SMRs formally introduced by NHS England (background)
clinical pharmacists surveyed
respondents who reported giving patients information in advance
typical SMR length, mostly by telephone

claims.claim: Some structured medication reviews start from a request by patients, carers or family members, or from patients self-referring.

claims.claim: GPs and pharmacists described the ideal review as finding out what the person actually takes, sharing concerns and discussing pros and cons of continuing or stopping; there is no clear evidence that reviews as practised improve clinical outcomes.
claims.supporting_passage: "Both the pharmacists and GPs described the ‘ideal’ scenario of a patient-centred medication review, whereby the clinician finds out what the patient is actually taking, shares concerns, and has an informative discussion about the pros and cons of continuing or stopping certain higher-risk medicines." "Although a patient-centred model of medication review appears to be a reasonable approach to reducing harmful polypharmacy, there is a lack of evidence that medication review, as currently practised, or in the ‘ideal’ form described, actually improves clinical outcomes."
claims.location: Full text, Discussion (Implications for research and practice)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C06-29-a
claims.safe_wording: A good review starts with what you actually take, what worries you, and the pros and cons of carrying on or stopping each medicine.
claims.qualifications: Supports the three questions on the visual as a description of good practice. Do not claim that a patient-involving review improves outcomes; the argument for involvement is a matter of respect and agreement (mark as judgement).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Cochrane 2023 (C06-04-g): uncertain effect of reviews on admissions.

claims.claim: Of 1,981 US Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 or over, 92.0% (weighted) agreed they would be willing to stop one or more regular medicines if their doctor said it was possible; 66.6% wanted to reduce the number of medicines they take.
claims.supporting_passage: "Responses to 2 statements ("If my doctor said it was possible, I would be willing to stop one or more of my regular medicines" and "I would like to reduce the number of medicines I am taking") were the main outcomes of interest." "Of the 1981 Medicare beneficiaries included in the study, 1149 (55.2%, weighted) were women, and the majority (n = 715 [54.6%, weighted]) were 65 to 74 years old. A total of 1752 (92.0%, weighted) older adults reported being willing to stop taking 1 or more of their medicines if their physician said it was possible, and 1241 (66.6%, weighted) older adults wanted to reduce the number of medicines that they were taking."
claims.pico_timeframe: US Medicare beneficiaries 65+, population-based in-person survey (NHATS round 6); agreement with two attitude statements; cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a national US survey of about 2,000 people aged 65 or over, 92 in 100 said they would be willing to stop one or more of their regular medicines if their doctor said it was possible. Two in three said they would like to take fewer medicines.
claims.qualifications: Stated, hypothetical willingness, conditional on the doctor saying it is possible (judge's note: make the conditional the point). US population; most respondents were 65 to 74. Not what people did later.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Pooled data from 29 studies give a similar figure (C06-06-d). Stated attitudes predict behaviour poorly (C06-06-e).

numbers.meaning: willing to stop 1 or more regular medicines if the doctor said it was possible
wanted to reduce the number of medicines
age of respondents; 54.6% were 65 to 74

claims.claim: People taking 6 or more medicines had higher odds of being willing to stop one (adjusted odds ratio 2.90) and of wanting fewer medicines (adjusted odds ratio 2.31).
claims.supporting_passage: "Older adults taking 6 or more medications had greater odds than those taking fewer than 6 medications of being willing to stop taking 1 or more of their medicines (adjusted odds ratio, 2.90; 95% CI, 1.74-4.82) and wanting to reduce the number of medicines that they were taking (adjusted odds ratio, 2.31; 95% CI, 1.71-3.13)."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C06-06-a; comparison 6+ vs fewer than 6 medicines; adjusted
claims.safe_wording: People on 6 or more medicines were more likely than people on fewer to say they would be willing to stop one.
claims.qualifications: Adjusted odds ratio; do not convert to 'times more likely' or to an absolute difference (no valid inputs). Optional claim.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Chock 2021 meta-analysis found willingness was not influenced by the number of medicines taken (C06-06-d), so present this as one survey's finding.

numbers.meaning: willing to stop, 6+ vs under 6 medicines
wanting fewer medicines, 6+ vs under 6

claims.claim: Prescribers report that patients may be reluctant to stop medicines, and cite this among barriers to deprescribing.
claims.supporting_passage: Duncan 2019 (UK interviews, Results): "For many interviewees the key perceived barriers to stopping medicines included: fear of causing problems; not wanting to stop medicines that had been started by hospital specialists; and a lack of clear evidence and guidelines around stopping medicines. Interviewees felt that patients might be reluctant or have no incentive to stop medicines, particularly those that they had taken for a long time and medicines for long-term pain". Anderson 2014 (abstract): "The first three themes are intrinsic to the prescriber (eg, beliefs, attitudes, knowledge, skills, behaviour) and the fourth is extrinsic (eg, patient, work setting, health system and cultural factors)." Reeve 2018 (background only): "Primary care physicians report that patient resistance to discontinuing medication use is a significant barrier to deprescribing."
claims.location: Duncan full text Results (Reducing and stopping inappropriate medicines); Anderson abstract; Reeve abstract Importance (background)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK GPs and pharmacists (2017 interviews); prescribers in 21 qualitative studies (to 2014)
claims.safe_wording: GPs and pharmacists interviewed in the UK said patients might be reluctant to stop medicines, especially ones they had taken for a long time.
claims.qualifications: Primary support is Duncan 2019 (a UK primary source); Reeve's sentence is background and must not be cited as its finding; Anderson's abstract names patient factors only generally. Patient reluctance was one of several barriers, alongside fear of causing problems, specialists' prescriptions and unclear guidance.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Across 29 studies (11,049 participants), 87.6% of patients said they were willing to deprescribe based on their doctor's suggestion; caregivers were less willing (74.8%); willingness did not vary with location, population or number of medicines.
claims.supporting_passage: "Twenty-nine unique studies involving 11,049 participants were included." "Overall, 87.6% (95% CI: 83.3 to 91.4%) patients were willing to deprescribe their medication, based upon the doctors' suggestions. This was lower among caregivers, with only 74.8% (49.8% to 93.8%) willing to deprescribe their care recipients' medications. Patients' or caregivers' willingness to deprescribe were not influenced by study location, study population, or the number of medications they took."
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients and caregivers in 29 quantitative attitude studies, various countries, to April 2021; stated willingness
claims.safe_wording: Across 29 studies in different countries, about 88 in 100 patients said they would be willing to stop a medicine if their doctor suggested it. Family carers were somewhat less willing, about 75 in 100.
claims.qualifications: Stated willingness; pooled across heterogeneous surveys. Caregiver estimate is imprecise (50% to 94%).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Conflicts with Reeve's finding that people on 6+ medicines were more willing.

numbers.meaning: pooled proportion of patients willing to deprescribe on doctor's suggestion
pooled proportion of caregivers willing
studies and participants

claims.claim: Attitude questionnaires predict actual deprescribing poorly, so stated willingness in a survey is different from agreement in a consultation.
claims.supporting_passage: "Most patients and their caregivers were willing to deprescribe their medications, whenever possible and thus should be offered a trial of deprescribing. Nevertheless, as these tools have a poor predictive ability, patients and their caregivers should be engaged during the deprescribing process to ensure that the values and opinions are heard, which would ultimately improve patient safety."
claims.pico_timeframe: Authors' conclusion about attitude tools
claims.safe_wording: What people say in a survey does not reliably predict what they decide when a doctor actually suggests stopping a medicine. The survey answers are a reason to raise the question, not a prediction of the answer.
claims.qualifications: Authors' statement in the conclusion; the underlying evidence on predictive ability was not opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: STOPP/START, the European checklist for prescribing in older people, covers both medicines that may be inappropriate (STOPP) and potential prescribing omissions, meaning indicated medicines that are missing (START); version 3 (2023) has 133 STOPP and 57 START criteria.
claims.supporting_passage: "STOPP/START criteria are designed to help identify and support deprescribing of adverse medication and introduction of beneficial medication (where inappropriately unprescribed) as part of routine medication review in multimorbid older people with polypharmacy." "START criteria are designed to detect potential prescribing omissions (PPOs) which represent another critically important aspect of inappropriate prescribing, i.e., undertreatment or failure to prescribe appropriate medications despite clear and valid indications." "Over the course of four rounds of Delphi validation, the panel achieved consensus on 133 STOPP criteria and 57 START criteria, i.e., 190 STOPP/START criteria in total" "These criteria cannot replace clinical judgment in individual cases"
claims.pico_timeframe: Explicit criteria for older people with multimorbidity and polypharmacy; European expert consensus (11 geriatricians, 8 countries)
claims.safe_wording: The main European checklist for medicines in older people has two halves: one lists medicines to consider stopping, the other lists medicines that may be missing. The 2023 version has 133 items of the first kind and 57 of the second.
claims.qualifications: Consensus criteria; the authors say they cannot replace clinical judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: criteria in version 3 (2023)
Delphi panel

claims.claim: An example of an omission: starting an anticoagulant for an older person with untreated persistent atrial fibrillation, while the same checklist also flags caution where bleeding risk is high.
claims.supporting_passage: "Similarly, avoidance of PPOs (START criteria) should reduce preventable morbidity such as major ischemic stroke through initiation of anticoagulants when untreated older patients have persistent atrial fibrillation." "The updated criteria continue to focus on situations that require caution in multimorbid older people, such as the prescribing of anticoagulants in patients with chronic atrial fibrillation and concurrent increased risk of bleeding (c.f. STOPP criteria C10, C12, C14)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people with persistent atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation
claims.safe_wording: One medicine that is often worth looking for is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) for someone with long-standing atrial fibrillation who is not on one, because it lowers the risk of stroke. The same checklist also asks for caution where the risk of bleeding is high.
claims.qualifications: Exact START v3 criterion wording not seen (Appendix 1 not accessible); paraphrase from the main text. Must carry 'when indicated and wanted' and the bleeding caution; the decision depends on the person's goals and risks.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: STOPP/START flags a regular opioid prescribed without a laxative.
claims.supporting_passage: te Winkel 2023 (STOPP/START Netherlands version 2; full-text excerpt): "The most frequently observed PIM was "stop benzodiazepines" (15.7% of all PIMs) and the most frequently observed PPO was "start laxatives in patients receiving opioids regularly" (14.7% of all PPOs)." Szoszkiewicz 2024 (STOPP/START version 3 study; full-text excerpt): "The most frequent PIMs were the use of regular opioids without concomitant laxatives (7.8%), drugs causing constipation in patients with constipation (7.3%), long-term opioids for osteoarthritis (6.2%), aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (6.2%), long-term aspirin at doses greater than 100 mg per day (5.6%), and the use of benzodiazepines for more than four weeks (5.6%)."
claims.location: te Winkel full text Results (via Scite); Szoszkiewicz full text Results (via Scite)
claims.pico_timeframe: Dutch primary care (v2-NL); Polish day-care centres (v3)
claims.safe_wording: The checklist flags a regular opioid painkiller taken without a laxative.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's claim that START version 3 contains 'laxative with regular opioids' is NOT verified: the v3 criteria appendix could not be opened, and the v3 study lists 'regular opioids without concomitant laxatives' among potentially inappropriate medicines (the STOPP side), not omissions. In version 2 (Netherlands) it appears as a START item. Word it as 'the checklist flags', without naming the version or side.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Szoszkiewicz excerpt does not state whether 7.8% is of patients or of all PIMs, so do not quote the figure.

numbers.meaning: share of all omissions that were 'start laxatives in patients receiving opioids regularly', Dutch primary care, 6 years

claims.claim: Potential prescribing omissions are about as common as potentially inappropriate medicines: in 25,854 Dutch primary care patients aged 65 or over, 74.3% had at least one omission and 72.2% at least one potentially inappropriate medicine over 6 years; the most common omission was a laxative for someone on regular opioids.
claims.supporting_passage: "All 25,854 patients aged 65 years and older having at least 5 contacts with their practice in 6 years were included." "In our population, 72.2% and 74.3% of patients had at least 1 PIM and PPO, respectively; 30.9% and 34.2% had at least 3 PIMs and PPOs, respectively." Full-text excerpt: "the most frequently observed PPO was "start laxatives in patients receiving opioids regularly" (14.7% of all PPOs)."
claims.location: Abstract (Methods, Results); full-text Results excerpt via Scite
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients 65+ in 48 Dutch family practices, 2013 to 2018; STOPP/START-NL v2 applied to routine data; any PIM or PPO over 6 years
claims.safe_wording: In a Dutch study of almost 26,000 people aged 65 or over, about 3 in 4 were missing at least one medicine the checklist says may be indicated at some point over 6 years; a similar share had at least one medicine it says may be inappropriate. The most common gap was a laxative for someone on a regular opioid.
claims.qualifications: Automated checklist applied to records over 6 years; 'potential' omissions, not confirmed after clinical review. Netherlands, not UK.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Single-time-point prevalence would be lower. Consistent with a small Polish v3 study: START v3 found an omission in 74 of 100 people with polypharmacy.

numbers.meaning: patients aged 65+ in 48 Dutch practices
had at least 1 potential prescribing omission over 6 years
had at least 1 potentially inappropriate medicine over 6 years
had 3 or more omissions

claims.claim: Underprescribing is linked with polypharmacy: in 150 geriatric patients, 42.9% of those on 5 or more drugs were undertreated vs 13.5% of those on 4 or fewer.
claims.supporting_passage: "Underprescription was defined as lack of an indicated drug, while no reason could be found for not prescribing it. Polypharmacy was defined as five or more drugs." "Polypharmacy was present in 61% of 150 patients. Underprescription was found in 47 (31%). Of patients with polypharmacy 42.9% were undertreated, in contrast to 13.5% of patients using four medicines or less (OR 4.8, 95% CI 2.0, 11.2). The estimated probability of underprescription increased significantly with the number of drugs."
claims.pico_timeframe: 150 geriatric patients, Netherlands; underprescription vs GP and national guidelines; cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a Dutch study of 150 older patients, people taking 5 or more medicines were more often missing an indicated medicine than people taking fewer: about 43 in 100 compared with about 14 in 100.
claims.qualifications: Small, older (2008), single-setting, cross-sectional association. Do not convert OR 4.8 to 'times more likely'; give the two percentages instead.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: One Serbian study (reported in a Scite result, not opened) found number of medications was not a significant predictor of omissions; treat the link as likely but not universal.

numbers.meaning: patients with underprescription
undertreated, polypharmacy (5+) vs 4 or fewer medicines

claims.claim: Trials increasingly address prescribing omissions; pharmaceutical care may slightly reduce the number of omissions (low certainty) and it is uncertain whether it reduces the proportion of people with one.
claims.supporting_passage: "Pharmaceutical care may slightly reduce the number of potential prescribing omissions (PPOs) (SMD -0.48, 95% CI -1.05 to 0.09; I= 92%; 3 studies, 691 participants; low-certainty evidence), however it must be noted that this effect estimate is based on only three studies, which had serious limitations in terms of risk of bias. Likewise, it is uncertain whether pharmaceutical care reduces the proportion of patients with one or more PPO (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.91; I= 95%; 7 studies, 2765 participants; very low-certainty evidence)." "Since the last update of this review in 2018, there appears to have been an increase in the number of studies seeking to address potential prescribing omissions and more interventions being delivered by multidisciplinary teams."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C06-04-g
claims.safe_wording: Research on medicines reviews has started to measure missing medicines as well as unnecessary ones, but the evidence on whether reviews close these gaps is weak.
claims.qualifications: Low and very low certainty; do not quote the SMD or RR in a post.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: number of omissions outcome, low certainty
proportion with an omission, very low certainty

claims.claim: Polypharmacy can be appropriate (medicines that improve or prolong life with minimal harm) or problematic (where harm outweighs benefit), a distinction made by Duerden and colleagues (King's Fund).
claims.supporting_passage: "Polypharmacy is not always harmful, however, and Duerdenmake the distinction between appropriate polypharmacy, such as where multiple medicines improve quality of life, prolong life, and cause minimal harm, and problematic polypharmacy, where the balance tips and the potential harm of some medicines outweighs the potential benefit."
claims.pico_timeframe: Conceptual distinction
claims.safe_wording: Taking many medicines is not always a problem. It depends on whether each one is doing more good than harm for that person.
claims.qualifications: Secondary citation of the King's Fund report (not opened). Attribute to 'experts' or to the concept, not a verbatim King's Fund quote.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: A medication review judged by the number of medicines removed will miss omissions.
claims.supporting_passage: No source states this directly. Supporting facts: omissions are as common as potentially inappropriate medicines (te Winkel: "72.2% and 74.3% of patients had at least 1 PIM and PPO, respectively"); STOPP/START is designed for "deprescribing of adverse medication and introduction of beneficial medication (where inappropriately unprescribed)".
claims.pico_timeframe: Argument
claims.safe_wording: We should judge a medicines review by how well the medicines fit the person, not by how many are stopped, because missing medicines are about as common as unnecessary ones.
claims.qualifications: This is a judgement; present it as the post's position ('we should'), not as a finding. No study found here measured whether reviews targeted at reducing counts miss omissions.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Among adults aged 66 or over with high blood pressure in Ontario, those newly given a calcium channel blocker were more often given a loop diuretic within 90 days than those newly given an ACE inhibitor or ARB or an unrelated drug (1.4% vs 0.7% and 0.5%).
claims.supporting_passage: "The cohort included 41 086 older adults (≥66 years) with hypertension who were newly dispensed a CCB, 66 494 individuals who were newly dispensed another antihypertensive medication, and 231 439 individuals who were newly dispensed an unrelated medication. At index (ie, the dispensing date), the mean (SD) age was 74.5 (6.9) years, and 191 685 (56.5%) were women. Individuals who were newly dispensed a CCB had a higher cumulative incidence at 90 days of being dispensed a loop diuretic than individuals in both control groups (1.4% vs 0.7% and 0.5%, P < .001)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling adults 66+ with hypertension, Ontario 2011 to 2016 / newly dispensed CCB / newly dispensed ACE inhibitor or ARB, or unrelated drug / dispensing of a loop diuretic / 90 days (and up to 1 year)
claims.safe_wording: In Ontario, among people aged 66 or over with high blood pressure, about 14 in every 1,000 people started on a calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine were given a loop diuretic (a strong water tablet such as furosemide) within 3 months. The figure was about 7 in 1,000 for people started on a different blood pressure tablet, and 5 in 1,000 for people started on an unrelated medicine.
claims.qualifications: Dispensing data: shows who was given a diuretic, not whether swelling was the reason. The gap (about 7 extra per 1,000 compared with other blood pressure tablets) is the best estimate of the cascade; it is small per person but large across a population. Association, not proof that each case was a cascade.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A US claims study (Vouri 2019) found a similar signal (see C06-18-i). No study found that contradicts the direction.

numbers.meaning: older adults newly dispensed a CCB (comparators 66,494 and 231,439)
cumulative incidence of loop diuretic dispensing at 90 days after starting a CCB
same, after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
same, after starting an unrelated medicine
absolute difference CCB vs ACE inhibitor/ARB at 90 days (derived: 1.4 minus 0.7)
mean age at index

claims.claim: The association persisted, slightly weaker, up to 1 year, and in people started on amlodipine alone; relative rates were 1.68 to 2.40 times higher than after an ACE inhibitor or ARB over the first 3 months.
claims.supporting_passage: "After adjustment, individuals who were newly dispensed a CCB had increased relative rates of being dispensed a loop diuretic compared with individuals who were newly dispensed an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker (HR, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.38-2.05 in the first 30 days after index [days 1-30]; 2.26; 95% CI, 1.76-2.92 in the subsequent 30 days [days 31-60]; and 2.40; 95% CI, 1.84-3.13 in the third month of follow-up [days 61-90]) ... This association persisted, although slightly attenuated, from 90 days to up to 1 year of follow-up and when restricted to a subgroup of individuals who were newly dispensed amlodipine."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C06-18-a; adjusted hazard ratios by 30-day window; sensitivity analyses to 1 year and amlodipine-only subgroup
claims.safe_wording: The pattern was still there a year after starting the drug, and it held when the analysis was limited to people started on amlodipine.
claims.qualifications: Hazard ratios are relative; give the absolute figures from C06-18-a first. The 1-year figures are not in the abstract, so give no number for them.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: A prescribing cascade is when a side effect of one drug is taken for a new condition and a second drug is prescribed to treat it; the term was described by Rochon and Gurwitz in the BMJ in 1997.
claims.supporting_passage: McCarthy 2022: "Prescribing cascades occur when a drug is prescribed to manage side effects of another drug, typically when a side effect is misinterpreted as a new condition." Savage 2020: "A prescribing cascade occurs when the edema is misinterpreted as a new medical condition and a diuretic is subsequently prescribed to treat the edema." Rochon 1997 record title: "Optimising drug treatment for elderly people: the prescribing cascade."
claims.location: McCarthy 2022 Abstract; Savage 2020 Abstract (Importance); Rochon 1997 PubMed record (title only)
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition
claims.safe_wording: A prescribing cascade is when a side effect of one medicine is mistaken for a new illness, and a second medicine is started to treat it.
claims.qualifications: Attribute the term to Rochon and Gurwitz (BMJ 1997) only by citation; no text from that article was read.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: ThinkCascades authors note that some cascades are intentional and appropriate (e.g., NSAID plus stomach protection), so not every drug added for a side effect is an error.

numbers.meaning: year of Rochon and Gurwitz BMJ article

claims.claim: Ankle swelling is a common, dose-related side effect of calcium channel blockers of the amlodipine type.
claims.supporting_passage: Makani 2011: "One hundred and six studies with 99 469 participants, mean age 56 ± 6 years, satisfied our inclusion criteria and were included in this analysis. The weighted incidence of peripheral edema was significantly higher in the CCBs group when compared with controls/placebo (10.7 vs. 3.2%, P < 0.0001). Similarly, the withdrawal rate due to edema was higher in patients on CCBs compared with control/placebo (2.1 vs. 0.5%, P < 0.0001). Both the incidence of edema and patient withdrawal rate due to edema increased with the duration of therapy with CCBs reaching 24 and 5%, respectively, after 6 months. ... Incidence of peripheral edema in patients on DHPs was 12.3% compared with 3.1% with non-DHPs (P < 0.0001). Edema with high-dose CCBs (defined as more than half the usual maximal dose) was 2.8 times higher than that with low-dose CCBs (16.1 vs. 5.7%, P < 0.0001)." Woodford 2020: "CCBs have no prognostic benefit in heart failure and have an absolute risk increase for oedema of around 8-18% (number needed to harm 6-13)."
claims.pico_timeframe: People with hypertension in RCTs (mean age 56) / CCB / placebo or control / peripheral oedema and withdrawal for oedema / trials at least 4 weeks, rising to 6 months
claims.safe_wording: In trials, ankle swelling affected about 11 in 100 people taking a calcium channel blocker, compared with about 3 in 100 on placebo or other treatment. It was about three times as common on higher doses (16 in 100) as on lower doses (6 in 100), and it became more common the longer people took the drug.
claims.qualifications: Trial participants averaged 56 years, so rates in older people may differ. The swelling mechanism in the abstract ('thought to occur secondary to arteriolar dilatation') is background, so say 'is thought to' if used.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Rates vary by drug type (lower with non-dihydropyridine and newer lipophilic dihydropyridine CCBs).

numbers.meaning: incidence of peripheral oedema, CCB vs control/placebo, pooled RCTs
oedema on high-dose vs low-dose CCB
oedema incidence and withdrawal due to oedema after 6 months of CCB therapy
dihydropyridine vs non-dihydropyridine CCBs
absolute risk increase for oedema cited in Woodford review

claims.claim: For calcium channel blocker ankle swelling the options are to lower the dose, switch to another drug, or reconsider the need for it; adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB also reduces the swelling; a loop diuretic is justified only where these fail.
claims.supporting_passage: Woodford 2020: "The best way to manage the oedema caused by CCBs is to switch to an alternative medication. Only where this is not possible or fails to achieve therapeutic goals would the CCB-loop diuretic combination appear to be justified. In many cases, therapeutic practice could be improved by targeting people on CCB-loop diuretic combinations for medication review." Makani (Am J Med) 2011: "The incidence of peripheral edema with calcium channel blocker/renin-angiotensin system blocker combination was 38% lower than that with calcium channel blocker monotherapy (P<.00001) (relative risk [RR] 0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.53-0.74)." Makani (J Hypertens) 2011: "The risk of peripheral edema with lipophilic DHPs was 57% lower than with traditional DHPs (relative risk 0.43; 95% confidence interval 0.34-0.53; P < 0.0001)."
claims.location: Woodford 2020 Abstract; Makani Am J Med 2011 Abstract, Results; Makani J Hypertens 2011 Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: People on CCBs with oedema / switch, dose reduction, or adding RAS blocker / continuing CCB or adding loop diuretic / oedema incidence / trials of weeks (mean 9.2 weeks for combination meta-analysis)
claims.safe_wording: If ankle swelling starts after a calcium channel blocker, the first question is whether the drug is the cause. The options include a lower dose, a different blood pressure medicine, or asking whether the drug is still needed. A UK geriatrician's review concluded that switching is the best way to manage it, and that adding a loop diuretic is justified only when other options fail. In trials, adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB cut the rate of swelling by about a third.
claims.qualifications: The switch advice is expert opinion in a narrative review, not a trial result. 'Reconsider the need for it' is a clinical judgement (no study opened tested stopping). Combination-trial participants were middle-aged and followed for about 9 weeks. Present the RAS-blocker option as one of several, since it adds a drug.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial compared 'reduce or switch' with 'add a diuretic' directly in older people.

numbers.meaning: oedema incidence with CCB plus ACE inhibitor/ARB vs CCB alone, 25 RCTs, 17,206 people, mean age 56 (relative)

claims.claim: Adding a loop diuretic brings its own harms, such as worse kidney function, dizziness or blood pressure drop on standing, abnormal salts in the blood and falls.
claims.supporting_passage: "In the 60 days following LD initiation, 28 patients (23.3%) experienced 37 events potentially attributable to LD initiation. The most common downstream events were worsening kidney function (n = 9 [7.5%]), orthostasis (n = 7 [5.8%]), electrolyte abnormalities (n = 6 [5.0%]), and falls (n = 5 [4.2%]). Six patients (5.0%) were evaluated in the emergency department and/or hospital for potential downstream events." Also: "Gabapentinoids were rarely noted in the differential (n = 4 [3.3%])."
claims.pico_timeframe: 120 US veterans aged 66+ (mostly men) who started a loop diuretic after a gabapentinoid / no comparison group / events potentially attributable to the loop diuretic / 60 days
claims.safe_wording: In a US record review of 120 older veterans who were started on a loop diuretic after a nerve-pain medicine caused swelling, about 1 in 4 had a problem within 2 months that may have come from the diuretic: worse kidney function, a drop in blood pressure on standing, abnormal salts in the blood, or a fall.
claims.qualifications: The first drug in this study was gabapentin or pregabalin, not a calcium channel blocker; state that if it is used in a CCB post. Small, mostly male sample; no comparison group; events 'potentially attributable'. The candidate's visual label 'passing urine often' was not checked against a source; the 'possible third drug' step must be labelled 'Illustrative example'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; the direction fits the ThinkCascades rationale but no CCB-specific harm study was opened.

numbers.meaning: patients with at least one event potentially attributable to the loop diuretic within 60 days

claims.claim: Calcium channel blocker ankle swelling responds poorly to diuretics.

claims.pico_timeframe: Not studied in opened sources
claims.safe_wording: Do not say that water tablets do not work for this swelling. Say instead that the swelling is a side effect of the first drug, and the first step is to review that drug.
claims.qualifications: The Sica 2003 lead could not be found in PubMed.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Unverified either way.

claims.claim: In a UK primary care study of 487,372 people on blood pressure drugs, taking an NSAID together with a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor or ARB was linked with a higher rate of acute kidney injury (rate ratio 1.31).
claims.supporting_passage: "A cohort of 487 372 patients using antihypertensive drugs met the study inclusion criteria (fig 1); they were followed for a mean of 5.9 (SD 3.4) years ... current use of a triple therapy combination was associated with a 31% higher rate of acute kidney injury (rate ratio 1.31, 95% confidence interval 1.12 to 1.53)." Table 1: cases mean (SD) age "76.9 (10.9)"; controls "76.9 (10.7)".
claims.location: Full text, Results and Table 1; Table 2

claims.safe_wording: In UK GP records, people taking an anti-inflammatory painkiller on top of both a water tablet and an ACE inhibitor or ARB (such as ramipril or losartan) had about a third more hospital admissions with sudden kidney injury than people taking the two blood pressure medicines without the painkiller.
claims.qualifications: Observational (linked with, not proven to cause). Prescribed NSAIDs only; shop-bought ibuprofen was not captured. The people who developed kidney injury averaged 77 years old. Relative figure: pair it with the absolute context in C06-32-c and C06-32-e.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Restricting to dialysis-requiring cases gave a non-significant result (rate ratio 1.13, 0.69 to 1.77; few cases).

claims.claim: Hospital admission with acute kidney injury was uncommon overall (about 7 per 10,000 person-years among users of blood pressure drugs).
claims.supporting_passage: "We identified 2215 cases of acute kidney injury during follow-up, yielding an overall incidence rate of 7/10 000 (95% confidence interval 7/10 000 to 8/10 000) person years."

claims.safe_wording: Hospital admission with sudden kidney injury was uncommon: about 7 per 10,000 people per year among everyone in the study taking blood pressure medicines.
claims.qualifications: This is the rate for the whole cohort, not for people on the triple combination, and it counts only hospital admissions coded as kidney injury. The Tayside study (C06-32-e), which counted blood-test rises, found about 68 per 10,000 per year.

claims.claim: An NSAID with only one of these drugs (a diuretic alone, or an ACE inhibitor or ARB alone) was not linked with extra kidney injury in the UK hospital-admission study, but a Scottish study counting blood-test rises found a similar relative increase with these double combinations.
claims.supporting_passage: Lapi 2013: "Overall, current use of a double therapy combination of a diuretic or an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker with NSAIDs was not associated with an increased rate of acute kidney injury." Dreischulte 2015: "The relative increase in AKI risk was similar for NSAID use in both triple (adjusted rate ratio 1.64 (95% CI 1.25-2.14)) and dual combinations with either renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (1.60 (1.18-2.17)) or diuretics (1.64 (1.17-2.29))."
claims.location: Lapi 2013 Full text, Results; Dreischulte 2015 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Lapi: hospital-coded AKI, UK CPRD. Dreischulte: community AKI defined as creatinine rise of 50% or more, 78,379 users of RAS inhibitors and/or diuretics, Tayside
claims.safe_wording: Do not say that ibuprofen with only one of these medicines is safe. A Scottish study found that taking an anti-inflammatory alongside either a water tablet or an ACE inhibitor or ARB was also linked with more kidney injury, though the extra risk in absolute terms was about half that seen with all three together.
claims.qualifications: The two studies used different definitions of kidney injury and reached different conclusions for double combinations; the Scottish study is the more sensitive.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Direct conflict between Lapi 2013 (no increase with doubles) and Dreischulte 2015 (increase with doubles). This conflict must shape the post.

claims.claim: In absolute terms, about 1 extra kidney injury occurs for every 158 people who take an NSAID for a year alongside both a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor or ARB, compared with 1 in over 300 for the double combinations; risk was highest in people over 75 and those with reduced kidney function.
claims.supporting_passage: "This nested case-control study characterized the risk of community-acquired AKI associated with NSAID use among 78,379 users of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors and/or diuretics, where AKI was defined as a 50% or greater increase in creatinine from baseline. The AKI incidence was 68/10,000 person-years. ... However, the absolute increase in AKI risk was higher for NSAIDs used in triple versus dual combinations with renin-angiotensin system inhibitors or diuretics alone (numbers needed to harm for 1 year treatment with NSAID of 158 vs. over 300). AKI risk was highest among users of loop diuretic/aldosterone antagonist combinations, in those over 75 years of age, and in those with renal impairment."
claims.pico_timeframe: Tayside users of RAS inhibitors and/or diuretics / NSAID use / same drugs without NSAID / creatinine-defined AKI / NNH per 1 year of NSAID treatment
claims.safe_wording: In a Scottish study, for every 158 people who took an anti-inflammatory painkiller for a year on top of both a water tablet and an ACE inhibitor or ARB, about 1 extra person had a kidney injury picked up on blood tests (roughly 6 in 1,000). With only one of the two blood pressure medicines, the extra risk was lower (fewer than 1 in 300). People over 75 and people with weaker kidneys were at highest risk.

claims.claim: Each of the three drugs affects the kidney differently, so together they reduce the kidney's ability to keep filtering.
claims.supporting_passage: "Use of diuretics can lead to hypovolaemia, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers cause a haemodynamic reduction in glomerular filtration rate due to efferent arteriolar vasodilation, and NSAIDs cause inhibition of prostacyclin synthesis (leading to renal afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction)." and "among users of the triple therapy combination, the decreased inflow to the glomerulus resulting from the diuretic and NSAID cannot be compensated owing to blockade of the renin-angiotensin system"
claims.location: Full text, Introduction and Discussion (Biological mechanisms)
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacological explanation offered by the authors
claims.safe_wording: The water tablet lowers the fluid reaching the kidneys, the anti-inflammatory narrows the blood vessel into the kidney's filters, and the ACE inhibitor or ARB stops the kidney from compensating.
claims.qualifications: Authors' explanation, not a finding of the study. Keep it short and literal.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Unverified.

claims.claim: DQIP was a cluster-randomised stepped-wedge trial in Tayside general practices (34 randomised, 33 completed) of a 48-week intervention combining professional education, informatics to find patients, and financial incentives for practices to review them.
claims.supporting_passage: "In this cluster-randomized, stepped-wedge trial conducted in Tayside, Scotland, we randomly assigned participating primary care practices to various start dates for a 48-week intervention comprising professional education, informatics to facilitate review, and financial incentives for practices to review patients' charts to assess appropriateness. ... A total of 34 practices underwent randomization, 33 of which completed the study."
claims.pico_timeframe: Tayside general practices; patients at risk of adverse drug events from NSAIDs or antiplatelets / DQIP intervention / preintervention period (stepped wedge) / high-risk prescribing / 48 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In Tayside, 33 general practices took part in a trial of a programme with three parts: training for prescribers, a computer search that listed each practice's patients on specific risky prescriptions, and payment for the practice to review each of those patients.
claims.qualifications: Stepped-wedge design: every practice got the intervention, at randomly assigned start dates.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: The programme targeted nine named high-risk prescribing measures involving NSAIDs and antiplatelet drugs (six for stomach bleeding, two for kidney harm, one for heart failure), and flags could be cleared by recording that the prescription was appropriate, stopping it, or adding stomach protection.
claims.supporting_passage: "The individual measures were related to three types of adverse drug events: gastrointestinal events (six measures; e.g., aspirin or clopidogrel prescription for a patient taking an oral anticoagulant without coprescription of a gastroprotective drug), renal events (two measures; e.g., NSAID prescription for a patient with chronic kidney disease), and heart failure (NSAID prescription for a patient with heart failure)." and "Physicians could clear the flag by recording an explicit decision that the prescribing was appropriate, by stopping prescription of the offending drugs, or by adding a gastroprotective drug (proton-pump inhibitor or histamine 2 -receptor antagonist) for measures targeting the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C06-31-a
claims.safe_wording: It focused on nine specific combinations, for example an anti-inflammatory painkiller in someone with kidney disease or heart failure, or aspirin with a blood thinner and no stomach protection. For each patient flagged, the doctor could stop the drug, add stomach protection, or record why the prescription was right for that person.
claims.qualifications: Review did not mean automatic stopping; the design allowed a documented decision to continue.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.
