claims.claim: UK consensus says the usual HbA1c targets (53 to 59 mmol/mol, 7 to 7.5%) are too tight for frail older people.
claims.supporting_passage: "Guidelines from organizations such as the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), the European Association for the Study of Diabetes, and the American Diabetes Association acknowledge the need for individualized care, but the glycaemic targets that are suggested to constitute good control [HbA 53-59 mmol/mol (7-7.5%)] are too tight for frail older individuals. We present a framework for the assessment of older adults and guidelines for the management of this population according to their frailty status..."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with type 2 diabetes, UK; consensus
claims.safe_wording: A UK consensus statement (2018, with NHS England and geriatric and diabetes specialists) says the usual HbA1c targets of 53 to 59 mmol/mol are too tight for older people living with frailty, and that targets should be set according to frailty.
claims.qualifications: Specific frailty targets in the body of the paper were not read; do not quote target numbers for frailty from this source.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: ADA Standards of Care 2026 (Older Adults section, PMID 41358888) could not be opened in full, so ADA wording is not verified here.

numbers.meaning: usual targets the statement calls too tight for frail older people

claims.claim: A deprescribing guideline recommends reducing or stopping glucose-lowering drugs that cause hypoglycaemia in older adults at risk, and individualising targets for people who are frail, have dementia or limited life expectancy.
claims.supporting_passage: "We recommend deprescribing antihyperglycemic medications known to contribute to hypoglycemia in older adults at risk or in situations where antihyperglycemic medications might be causing other adverse effects, and individualizing targets and deprescribing accordingly for those who are frail, have dementia, or have a limited life expectancy."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults on glucose-lowering drugs; GRADE guideline
claims.safe_wording: An evidence-based guideline on stopping diabetes medicines recommends reducing or stopping those that can cause low blood sugar in older people at risk, and setting targets to suit people who are frail, have dementia or have limited life expectancy.
claims.qualifications: Canadian guideline (2017).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Low blood sugar episodes in older people treated for diabetes are linked with falls and fractures.
claims.supporting_passage: "Similarly, our meta-analysis of six studies demonstrated an association between hypoglycemia and falls and fractures, pooled OR 1.78 (95% CI 1.44-2.21) and 1.68 (95% CI 1.37-2.07) respectively." and "Studies assessing mortality signal a time-response relationship with a higher risk of adverse events occurring within the first 90 days after hypoglycemia."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people on glucose-lowering drugs / hypoglycaemia (mostly severe, from healthcare databases) / no hypoglycaemia / falls, fractures / various
claims.safe_wording: In studies of older people treated for diabetes, those who had episodes of low blood sugar were more likely to have falls and fractures. This link does not prove the low sugars caused them.
claims.qualifications: Association from observational studies; odds ratios cannot be turned into 'X times more likely' in plain terms or into absolute risks. Mostly severe hypoglycaemia.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: falls, six studies (relative, association)
fractures, six studies (relative, association)

claims.claim: HbA1c does not reveal low blood sugars: in older adults with high HbA1c (8% or more), most on insulin, two thirds had low glucose on 3 days of monitoring, and almost all episodes went unnoticed.
claims.supporting_passage: "Forty adults (mean [SD] age, 75 [5] years; HbA(1C) value, 9.3% [1.3%]; diabetes duration, 22 [14] years; 28 patients [70%] with type 2 diabetes mellitus; and 37 [93%] using insulin) were evaluated. Twenty-six patients (65%) experienced 1 or more episodes of hypoglycemia (glucose level <70 mg/dL). ... Of the total of 102 hypoglycemic episodes, 95 (93%) were unrecognized by finger-stick glucose measurements performed 4 times a day or by symptoms." Conclusion: "Raising HbA(1C) goals may not be adequate to prevent hypoglycemia in this population."
claims.pico_timeframe: 40 adults 69+ with HbA1c 8%+, 93% on insulin / blinded CGM / none / glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) / 3 days
claims.safe_wording: An HbA1c result does not show whether someone is having low blood sugars. In a small US study of 40 older people on insulin whose HbA1c was high, 26 had low glucose readings over 3 days of continuous monitoring, and 93 in 100 episodes were not picked up by finger-prick tests or symptoms.
claims.qualifications: Very small; high-HbA1c group, mostly insulin users, some with type 1 diabetes. Use it to show HbA1c alone cannot rule low sugars in or out, not to say a low HbA1c causes them.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: This refines the candidate's core insight: the evidence opened shows potential overtreatment with low HbA1c, and frequent unrecognised hypoglycaemia even with high HbA1c; no opened source measured hypoglycaemia frequency in frail people with low HbA1c.

numbers.meaning: had at least one glucose below 70 mg/dL over 3 days
episodes not recognised by finger-stick tests or symptoms
mean HbA1c (about 78 mmol/mol, conversion not from source)

claims.claim: HbA1c can be misleading in anaemia: non-iron-deficiency anaemia may lower it and iron deficiency may raise it.
claims.supporting_passage: "HbA1c is likely to be affected by iron deficiency and IDA with a spurious increase in HbA1c values; conversely, non-IDA may lead to a decreased HbA1c value."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults not known to have diabetes; 12 studies
claims.safe_wording: Some types of anaemia can make HbA1c read lower than the true blood sugar level, and iron deficiency can make it read higher.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is limited and in people without known diabetes; say 'can' not 'does'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors call for more evidence.

claims.claim: Tight glucose control in older adults reduces some complications but more than doubles severe hypoglycaemia, without a clear difference in deaths.
claims.supporting_passage: "No difference was noted in all-cause mortality with intensive control (pooled hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval 0.90-1.03), but risk of severe hypoglycemia increased (2.45, 2.22-2.72). Intensive control was associated reductions in microvascular (0.73, 0.68-0.79) and macrovascular complications (0.84, 0.79-0.89). Outcome data for risk of hospitalization, cognition, and falls/fractures were limited."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 60+ or frail with type 2 diabetes / intensive control (HbA1c target 58 mmol/mol or lower) / standard care / mortality, severe hypoglycaemia, complications / study durations varied
claims.safe_wording: Across 15 studies in people aged 60 or over, aiming for tight control was linked with fewer blood vessel complications, but more than twice the rate of severe low blood sugars, and no clear difference in deaths.
claims.qualifications: Mixed RCT and observational data with significant heterogeneity; population mostly 60 plus rather than frail. Relative figures only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Gives the benefit side: the post must not imply tight control has no benefits.

numbers.meaning: severe hypoglycaemia, intensive vs standard (relative)
all-cause mortality
microvascular and macrovascular complications (relative)

claims.claim: The American Diabetes Association recommends less stringent targets and deintensifying hypoglycaemia-causing drugs in older adults with complex or poor health.
claims.supporting_passage: Not opened. ADA Standards of Care 2026 Older Adults section (PMID 41358888, PMC12690186): PMC full text returned empty, Scite returned abstract only; 2024 and 2025 editions also not readable.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not cite ADA wording. Use the UK consensus (C06-25-d) and the deprescribing guideline (C06-25-e) instead.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Unverified in this project.

claims.claim: In the trials of direct oral anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation, eligibility and dosing were based on creatinine clearance from the Cockcroft-Gault equation.
claims.supporting_passage: MacCallum 2013: "In clinical trials of dabigatran and rivaroxaban for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF), drug eligibility and dosing were determined using the Cockcroft-Gault equation to estimate creatine clearance as a measure of renal function." Chan 2022: "Randomized trials of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) adopted the Cockcroft-Gault (CG) formula to calculate estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) to determine the dosages of DOACs."
claims.location: MacCallum 2013 Abstract, Objectives; Chan 2022 Abstract, Background
claims.pico_timeframe: DOAC trials in AF (background statements)
claims.safe_wording: The trials that tested the newer blood thinners (DOACs) worked out doses from creatinine clearance calculated with the Cockcroft-Gault formula, which uses age, weight and sex, not from the eGFR printed on lab reports.
claims.qualifications: Background statement in both abstracts; 'uses age, weight and sex' is general knowledge of the formula not quoted in an opened source (confirm or omit).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Using eGFR instead of Cockcroft-Gault overestimates kidney function mainly in people over 75 and under 50 kg, leading to overdosing of DOACs; only dosing that was correct by Cockcroft-Gault was linked with less major bleeding than warfarin.
claims.supporting_passage: "At the cutoff values of eGFR of <15, 15-50, and >50 mL/min, the agreements were 78% between MDRD and CG and 81% between CKD-EPI and CG. The disagreements among the different equations were largely due to overestimations, especially for patients aged >75 years and with a body weight of <50 kg (58.8% for MDRD and 50.9% for CKD-EPI). Among patients receiving DOACs whose dosages were defined as "on label" based on MDRD or CKD-EPI, only those whose dosages were "truly on label" based on CG were associated with a lower risk of major bleeding (adjusted HR: 0.34; 95% CI: 0.26-0.45) compared to warfarin."
claims.pico_timeframe: 39,239 people with AF in Taiwan; 11,185 on DOACs / dosing by eGFR vs CG / warfarin / major bleeding / retrospective
claims.safe_wording: In a Taiwanese study of 39,239 people with atrial fibrillation, the lab eGFR and the Cockcroft-Gault calculation disagreed for about 1 in 5 people, mostly because eGFR made kidney function look better. The disagreement was most common in people over 75 who weighed under 50 kg.
claims.qualifications: East Asian population with lower body weight; observational. The 58.8% and 50.9% figures are ambiguous in the abstract (proportion overestimated in that subgroup); do not quote them without the full text.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Villain 2023 (C06-19-e) found no difference in outcomes by equation in very old Germans.

numbers.meaning: agreement of MDRD and CKD-EPI with CG at dosing cut-offs
major bleeding vs warfarin for doses on label by CG (relative)

claims.claim: In east London, using MDRD eGFR instead of Cockcroft-Gault would have made about 15% of people aged 80 or over with AF eligible for dabigatran who were ineligible, and led to too-high rivaroxaban doses in 13.5%.
claims.supporting_passage: "Of 4120 patients, 2706 were <80 years and 1414 were ≥80 years of age. Among those ≥80 years, 14.9% were ineligible for dabigatran according to Cockcroft-Gault equation but would have been judged eligible applying MDRD method. For those <80 years, 0.8% would have been incorrectly judged eligible for dabigatran and 5.3% would have received too high a dose. For rivaroxaban, 0.3% would have been incorrectly judged eligible for treatment and 13.5% would have received too high a dose."
claims.pico_timeframe: 4,120 people with AF in east London general practices / MDRD eGFR / Cockcroft-Gault / modelled eligibility and dose category / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In east London GP records, among people aged 80 or over with atrial fibrillation, about 15 in 100 who were too frail in kidney terms for dabigatran by the Cockcroft-Gault calculation would have looked eligible using the lab eGFR.
claims.qualifications: Uses the older MDRD equation, not CKD-EPI; modelled dosing, not outcomes. The rivaroxaban 13.5% and dabigatran '<80 years' figures are ambiguous in the abstract; use only the 14.9% figure for people aged 80 or over.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Villain 2023 (C06-19-e).

numbers.meaning: people 80+ ineligible for dabigatran by CG but eligible by MDRD
people 80+ in the sample

claims.claim: MHRA advised in 2019 that creatinine clearance by Cockcroft-Gault should be used to dose DOACs and some other drugs.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine summary only (not verbatim from the MHRA page): 'Creatinine clearance should be calculated using the Cockcroft-Gault formula to determine dosage adjustments for patients taking direct-acting oral anticoagulants, patients taking nephrotoxic drugs (such as vancomycin and amphotericin B), and patients taking medicines that are largely renally excreted and have a narrow therapeutic index (such as digoxin and sotalol).'
claims.pico_timeframe: UK regulatory advice, October 2019
claims.safe_wording: Do not state MHRA wording until it is checked in an opened copy. If it cannot be opened, rely on the published studies (C06-19-a to c).
claims.qualifications: Search extract; which body weight and patient groups the MHRA specifies is unverified.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The judge noted some product information may now allow eGFR for some drugs; unverified.

numbers.meaning: date of the MHRA Drug Safety Update, from search extract

claims.claim: In very old people with AF on DOACs, whether the dose was judged appropriate by Cockcroft-Gault or by eGFR made no difference to the link with deaths, clots or bleeding.
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 224 patients were included in the analysis (median age 87 years). Using CrCl, 154 (69%) had an appropriate dose of DOACs, 52 (23%) were underdosed and 18 (8%) were overdosed. ... In participants with discrepancies in dose status using CrCland eGFR equations, the occurrence of endpoints did not differ between participants having an appropriate dose using CrClor eGFR." Conclusions: "In older adults with AF, the association of DOAC dose status with adverse events did not differ when using CrClor eGFR. Our results suggest that eGFR equations are not inferior to CrClwithin this context."
claims.pico_timeframe: 224 people with AF on DOACs, median age 87, Berlin / dose status by CrCl vs eGFR / mortality, thromboembolism, bleeding / median 39 months
claims.safe_wording: A Berlin study of 224 people with a median age of 87 found that outcomes did not differ according to which kidney formula was used to judge the dose.
claims.qualifications: Small study; wide uncertainty. Conflicts with Chan 2022.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Direct conflict with C06-19-b; the post must say the evidence on outcomes is mixed.

numbers.meaning: participants
median age
appropriate / underdosed / overdosed by CrCl

claims.claim: eGFR is adjusted to a standard body size (1.73 m2) and creatinine depends on muscle mass, so eGFR can overestimate kidney function in small people with low muscle mass.
claims.supporting_passage: Not found in opened sources (the 1.73 m2 unit appears in Hambling 2017 but without explanation).
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Say only what Chan 2022 supports: eGFR tended to overestimate kidney function compared with Cockcroft-Gault, especially in people over 75 and under 50 kg.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Unverified.

claims.claim: The European labelling convention used in UK and EU medicine leaflets defines frequency words as fixed bands: very common 1 in 10 or more; common 1 in 100 up to 1 in 10; uncommon 1 in 1,000 up to 1 in 100; rare 1 in 10,000 up to 1 in 1,000; very rare fewer than 1 in 10,000.
claims.supporting_passage: Buchter 2014, Table 1 'European commission nomenclature for communicating frequency of adverse effects of drugs': "Very common (≥1/10) Common (≥1/100 to <1/10) Uncommon (≥1/1000 to <1/100) Rare (≥1/10000 to <1/1000) Very rare (<1/10000) Not known cannot be estimated from the available data". Knapp 2004 abstract: "verbal descriptors suggested by the European Union (EU) such as \"common\" (1-10% frequency) and \"rare\" (0.01-0.1%)"
claims.location: Buchter 2014 Background, Table 1 (PMC full text); Knapp 2004 Abstract (Objective)
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition from the European Commission 1998 readability guideline, carried into later guidance; not a study finding
claims.safe_wording: In a medicine leaflet, 'common' means between 1 in 100 and 1 in 10 people: at most 10 in 100, and often fewer. 'Uncommon' means between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 100. 'Rare' means between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 1,000. 'Very rare' means fewer than 1 in 10,000.
claims.qualifications: 'Up to 1 in 10' is only the upper edge of 'common'; say so. The current EU/UK template wording printed in leaflets (for example 'may affect up to 1 in 10 people') was not opened in this project, so quote the bands, not the leaflet phrase.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the definitions.

numbers.meaning: definition of 'common' (1% to under 10% of people taking the medicine)
definition of 'uncommon'
definition of 'rare'
definition of 'very rare'
definition of 'very common'

claims.claim: In a UK randomised study of 120 adults taking statins, those told constipation was 'common' estimated its likelihood at 34.2% on average, against 8.1% for those told the figure 2.5%; for pancreatitis described as 'rare', estimates were 18% with the word and 2.1% with the number 0.04%.
claims.supporting_passage: "120 adults taking simvastatin or atorvastatin after cardiac surgery or myocardial infarction." "Cardiac rehabilitation clinics at two hospitals in Leeds, UK." "Within each side effect condition half the patients were given the information in verbal form and half in numerical form (for constipation, \"common\" or 2.5%; for pancreatitis, \"rare\" or 0.04%)." "The mean likelihood estimate given for the constipation side effect was 34.2% in the verbal group and 8.1% in the numerical group; for pancreatitis it was 18% in the verbal group and 2.1% in the numerical group."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults on statins after cardiac events, Leeds / written statement giving side-effect frequency as a word / same frequency as a percentage / estimated likelihood of the side effect / measured immediately
claims.safe_wording: In a UK study, 120 people taking a statin read that constipation was a 'common' side effect. On average they guessed about 34 in 100 people would get it. People given the actual figure, 2.5 in 100, guessed about 8 in 100. For a 'rare' side effect (4 in 10,000), the word led to an average guess of 18 in 100.
claims.qualifications: Small study; allocation not concealed; estimates were made immediately after reading one statement, so the study shows how the words are read, not what people later did. Even the group given numbers overestimated (8.1% against 2.5%): say this plainly.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with the Buchter 2014 meta-analysis (C06-11-d).

numbers.meaning: participants, adults taking simvastatin or atorvastatin, Leeds
mean estimated likelihood of constipation when told 'common' (verbal group)
mean estimate when told 2.5% (numerical group)
stated frequency of constipation used in the study
mean estimate of pancreatitis when told 'rare'
mean estimate of pancreatitis when told 0.04%
stated frequency of pancreatitis (4 in 10,000)

claims.claim: The frequency words were associated with more negative views of the medicine than the equivalent numbers.
claims.supporting_passage: Knapp 2004: "The verbal descriptors were associated with more negative perceptions of the medicine than their equivalent numerical descriptors." Berry 2003: "In all studies it was found that people significantly over-estimated the likelihood of adverse effects occurring, given specific verbal descriptors. This in turn resulted in significantly higher ratings of their perceived risks to health and significantly lower ratings of their likelihood of taking the medicine."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C06-11-b; Berry 2003 summarises the same group's studies in public, patients and doctors
claims.safe_wording: People given the words also rated the medicine more negatively, and in related studies said they were less likely to take it.
claims.qualifications: Stated intentions on a rating scale, measured once; no study measured whether people actually stopped their medicine.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No behavioural outcome data (Buchter 2014 notes this gap).

claims.claim: A systematic review of 10 randomised trials found that verbal frequency words consistently led to overestimation of side-effect risk; numbers also led to overestimation but less.
claims.supporting_passage: "Ten trials were included. Participants perceived probabilities presented in verbal terms as higher than in numeric terms: commonly used verbal descriptors systematically led to an overestimation of the absolute risk of adverse effects (Range of means: 3% - 54%). Numbers also led to an overestimation of probabilities, but the overestimation was smaller (2% - 20%)." Results: "MD for common side effects: -35.36 [CI: -39.92 to -30.81]". "Only between 9% and 50% of the participants in the numerical groups gave a correct probability for the adverse effects". Limitations: "Many studies were conducted with healthy volunteers and used fictional scenarios." "All outcomes were measured shortly after distribution of the information leaflets, and none of the studies had a follow-up."
claims.location: Abstract (Results); Results (Estimation of probabilities); Description of studies; Limitations of the included studies
claims.pico_timeframe: Mostly general-public volunteers, hypothetical leaflets / verbal EU descriptors / numerical frequency / estimated probability / immediate
claims.safe_wording: Across 10 trials, people given the leaflet words overestimated the chance of a side effect every time. People given numbers also overestimated, but by less.
claims.qualifications: Mostly volunteers reading made-up leaflets; all trials from two UK research groups; measured immediately; no data on behaviour. For 'common' side effects the average overestimate with words was about 35 percentage points larger than with numbers: if used, call it percentage points.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: One trial suggested adding the word to the number may dilute the benefit of the number (post hoc, single trial of 100 people).

numbers.meaning: randomised trials in the review (19 comparisons, 2,145 observations for probability estimates)
range of mean estimates with verbal descriptors across comparisons
range of mean overestimation with numbers
pooled mean difference (verbal higher than numeric) for 'common' side effects
share of numeric-group participants who gave the correct probability

claims.claim: Current EU guidance on leaflets pairs the frequency word with a number, rather than the word alone.
claims.supporting_passage: Buchter 2014 Discussion: "Different preferences imply that using a combined verbal and numerical format may be the best compromise to suit various needs. This is also reflected in the current European Commission Guideline on readability from 2009 as well as the current EU template for patient leaflets". Also: "One study examined a combination of a verbal and numerical description, as it is currently included in the 2009 European Commission Guideline on the readability of package leaflets". EMA search extract (not opened): user testing showed double-sided expressions such as "affects more than 1 in 100 but less than 1 in 10" are not well understood and should not be used in package leaflets.
claims.location: Buchter 2014 Discussion and Description of studies; EMA QRD search extract
claims.pico_timeframe: Regulatory guidance as described in 2014
claims.safe_wording: Many leaflets now print a number beside the word. The Leeds study tested the word alone, so it shows what the word on its own conveys.
claims.qualifications: Do not claim leaflets use words only. The exact current leaflet phrase was not verified.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether the combined word-plus-number format fully fixes the overestimate is uncertain (one trial).

claims.claim: About 1 in 7 older people living at home report difficulty swallowing their medicines, and modifying medicines is common when older people are given them, though the evidence base is small.
claims.supporting_passage: "Five studies met the inclusion criteria. The results suggest that approximately 14 % of community-dwelling older patients experience difficulty swallowing medicines. Between one quarter and one third of occasions of medicine administration to older patients involve the modification of oral medicines." "Difficulty swallowing oral medicines and the modification of medicines are reported as being common issues in the older cohort. However, evidence to support such contentions is limited."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older patients in community and care settings / difficulty swallowing medicines; modification of oral medicines / studies to November 2014
claims.safe_wording: About 1 in 7 older people living at home say they have difficulty swallowing their medicines. Where older people are given medicines by staff, tablets are altered (crushed, split or opened) at between a quarter and a third of doses.
claims.qualifications: Based on only five studies; the authors call the evidence limited.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Schiele 2013 found swallowing difficulty was more common in younger than older primary care patients (C06-01-b), so do not say it is mainly a problem of old age.

numbers.meaning: community-dwelling older patients reporting difficulty swallowing medicines (about 1 in 7)
share of medicine administrations to older patients that involved modifying the medicine
studies included

claims.claim: Difficulty swallowing tablets is often not known to the doctor, and many affected people alter their medicines themselves.
claims.supporting_passage: Schiele 2013: "Of all participants (N = 1,051), 37.4 % reported having had difficulties in swallowing tablets and capsules. The majority (70.4 %) of these patients was not identified by their GP. The occurrence of swallowing difficulties was related to gender (f>m), age (young>old), dysphagia [adjusted odds ratio (adOR): 7.9; p < 0.0001] and mental illness (adOR: 1.8; p < 0.05)." "Because of these difficulties, 58.8 % of the affected patients had already modified their drugs in a way that may alter safety and efficacy and 9.4 % indicated to be non-adherent." "One in 11 primary care patients had frequent difficulties in swallowing tablets and capsules while GPs grossly underestimated these problems." Mc Gillicuddy 2019: "However, when challenges arise, they tend to feel resigned to coping within the constraints of the current medication regimen, resulting in a lack of focused communication with healthcare professionals. Thus, healthcare professionals were unaware of their difficulties and unable to offer advice or solutions."
claims.location: Schiele 2013 Abstract (Results, Conclusions); Mc Gillicuddy 2019 Abstract (Results)
claims.pico_timeframe: German general practice patients of all adult ages on regular tablets (survey); Irish older adults and carers (interviews)
claims.safe_wording: In a survey of 1,051 patients in German general practices, 1 in 11 had frequent trouble swallowing tablets, and GPs had not recognised 7 in 10 of those with any difficulty. More than half of those affected had already altered their tablets themselves. Older people and carers interviewed in Ireland described coping quietly rather than raising it.
claims.qualifications: The survey was of all adult ages and difficulty was commoner in younger patients. Self-report. Avoid 'quietly' (banned word) in the post: use 'without telling anyone' or similar.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None directly conflicting.

numbers.meaning: survey participants, 11 general practices, Germany
reported ever having difficulty swallowing tablets or capsules
primary care patients with frequent difficulty
of those with difficulty, not identified by their GP
of those with difficulty, had modified their medicines in a way that may alter safety or effect

claims.claim: Crushing a slow-release (modified-release) tablet can release the dose all at once and cause overdose; crushing a tablet with a stomach-acid-resistant coating is likely to make it underdose.
claims.supporting_passage: "The clinical consequences for the patient of crushing tablets or opening capsules can be serious: alteration of the drug's absorption can result in sometimes fatal overdose, or conversely underdosing, rendering the treatment ineffective. When it disrupts a drug's sustained-release properties, the active ingredient is no longer released and absorbed gradually, resulting in overdose. When a gastro-resistant layer is destroyed by crushing, underdosing is likely." "In practice, there are many drugs that should never be crushed or opened."
claims.pico_timeframe: Review of evidence on crushing tablets or opening capsules, all patients
claims.safe_wording: Crushing a slow-release tablet (often marked MR, SR or XL) destroys the slow release, so the dose is absorbed at once and can cause an overdose. Crushing a tablet with a coating that protects it from stomach acid can stop it working properly. Some medicines should never be crushed or opened.
claims.qualifications: The review describes mechanisms and case harms, not how often harm follows. The label abbreviations (MR, SR, XL) are common examples, not a complete list; the post should say 'often marked'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Another form of the medicine, or another medicine, is sometimes a better solution than crushing; pharmacists are well placed to advise.
claims.supporting_passage: Prescrire 2014: "Before crushing a tablet or opening a capsule, it is better to consider and research the impact it will have on the drug's effects. It is sometimes preferable to use a different dosage form, or a different active ingredient." Mc Gillicuddy 2019: "Whilst the input and expertise of all healthcare professionals will be required, as medication experts, the pharmacy profession should take ownership and become the champion of, and for, the patient."
claims.pico_timeframe: Review and qualitative study; recommendation rather than trial evidence
claims.safe_wording: Before crushing, ask a pharmacist. There may be a liquid, a dispersible tablet or a different medicine that avoids crushing altogether.
claims.qualifications: Do not promise that an alternative always exists ('sometimes' / 'may be'). Naming specific alternatives (liquid, dispersible) is general knowledge consistent with Prescrire's 'different dosage form'; avoid naming patches as a routine alternative. The candidate's pharmacy guidance sources (SPS, NEWT) were not opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Slow-release tablets should not be split, but for most other tablets the evidence gives little support to concerns about splitting (apart from physical difficulty splitting them).
claims.supporting_passage: "No substantive evidence was found to support concerns regarding loss of mass, weight variability, chemical instability, or non-compliance. Evidence does support some older adults struggling to split tablets without tablet splitters, and the inappropriateness of splitting sustained-release preparations, given the potential for alteration of the rate of drug release for some products." "With the exception of sustained-release tablets, which should not be split, and excepting those older people who may struggle to split tablets based on physical limitations, there is little evidence to support tablet-splitting concerns."
claims.pico_timeframe: Systematic review of 138 articles on tablet splitting
claims.safe_wording: Splitting is a different matter from crushing: many tablets can be halved safely, but slow-release tablets should not be split. If in doubt, ask the pharmacist.
claims.qualifications: This corrects the candidate's position: do not say 'no tablet should be split'. No studies were found on splitting enteric-coated tablets.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Manufacturer and pharmacy guidance may still advise against splitting particular products.

claims.claim: In an observational study in English care homes with nursing, medicine administration errors were observed in 57.3% of administrations for residents with swallowing difficulty and 30.8% for residents without.
claims.supporting_passage: "A pharmacist specialised in dysphagia observed nurses during drug rounds and compared these practices with national guidelines. Deviations were classified as types of medication administration errors (MAEs)." "Overall, 738 administrations were observed from 166 patients of which 38 patients (22.9%) had dysphagia. MAE rates were 57.3% and 30.8% for PWD and those without respectively (p<0.001)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Care homes with nursing, North Yorkshire / residents with dysphagia / residents without / deviations from national guidance during observed drug rounds / single observation period

This practice occurs among vulnerable groups, including children, people with intellectual disabilities, people experiencing mental ill-health, and older people, particularly those living with dementia." claims.claim: A used fentanyl patch still contains a substantial amount of drug after its wearing period, enough to harm a child.

claims.claim: Heat over a fentanyl patch increases the amount of drug absorbed, and heat exposure has been identified by the UK regulator as a factor in unintentional overdose.

"However, significant differences were seen during the first 4 hours, with C(max) and AUC values almost 3 times higher for the heated administrations than for the administrations without heat." claims.claim: Putting on a new patch without removing the old one is a recognised cause of too-high doses of opioid patches.
claims.supporting_passage: Lovborg 2014 Abstract: "In the study 151 MEs were identified. The three most common error types were wrong administration time 67 (44%), wrong dose 34 (23%), and omission of dose 20 (13%)." Of the cases with too high dose, 7 were cases where the old patch were not removed before a new patch was applied." "The second case concerns a patient who received a higher dose than prescribed. At admittance to hospital health care personnel found two sets of patches of the prescribed dose on the patient". "Educating healthcare personnel in transdermal opioid pain management and the importance of carefully checking patient for old patches before applying new ones would likely reduce the risk of overdosing." Thereby, the lack of knowledge and awareness of the importance of a correct administration practice were a major source of risk."

claims.pico_timeframe: Incident reports of fentanyl and buprenorphine patch errors, Swedish region, 2004 to 2011; systematic review of published errors
claims.safe_wording: One of the commonest ways a patch dose ends up too high is simple: the old patch is still on when the new one goes on. In one Swedish region's incident reports, this explained 7 of the 13 reports of too high a dose. Check for the old patch, take it off, and write down where and when the new one went on.
claims.qualifications: Incident reports cannot give how often this happens overall. The site-and-time record is a recommended practice (Lovborg; Lampert), not tested in a trial.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The commonest reported error overall was late changing of patches (44%), not duplication.

claims.claim: Used patches should be folded in half with the sticky sides together before disposal, and disposed of as advised so children and pets cannot reach them.

However, it is ideal to hand them over to a drug take-back site where they can be properly discarded [10]." Finlay and Dunne 2019: "Discarded patches should be folded putting the sticky sides of each patch together so that it sticks to itself. They should then be wrapped in paper or plastic before disposal". "Used patches should be disposed of carefully and not be put in a wastepaper bin where pets may find and ingest them". claims.qualifications: Do not advise flushing (US advice). The UK disposal route (for example returning to a pharmacy) was not confirmed from an opened UK document, so say 'as the pharmacist advises'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Disposal routes differ between countries.

claims.safe_wording: Watch for unusual sleepiness or slow, shallow breathing. If you see this, or a child or pet has touched or chewed a patch, get urgent medical help.
claims.qualifications: 'Unusual sleepiness' is the standard presentation of opioid excess; the sources name respiratory depression and respiratory failure explicitly. Do not describe confusion (delirium is out of scope). The urgent-help instruction rests on a search extract plus general safety judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Errors in the medicines history taken at hospital admission are common, most often a medicine left off.
claims.supporting_passage: "We identified 22 studies involving a total of 3755 patients (range 33-1053, median 104). Errors in prescription medication histories occurred in up to 67% of cases: 10%- 61% had at least 1 omission error (deletion of a drug used before admission), and 13%- 22% had at least 1 commission error (addition of a drug not used before admission); 60%- 67% had at least 1 omission or commission error." claims.claim: About a third of older people taking prescribed medicines also take herbal remedies or supplements, and some of these combinations carry a potential for interactions.

"The most commonly used dietary supplements were cod liver oil, glucosamine, multivitamins, and vitamin D." "Sixteen participants (32.6%) were at risk of potential adverse drug interactions." claims.claim: In hospital, Parkinson's medicines are often given late: in one study half of doses were more than 30 minutes late.
claims.supporting_passage: Richard 2022: "A total of 102 admissions of 70 patients (67% men) were included for analysis." "Of the admission days with known outpatient timing regimens, 47% had an average deviation of more than 30 min and 22% had at least one missed levodopa dose."

claims.qualifications: Single-centre studies outside the UK; the second figure is per hospital day, not per dose. Present each figure with its own denominator.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Rates vary between hospitals; improvement programmes have raised on-time rates (not researched in depth here).

claims.claim: Missed and mistimed Parkinson's doses in hospital are linked with longer stays and, for omitted doses, higher in-hospital death rates; the studies are observational.
claims.supporting_passage: Lertxundi 2017: "All PD patients admitted to any of the 11 public acute-care hospitals in the Basque Country in 2011-2012 were included." "The study included 1628 patients admitted 2546 times. Medication errors, affecting almost one third of admissions and half of patients, were associated with higher mortality: inappropriately omitted dopaminergic drug doses OR = 1.92 CI 95% (1.34-2.76)" "Inappropriately omitted doses and both inappropriate antipsychotic and antiemetic administration were associated with a significant 4-day increase in median hospital stay." Yu 2023: "LOS was longer with each additional day of over-dose (4%), under-dose (14%), missed dose (21%), timing deviation (15%) and substitution (19%), (all p < 0.0001)." "Deviations between outpatient and hospital regimens, and administration of antidopaminergic medications, were associated with poor outcomes."

A US study found each extra day with a missed dose or badly timed doses was linked with a longer stay. These studies show a link; they do not prove the late doses caused the longer stays.
claims.qualifications: Observational: sicker people may both miss doses and stay longer. Do not turn the odds ratio (1.92) into 'twice as likely to die'. Per the editor, do not list drugs to avoid: the 'almost one third of admissions' headline includes dopamine-blocking drugs, so if quoted it must be described as 'errors with Parkinson's medicines, including missed doses'; prefer the omitted-dose results. The antipsychotic odds ratio in the abstract has an inconsistent confidence interval and must not be used.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Causation not established; residual confounding likely.

The rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001)." claims.claim: STAREE (2026): in 9971 Australians aged 70 and over without CVD, diabetes or dementia, atorvastatin 40 mg reduced major cardiovascular events but did not clearly lengthen disability-free survival over a median 5.9 years; serious adverse events were similar.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Community-dwelling adults at least 70 years of age with no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or dementia were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive atorvastatin at a dose of 40 mg once daily or identical placebo." ... "A total of 9971 participants were enrolled: 4984 were assigned to receive atorvastatin and 4987 to receive placebo. The mean (±SD) age of the participants was 74.7±4.5 years, and 51.9% were women. After a median of 5.9 years, a primary cardiovascular event had occurred in 297 participants (10.9 events per 1000 person-years) in the atorvastatin group and in 412 participants (15.5 events per 1000 person-years) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.61 to 0.82; P<0.001). Death from any cause, dementia, or persistent physical disability occurred in 637 participants (21.6 events per 1000 person-years) in the atorvastatin group and in 676 participants (23.0 events per 1000 person-years) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.84 to 1.05; P = 0.25). Serious adverse events occurred in 131 participants (2.7%) in the atorvastatin group and in 129 (2.7%) in the placebo group, with musculoskeletal, hepatobiliary, and diabetes-related adverse events occurring more commonly in the atorvastatin group."
claims.pico_timeframe: 9971 community-dwelling Australians aged 70+ (mean 74.7) without CVD, diabetes or dementia / atorvastatin 40 mg / placebo / major CV events (CV death, non-fatal MI or stroke, coronary revascularisation); disability-free survival / median 5.9 years
claims.safe_wording: A trial published in August 2026 gave 9971 Australians aged 70 and over (average age 75), without heart disease, stroke, diabetes or dementia, a statin or a dummy tablet. Over about 6 years, about 6 in 100 on the statin and 8 in 100 on the dummy tablet had a heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death or a procedure to open a heart artery. The statin did not clearly change the chance of staying alive without dementia or lasting disability (about 13 in 100 vs 14 in 100 lost it).
claims.qualifications: The '6 vs 8 in 100' and '13 vs 14 in 100' figures are crude proportions calculated here from the counts in the abstract (297/4984, 412/4987; 637/4984, 676/4987), not Kaplan-Meier estimates. Only the abstract was read: results for those aged 75 and over, and the size of the excess muscle, liver and diabetes-related events, were not seen. The cardiovascular composite includes coronary revascularisation. People with diabetes were excluded.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Adds direct evidence of cardiovascular benefit in over-70s that earlier sources lacked (C07-12-d). No clear effect on disability-free survival; 'did not show a clear difference' is the correct phrasing, not 'no effect'.

claims.claim: Switching off the shocks needs no operation, is painless and reversible, leaves pacing working, and does not in itself cause death.

claims.pico_timeframe: Technical and practice facts about ICD deactivation (Canada; UK guidance cited by an Australian and US survey).
claims.safe_wording: Switching off the shocks needs no operation. A member of the heart rhythm or pacemaker team reprograms the device from outside the body. It is painless and can be reversed. The device's pacing (the part that stops the heart going too slowly) keeps working. It does not cause death by itself. It means that a dangerous heart rhythm near the end of life will not be shocked.
claims.qualifications: Say 'shock function', not 'the device'. Pacing continues. Deactivation removes a possible life-saving shock, so avoid implying it has no effect on how death happens. The magnet method is an emergency, temporary measure.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found. The UK guidance (Pitcher 2016; BHRS 2024) says the same, but its practical sections were not readable here.

claims.qualifications: The candidate's 2013 BHF document has been superseded by the British Heart Rhythm Society consensus guideline (Age and Ageing, 2024); cite that. Keep the tone to planning ('when the time is right'), not expectation of death.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; the UK scenario study (Moffat 2016) and UFTO evaluation (Fritz 2013) point the same way.

With the order, fewer said they would give a blood transfusion (75 in 100 versus 87 in 100 in one scenario) or send blood tests for infection (91 versus 98 in 100).

claims.claim: A time-limited trial is an agreed plan to use a treatment for a defined period, after which the person's response decides whether to continue, stop and focus on comfort, or extend.
claims.supporting_passage: ATS 2024, Key Conclusions: "The time-limited trial in critical care is operationally defined as a collaborative plan among clinicians and a patient and/or their surrogate decision maker(s) to use life-sustaining therapy for a defined duration, after which the patient’s response to therapy informs the decision to continue care directed toward recovery, transition to care focused exclusively on comfort, or extend the trial’s duration." | Vink 2018, Abstract: "A TLT is an agreement to initiate all necessary treatments or treatments with clearly delineated limitations for a certain period of time to gain a more realistic understanding of the patient's chances of a meaningful recovery or to ascertain the patient's wishes and values."
claims.location: ATS: Overview, Key Conclusions; Section 1. Vink: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Critical care; consensus definition (Delphi with 100 stakeholders).
claims.safe_wording: A time-limited trial is an agreed plan to give a treatment for a set time. At the end, how the person has responded guides the next step: carry on, stop and focus on comfort, or extend the trial.
claims.qualifications: The consensus definition is written for life-sustaining treatment in critical care. Applying it to other decisions in older people is reasonable but is extrapolation; the report notes the approach is also promoted in nephrology, neurology and surgery. Quill & Holloway 2011 (JAMA) has no abstract and was not opened; cite ATS 2024 instead.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: The plan should state the treatment, how long it will run, the clinical signs that will show improvement or deterioration, and what will happen at review; it is proposed to and agreed with the person or family.
claims.supporting_passage: ATS 2024, Introduction: "This approach has been described as an attempt or “trial” of life-sustaining therapy, with specific, agreed-on guidelines designed to help clinicians, patients, and surrogates evaluate whether the therapy is providing benefit to the patient. These guidelines typically include a boundary on how long the trial lasts and clinical criteria that help determine the patient’s response to the therapy. After the trial is over, patients (if able), surrogates, and clinicians use these criteria to consider whether to continue life-sustaining therapies or, instead, focus exclusively on comfort ()." | Section 1: "Our committee concluded that the time-limited trial approach is distinct from current “usual care” for patients with critical illness, largely because of strong consensus that the trial is explicitly proposed to the patient and/or surrogate(s) who can then endorse the structured plan." | Section 2: "we measured participants’ views on these respective roles for three major elements of a time-limited trial:) the clinical criteria of improvement and deterioration,) the duration, and) the acceptable degree of recovery or the clinical outcome after the time-limited trial." | Key Conclusions: "A time-limited trial is composed of 16 essential elements that follow four sequential phases: consider, plan, support, and reassess."
claims.location: ATS 2024 full text: Introduction; Section 1; Section 2; Key Conclusions.
claims.pico_timeframe: Critical care consensus, US-led, 2024.
claims.safe_wording: Expert consensus describes what separates a time-limited trial from 'let's see how it goes'. The plan is offered to the person or family, who can agree to it. It names the treatment, how long it will run, the signs that would show it is working or not, and what happens at the review.
claims.qualifications: The four-item list simplifies the ATS consensus, which has 16 elements in four phases (consider, plan, support, reassess). Present the four as core items, not the full standard. The consensus is flexible: trials can be extended and should not be binding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The ATS report says there is little evidence on how best to conduct trials. Kruser 2024 found them often carried out incompletely in practice.

numbers.meaning: essential elements in the ATS consensus, across 4 phases

claims.claim: In a US ICU quality-improvement study, training clinicians to use time-limited trials was associated with better family meetings, shorter ICU stays and fewer invasive procedures, without a change in hospital mortality.
claims.supporting_passage: Chang 2021, Abstract: "This prospective quality improvement study was conducted from June 1, 2017, to December 31, 2019, at the medical ICUs of 3 academic public hospitals in California." ... "A total of 209 patients were included (mean [SD] age, 63.6 [16.3] years" ... "identifying clinical markers of improvement (9 [20.9%] vs 52 [88.1%]; P < .01), were discussed more frequently after intervention. Median ICU length of stay was significantly reduced between preintervention and postintervention periods (8.7 [interquartile range (IQR), 5.7-18.3] days vs 7.4 [IQR, 5.2-11.5] days; P = .02). Hospital mortality was similar between the preintervention and postintervention periods (66 of 113 [58.4%] vs 56 of 96 [58.3%], respectively; P = .99). Invasive ICU procedures were used less frequently in the postintervention period (eg, mechanical ventilation preintervention, 97 [85.8%] vs postintervention, 70 [72.9%]; P = .02)." | ATS 2024, Section 4: "To our knowledge, the time-limited trial approach has been tested in only one pre-post study of a quality improvement program focused on implementation. In that study, surrogates experienced earlier and more frequent family meetings, though there was no change in their satisfaction with medical care or amount of decision making conflict ()."
claims.pico_timeframe: 209 critically ill adults with advanced medical illness (mean age 63.6), 3 California public-hospital ICUs; before (113) vs after (96) clinician training; ICU length of stay, procedures, hospital mortality; 2017 to 2019.
claims.safe_wording: In one US study in three intensive care units, before-and-after training doctors to use time-limited trials: family meetings named the signs of improvement far more often (about 1 in 5 meetings before, almost 9 in 10 after). Median intensive care stay fell from 8.7 to 7.4 days, and fewer people were put on a ventilator (86 in 100 before, 73 in 100 after). Hospital deaths did not change (58 in 100 in both periods).
claims.qualifications: Before-and-after quality-improvement study, not randomised; not specific to older people (mean age 64). Label it as 'a US intensive care before-and-after study' in the caption. According to ATS 2024, family satisfaction and decisional conflict did not change. The claim that trials protect against both premature withdrawal and open-ended treatment is the rationale (C07-26-e), not a measured result.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Only one interventional study exists (ATS 2024), so the effect may not hold elsewhere.

numbers.meaning: patients (113 before, 96 after)
family meetings that identified clinical markers of improvement, before vs after
median ICU length of stay, before vs after
mechanical ventilation, before vs after
hospital mortality, before vs after

claims.claim: Time-limited trials are often carried out incompletely and are rarely documented.
claims.supporting_passage: Kruser 2024 (Chest), Abstract: "When time-limited trials are used, they are often implemented incompletely and challenged by systematic barriers (eg, continually rotating ICU staff)." ... "some older adults appear to favor time-limited trial strategies over indefinite life-sustaining therapy or care immediately focused on comfort." | Piscitello 2025, Abstract: "Of 5475 GOC-template notes, we found reference to a TLT in 1% (n = 69/5475)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Kruser: review of 18 empirical studies (ICU). Piscitello: goals-of-care notes for seriously ill adults, 21 US hospitals, 2021 to 2023.
claims.safe_wording: Reviews find that when time-limited trials are used, parts of the plan are often missing. In one US health system, only about 1 in 100 goals-of-care notes recorded a time-limited trial. Some older adults say they would prefer this approach to open-ended treatment or an immediate switch to comfort care.
claims.qualifications: US data. Low documentation may partly reflect under-recording rather than non-use. Kruser's finding on older adults' preferences is phrased 'appear to'; keep that tentativeness.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: goals-of-care notes that referred to a time-limited trial, 21 US hospitals

claims.claim: The purpose of a time-limited trial is to avoid both open-ended treatment without benefit and giving up too early.
claims.supporting_passage: ATS 2024, Key Conclusions: "This specific approach to patient care aims to uphold a set of goals held by many patients: to extend life when possible and to avoid prolonged life-sustaining therapy if the chance of survival is low or the impact on quality of life is unacceptable." | Introduction: "In critical care, the time-limited trial approach aims to provide greater nuance to a clinical decision that is often oversimplified as a dichotomous choice between either open-ended life-sustaining therapy or an immediate transition to comfort-focused, end-of-life care." | Table 3: "Trials of high-quality, standard-of-care therapies" (should be) vs "Lower quality care" (should not be).
claims.pico_timeframe: Consensus rationale; not an outcome measure.
claims.safe_wording: The aim is a middle path between open-ended treatment and stopping at once: give the treatment a fair chance, with full-quality care, and agree in advance how you will judge it.
claims.qualifications: This is the stated aim of the approach, from expert consensus, not a measured effect; mark it as the rationale. The ATS report also warns that poorly carried out trials may cause harm or conflict.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: ATS 2024: 'there is a small evidence base for efficacy'.

claims.claim: The Serious Illness Conversation Guide begins by asking what the person understands about their illness and how they want information and decisions handled, before sharing prognosis and then exploring goals, fears, trade-offs and family involvement.
claims.supporting_passage: Bloom 2022, Results (Scite full-text excerpt): "The guide recommends to: elicit illness understanding, elicit decision-making preferences, share prognostic information according to preference, understand goals and fears, explore views on trade-offs and impaired function, and understand desire for family involvement (table 1).33" | Bloom 2022: "There are three core components that each framework includes: assessing patients’ illness understanding and preferences, communicating prognosis and responding to emotion." | Bernacki 2015, Abstract: "The Serious Illness Care Program is a multicomponent, structured communication intervention designed to identify patients, train clinicians to use a structured guide for advanced care planning discussion with patients, 'trigger' clinicians to have conversations, prepare patients and families for the conversation, and document outcomes of the discussion in a structured format in the electronic medical record." | Paladino 2026, Abstract: "Major revisions were made to specific Guide sections, including the introduction, prognosis, illness understanding, and critical abilities. Other additions included a question to align around patient hopes and a prompt for clinicians to respond to emotion."
claims.location: Bloom: Results (description of SICG, citing Bernacki 2015). Bernacki 2015: Abstract. Paladino 2026: Abstract, Results.
claims.pico_timeframe: Published descriptions of the Ariadne Labs Serious Illness Conversation Guide (oncology origin); 2026 revision.
claims.safe_wording: One widely used, tested conversation guide takes a set order. First, ask what the person understands about their illness, and how much they want to know and to be involved. Then share what is likely to happen, at the level they asked for. Only then explore their goals, worries, what they would and would not trade for more time, and who they want involved.
claims.qualifications: Paraphrase; do not reproduce the guide's copyrighted wording. The guide was revised in 2025 to 2026 (a question on hopes added and the understanding section reworded), so describe the sequence, not the exact questions. The claim that asking first 'shows where to begin' and 'brings misunderstandings out early' is the design rationale and teaching judgement, not a tested finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the sequence itself.

claims.claim: In a cluster randomised trial in US outpatient oncology, the Serious Illness Care Program did not improve its main outcomes (goal-concordant care, peacefulness at the end of life); it reduced moderate to severe anxiety and depression symptoms (secondary outcomes).
claims.supporting_passage: Bernacki 2019, Abstract: "A cluster randomized clinical trial of the Serious Illness Care Program in an outpatient oncology setting was conducted. Patients with advanced cancer (n = 278) and oncology clinicians (n = 91) participated between September 1, 2012, and June 30, 2016." ... "The coprimary outcomes were evaluated in 64 patients; no significant differences were found between the intervention and control groups. However, the trial demonstrated significant reductions in the proportion of patients with moderate to severe anxiety (10.2% vs 5.0%; P = .05) and depression symptoms (20.8% vs 10.6%; P = .04) in the intervention group at 14 weeks after baseline. Anxiety reduction was sustained at 24 weeks (10.4% vs 4.2%; P = .02), but depression reduction was not sustained (17.8% vs 12.5%; P = .31). Survival and therapeutic alliance did not differ between groups." ... "The results of this cluster randomized clinical trial were null with respect to the coprimary outcomes of goal-concordant care and peacefulness at the end of life. Methodologic challenges for the primary outcomes, including measure selection and sample size, limit the conclusions that can be drawn from the study." ... "of 39 who received a reminder, 34 (87.2%) completed at least 1 conversation (median duration, 19 minutes; range, 5-70)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 278 adults with advanced cancer and 91 clinicians, Dana-Farber outpatient oncology, Boston; programme (training, guide, reminders) vs usual care; co-primary: goal-concordant care, peacefulness (64 evaluable); secondary: anxiety, depression at 14 and 24 weeks; 2012 to 2016.
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial in cancer clinics (278 patients), the programme built around this guide did not show a clear difference in its two main aims: care matching people's goals, and peace at the end of life. It did lower the share of people with moderate to severe anxiety (10 in 100 to 5 in 100 at 14 weeks) and depression symptoms (21 to 11 in 100); these were secondary measures. "Compared to dialysis, CKM had uncertain effects on death (any cause) (23 studies, 24,628 participants: 813 per 1000 with CKM versus 630 per 1000 with dialysis) (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.41; I² = 89%; very low-certainty evidence)" ... "We found no randomised controlled trials. The certainty of evidence from non-randomised studies was very low due to a high risk of bias, because of significant imbalances in prognostic factors that could not be fully addressed." | Bergen 2026, full text: "Taken together, the available observational evidence suggests that dialysis is generally associated with longer survival compared with CKM, but this advantage appears to diminish substantially with increasing age, frailty, and comorbidity." | Verberne 2016, Abstract: "Patients choosing CM were older (mean±SD: 83±4.5 versus 76±4.4 years; P<0.001)." ... "However, the survival advantage of patients choosing RRT was no longer observed in patients ages ≥80 years old (median; 75th to 25th percentiles: 2.1, 1.5-3.4 versus 1.4, 0.7-3.0 years; log-rank test: P=0.08)." | Foote 2016, Abstract: "While the available literature demonstrates a broadly similar 1-year survival in elderly ESKD patients, it does not allow a confident estimate of the relative survival benefits of dialysis or supportive care."

claims.pico_timeframe: People aged 65+ (Cochrane) or 70+ (Verberne) with kidney failure choosing CKM vs dialysis; observational; death over variable follow-up.
claims.safe_wording: No randomised trial has compared dialysis with conservative care. In observational studies, people who have dialysis usually live longer, but they are also usually younger and fitter, so part of the gap is not caused by dialysis. In one Dutch hospital, among people aged 80 or over, those choosing dialysis lived a median of 2.1 years and those choosing conservative care 1.4 years; the study did not show a clear difference.

Do not quote the Cochrane crude figures (813 vs 630 deaths per 1000) without saying they are very low certainty and confounded, and not the effect of dialysis. Verberne is small (311 people) and single-centre, and P=0.08 is not evidence of no difference. Replace 'adds little time' with these findings.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Montez-Rath 2024 found that the survival gain from starting dialysis was larger (not smaller) in people aged 80 or over (60 days over 3 years), which conflicts with Verberne. Present the uncertainty in both directions.

claims.claim: In older US veterans, starting dialysis when kidney function fell very low made little clear difference to survival over 3 years compared with continuing medical care, and meant about 2 weeks fewer days at home; compared with never having dialysis, it added about 11 weeks of life and still meant fewer days at home.

Over a 3-year horizon, the group starting dialysis survived 770 days and the group continuing medical management survived 761 days (difference, 9.3 days [95% CI, -17.4 to 30.1 days]). Compared with the group continuing medical management, the group starting dialysis had 13.6 fewer days at home (CI, 7.7 to 20.5 fewer days at home). Compared with the group continuing medical management and forgoing dialysis completely, the group starting dialysis had longer survival by 77.6 days (CI, 62.8 to 91.1 days) and 14.7 fewer days at home (CI, 11.2 to 16.5 fewer days at home)." | Full text, Methods: "We defined home time as the number of days the patient was alive and not receiving inpatient care in a hospital, skilled nursing facility, nursing home, or rehabilitation facility." | Results: "In age-stratified analyses, compared to continuing medical management, starting dialysis was associated with longer survival by 60.0 days among adults ≥80 years (95% CI 3.5, 108.8) but 12.9 fewer days at home (95% CI −28.7, −0.2)." | Discussion: "we did not impose requirements on the frequency of medical visits or type of care provided in the medical management arm; therefore this treatment arm should not be considered equivalent to structured clinical programs for patients who proactively choose to forgo dialysis." ... "Finally, the results may not be generalizable to women, non-Veterans, or patients who start peritoneal dialysis."
claims.location: Abstract; full text Methods (Outcomes), Results, Discussion (Limitations).
claims.pico_timeframe: 20,440 US veterans aged 65+ (mean 77.9), eGFR below 12, not referred for transplant; start dialysis within 30 days vs continue medical management (49% later started dialysis) or forgo dialysis entirely (per-protocol); survival and home time over 3 years; 2010 to 2018.
claims.safe_wording: In a large US study of about 20,000 veterans aged 65 or over (average age 78) who were not having a transplant, the researchers compared starting dialysis as soon as kidney function fell very low with carrying on with medical care. Over 3 years, starting at once made little clear difference to survival (about 9 days longer on average, anywhere from 17 days shorter to 30 days longer). It meant about 2 weeks fewer days at home rather than in hospital or a care home. Compared with never having dialysis, it added about 11 weeks of life but still meant about 2 weeks fewer at home.

'Days at home' means days alive and not in hospital, a nursing or care home, or rehabilitation. Outpatient dialysis sessions count as days at home, so the time spent at dialysis is not included in the loss. The comparison group got usual medical care, not a structured conservative care programme. In people aged 80 or over, starting dialysis was linked with about 2 months longer survival, so do not say dialysis helps the oldest least.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Direction of benefit varied by subgroup (in people aged 65 to 79 with eGFR 9 to 12, survival favoured continuing medical management). Verberne 2016 found no clear survival gain in people aged 80 or over. The uncertainty runs both ways.

claims.claim: IST-3 enrolled 3035 people with acute ischaemic stroke, of whom 1617 (53%) were older than 80.

'Largest-ever trial of thrombolysis for stroke' was the authors' description in 2012; later trials (for example of tenecteplase or of alteplase doses) were not checked, so do not call IST-3 'the largest' in 2026 without that qualification ('at the time, the largest').

"Thrombolytic therapy with intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA), when approved in Europe, was restricted to the treatment of patients younger than 80 years of age with acute ischaemic stroke who could be treated within 3 h." "We defined a good stroke outcome as no significant disability at 3-6 months, defined by a modified Rankin Score of 0 or 1." ... "Proportional treatment benefits were similar irrespective of age or stroke severity." claims.pico_timeframe: Adults over 80 with acute ischaemic stroke under 4.5 h / IV alteplase / guideline recommendation
claims.safe_wording: European stroke guidelines strongly recommend clot-busting treatment for people over 80 whose stroke started less than 4.5 hours ago. All nine members of the guideline group agreed that age alone should not be a reason to withhold it.
claims.qualifications: This is the European Stroke Organisation guideline (2021). It recommends treatment when other criteria (timing, brain scan, no contraindication) are met; it does not mean everyone over 80 is eligible.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: UK wording (National Clinical Guideline for Stroke 2023, 'regardless of age') seen only as a search extract (claim C07-30-g).

numbers.meaning: time from stroke onset within which the recommendation applies
guideline group members agreeing age alone should not limit thrombolysis (expert consensus)

claims.claim: The 2023 National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland recommends that thrombolysis be considered regardless of age.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine extract (not the guideline itself): "Patients with acute ischaemic stroke, regardless of age or stroke severity, in whom treatment can be started within 4.5 hours of known onset, should be considered for thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase."
claims.location: Search-engine summary of guideline summary pages (Medscape, Medical Independent)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK and Ireland adults with acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 h
claims.safe_wording: Do not quote the UK guideline's wording. If a UK reference is needed, say 'European stroke guidelines' (C07-30-f) instead.
claims.qualifications: Access was search_extract only; the guideline and its summary pages could not be opened, and it is not in Drive. The Clinical Medicine 2024 summary by the guideline authors (PMID 38387534, full text) does not reproduce the age wording.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not verified.

claims.claim: Whether someone can have emergency stroke treatment depends on time since onset and a brain scan, not age; earlier treatment gives more benefit, so call 999 at once.
claims.supporting_passage: Emberson abstract: "Alteplase increased the odds of a good stroke outcome, with earlier treatment associated with bigger proportional benefit. Treatment within 3·0 h resulted in a good outcome for 259 (32·9%) of 787 patients who received alteplase versus 176 (23·1%) of 762 who received control (OR 1·75, 95% CI 1·35-2·27); delay of greater than 3·0 h, up to 4·5 h, resulted in good outcome for 485 (35·3%) of 1375 versus 432 (30·1%) of 1437 (OR 1·26, 95% CI 1·05-1·51); and delay of more than 4·5 h resulted in good outcome for 401 (32·6%) of 1229 versus 357 (30·6%) of 1166 (OR 1·15, 95% CI 0·95-1·40)." Emberson full text: "We found no evidence that old age shortened the period during which alteplase could effectively be given". IST-3 Methods (Scite citation snippet): "patients were eligible according to the following criteria: they had symp-toms and signs of clinically definite acute stroke; the time of stroke onset was known; treatment could be started within 6 h of onset; and CT or MRI had reliably excluded both intracranial haemorrhage and structural brain lesions, which could mimic stroke (eg, cerebral tumour)." ESO abstract: "Appropriate patient selection and timely treatment are crucial." Bhalla 2024 (full text): "clinicians in high-risk clinical areas ... should have a high level of awareness of acute stroke and time-critical nature of interventions." ... "To maximise the population benefit from thrombolysis, a renewed focus needs to be directed towards improving thrombolysis rates (currently between 10–11%) as well as door to needle times."
claims.location: Emberson abstract and Results excerpt; IST-3 Methods; ESO abstract; Bhalla 2024 full text
claims.pico_timeframe: People with acute ischaemic stroke / alteplase by time to treatment / control / mRS 0-1 at 3-6 months
claims.safe_wording: Whether clot-busting treatment is possible depends on how long ago the stroke started, and on a brain scan to rule out bleeding. The sooner it is given, the more it helps: within 3 hours, 33 in 100 treated people had no significant disability afterwards, against 23 in 100 untreated. So call 999 straight away for stroke symptoms, whatever the person's age.
claims.qualifications: The 999 instruction is standard UK practice and follows from the time dependence; it is advice, not a trial finding. Eligibility also depends on other factors (bleeding risk, some medicines, pre-stroke function) that the post should not list as if complete. Thrombolysis rates in the UK were 10 to 11% of strokes (guideline authors, 2024); this is not an age-specific figure.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Beyond 4.5 h without advanced imaging, the pooled trials did not show a clear benefit (32.6% vs 30.6%).

numbers.meaning: no significant disability at 3-6 months when treated within 3 h, alteplase vs control (259/787 vs 176/762)
same outcome when treated after 3 h up to 4.5 h
UK thrombolysis rate cited by guideline authors in 2024 (all ages)

claims.claim: GAP70+ was a cluster-randomised trial in 718 people aged 70 and over with incurable cancer and at least one ageing-related problem, starting a high-risk treatment; oncologists in the intervention practices received a geriatric assessment summary with management recommendations.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "In this cluster-randomised trial, we enrolled patients aged 70 years and older with incurable solid tumours or lymphoma and at least one impaired geriatric assessment domain who were starting a new treatment regimen. 40 community oncology practice clusters across the USA were randomly assigned (1:1) to the intervention (oncologists received a tailored geriatric assessment summary and management recommendations) or usual care (no geriatric assessment summary or management recommendations were provided to oncologists)" ... "we enrolled 718 patients. Patients had a mean age of 77·2 years (SD 5·4)" ... "The mean number of geriatric assessment domain impairments was 4·5 (SD 1·6)". Full text (Methods): "Patients in both arms underwent a GA that evaluated eight domains using patient-reported and objective measures prior to starting the new treatment regimen."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 70+ with incurable solid tumour or lymphoma and >=1 impaired GA domain starting high-toxicity treatment, US community oncology / GA summary + management recommendations to oncologist / usual care / grade 3-5 toxicity over 3 months
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial of 718 people aged 70 and over (average age 77) starting treatment for cancer that could not be cured, some cancer teams were given a geriatric assessment of each person: a check of daily function, falls, memory, mood, nutrition, medicines and support at home, with advice on what to do about each problem.
claims.qualifications: The effect belongs to the whole package (assessment plus recommendations to the oncologist), in people with advanced cancer starting a high-risk regimen. Community oncology practices in the USA, not the NHS.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Cluster randomisation produced some imbalances between arms (race, prior chemotherapy, cancer type).

numbers.meaning: patients enrolled
mean age in years
practice clusters randomised
mean number of impaired assessment domains

claims.claim: In GAP70+, serious side effects (grade 3 to 5) over 3 months occurred in about 51 in 100 people in the intervention group vs 71 in 100 with usual care.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "A lower proportion of patients in the intervention group had grade 3-5 toxic effects (177 [51%] of 349 patients) compared with the usual care group (263 [71%] of 369 patients; relative risk [RR] 0·74 (95% CI 0·64-0·86; p=0·0001)." Full text: "In 718 evaluable patients, the prevalence of patients experiencing any grade 3–5 toxicity was 61·3% (440/718) within three months of starting a new treatment regimen"
claims.pico_timeframe: As C07-23-a / grade 3-5 toxic effects (CTCAE v4) / 3 months
claims.safe_wording: Over the next 3 months, serious side effects happened to about 51 in 100 people whose cancer team had the assessment, compared with 71 in 100 whose team did not.
claims.qualifications: Absolute figures first: 177 of 349 vs 263 of 369. The relative figure (26% lower risk) should come second if used. 'Serious' here means grade 3 to 5 on the standard cancer side-effect scale, which includes hospital-level problems and death (5 deaths from toxicity in total).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Blood-count toxicity alone did not differ clearly (37% vs 44%, not significant); the reduction was mainly in non-blood side effects (32% vs 52%).

numbers.meaning: intervention group with grade 3-5 toxicity over 3 months
usual care group with grade 3-5 toxicity over 3 months
relative risk (relative, second)

claims.claim: In GAP70+, survival was similar in the two groups at 6 months and 1 year.
claims.supporting_passage: Full text (Results): "The proportion of patients alive at six months was similar for the intervention arm compared to usual care (250/349, 71·6% vs 275/369, 74·5%; p=0·38). There were no survival differences between arms at six months (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1·13; 95% CI: 0·85–1·50; p=0·39; CE p=0·04) or one year (aHR 1·05; 95% CI 0·85–1·29; p=0·68; CE p=0·05)". Discussion: "Because survival was a secondary aim and only captured for one year, the study was not designed to examine non-inferiority between the arms; further research is required to evaluate the effects of GA interventions on survival as a primary aim and for tumor control."
claims.location: Full text Results (Overall Survival) and Discussion (limitations)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C07-23-a / overall survival / 6 months and 1 year
claims.safe_wording: About 72 in 100 people in the assessment group and 75 in 100 in the usual care group were alive at 6 months, a difference that could be chance. Survival at 1 year was also similar. The trial was not designed to prove that survival was unaffected.
claims.qualifications: Do not say the assessment 'did not shorten survival' as a proven fact; say survival was similar and the trial was not built to test it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Confidence interval for the 6-month hazard ratio (0.85 to 1.50) is compatible with modest harm or benefit.

numbers.meaning: alive at 6 months, intervention vs usual care (250/349 vs 275/369)

claims.claim: The assessment changed care: more people started on a reduced dose, fewer fell, and more medicines were stopped; a geriatric assessment covers function, memory, mood, other illnesses, medicines, nutrition and social support.
claims.supporting_passage: GAP70+ full text: "A higher proportion of patients in intervention received treatment at a reduced dose intensity than standard at cycle one (170/349; 48·7%) compared to usual care (129/369; 35·0%)." Abstract: "Patients in the intervention group had fewer falls over 3 months (35 [12%] of 298 patients vs 68 [21%] of 329 patients; adjusted RR 0·58, 95% CI 0·40-0·84; p=0·0035) and had more medications discontinued (mean adjusted difference 0·14, 95% CI 0·03-0·25; p=0·015)." Full text: "Frequent toxicity checks, adjusting cancer treatment schedule or dosing, reviewing medications for duplications or interactions, providing education materials on aging-related conditions, and referrals to relevant disciplines (i.e., social worker, nutritionist) were among the most common recommendations selected by oncologists."
