claims.qualifications: Ratings came from participants and family members, who knew whether therapy had been given; the researchers who collected the ratings were blind. The 2.57 vs 0.86 figures are average changes in the goal score, not the proportion of people who improved. A 2-point gain on a single goal is the trial's threshold for a clinically significant change.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Because the raters knew their allocation and the therapy worked directly on these goals, some of the gain may reflect expectation or attention; the authors say the design could not rule out non-specific effects of therapist contact (see C08-06-f).

numbers.meaning: participant-rated effect size at 3 months, rehabilitation vs usual care; 'large'
carer-rated effect size at 3 months
participant and carer effect sizes at 9 months
mean change in average goal attainment rating (0 to 10 scale) at 3 months, rehabilitation vs usual care
trial's threshold for clinically significant change on any individual goal

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in quality of life, mood, self-efficacy or cognition (or in carer stress and quality of life).
claims.supporting_passage: IJGP abstract: "Secondary outcomes at 3 and 9 months included informant-reported goal attainment, quality of life, mood, self-efficacy, and cognition and study partner stress and quality of life." ... "There were no significant differences in secondary outcomes." Full text, Results: "Following Bonferroni correction, there were no significant differences. Effect sizes were small to negligible, although in some cases with wide confidence intervals."
claims.pico_timeframe: Same trial; standard scales of quality of life, mood, self-efficacy, cognition and carer outcomes at 3 and 9 months.
claims.safe_wording: On the standard questionnaires for quality of life, mood, confidence and memory and thinking, the trial did not show a clear difference between the groups.
claims.qualifications: 'No significant difference' after Bonferroni correction, with small to negligible effect sizes and some wide confidence intervals: not proof of no effect.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors say no change in cognitive scores was expected, because the therapy does not aim to improve cognition, and few participants had depression or anxiety at the start (C08-06-f). So the standard scales were not a fair test of what the therapy targets; the post should say this and not imply the scales 'failed'.

claims.claim: The gains related to the goals directly targeted in therapy; for the goals actually worked on, the improvement was larger (2.84 points at 3 months).
claims.supporting_passage: IJGP abstract: "The observed gains related to goals directly targeted in the therapy." Full text, Results: "The CR group participants identified 679 goals and worked on 481 (71%) of these with the therapists. Taking just the 481 goals that were addressed in therapy, the mean change in participants' goal attainment ratings was an improvement of 2.84 points (SD 2.84) at 3 months and 2.77 points (SD 3.18) at 9 months, while." Limitations: "While participants were invited to select up to three goals, on average, the therapists were able to address two goals per participant. The primary outcome was based on ratings of progress with all goals identified at baseline, rather than just those goals that were actually addressed; therefore, the overall estimate of improvement in goal attainment is a conservative one. Ratings for the goals that were directly addressed showed a clinically meaningful degree of change."
claims.location: IJGP abstract (Results); Results (goal attainment); Discussion (Strengths and limitations)
claims.pico_timeframe: Rehabilitation group only: 679 goals identified, 481 worked on; change from baseline at 3 and 9 months.
claims.safe_wording: The improvement was in the specific goals people worked on with the therapist. It did not spread to general measures.
claims.qualifications: The 2.84-point figure is a within-group change for goals addressed in therapy, with no control comparison; use the between-group result (C08-06-c) as the headline.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: goals identified by the rehabilitation group, and goals worked on in therapy
mean improvement at 3 months in ratings for goals addressed in therapy, rehabilitation group only
average number addressed per participant

claims.claim: Reading cautiously: the trial was single-blind (only researchers blinded) and the authors say it could not separate the specific effect of rehabilitation from non-specific effects of therapist contact; they also say the standard scales were not expected to change and may have missed wider benefits.
claims.supporting_passage: Full text, Methods: "This was a multicentre, single‐blind pragmatic RCT comparing CR added to usual treatment (CR) with usual treatment alone (TAU). Outcomes were assessed 3 and 9 months post randomisation." ... "All assessments were conducted in participants' homes by trained researchers blind to group allocation." Limitations: "The trial design did not allow us to conclusively demonstrate that benefits were due to the specific effects of CR rather than nonspecific effects of contact with a therapist; however, the observed gains related specifically to improvements in functional ability for goals directly targeted in the therapy, and in the pilot trial, CR demonstrated benefits over an active control condition." Discussion: "The finding of no differences in cognitive test scores was unsurprising as the intervention does not directly seek to improve cognitive function. As only a small proportion of participants reported clinical levels of depression or anxiety at baseline, there was little scope for the intervention to demonstrate improvements in these domains." ... "However, the qualitative findings were at odds with the results from secondary outcome measures. The intervention may therefore have provided wider benefits that were not detected by available standardised measures."
claims.location: IJGP Methods (Design; Assessments); Discussion (Strengths and limitations; How the findings relate to other evidence)
claims.pico_timeframe: Same trial.
claims.safe_wording: Two cautions. The people rating the goals knew they had had therapy, and the trial could not rule out that some of the benefit came from having an attentive visitor. Also, the therapy was never aimed at memory scores, so no change there is not a failure. The goal ratings measured what the therapy set out to change.
claims.qualifications: 'Single-blind' here means the researchers collecting outcomes were blind; participants and carers were not. The authors' suggestion that the questionnaires missed wider benefits rests on qualitative interviews and is their interpretation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors point to their earlier pilot trial, in which rehabilitation beat an active control condition, as partial reassurance about non-specific effects.

claims.claim: Measured by quality-adjusted life years, the standard economic yardstick, the trial found no evidence of cost-effectiveness; measured against the goals, rehabilitation was cost-effective at willingness-to-pay values of £2,500 or more per unit improvement.
claims.supporting_passage: HTA abstract: "In the cost-utility analyses, there was no evidence of cost-effectiveness in terms of gains in the quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) of the person with dementia (measured using the DEMentia Quality Of Life questionnaire utility score) or the QALYs of the carer (measured using the EuroQol-5 Dimensions, three-level version) from either cost perspective. In the cost-effectiveness analyses, by reference to the primary outcome of participant-rated goal attainment, CR was cost-effective from both the health and social care perspective and the societal perspective at willingness-to-pay values of £2500 and above for improvement in the goal attainment measure."
claims.pico_timeframe: Economic evaluation alongside GREAT, 9 months.
claims.safe_wording: The same pattern showed up in the costings. Judged by the usual economic measure (quality-adjusted life years), the therapy showed no evidence of value for money. Judged by the goals people chose, it did.
claims.qualifications: Cost-effectiveness against the goal measure depends on how much a service is willing to pay per point of goal improvement (£2,500 or more); there is no agreed threshold for that measure.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; this is the trial's own analysis.

numbers.meaning: willingness-to-pay per unit improvement in goal attainment at and above which rehabilitation was cost-effective

claims.claim: Examples of the kinds of goals GREAT participants chose.
claims.supporting_passage: No passage found. IJGP full text describes goals only as "personally relevant and meaningful goals relating to everyday activities"; the protocol gives compensatory-strategy examples ("calendars, diaries, reminder systems") and an example from earlier, pre-GREAT studies ("learning names of other participants in a social club helped to maintain attendance and participation").
claims.location: IJGP Introduction; GREAT protocol Background and Intervention
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not name specific goal types as GREAT participants' goals. The post may say people chose 'everyday activities they wanted to manage better', and may name the methods (prompts, memory aids, practising the skill).
claims.qualifications: The HTA report body, which may list goal categories, was not available.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable.

claims.claim: NICE (NG97) says to consider cognitive rehabilitation or occupational therapy to support functional ability in mild to moderate dementia.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine extract (nice.org.uk NG97 recommendations): "NICE NG97 Recommendation 1.4.4 states: 'Consider cognitive rehabilitation or occupational therapy to support functional ability in people living with mild to moderate dementia.'"
claims.pico_timeframe: England; people living with mild to moderate dementia.
claims.safe_wording: Optional and non-essential. If used: 'NICE guidance in England says services should consider cognitive rehabilitation or occupational therapy for people with mild to moderate dementia.' Better left out, as only a search extract supports it.
claims.qualifications: 'Consider' is a weaker recommendation than 'offer'. Page not opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: NICE recommends offering group cognitive stimulation therapy to people living with mild to moderate dementia.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine extract (nice.org.uk NG97): "NICE NG97 Recommendation 1.4.2 states: 'Offer group cognitive stimulation therapy to people living with mild to moderate dementia.'" | Crawley 2023, Abstract: "Cognitive stimulation therapy (CST) is the only non-pharmacological, treatment for dementia recommended by the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, following multiple international trials demonstrating beneficial cognitive outcomes in people with mild-to-moderate dementia." | Fisher 2025, Abstract: "Cognitive stimulation and reminiscence therapy are recommended by the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence to support the cognition, independence, and wellbeing of people with dementia, and crucially, they can be delivered by care home staff or non-specialist interventionists."
claims.location: NG97 rec 1.4.2 (search extract); Crawley 2023 abstract; Fisher 2025 abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: England (NICE); people living with mild to moderate dementia.
claims.safe_wording: In England, NICE guidance says people with mild to moderate dementia should be offered group cognitive stimulation therapy.
claims.qualifications: Exact NICE wording comes from a search extract; two peer-reviewed papers confirm the recommendation. NICE guidance applies to England (and is often used elsewhere); do not claim it for Scotland. Do not say CST is the 'only' non-drug treatment NICE recommends (NG97 also says to consider cognitive rehabilitation or occupational therapy).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found on the recommendation itself.

claims.claim: Standard CST is 14 sessions over 7 weeks in a small group, with themed activities such as discussion of past and present events, word games, puzzles, music and creative activities; sessions usually run about 45 minutes twice a week.
claims.supporting_passage: Crawley 2023, Background: "CST follows a format of 14 sessions over 7 weeks, with enrolment immediately post-diagnosis." ... "As a non-specialist intervention, any health or social care professional can be trained to deliver CST, and there is good evidence of its cost-effectiveness." | Woods 2023, plain-language summary: "It involves a wide range of activities aiming to stimulate thinking and memory generally, including discussion of past and present events and topics of interest, word games, puzzles, music and creative practical activities. Usually delivered by trained staff working with a small group of people with dementia for around 45 minutes twice‐weekly, it can also be provided on a one‐to‐one basis."
claims.location: Crawley 2023, Background (full text); Woods 2023, plain-language summary
claims.pico_timeframe: Programme description.
claims.safe_wording: Cognitive stimulation therapy is a small group that usually meets twice a week for about 45 minutes, 14 sessions over 7 weeks. Sessions use themed activities such as talking about the news and the past, word games, puzzles and music, run by trained staff.
claims.qualifications: Local formats vary: studies in the Cochrane review ran from 1 to 6 sessions a week and from 8 to 520 sessions in total. Say 'usually'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: standard CST programme
usual session length and frequency (Cochrane plain-language summary)

claims.claim: In the original UK trial of 201 older people with dementia, the CST group improved relative to controls on the MMSE, ADAS-Cog and a dementia quality-of-life scale; about 1 in 6 treated people had a 4-point or greater ADAS-Cog improvement attributable to CST (NNT 6).
claims.supporting_passage: "A single-blind, multi-centre, randomised controlled trial recruited 201 older people with dementia." ... "One hundred and fifteen people were randomised within centres to the intervention group and 86 to the control group. At follow-up the intervention group had significantly improved relative to the control group on the Mini-Mental State Examination (P=0.044), the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale - Cognition (ADAS-Cog) (P=0.014) and Quality of Life - Alzheimer's Disease scales (P=0.028). Using criteria of 4 points or more improvement on the ADAS-Cog the number needed to treat was 6 for the intervention group."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 201 older people with dementia, UK. I: CST programme. C: control group (not described in abstract). O: MMSE, ADAS-Cog, QoL-AD. T: end of programme follow-up.
claims.safe_wording: In the first large trial, 201 people with dementia took part. Those who went to the group scored better afterwards on memory and thinking tests and on a quality-of-life scale than those who did not.
claims.qualifications: Abstract gives p-values but no size of difference; one trial from 2003. The candidate's phrase 'compared with usual activities' and '14 sessions over 7 weeks' are not in this abstract: attribute the format to C08-18-b. Use NNT only with its definition (about 6 people need to attend for one extra person to gain 4 or more points on the ADAS-Cog), or leave it out for a public post.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Later trials vary a lot (Cochrane reports high inconsistency).

numbers.meaning: people randomised (115 CST, 86 control)
number needed to treat for one extra person to improve by 4 or more ADAS-Cog points

claims.claim: The 2023 Cochrane review (37 trials, 2,766 people) found a small short-term benefit to cognition (moderate-quality evidence; about 2 MMSE points, roughly equal to a six-month delay in expected decline), clinically relevant gains in communication and social interaction (high quality), and slight gains in quality of life, mood and day-to-day activities; no negative effects; little or no difference to carers' mood.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "We included 37 RCTs (with 2766 participants), 26 published since the previous update." ... "No negative effects were reported. Overall, we found moderate-quality evidence for a small benefit in cognition associated with CS (standardised mean difference (SMD) 0.40, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.55). In the 25 studies, with 1893 participants, reporting the widely used MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination) test for cognitive function in dementia, there was moderate-quality evidence of a clinically important difference of 1.99 points between CS and controls (95% CI: 1.24, 2.74)." ... "we found moderate-quality evidence of a slight improvement in self-reported QoL (18 studies, 1584 participants; SMD: 0.25 [95% CI: 0.07, 0.42]) as well as in QoL ratings made by proxies (staff or caregivers). We found high-quality evidence for clinically relevant improvements in staff/interviewer ratings of communication and social interaction (5 studies, 702 participants; SMD: 0.53 [95% CI: 0.36, 0.70])" ... "We found moderate-quality evidence that overall CS made little or no difference to caregivers' mood or anxiety." ... "We found a high level of inconsistency between studies in relation to both cognitive outcomes and QoL." Plain-language summary: "This benefit equates roughly to a six‐month delay in the cognitive decline usually expected in mild‐to‐moderate dementia." Authors' conclusions: "There remains an evidence gap in relation to the potential benefits of longer-term CS programmes and their clinical significance."
claims.location: Woods 2023, Abstract (Main results, Authors' conclusions) and plain-language summary
claims.pico_timeframe: P: people with mild to moderate dementia, community and care homes. I: cognitive stimulation (mostly group). C: usual care or unstructured activity. O: cognition, QoL, communication, mood, ADL, behaviour, carer outcomes. T: end of treatment (median 10 weeks); few data on maintenance.
claims.safe_wording: A 2023 review of 37 trials found the groups probably give a small boost to memory and thinking by the end of the course: about 2 points on a standard memory test, which the reviewers equate to roughly a six-month delay in the usual decline. People also communicated and joined in more. Gains in well-being and mood were slight, and it is not known how long the benefits last.
claims.qualifications: Short-term benefit at the end of the course; results varied a lot between studies; quality-of-life gain is 'slight'. The six-month comparison is the review authors' plain-language translation, not a measured delay. Benefits were larger with twice-weekly sessions and in mild dementia (exploratory).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Judge's note: certainty for quality of life is moderate (same grade as cognition), but the effect is slight and inconsistent, so 'benefits for thinking and quality of life' must be qualified as small and slight.

numbers.meaning: included in the review
small standardised benefit in cognition at end of treatment, moderate quality
difference vs controls at end of treatment, 25 studies, 1,893 people
review authors' equivalence: benefit roughly equals a six-month delay in usual decline
slight improvement in self-rated quality of life
communication and social interaction, high quality

claims.claim: Cognitive stimulation groups are often available through memory services or charities, and availability varies by area.
claims.supporting_passage: No source found. PubMed searches for audits or surveys of CST provision in UK memory services returned nothing; NICE and audit web pages could not be opened.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not state how widely CST is available or that it varies by area. Advise asking: 'Ask the memory service or GP whether a cognitive stimulation group runs near you.'

claims.claim: DAPA randomised 494 people with mild to moderate dementia in 15 English regions to usual care plus 4 months of supervised moderate to high intensity aerobic and strength exercise (twice-weekly gym groups of 60 to 90 minutes, plus home exercise and support to stay active) or usual care alone.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "494 people with dementia: 329 were assigned to an aerobic and strength exercise programme and 165 were assigned to usual care. Random allocation was 2:1 in favour of the exercise arm." ... "Usual care plus four months of supervised exercise and support for ongoing physical activity, or usual care only. Interventions were delivered in community gym facilities and NHS premises." Full text, Study treatments: "Thereafter, people with dementia attended group sessions in a gym twice a week for four months; each session lasted 60 to 90 minutes. We also asked the participants to do home exercises for one additional hour each week during this period." Setting: "National Health Service primary care, community and memory services, dementia research registers, and voluntary sector providers in 15 English regions."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 494 community-dwelling people with mild to moderate dementia (sMMSE above 10), average age 77, 61% men, England. I: 4 months supervised aerobic and strength training plus ongoing support. C: usual care. O: ADAS-cog at 12 months; ADL, behaviour, QoL, carer outcomes, falls. T: 12 months.
claims.safe_wording: A trial in England, DAPA, randomly assigned 494 people with mild to moderate dementia to a 4-month gym programme of fairly hard aerobic and strength exercise, twice a week, or to usual care.
claims.qualifications: 'Largest UK trial' is not verified: the authors say only that they recruited 'a substantially larger sample size' than previous trials. Say 'a large trial in England'. The programme was moderate to high intensity; the result may not apply to gentler exercise.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: people randomised (329 exercise, 165 usual care; 2:1)
supervised programme, twice weekly, 60 to 90 minutes per session
English regions
average age; proportion of men

claims.claim: At 12 months, ADAS-cog scores were slightly worse in the exercise group (adjusted difference 1.4 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 2.6, on a 0 to 70 scale where higher is worse); the programme did not slow cognitive decline, and the authors judged the difference small with uncertain clinical relevance.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "By 12 months the mean ADAS-cog score had increased to 25.2 (SD 12.3) in the exercise arm and 23.8 (SD 10.4) in the usual care arm (adjusted between group difference -1.4, 95% confidence interval -2.6 to -0.2, P=0.03). This indicates greater cognitive impairment in the exercise group, although the average difference is small and clinical relevance uncertain." ... "A moderate to high intensity aerobic and strength exercise training programme does not slow cognitive impairment in people with mild to moderate dementia." Full text, Outcomes: "(ADAS-cog 11 item scale, scored 0 to 70; higher scores indicate worse cognitive impairment)". Interpretation: "We did not prespecify a value for a negative effect, but the average effect observed was smaller than our prespecified superiority target of 2.45 ADAS-cog points. An influential international consensus group suggests that a between group difference of 2 points (or 25%) might be worthwhile depending on the cost and safety profile of the intervention." ... "the treatment difference was at least half as much as the annual rate of decline." Conclusion: "does not slow cognitive decline and might worsen cognitive impairment in people with mild to moderate dementia."
claims.pico_timeframe: ADAS-cog at 12 months, exercise vs usual care, adjusted for baseline covariates; 281 and 137 analysed.
claims.safe_wording: A year later, memory and thinking scores had not declined more slowly in the exercise group. If anything they were slightly worse, by about 1.4 points on a 70-point test. The researchers were unsure whether a difference that size matters.
claims.qualifications: Do not say 'too small to notice': the authors call its importance uncertain, and note it was at least half the usual annual decline. Do not say exercise 'harms memory' either: possible slight harm, not proven harm. The complier analysis was larger (2.0 points worse).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Several smaller earlier trials reported cognitive benefit; the authors attribute this to weaker methods. Result applies to this moderate to high intensity programme.

numbers.meaning: adjusted between-group difference in ADAS-cog at 12 months, worse in exercise arm; scale 0 to 70
mean ADAS-cog at 12 months, exercise vs usual care
consensus threshold for a worthwhile between-group difference cited by the authors
complier average causal effect, worse cognition among those who attended most sessions

claims.claim: Physical fitness improved in the short term with exercise: six-minute walk distance improved by 18.1 m over six weeks, and weights lifted increased.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Physical fitness (including the six minute walk test) was measured in the exercise arm during the intervention." ... "Six minute walking distance improved over six weeks (mean change 18.1 m, 95% confidence interval 11.6 m to 24.6 m)." Full text, Intervention: "Weight lifted improved in all strengthening exercises across the sessions, as did the duration of higher intensity aerobic activity." Limitations: "Physical fitness improved, but we are limited to data in the exercise arm and during the structured exercise intervention period only. Hence we cannot conclude definitively that the intervention improves physical fitness. It is unlikely that fitness would have improved in the usual care arm as there was no evidence of engagement in exercise or physiotherapy."
claims.location: Abstract (Main outcome measures, Results); Results (Intervention); Discussion (Strengths and limitations)
claims.pico_timeframe: Exercise arm only, baseline to 6 weeks; no control comparison.
claims.safe_wording: People in the exercise group got fitter and stronger while the classes ran: after six weeks they walked about 18 metres further in six minutes, and they lifted heavier weights.
claims.qualifications: Fitness was measured only in the exercise group and only during the classes, so the authors say they cannot be definite that the programme caused it. No between-group comparison.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: mean increase in six-minute walk distance over 6 weeks, exercise arm only

claims.claim: There were no differences in secondary outcomes: activities of daily living, behavioural symptoms, health-related quality of life, carer burden or quality of life, or falls.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "No differences were found in secondary outcomes or preplanned subgroup analyses by dementia type (Alzheimer's disease or other), severity of cognitive impairment, sex, and mobility." Full text, Outcomes: "No evidence was found of differences in other secondary outcomes, including the rate of falls over 12 months (incident rate ratio 1.1, 95% confidence interval 0.8 to 1.6; P=0.69)." Discussion: "The exercise improved physical fitness in the short term, but this did not translate into improvements in activities of daily living, behavioural outcomes, or health related quality of life."
claims.pico_timeframe: Secondary outcomes at 6 and 12 months, exercise vs usual care.
claims.safe_wording: The trial found no clear difference in everyday activities, behaviour, quality of life, carers' strain or falls.
claims.qualifications: 'No difference' means the trial did not show one, not proof of none; falls were carer-recalled.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None within the trial.

numbers.meaning: rate of falls over 12 months, exercise vs usual care; no clear difference

claims.claim: Strength and function training adapted for people with dementia improves strength and physical performance.
claims.supporting_passage: Hauer 2012, Abstract: "Supervised, progressive resistance and functional group training for 3 months specifically developed for people with dementia (intervention, n = 62) compared with a low-intensity motor placebo activity (control, n = 60)." ... "Training significantly improved both primary outcomes" ... "Training gains were partly sustained during follow-up. Low baseline performance on motor tasks but not cognitive impairment predicted positive training response." ... "The intensive, dementia-adjusted training was feasible and substantially improved motor performance in frail, older people with dementia"
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 122 frail older people with mild to moderate dementia, German outpatient geriatric rehabilitation. I: 3 months progressive resistance and functional group training. C: low-intensity placebo activity. O: leg-press strength and five-chair-stand time. T: 3 months, with 3-month follow-up.
claims.safe_wording: Other trials show that people with dementia can build strength: in a German trial, 3 months of strength and balance-type training made people stronger and quicker at standing up from a chair than a gentle comparison activity.
claims.qualifications: Small single-country trial; motor outcomes only; gains partly sustained. Supports 'offer exercise for strength and mobility', not for memory or falls.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: DAPA found fitness gains did not translate into better daily activities.

numbers.meaning: participants in training vs placebo groups

claims.claim: Exercise reduces falls in older people living in the community; evidence specific to people with dementia is less certain.
claims.supporting_passage: Sherrington 2019, Abstract: "We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of any form of exercise as a single intervention on falls in people aged 60+ years living in the community. We excluded trials focused on particular conditions, such as stroke." ... "Exercise reduces the rate of falls by 23% (rate ratio (RaR) 0.77, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.71 to 0.83; 12,981 participants, 59 studies; high-certainty evidence)." | DAPA full text: "No evidence was found of differences in other secondary outcomes, including the rate of falls over 12 months (incident rate ratio 1.1, 95% confidence interval 0.8 to 1.6; P=0.69)."
claims.location: Sherrington 2019 Abstract (Selection criteria, Main results); DAPA Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Sherrington: community-dwelling people 60+, trials of specific conditions excluded. DAPA: people with dementia, 12 months.
claims.safe_wording: Do not claim that exercise prevents falls in people with dementia. If falls are mentioned: 'Exercise with balance training reduces falls in older people generally; in the DAPA trial of people with dementia, falls were no different.'
claims.qualifications: The general-population finding cannot be transferred to dementia without a dementia-specific source; none was opened in this batch.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: DAPA itself found no difference in falls.

numbers.meaning: relative reduction in rate of falls with exercise, community-dwelling older people generally (Sherrington 2019)

claims.claim: Serious exercise-related adverse events were uncommon but occurred; many people approached declined to take part.
claims.supporting_passage: Full text, Adverse events: "Twenty five adverse events occurred (eight were possibly related, nine probably related, and eight definitely related) and four serious related adverse events (one hospital admission for exercise induced angina, two injurious falls, and one case of substantially worsening hip pain) in the exercise arm and no reports in the usual care arm. In the exercise arm an adverse event was reported by 23/329 (7.0%, 95% confidence interval 4.7% to 10.3%) participants." Recruitment: "2929 people were screened, 1847 were found potentially eligible and approached, and 494 were randomised". Discussion: "The numbers of people who declined participation in the trial was high and suggests that exercise might not be an attractive proposition."

claims.safe_wording: Optional context: about 7 in 100 people in the exercise group had a related problem such as muscle soreness or a fall, and 4 had a serious one.
claims.qualifications: Adverse events were recorded only in the exercise arm.

claims.claim: The 2025 Cochrane review included 30 randomised trials with 1,720 participants; interventions had at least five sessions, most were delivered to groups, and most participants lived in institutions such as care homes.
claims.supporting_passage: "We included randomised controlled trials of music-based therapeutic interventions (of at least five sessions) for people with dementia that measured any of our outcomes of interest. Control groups either received usual care or other activities with or without music." ... "We included 30 studies with 1720 randomised participants that were conducted in 15 countries. Twenty-eight studies with 1366 participants contributed data to meta-analyses. Ten studies contributed data to long-term outcomes. Participants had dementia of varying degrees of severity and resided in institutions in most of the studies. Seven studies delivered an individual intervention; the other studies delivered the intervention to groups. Most interventions involved both active and receptive elements of musical experience. The studies were at high risk of performance bias and some were at high risk of detection or other bias."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: people with dementia, mostly in institutions. I: structured music-based therapeutic interventions, 5 or more sessions. C: usual care or other activities. O: mood, behaviour, agitation, well-being, cognition. T: end of treatment and 4 or more weeks after.
claims.safe_wording: A 2025 Cochrane review pooled 30 trials with 1,720 people with dementia. The trials tested planned music sessions, at least five of them, mostly in groups and mostly in care homes, usually with people both listening and taking part.
claims.qualifications: Not a test of background music, the radio or casual listening at home.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: High risk of performance bias across studies.

numbers.meaning: included; 28 studies (1,366 people) in meta-analyses
sessions required for inclusion
countries

claims.claim: Compared with usual care, music-based interventions probably improve depressive symptoms slightly at the end of treatment (moderate certainty) and may improve overall behavioural problems (low certainty), but likely do not improve agitation or aggression (moderate certainty).
claims.supporting_passage: "For music-based therapeutic interventions compared to usual care, we found moderate-certainty evidence that, at the end of treatment, music-based therapeutic interventions probably improved depressive symptoms slightly (standardised mean difference (SMD) -0.23, 95% confidence interval (CI) -0.42 to -0.04; 9 studies, 441 participants), and we found low-certainty evidence that it may have improved overall behavioural problems (SMD -0.31, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.02; 10 studies, 385 participants). We found moderate-certainty evidence that music-based therapeutic interventions likely did not improve agitation or aggression (SMD -0.05, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.17; 11 studies, 503 participants). Low to very low certainty evidence showed that they did not improve emotional well-being (SMD 0.14, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.56; 4 studies, 154 participants), anxiety (SMD -0.15, 95% CI -0.39 to 0.09; 7 studies, 282 participants), social behaviour (SMD 0.22, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.57; 2 studies; 121 participants) or cognition (SMD 0.19, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.41; 7 studies, 353 participants)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Music-based intervention vs usual care, at end of treatment.
claims.safe_wording: Compared with usual care, the review found music sessions probably ease low mood slightly by the end of a course (moderate-certainty evidence). They probably do not reduce agitation or aggression (moderate-certainty evidence). They may reduce behaviour problems overall, but that evidence is weak.
claims.qualifications: Quote certainty words exactly: 'probably improved ... slightly' (moderate), 'may have improved' (low), 'likely did not improve' (moderate). The mood effect is small (SMD 0.23) and is against usual care, not against other activities.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The MIDDEL trial (2025), published after the review's search, found no reduction in depressive symptoms at 6 months (C08-25-e).

numbers.meaning: depressive symptoms vs usual care, end of treatment, 9 studies, 441 people; small
agitation or aggression vs usual care, 11 studies, 503 people; no clear effect
overall behavioural problems, low certainty

Authors' conclusions: "There was no evidence of long-term effects from music-based therapeutic interventions."
claims.pico_timeframe: 4 or more weeks after the end of treatment; 10 studies contributed.
claims.safe_wording: Once the sessions stopped, the trials did not show benefits lasting a month or more, though this evidence is weak.
claims.qualifications: Absence of evidence from 10 studies with low or very low certainty, not proof that no benefit lasts.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Compared with other activities, music-based interventions showed no clear advantage for mood, agitation or behaviour, but may improve social behaviour (low certainty).
claims.supporting_passage: "For music-based therapeutic interventions compared to other interventions, we found low-certainty evidence that, at the end of treatment, music-based therapeutic interventions may have been more effective than the other activities for social behaviour (SMD 0.52, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.96; 4 studies, 84 participants)." ... "For all other outcomes, low-certainty evidence showed no evidence of an effect: emotional well-being (SMD 0.20, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.49; 9 studies, 298 participants); depressive symptoms (SMD -0.14, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.08; 10 studies, 359 participants); agitation or aggression (SMD 0.01, 95% CI -0.31 to 0.32; 6 studies, 168 participants); overall behavioural problems (SMD -0.08, 95% CI -0.33 to 0.17; 8 studies, 292 participants) and cognition (SMD 0.12, 95% CI -0.21 to 0.45; 5 studies; 147 participants)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Music-based intervention vs other activities, end of treatment.

claims.qualifications: Low-certainty evidence; small studies.

claims.claim: The largest trial since, MIDDEL (1,021 care home residents with dementia and depressive symptoms in 6 countries), found that neither group music therapy nor recreational choir singing reduced depressive symptoms at 6 months compared with standard care.
claims.supporting_passage: "The trial was done in 86 care home units across Australia, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Türkiye, and the UK." ... "have mild depressive symptoms as indicated by a Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) score of at least 8" ... "The primary outcome was MADRS assessed at 6 months in the intention-to-treat population" ... "Between July 18, 2018, and Feb 1, 2023, 86 care home units with 1021 residents were enrolled and randomly assigned to one of the four groups." ... "Intention-to-treat analysis of 751 residents with data at 6 months showed no significant effect on MADRS scores of either recreational choir singing versus no recreational choir singing (β 0·4 [95% CI -1·3 to 2·1]; p=0·68), group music therapy versus no group music therapy (β 0·8 [-1·0 to 2·6]; p=0·37), or the interaction between recreational choir singing and group music therapy (β -0·6 [-3·1 to 1·9], p=0·63; β represents mean difference estimated from ANCOVA). Effects varied between countries." ... "Internationally, active group music interventions as conducted in this study do not reduce depressive symptoms more than standard care in the long term."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 1,021 care home residents 65+, dementia and at least mild depressive symptoms, 6 countries. I: group music therapy, choir singing, or both. C: standard care. O: MADRS depressive symptoms. T: 6 months.
claims.safe_wording: Since then, the largest trial so far, in 86 care home units in six countries including the UK, found that neither music therapy groups nor choir singing eased depressive symptoms more than usual care after 6 months.
claims.qualifications: Results varied by country; residents all had at least mild depressive symptoms; 751 of 1,021 had 6-month data. 'Largest trial' is safe in the form 'a large trial of 1,021 residents'; the Cochrane review's biggest pooled comparison was 503 people.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Conflicts with the Cochrane 'probably improves slightly' finding for depressive symptoms; the two should be presented together.

claims.claim: Daily personalised recorded music built into care did not reduce agitation or other neuropsychiatric symptoms in a Norwegian nursing home trial.
