claims.claim: The basis for asking is the Equality Act 2010 duty to make reasonable adjustments and, in England, the Accessible Information Standard, which requires NHS and adult social care to meet communication needs and to use qualified interpreters.
claims.supporting_passage: Ahmed 2022, Conclusion: "Sensory impairments are common within the UK and dental practitioners have a legislative duty to make reasonable adjustments to dental care for this population, including considering alternative communication methods." | Introduction: "All organisations offering NHS care are legally required to follow the Standard (commenced 1 August 2016), including dental services. The Standard sets out a consistent approach to identifying, recording, flagging, sharing and meeting the information and communication support needs of patients, service users, carers and parents with a disability, impairment or sensory loss." | Box 1: "Organisations must ensure that communication professionals (including BSL interpreters and deafblind manual interpreters) used in health and social care settings have: Appropriate qualifications; Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) clearance; Signed up to a relevant professional code of conduct." | Nursing Management 2017, Abstract: "All organisations that provide NHS or adult social care are legally required to follow the Accessible Information Standard" | Selby 2025, Discussion: "Currently, there is no process in the NHS to ensure that this legal requirement is met."
claims.location: Ahmed 2022: Introduction, Box 1, Conclusion; Nursing Management 2017: Abstract; Selby 2025: Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: UK law and NHS England standard, as summarised in secondary sources
claims.safe_wording: In England, NHS and social care services must record a person's communication needs and meet them, and any BSL interpreter they use must be qualified. Across the UK, the Equality Act expects services to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, including how they communicate.
claims.qualifications: Secondary sources only; the Standard (DCB1605) and the Act were not opened. The Accessible Information Standard applies in England, not Scotland or Wales; do not present it as UK-wide. Do not state that the law guarantees an interpreter in every case. Ahmed 2022 has a published correction whose content could not be read.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Selby 2025 reports frequent non-compliance with the Standard.

numbers.meaning: date the Accessible Information Standard commenced (Ahmed 2022)

claims.claim: Of 67 studies of how doctors communicate with older patients (published since 2000), 16 mentioned hearing loss at all: 6 only mentioned it, 4 used it to exclude people, 2 measured it without further analysis, 3 examined its link with communication, and 1 included an intervention.
claims.supporting_passage: Cohen 2017, Abstract: "We identified 409 papers in the initial search, and included 67 in this systematic review. Of the 67 papers, only 16 studies (23.9%) included any mention of hearing loss. In six of the 16 studies, hearing loss was mentioned only; in four studies, hearing loss was used as an exclusion criterion; and in two studies, the extent of hearing loss was measured and reported for the sample, with no further analysis. Three studies examined or reported on an association between hearing loss and the quality of physician-patient communication. One study included an intervention to temporarily mitigate hearing loss to improve communication."
claims.pico_timeframe: Original studies of physician-patient communication with older patients, published from 2000 to about 2016, PubMed only
claims.safe_wording: A review of 67 studies of how doctors talk with older patients, published from 2000 to 2016, found that 16 mentioned hearing loss at all. Four used it to exclude people. Only 3 looked at whether it affected the conversation.
claims.qualifications: Say the date range (judge's request). One database, one search phrase.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Newer studies may do better; not checked.

numbers.meaning: included studies
mentioned hearing loss
mentioned only / exclusion criterion / measured not analysed / examined association / intervention

claims.claim: Hearing loss affects nearly two in three adults aged 70 and over, and most with mild loss do not use hearing aids.
claims.supporting_passage: Lin 2011, Abstract: "The prevalence of hearing loss defined as a speech frequency pure tone average of more than 25 dB in the better ear was 63.1% (95% confidence interval: 57.4-68.8)." ... "Hearing aids were used in 40.0% (95% confidence interval: 35.1-44.8) of adults with moderate hearing loss, but in only 3.4% (95% confidence interval: 0.8-6.0) of those with a mild hearing loss." ... "Hearing loss is prevalent in nearly two thirds of adults aged 70 years and older in the U.S. population."
claims.pico_timeframe: US national sample, 717 adults aged 70 and over with audiometry, 2005 to 2006; weighted prevalence
claims.safe_wording: In a US national survey with hearing tests, about 63 in 100 adults aged 70 and over had hearing loss. Hearing aids were used by 40 in 100 of those with moderate loss and about 3 in 100 of those with mild loss.
claims.qualifications: US data from 2005 to 2006. Replace the candidate's 'most people over 80 have bilateral loss', which appears only in Cohen 2017's introduction (background, not a finding) and was not checked in a primary source.

numbers.meaning: of US adults aged 70 and over with hearing loss (>25 dB, better ear)
hearing aid use among those with moderate loss
hearing aid use among those with mild loss
adults aged 70 and over tested

claims.claim: Across 13 studies, nearly 4 in 10 adults at routine medical visits were accompanied, usually by a spouse or an adult child; accompanied patients were older and in worse health.
claims.supporting_passage: The weighted mean rate of patient accompaniment to routine adult medical visits was 37.6% in 13 contributing studies. Accompanied patients were significantly older and more likely to be female, less educated, and in worse physical and mental health than unaccompanied patients. Companions were on average 63 years of age, predominantly female (79.4%), and spouses (54.7%) or adult children (32.2%) of patients.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults at routine physician visits (13 studies) / accompanied by a family companion / unaccompanied / rate and characteristics / single visits
claims.safe_wording: Across 13 studies, nearly 4 in 10 adults at routine medical appointments brought someone with them, most often a husband, wife or grown-up child. The people who brought someone were, on average, older and in poorer health.
claims.qualifications: Say 'routine medical appointments'; the figure is a weighted average across studies, not a UK figure. Do not describe the companions as mainly daughters: the review reports spouses 54.7% and adult children 32.2%.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The review is from 2011; accompaniment rates may differ now and by country. Country mix of the 13 studies not confirmed from the abstract.

numbers.meaning: weighted mean rate of accompaniment to routine adult medical visits, 13 studies; 'nearly 4 in 10'
share of companions who were spouses and adult children respectively
average age of companions in years

claims.claim: In videotaped US geriatric primary care visits with 93 patients, those whose companions asked them questions, prompted them to talk and asked their opinion were more likely to be active in decision-making (cross-sectional association).
claims.supporting_passage: Patients (N = 93) in this cross-sectional sample range in age from 65 to 95 years and are mostly white (n = 73, 79%) and female (n = 67, 72%). ... Patients whose companions facilitated their involvement in the medical visit by asking the patient questions, prompting the patient to talk, and asking for the patient's opinion were more than four times as likely to be active in decision-making as patients whose companions did not assist in this manner (unadjusted OR 3.5, CI 1.4-8.7, p < .01; adjusted OR 4.5, CI 1.6-12.4, p < .01).
claims.pico_timeframe: 93 accompanied patients aged 65 to 95, US geriatric primary care / companion facilitates patient involvement (asks patient questions, prompts talk, asks opinion) / companions who did not / patient active in decision-making during the visit / single visit, cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a US study that filmed 93 GP visits by people aged 65 to 95 who came with a relative or friend, patients were more likely to take an active part in decisions when the companion asked them questions, prompted them to speak and asked what they thought. The study looked at one visit each, so it shows a link, not proof that the companion's behaviour caused the difference.
claims.qualifications: Association only (cross-sectional). Do not write 'four times as likely' or any multiplier: the figure is an odds ratio (adjusted OR 4.5, 95% CI 1.6 to 12.4) with a wide interval. Say 'more likely'. Small, mostly white, mostly female US sample. Sicker patients' companions were more likely to facilitate, so the groups differed.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Reverse direction is possible: patients who wish to be active may draw their companions into prompting them. No trial tests coaching companions to do this.

numbers.meaning: patients aged 65 to 95 in the study
odds of active patient decision-making with vs without companion facilitation; practitioner posts only, as an odds ratio; never 'times more likely'

claims.claim: When a third person was present, older patients raised fewer topics, were less assertive, and were frequently excluded from the conversation (small US matched comparison).
claims.supporting_passage: In a sample of 96 audiotaped initial medical visits, 15 encounters involved three persons. These 15 cases were matched with 15 dyadic interviews for gender and race of the patient and for gender and race of the physician. ... The specific content and the quality of interactional processes of physicians were not affected by the presence of a third person. However, older patients raised fewer topics in all content areas (medical, personal habits, psychosocial, and physician-patient relationship) in triads than in dyads. ... Patients were rated as less assertive and expressive, and there was less joint decision-making and shared laughter in triads than in dyads. Patients were frequently excluded from conversations in visits in which a third person was present.
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients aged 60 and over at a first visit to hospital-based primary care physicians, US / third person present (15 visits) / matched visits without (15) / patient topics raised, assertiveness, joint decision-making, exclusion / single audiotaped visit
claims.safe_wording: In a small US study that compared 15 first appointments where an older patient came with someone against 15 where they came alone, patients who were accompanied raised fewer topics themselves and were often left out of the conversation.
claims.qualifications: Small (15 vs 15), 1994, US, audiotaped first visits only. It does not show that doctors 'turn to the companion': the authors found the doctors' content and interaction quality were not affected; the change was in the patient's participation and exclusion from conversations. Use 'often left out of the conversation', not 'doctors talk to the relative instead'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Wolff and Roter 2011 found accompanied patients plus companions contributed about as much talk as unaccompanied patients, and Clayman 2005 found companions did more enabling than detracting things, so exclusion is not universal.

numbers.meaning: matched three-person and two-person visits, out of 96 recorded

claims.claim: Some companion behaviours (informational support) are seen as helpful and others (dominating or demanding) as less helpful; preferences vary, and agreeing roles is a proposed strategy.
claims.supporting_passage: Of the 8409 titles identified, 52 studies were included. ... Results indicated companions regularly attended consultations, were frequently perceived as helpful, and assumed a variety of roles. However, their involvement often raised challenges. Patients with increased need were more often accompanied. Some companion behaviours were felt to be more helpful (e.g. informational support) and less helpful (e.g. dominating/demanding behaviours), and preferences for involvement varied widely. ... Preliminary strategies for health professionals include (i) encourage/involve companions, (ii) highlight helpful companion behaviours, (iii) clarify and agree upon role preferences of patient/companions.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult patients with adult companions in medical consultations (52 studies) / companion behaviours and roles / not applicable / perceived helpfulness, role preferences / cross-sectional and qualitative
claims.safe_wording: A review of 52 studies found that companions were often seen as helpful, but taking over or making demands was seen as less helpful, and people differed widely in how much they wanted a companion to do. That is why it helps to agree beforehand what your parent wants to say themselves and what they want you to add.
claims.qualifications: The 'agree beforehand' step is practical advice consistent with the review's proposed strategy for professionals (clarify and agree role preferences); it has not been tested as a family intervention. Present it as advice, not as a finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Strategies are described by the authors as preliminary.

numbers.meaning: studies in the systematic review

claims.claim: Companions showed autonomy-detracting behaviours (controlling the patient, building alliances with the doctor), and these go with less patient involvement.
claims.supporting_passage: These behaviors were coded throughout the visit using an autonomy-based framework that included both autonomy enhancing (i.e. facilitating patient understanding, patient involvement, and doctor understanding) and detracting behaviors, (i.e. controlling the patient and building alliances with the physician). ... Companions are active participants in medical visits and engage in more autonomy enhancing than detracting behaviors.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C09-09-b
claims.safe_wording: In the same study, companions did more to help the patient take part than to take over.
claims.qualifications: The abstract confirms that controlling and alliance-building behaviours were coded and were less common than enabling behaviours. It does not report that they were linked with less patient involvement, so the candidate's clause 'controlling or siding with the doctor goes with less [involvement]' must be dropped.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Full text not available in this project to check the detracting-behaviour analysis.

claims.claim: When a companion was present, clinicians gave more biomedical information; effects of accompaniment on patient outcomes were inconclusive or favourable.
claims.supporting_passage: Accompanied patient visits were significantly longer, but verbal contribution to medical dialog was comparable when accompanied patients and their family companion were compared with unaccompanied patients. When a companion was present, health care providers engaged in more biomedical information giving. Given the diversity of outcomes, pooled estimates could not be calculated: of 5 contributing studies 0 were unfavorable, 3 inconclusive, and 2 favorable for accompanied relative to unaccompanied patients.
claims.pico_timeframe: Routine adult physician visits / companion present / companion absent / visit length, talk, information giving, patient outcomes (5 studies) / single visits
claims.safe_wording: When someone came with the patient, appointments were longer and doctors gave more medical information. None of five studies found worse outcomes for patients who were accompanied.
claims.qualifications: Only 5 studies on outcomes; 3 inconclusive. Do not claim companions improve outcomes.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None beyond the small number of outcome studies.

numbers.meaning: outcome studies unfavourable, inconclusive and favourable for accompanied patients

claims.claim: In a 2026 systematic review of 18 RCTs (1985 participants), there was no clear pattern of effect of teach-back on patient knowledge (very low certainty); the 9 knowledge trials could not be pooled.
claims.supporting_passage: Our systematic review included 18 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1985 participants. Across 9 RCTs assessing knowledge acquisition, conceptual inconsistencies precluded meta-analysis. Overall, there was no clear pattern of the effect of teach-back on knowledge (very low COE). ... In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we did not identify a clear benefit of teach-back on knowledge acquisition
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult patients and/or care partners / teach-back in a single encounter / comparator (usually usual care) / knowledge acquisition / proximal outcomes, short term
claims.safe_wording: A 2026 review of 18 randomised trials, with about 2,000 people, found no clear effect of teach-back on what patients knew afterwards. The evidence was rated very low certainty, and the 9 trials that measured knowledge were too different to combine.
claims.qualifications: This is an evidence gap, not evidence that teach-back fails: say 'has not been shown' or 'no clear effect', never 'does not work'. The review covered teach-back in a single encounter only; multi-session education programmes that include teach-back were outside its scope. The trials were in adults generally, not older people specifically.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Talevski 2020 (20 studies of mixed design and quality) reported teach-back effective in 19 of 20 studies, including knowledge outcomes. The difference probably reflects Vick's RCT-only, single-encounter criteria and GRADE rating; state that the newer, stricter review is less certain than earlier ones.

numbers.meaning: randomised controlled trials in the review
participants across the 18 trials ('about 2,000')
trials that measured knowledge; not pooled

claims.claim: Teach-back increased self-efficacy (5 RCTs, very low certainty) and self-reported short-term adherence (7 RCTs, low certainty), with wide confidence intervals and substantial heterogeneity.
claims.supporting_passage: In a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs assessing self-efficacy (416 participants), we found that teach-back interventions led to a large increase in self-efficacy relative to usual care (SMD = 2.40; 95%CI 0.37-4.44) (very low COE). In a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs assessing adherence to health behaviors (571 participants), teach-back interventions led to a large increase in adherence (SMD = 1.04; 95%CI 0.45-1.64) (low COE). Meta-analyses for both self-efficacy and adherence had large confidence intervals that ranged from small to large effect sizes and had substantial heterogeneity. ... but did find evidence that teach-back improves self-efficacy and self-reported, short-term adherence to health behaviors.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult patients and/or care partners / single-encounter teach-back / usual care / self-efficacy; self-reported adherence to health behaviours / short term
claims.safe_wording: Teach-back did improve patients' confidence in managing their health and their own reports of sticking to advice in the short term, but the certainty was low or very low and the size of the effect was very uncertain.
claims.qualifications: Say 'self-reported' and 'short term' for adherence. Do not present standardised mean differences to the public; for practitioners give them only with the certainty rating. Do not describe the effects as 'large' without the certainty caveat.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Wide confidence intervals (self-efficacy 0.37 to 4.44; adherence 0.45 to 1.64) and substantial heterogeneity.

numbers.meaning: self-efficacy meta-analysis; SMD 2.40 (95% CI 0.37 to 4.44); very low certainty
adherence meta-analysis; SMD 1.04 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.64); low certainty; self-reported, short term

claims.claim: Teach-back is widely presented as an effective, high-quality communication strategy.
claims.supporting_passage: Vick 2026: "Teach-back has been identified as a high-quality clinical communication strategy." Talevski 2020: "Use of 'teach-back' has been shown to improve patients' knowledge and self-care abilities, however there is little guidance for healthcare services seeking to embed teach-back in their setting." ... "Overall, 20 studies of moderate quality were included in this review (four rated high, nine rated moderate, seven rated weak)." ... "Use of teach-back proved effective in 19 of the 20 studies, ranging from learning-related outcomes (e.g. knowledge recall and retention) to objective health-related outcomes (e.g. hospital re-admissions, quality of life)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Description of how teach-back is presented in the literature; Talevski: 20 studies of mixed design to July 2019
claims.safe_wording: Teach-back is often taught as a proven way to improve understanding: an earlier review reported it worked in 19 of 20 studies. The newer review, which included only randomised trials and graded their certainty, is much less sure about knowledge.
claims.qualifications: The NHS or Health Education England guidance recommending teach-back could not be identified or opened, so do not name any NHS body as recommending it. 'Often taught as proven' is supported only as a description of the literature.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The two reviews differ in inclusion criteria (Talevski included non-randomised studies and teach-back within structured education; Vick only RCTs of single-encounter teach-back).

numbers.meaning: studies in Talevski 2020 reporting teach-back effective on some outcome (mixed designs, 7 rated weak)

claims.claim: Older patients remember less than younger patients when more information is given in a consultation.
claims.supporting_passage: Recall decreased significantly with age, but only when total amount of information presented was taken into account. This indicates that if more information is discussed, older patients have more trouble remembering the information than younger ones. ... Recall is not simply a function of patient age. Age only predicts recall when controlling for amount of information presented. Both prognosis and information about prognosis are better predictors of recall than age.
claims.pico_timeframe: 260 patients with cancer at a first oncology consultation / age, amount of information given / younger patients / recall measured by structured telephone interview against audio recordings / shortly after consultation
claims.safe_wording: In a study that checked what 260 people with cancer remembered against recordings of their first oncology appointment, older patients recalled less than younger ones when a lot of information was given. Age alone was a weaker guide than how much was said, and how serious the news was.
claims.qualifications: Oncology only; the age effect depends on the amount of information. Do not say 'older people forget most of what they are told'. This replaces the candidate's Kessels 2003 claim (see C09-23-f).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Prognosis and information about prognosis predicted recall better than age.

numbers.meaning: patients with cancer in the recall study

claims.claim: Teach-back is recommended in NHS health literacy guidance.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not name any NHS document or body as recommending teach-back.
claims.qualifications: No NHS, NHS England or Health Education England document was identified or opened in this project.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not searched further to conserve usage; the post does not need it (C09-23-c covers 'widely taught').

claims.claim: Patients forget a large share of medical information soon after a consultation, and older age is associated with poorer recall (Kessels 2003).
claims.location: Not found: PubMed record PMID 12724430 has no abstract, and the PMC record PMC539473 returned no text
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not quote a percentage of information forgotten. Use C09-23-d (Jansen 2008) for the older-patient point.
claims.qualifications: Kessels 2003 is a narrative review whose often-quoted figures come from older studies; the text could not be read here.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable

claims.claim: The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges 2018 guidance 'Please, write to me' recommends that outpatient clinic letters be written directly to patients.
claims.supporting_passage: Ong 2026 (full text, Introduction): "Key drivers for this shift include the 2018 Academy of Medical Royal Colleges (AoMRC) guidance, ‘Please, write to me’, which established the best practice of writing letters directly to patients rather than about them." Lonergan 2019 (abstract): "Recent guidelines from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges recommend that all OPD letters should be written directly to the patient." Gupta 2021 (abstract): "The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges have recently recommended all outpatient letters to be written directly to patients." Search extract (not opened): the guidance "aims to encourage doctors to write most of their outpatient clinic letters directly to patients and send a copy to the patient's General Practitioner".
claims.location: Ong 2026 Introduction and Discussion; Lonergan 2019 and Gupta 2021 abstracts; AoMRC web page search extract
claims.pico_timeframe: UK hospital doctors writing outpatient clinic letters / guidance from 2018
claims.safe_wording: National guidance from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges (2018) recommends that hospital doctors write outpatient clinic letters to the patient, rather than about the patient to the GP. If your letters are written to your GP, you can ask whether future letters could be written to you.
claims.qualifications: Follow the editor: say 'national guidance recommends', never 'entitled to' or 'your right'. It is professional guidance, not law. Avoid 'all' and 'most' (secondary sources disagree on which word the guidance uses). The primary document was not opened; three peer-reviewed papers describe the recommendation consistently. The 'copy to the GP' detail rests on a search extract only, so leave it out or keep it general.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Uptake is low: Ong 2026 describes a 'persistent gap between policy recommendations and real-world practice'.

numbers.meaning: year of the AoMRC guidance

claims.claim: Of 4.6 million outpatient letters at Moorfields Eye Hospital (2013 to 2025), about 2 in 100 were classified as addressed to patients and about 95 in 100 were less readable than recommended.
claims.supporting_passage: The dataset comprised 4 648 289 letters from 804 986 patients (median 3, IQR 1–6 letters per patient) over the 13 year study period. ... age of 53 (IQR 31–69) years at the baseline visit. ... FRE had a median value of 51.1 (IQR 41.9–58.5), indicating substantially lower readability than the suggested reference range of 70–90 for patient-facing materials. ... Overall, 95.3% of letters fell below the recommended FRE range ... Only a minority of letters (2.25%) were classified as patient-addressed. There was a small annual increase in the likelihood of letters being addressed directly to patients over time ... Based on this exploratory review, a pragmatic threshold of at least six second-person pronouns per 100 words was selected to classify letters as patient addressed for subsequent analyses.
claims.pico_timeframe: All outpatient clinic letters, Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust (London), 17 subspecialties, 1 Jan 2013 to 1 Nov 2025 / letter text / recommended Flesch Reading Ease range 70 to 90 / readability and patient-addressed classification
claims.safe_wording: At one large London eye hospital, researchers analysed 4.6 million clinic letters written between 2013 and 2025. About 2 in 100 were written to the patient. About 95 in 100 were harder to read than the level recommended for patients.
claims.qualifications: Always name it as one eye hospital; do not generalise to all clinics or all of the NHS. 'Written to the patient' was judged by a computer rule (at least 6 uses of 'you' or 'your' per 100 words), which the authors call imperfect. Patients were all ages (median 53), not an older-age sample. The study measured reading level, not whether patients understood.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The share addressed to patients rose slightly each year, from a low base.

numbers.meaning: clinic letters analysed, 2013 to 2025, one eye hospital
letters classified as written to the patient; 'about 2 in 100'
letters below the recommended Flesch Reading Ease range of 70 to 90; 'about 95 in 100'
median Flesch Reading Ease score (recommended 70 to 90); practitioner posts only

claims.claim: In the NHS, patients often receive a copy of the clinic letter even when it is addressed to the GP.
claims.supporting_passage: The practice of sending copies of clinical letters directly to patients is well established in the National Health Service (NHS) in the United Kingdom (UK), where these letters serve several key purposes simultaneously ... Letters could be addressed to—and therefore written for—healthcare professionals or patients and copied to the other party.
claims.pico_timeframe: UK NHS outpatient correspondence (background statement)
claims.safe_wording: Many people already get a copy of the clinic letter, but it is usually written to the GP and about them.
claims.qualifications: Background statement from a paper's introduction, not a measured finding; do not give a figure for how many people receive copies. Rephrase the candidate angle: do not say the letter is 'the only lasting record most older people get' (unsupported).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No data on how often older patients receive copies.

claims.claim: In a urology quality improvement project, most patients interviewed after receiving a restructured clinic letter found it easy to understand and said it improved their understanding.
claims.supporting_passage: In one OPD, 71% of patients stated that they wished to receive a copy of their letter. ... Following the implementation of the intervention, letters were sent to 120 patients and feedback was obtained from 63 patients with either a feedback postcard or telephone interview. Of the 53 patients who agreed to participate in the telephone feedback, 39 (74%) found the letter easy to understand, 49 (92%) reported it was accurate and summarised the consultation as they remembered it and 38 (72%) reported that reading the letter improved their understanding of their OPD visit. All patients said they would like to receive similar letters from future OPD consultations.
claims.pico_timeframe: Urology outpatients, Tallaght University Hospital, Dublin / restructured clinic letter sent to patient / no comparator / self-reported understanding and accuracy / after a 90-day improvement cycle
claims.safe_wording: In one Dublin urology clinic that redesigned its letters and sent them to patients, 39 of the 53 patients interviewed found the letter easy to understand, and 38 said it helped them understand their visit.
claims.qualifications: Irish, not UK. Small, uncontrolled, self-reported; only 53 of 120 recipients gave telephone feedback. The abstract does not say the letters were addressed to the patient, so say 'sent to patients' rather than 'written to them'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Responder bias likely.

numbers.meaning: telephone respondents who found the letter easy to understand
said reading the letter improved understanding of their visit
patients sent letters; 63 gave any feedback

claims.claim: In a UK head and neck clinic survey, about half of patients preferred letters written to them and very few preferred letters to the GP, yet all sampled surgeon letters were addressed to GPs.

All 54 surgeon letters (100%) were addressed to GPs.

claims.safe_wording: In a survey at one English hospital clinic, 42 of 80 patients wanted letters written to them, 4 wanted them written to their GP and the rest had no preference. Every one of the 54 surgeons' letters checked was written to the GP.
claims.qualifications: One clinic, small sample, not an older-age sample.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A large share (34 of 80) had no preference, so do not say 'most patients want letters written to them'.

numbers.meaning: preferred letters written to the patient
preferred letters written to the GP
no preference

claims.claim: Patients who need a different format (large print, easy read) can ask for it under the Accessible Information Standard (England) or as a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010; and patients can say if they would rather letters were not sent to their home.
claims.location: Not found. A web search returned only a law firm's summary for the home-delivery point, which is not an official source and was not opened.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Leave both points out of the post, including the judge's suggested line about letters not coming to the home, unless a later batch opens the Accessible Information Standard or the AoMRC guidance itself.
claims.qualifications: Official web pages could not be opened; no copy was found in Drive.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable

claims.claim: In 16 studies with 2595 patient-surrogate pairs answering hypothetical scenarios, surrogates predicted patients' treatment preferences with 68% accuracy.
claims.supporting_passage: The search identified 16 eligible studies, involving 151 hypothetical scenarios and 2595 surrogate-patient pairs, which collectively analyzed 19 526 patient-surrogate paired responses. Overall, surrogates predicted patients' treatment preferences with 68% accuracy. ... Patient-designated and next-of-kin surrogates incorrectly predict patients' end-of-life treatment preferences in one third of cases.
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients and their patient-designated or next-of-kin surrogates / surrogate predicts patient's answer / patient's own answer / agreement on hypothetical end-of-life treatment scenarios / single time point
claims.safe_wording: When researchers asked people and the relative who would speak for them the same questions about treatment near the end of life, the relatives gave the same answer as the person about 2 times in 3, and a different answer about 1 time in 3. These were imagined situations, not real decisions.
claims.qualifications: Hypothetical end-of-life scenarios, not real decisions. 68% is across answers (19,526 paired responses), not the proportion of relatives who were 'right' overall. Do not say 'mostly US' (not verified from the abstract). The review is from 2006.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Some agreement is expected by chance on yes/no questions, so 68% is not directly comparable with zero. Later structured-planning trials improved agreement (C09-25-d).

numbers.meaning: accuracy of surrogates' predictions across 19,526 paired responses; 'about 2 in 3'
share of predictions that were wrong; 'about 1 in 3'
size of the evidence base

claims.claim: Neither the patient choosing the surrogate nor prior discussion of preferences improved surrogates' accuracy.
claims.supporting_passage: Neither patient designation of surrogates nor prior discussion of patients' treatment preferences improved surrogates' predictive accuracy.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C09-25-a; comparison of surrogates chosen by the patient vs next of kin, and pairs who had vs had not discussed preferences (observational comparisons within the included studies)
claims.safe_wording: In those studies, relatives the person had chosen were no more accurate than next of kin, and couples or families who said they had talked about it beforehand were no more accurate than those who had not.
claims.qualifications: This applies to ordinary, unstructured prior discussion in the observational studies reviewed. It must not be presented as 'talking does not help'. Pair it with C09-25-d. The judge's values note applies: keep encouraging conversations alongside writing things down.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Kirchhoff 2010 (RCT) found that a structured, facilitated planning interview greatly improved surrogate understanding.

claims.claim: The studies used hypothetical end-of-life scenarios, mostly in the US.
claims.supporting_passage: The search identified 16 eligible studies, involving 151 hypothetical scenarios and 2595 surrogate-patient pairs
claims.pico_timeframe: As C09-25-a
claims.safe_wording: The studies used imagined end-of-life situations rather than real decisions.
claims.qualifications: 'Hypothetical' is confirmed; 'mostly in the US' is not verified (full text not accessible), so leave the country out.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable

claims.claim: A structured, facilitated planning conversation improved surrogates' understanding of patients' goals in a randomised trial; reviews of joint patient-family planning suggest it may improve agreement.
claims.supporting_passage: Kirchhoff 2010: "Trained health professionals conducted a structured, patient-centered interview intended to promote informed decision-making and to result in the completion of a document clarifying the goals of the patient with regard to four disease-specific health outcome situations and the degree of decision-making latitude granted to the surrogate. ... Three hundred thirteen patient-surrogate pairs completed the study. As measured according to kappa scores and in all four situations and in the degree of latitude, intervention group surrogates demonstrated a significantly higher degree of understanding of patient goals than control group surrogates. Intervention group kappa scores ranged from 0.61 to 0.78, whereas control group kappa scores ranged from 0.07 to 0.28." Liu 2024: "In total, 14 randomized controlled trials were included. ... In addition, interventions may improve dyad's congruence on end-of-life care, family caregivers' confidence in surrogate decision-making, and quality of end-of-life communication."
claims.pico_timeframe: Kirchhoff: competent adults with chronic heart failure or chronic kidney disease and their surrogates, six Wisconsin clinics, 2004 to 2007 / facilitated disease-specific planning interview with a written document / usual care / surrogate understanding of patient goals (kappa agreement) / timing not stated in abstract. Liu: 14 RCTs of patient-caregiver advance care planning / usual care / congruence (narrative), documentation (pooled)
claims.safe_wording: Talking in a structured way can help. In a US trial with 313 people with heart or kidney disease and the relatives who would speak for them, a planning conversation led by a trained professional, which ended in a written record of the person's goals, left relatives with a much better understanding of those goals than usual care.
claims.qualifications: One US trial in adults with heart failure or kidney disease; facilitated by trained staff, with a written document. For the public describe the agreement as 'much better understanding'; do not quote kappa values to the public. Liu 2024's congruence finding is narrative ('may improve'), not pooled.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Liu 2024 notes the need for further studies; the companion trial (Kirchhoff 2012) (PMID 22458336, abstract read) found fewer unmet resuscitation wishes with planning (1 of 62 vs 6 of 48) but the difference was not statistically significant; not needed for this post, so not listed as a source.

numbers.meaning: patient-surrogate pairs completing the Kirchhoff trial
agreement between surrogate and patient goals, intervention vs control; practitioner posts only, with a plain reading (good vs slight agreement)
RCTs in Liu 2024 review

claims.claim: Opioid doses tend to rise as death approaches, but reviews of palliative care studies found no evidence that starting or increasing opioids to control symptoms brings death forward.
claims.supporting_passage: Sykes 2003: "We conclude that patients are more likely to receive higher doses of both opioids and sedatives as they get closer to death. However, there is no evidence that initiation of treatment, or increases in dose of opioids or sedatives, is associated with precipitation of death." Boland 2015: "Thirteen end-of-life studies, including 11 very low-quality retrospective studies, did not find a consistent association between opioid analgesic treatment and survival; this evidence comes from low-quality studies, so should be interpreted with caution."
claims.pico_timeframe: People with advanced illness (almost all cancer) in hospices and palliative care units / opioids given or increased for symptom control near death / no increase or lower doses / survival / last days to weeks of life
claims.safe_wording: Doses of morphine and similar medicines often go up in the last days of life because symptoms change. Studies of people dying in hospices and palliative care units have not found that giving or increasing these medicines to relieve symptoms shortens life.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is observational and mostly retrospective and low quality; almost all participants had cancer. Say 'have not found' or 'no consistent link'; never 'morphine does not shorten life' or 'proves'. Keep to doses adjusted to symptoms.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Portenoy 2006 found a small statistical association between higher dose and shorter survival (claim C10-25-c). Boland 2015 found that in longer-term (not end-of-life) cancer treatment six of seven studies suggested an association with shorter survival, possibly because more pain reflects more advanced cancer.

numbers.meaning: Studies in Boland 2015 systematic review that addressed survival at the end of life

claims.claim: In 238 consecutive deaths in a palliative care unit, people whose opioid doses were increased at the end of life did not live for a shorter time than those with no increase.
claims.supporting_passage: "We retrospectively analysed the pattern of opioid use in the last week of life in 238 consecutive patients who died in a palliative care unit. Median doses of opioid were low (26.4 mg) in the last 24 h of life and patients who received opioid increases at the end of life did not show shorter survival than those who received no increases."
claims.pico_timeframe: 238 consecutive patients dying in one UK palliative care unit / opioid increases in the last week of life / no increases / survival / last week of life
claims.safe_wording: In one UK palliative care unit, among 238 people who died, those whose opioid dose was increased near the end did not die sooner than those whose dose was not increased.
claims.qualifications: Single-unit retrospective study published as a letter; use as an example, not as the main evidence. Do not quote the 26.4 mg figure (units and drug not specified in the abstract).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See Portenoy 2006 (C10-25-c).

numbers.meaning: Consecutive patients who died in one palliative care unit; retrospective

claims.claim: A larger US hospice study found higher opioid doses were statistically linked with shorter survival, but dose explained very little of the difference in how long people lived, and the authors concluded that concern about hastening death does not justify withholding opioids.
claims.supporting_passage: "Multivariate models demonstrated a significant association between shorter survival and higher opioid dose, a cancer diagnosis, unresponsiveness, and pain of <5 on a 0-10 scale, but none of these models explained >10% of the variance in time till death." ... "This analysis revealed that opioid dosing was associated with time till death, but this factor would explain very little of the variation in survival." ... "Based on these findings, concern about hastening death does not justify withholding opioid therapy."
claims.pico_timeframe: 1,306 patients in 13 US hospices, 725 with an opioid dose change / higher dose and larger increases / lower doses / days from final dose change to death (mean 12.46) / hospice stay
claims.safe_wording: The evidence is not perfectly clean: one large hospice study found a small statistical link between higher doses and shorter survival, but dose accounted for very little of the difference, and the authors said fear of shortening life should not stop pain relief.
claims.qualifications: Observational; people on higher doses are often sicker, so the link may reflect illness rather than the drug.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: This is itself the main conflicting evidence; it should be acknowledged in the post rather than hidden.

numbers.meaning: US hospice cohort (13 programmes)
Share of variation in time to death explained by the models including dose

claims.claim: NICE NG31 recommends individualised as-needed and regular medicines for pain and breathlessness in the last days of life.
claims.supporting_passage: Not found in opened sources. The NICE NG31 records surfaced by PubMed search (PMIDs 26741019, 41604500) returned no metadata; no copy of NG31 was found in Drive; nice.org.uk could not be opened from this environment.
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Do not cite NICE NG31 in this post.
claims.qualifications: Non-essential; the post stands on the observational evidence.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: n/a

claims.claim: Tramadol blocks the reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline, and its opioid effect comes mainly from its breakdown product O-desmethyltramadol.
claims.supporting_passage: Faria 2018: "Tramadol is a prodrug that acts through noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition, with a weak opioid component added by its metabolite O-desmethyltramadol." Coluzzi 2020: "Tramadol is the most commonly involved opioid in the reported cases of serotonin syndrome, alone or in combination with other serotoninergic medications, because of its dual mechanism of action, including inhibition of 5-HT reuptake."
claims.location: Faria 2018 abstract; Coluzzi 2020 full text, section 'Combination Therapy with Opioids: Patient Safety Issues in CKD'
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacology (mechanism statement)
claims.safe_wording: Tramadol is an opioid that also raises serotonin and noradrenaline levels by blocking their reuptake. Much of its opioid effect comes from a breakdown product made in the liver.
claims.qualifications: Mechanism statement; no numbers.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: Tramadol's opioid effect depends on conversion by the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which varies widely between people, making its effect less predictable than morphine's.
claims.supporting_passage: Prescrire 2016: "The potency of codeine and tramadol is strongly influenced by the cytochrome P450 isoenzyme CYP2D6 genotype, which varies widely from one person to another. This explains reports of overdosing or underdosing after administration of standard doses of the two drugs. The potency of morphine and that of buprenorphine, an opioid receptor agonist-antagonist, appears to be independent of CYP2D6 activity." Roulet 2021: "...thus overcoming some limitations of tramadol, including the potential for pharmacokinetic drug-drug interactions and interindividual variability due to genetic polymorphisms of cytochrome P450 enzymes." Nelson 2012: "Tramadol is metabolized through CYP2D6 enzymes and all SSRIs are inhibitors of these enzymes."
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacology and pharmacogenetics review
claims.safe_wording: Like codeine, tramadol relies partly on a liver enzyme (CYP2D6) whose activity varies a great deal between people and is blocked by some antidepressants, so the same dose can have quite different effects in different people.
claims.qualifications: Say 'partly' or 'much of'; tramadol itself has non-opioid actions.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: Tramadol taken with SSRIs (and other serotonergic medicines) has caused serotonin toxicity; tramadol is the opioid most often involved in reported cases.
claims.supporting_passage: Nelson 2012: "Published documentation describing the interaction between tramadol and SSRIs and its relevance to serotonin syndrome is limited to a few case reports and 1 case series. While both tramadol and SSRIs increase the amount of serotonin in the brain, the interaction is much more complicated. Tramadol is metabolized through CYP2D6 enzymes and all SSRIs are inhibitors of these enzymes. Inhibitors of CYP2D6 can increase the concentration of tramadol in the blood and thus increase its effects on serotonin in the brain, contributing to the development of serotonin syndrome." ... "Coadministration of tramadol and SSRIs has caused serotonin syndrome." Coluzzi 2020: "Tramadol is the most commonly involved opioid in the reported cases of serotonin syndrome, alone or in combination with other serotoninergic medications, because of its dual mechanism of action, including inhibition of 5-HT reuptake."
claims.pico_timeframe: Case reports, case series and pharmacovigilance summaries
claims.safe_wording: Tramadol taken with some antidepressants has caused serotonin toxicity (agitation, twitching, shaking, sweating, fever). Among opioids, tramadol is the one most often named in reported cases.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is case reports and pharmacovigilance, so frequency is unknown; do not state a rate. Some SSRIs also block CYP2D6 and reduce tramadol's pain relief (Roulet 2021 citation snippet via Scite), so the combination can bring both more side effects and less relief. Roulet 2021 full-text passage (Scite citation snippet): "The bioactivation of tramadol by CYP2D6 is an important source of variability due to drug interaction. The analgesic efficacy of tramadol can be significantly reduced by CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as some SSRIs or terbinafine."
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No controlled estimate of risk.

claims.claim: Tramadol has been linked with low sodium, low blood sugar and seizures, adverse effects not shared to the same degree by other opioids.
claims.supporting_passage: Prescrire 2016: "In addition, tramadol can cause a serotonin syndrome, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and seizures." ... "Tramadol has additional adverse effects unrelated to its opioid effects." Roulet 2021: "tapentadol is likely to result in less exposure to serotoninergic adverse effects (nausea, vomiting, hypoglycaemia)" ... "its residual serotonergic activity (serotonin syndrome, seizures)". Owsiany 2019: "There is also concern for increased risk of seizures and central nervous system adverse effects in older adults with prolonged tramadol use."
claims.location: Prescrire 2016 abstract; Roulet 2021 abstract; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Reviews of trial and pharmacovigilance data
claims.safe_wording: Tramadol can also cause low sodium, low blood sugar and seizures, effects that come from its non-opioid actions.
claims.qualifications: 'Can cause' is supported by reviews; frequencies come only from the Fournier studies (C10-18-e, -f).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: In a UK primary care cohort of 332,880 people starting tramadol or codeine, hospital admission for low sodium in the first 30 days was 4.6 per 10,000 person-months with tramadol versus 1.9 with codeine (adjusted HR 2.05).
claims.supporting_passage: "Using the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink and Hospital Episodes Statistics database, a population-based cohort of 332,880 patients initiating tramadol or codeine was assembled from 1998 through 2012." ... "The incidence rates of hospitalization for hyponatremia were 4.6 (95% CI, 2.4-8.0) and 1.9 (95% CI, 1.4-2.5) per 10,000 person-months for tramadol and codeine users, respectively. In the adjusted model, the use of tramadol was associated with a 2-fold increased risk of hospitalization for hyponatremia, compared with codeine (adjusted HR 2.05; 95% CI, 1.08-3.86)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults starting tramadol or codeine for non-cancer pain, UK primary care / tramadol / codeine / hospital admission for hyponatraemia / first 30 days after starting
claims.safe_wording: In UK GP records of over 330,000 people starting tramadol or codeine, about 4.6 in every 10,000 people taking tramadol for a month were admitted to hospital with low sodium, compared with about 1.9 for codeine: roughly twice the rate, but still uncommon.
claims.qualifications: Absolute rate first; 'per 10,000 person-months' means per 10,000 people each taking the drug for one month. Wide confidence interval (1.08 to 3.86) from few events. Adults of all ages, not only older people; observational (association, adjusted by propensity score).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Only one large study; restricted sub-cohort gave HR 3.54 (1.32 to 9.54), consistent in direction. Do not quote both HRs.

numbers.meaning: Adults starting tramadol or codeine, UK CPRD, 1998 to 2012
Absolute rates of hospital admission for hyponatraemia, tramadol vs codeine, first 30 days
Relative rate, tramadol vs codeine, propensity-score adjusted

claims.claim: In the same UK data, starting tramadol was linked with more hospital admissions for low blood sugar than starting codeine, especially in the first 30 days.
claims.supporting_passage: "The cohort included 334,034 patients, of whom 1105 were hospitalized for hypoglycemia during follow-up (incidence, 0.7 per 1000 per year) and matched to 11,019 controls. Compared with codeine, tramadol use was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization for hypoglycemia (OR, 1.52 [95% CI, 1.09-2.10]), particularly elevated in the first 30 days of use (OR, 2.61 [95% CI, 1.61-4.23]). This 30-day increased risk was confirmed in the cohort (HR, 3.60 [95% CI, 1.56-8.34]) and case-crossover analyses (OR, 3.80 [95% CI, 2.64-5.47])." ... "Additional studies are needed to confirm this rare but potentially fatal adverse event."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults newly treated with tramadol or codeine for non-cancer pain, UK / tramadol / codeine / hospital admission for hypoglycaemia / whole follow-up and first 30 days
claims.safe_wording: The same UK research group found that people starting tramadol were more likely to be admitted to hospital with low blood sugar than people starting codeine, mainly in the first month. It is rare.
claims.qualifications: Nested case-control design (odds ratios); no absolute excess risk can be derived from the abstract, so do not turn the ORs into 'X times' statements or absolute numbers. The 0.7 per 1000 per year incidence is for the whole cohort (both drugs), not tramadol.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors call for confirmation.

numbers.meaning: Incidence of hospitalisation for hypoglycaemia in the whole cohort (tramadol and codeine users together)

claims.claim: There is no evidence that tramadol (or codeine) is less risky than morphine at its lowest effective dose, and its effects vary more between people.
claims.supporting_passage: "In practice, when opioid therapy is needed, there is no evidence that codeine, dihydrocodeine or tramadol is less risky than morphine at its lowest effective dose. Compared to morphine, the efficacy of these drugs varies more from one patient to another, and their multiple pharmacokinetic interactions can be difficult to manage. There is also a sometimes unpredictable risk of serious over-dose. Tramadol has additional adverse effects unrelated to its opioid effects. Weak opioids require at least as much vigilance as morphine, despite the major differences in their reputation and regulation."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults needing opioid analgesia; review of trials and pharmacovigilance
claims.safe_wording: Calling tramadol a 'weak' opioid does not make it a safer one: an independent review found no evidence that it is less risky than a low dose of morphine, and its effects are less predictable.
claims.qualifications: Frame the 'low dose of another opioid' point as a prescribing judgement, and add that morphine itself needs adjusting when kidney function is reduced (see C10-19). Evidence gap, not proof of equal or greater harm.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Morphine accumulates in reduced kidney function (C10-19-a), so the alternative depends on the person.

claims.claim: Tramadol and its active breakdown products are cleared mainly by the kidneys, so its dose needs adjusting when kidney function is reduced.
claims.supporting_passage: Coluzzi 2020: "With the regard to the use of the “weak opioid” tramadol, it is relevant to point out that 90% is renally excreted and its half-life may increase up to twofold in CKD patients." Owsiany 2019: "Tramadol (immediate release) is not recommended for usage in older chronic kidney disease patients. Tramadol and its active metabolites are predominantly renally cleared."
claims.location: Coluzzi 2020 full text, 'Pharmacological Update'; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacokinetics in chronic kidney disease
claims.safe_wording: Tramadol leaves the body mainly through the kidneys, so kidney function belongs on the pre-prescribing check along with the antidepressant list, sodium and any history of seizures.
claims.qualifications: Reviews differ on whether to avoid (Owsiany) or dose-adjust (Coluzzi); say 'check and adjust', not 'contraindicated'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Coluzzi says older people with GFR over 30 need no dose change up to 300 mg; Owsiany recommends avoiding immediate-release tramadol in older people with CKD.

numbers.meaning: Share of tramadol excreted by the kidneys (Coluzzi 2020 narrative review)

claims.claim: The AGS Beers Criteria 2023 list tramadol among drugs to use with caution because of hyponatraemia or SIADH.
claims.supporting_passage: Not found: PMC full text (PMC12478568) opened, but the criteria tables were not rendered in the text returned; the narrative does not mention tramadol.
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Do not cite the Beers Criteria for tramadol.
claims.qualifications: Non-essential.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: n/a

claims.claim: Morphine is broken down in the liver into M3G and M6G, which leave the body through the kidneys; when kidney function is reduced they build up, and M6G build-up can cause toxicity.
claims.supporting_passage: Coluzzi 2020: "In the liver, morphine is metabolized into two primary metabolites named 3 (M3G) and 6 glucuronide (M6G), which are eliminated via kidney pathways. In CKD condition, a significant renal retention of active or toxic metabolites occurs; for this reason, morphine is contraindicated in cases of renal failure, because the M6G accumulation may cause neurotoxic symptoms." Owsiany 2019: "Specifically, greater accumulation of morphine and its metabolite, morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), was found with decreased renal function." ... "Morphine and its metabolites are renally cleared, and in patients with significant renal impairment, these compounds are likely to accumulate."
claims.location: Coluzzi 2020 full text, 'Pharmacological Update on Opioid Analgesics in CKD'; Owsiany 2019 full text, sections 2 and 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacokinetics; adults and older adults with chronic kidney disease
claims.safe_wording: Morphine is broken down in the liver into active products that leave the body through the kidneys. When the kidneys work less well, these products build up with repeated doses.
claims.qualifications: Mechanism is well established; clinical evidence on how often it causes harm is very low quality.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Owsiany 2019: two studies found no relationship between morphine metabolite levels and adverse events (see C10-19-f).

claims.claim: Build-up of morphine and its metabolites in people with reduced kidney function can cause drowsiness, confusion, twitching (myoclonus), slowed breathing, nausea and constipation.
claims.supporting_passage: Owsiany 2019: "Because of the increased risk for adverse events, such as nausea, confusion, constipation, sedation, respiratory depression, and myoclonus, safe prescription of opioids is critical in the older, non-dialysis chronic kidney disease patient population." ... "Accumulation of morphine and its metabolites can cause adverse events such as nausea, vomiting, confusion, severe constipation, and cognitive dysfunction." Dubs 1999 (case report): "On the 7th day of morphine administration she became somnolent and breathing became markedly depressed, indicating overdosage" ... "As M6G is excreted by the kidney, its concentration rises in renal failure and can lead to severe intoxication."
claims.location: Owsiany 2019 full text, Introduction and section 2; Dubs 1999 abstract (English)
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with non-dialysis CKD (review); one case with chronic renal failure (case report)
claims.safe_wording: In a person with reduced kidney function who is on regular morphine, new drowsiness, confusion, muscle twitching or slowed breathing can be signs that it is building up.
claims.qualifications: Hallucinations were NOT found in the opened sources for morphine in renal impairment: leave them out. 'Twitching is an early sign' is NOT supported: do not say it. 'Develops over days' rests on pharmacology plus a single case report (day 7): say 'with repeated doses' or 'can appear after several days', not a fixed timescale.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The Owsiany introduction lists these effects for opioids in older people with CKD generally, not morphine alone.

claims.claim: European palliative care guidance based on a systematic review advises that morphine side effects in renal impairment can be managed by lengthening the dosing interval, reducing the 24-hour dose or switching opioid, and names fentanyl, alfentanil and methadone as least likely to cause harm; the evidence is very low quality.
claims.supporting_passage: "All of the studies identified have a significant risk of bias inherent in the study methodology and there is additional significant risk of publication bias. Overall evidence is of very low quality." ... "Fentanyl, alfentanil and methadone are identified, with caveats, as the least likely to cause harm when used appropriately. Morphine may be associated with toxicity in patients with renal impairment. Unwanted side effects with morphine may be satisfactorily dealt with by either increasing the dosing interval or reducing the 24 hour dose or by switching to an alternative opioid."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with cancer pain and renal impairment / opioids / other opioids / toxicity and pain relief / not specified
claims.safe_wording: European palliative care guidance suggests a lower daily dose, a longer gap between doses, or a switch to an opioid less dependent on the kidneys, such as fentanyl or alfentanil, with specialist advice.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is very low quality and from cancer pain; recommendations rest on pharmacokinetics and experience. Name only fentanyl and alfentanil (methadone needs specialist use). Do not name oxycodone as a safe swap (C10-19-d).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Sande 2016 found fentanyl/alfentanil/sufentanil recommendations rest on pharmacokinetics with very little clinical evidence.

numbers.meaning: Studies included in King 2011 systematic review

claims.claim: Oxycodone's breakdown products are also cleared by the kidneys and can accumulate, so it is not a straightforward substitute.
claims.supporting_passage: Coluzzi 2020: "its hepatic metabolism produces multiple metabolites, including the noroxycodone and oxymorphone (further metabolized to noroxymorphone), which could accumulate in patients with renal failure, since oxycodone elimination is relatively impaired in ESRD patients." Owsiany 2019: "Oxycodone and its active metabolites are cleared renally, and this clearance may be greatly reduced in older, renally-impaired patients."
claims.location: Coluzzi 2020 full text; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 4
claims.pico_timeframe: Pharmacokinetics in CKD
claims.safe_wording: Switching to oxycodone does not remove the problem: its breakdown products also depend on the kidneys.
claims.qualifications: Both reviews say oxycodone can be used with dose adjustment and monitoring.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: Kidney function falls with age, and creatinine-based eGFR can overestimate kidney function in people with little muscle.
claims.supporting_passage: Owsiany 2019: "Given the decreased kidney function associated with aging and chronic kidney disease, these patients are at increased risk for drug accumulation and adverse events." Hanna 2024: "Creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) may overestimate kidney function in patients with sarcopenia. While cystatin C-based eGFR (eGFR) is less affected by muscle mass, it may underestimate kidney function in patients with obesity." ... "After adjustment for potential confounders, CT-defined sarcopenia and high adiposity were both associated with >30% eGFR discordance (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.90, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.12-3.24; aOR 2.01, 95% CI 1.15-3.52, respectively)" ... "A spline model demonstrated that as skeletal muscle index decreases, the predicted difference between eGFRand eGFRwidens considerably."
claims.location: Owsiany 2019 abstract; Hanna 2024 abstract (Background and Results; subscripts cr/cys lost in the PubMed text)
claims.pico_timeframe: 545 adults with cancer, mean age 63 / CT-defined sarcopenia / no sarcopenia / cystatin C eGFR more than 30% below creatinine eGFR / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: A creatinine result in the normal range can hide low kidney function in someone with little muscle, because creatinine comes from muscle. In a study of people with low muscle mass, creatinine-based estimates often read well above cystatin C-based estimates.
claims.qualifications: Hanna 2024 studied people with cancer (mean age 63), not frail older people specifically, and compared two estimates rather than measured GFR. The 'creatinine comes from muscle' explanation is standard physiology but was not stated verbatim in the opened sources beyond 'less affected by muscle mass'; keep it brief. Prefer 'can' to 'often' for the general statement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: C06-B2 (claim C06-19-e) records that in very old people on DOACs the choice of kidney equation did not change outcomes; the size of the problem for opioid dosing is unmeasured.

numbers.meaning: Adjusted odds of more than 30% discordance between cystatin C and creatinine eGFR with sarcopenia (do not quote in a public post)

claims.claim: The clinical evidence linking morphine, kidney function and side effects is limited and partly conflicting.
claims.supporting_passage: Sande 2016: "There is lack of consensus within the existing literature on the relationship between morphine, creatinine levels and morphine-related side effects. Based on the current evidence, morphine should be used with caution; however, more evidence is needed." Owsiany 2019: "Alternatively, two studies found no relationship between serum concentrations of morphine, M6G, and morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) and pain intensity or adverse events."
claims.location: Sande 2016 abstract, Conclusions; Owsiany 2019 full text, section 2
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with cancer pain and renal impairment (18 studies, n = 2,422)
claims.safe_wording: The studies are small and do not all agree, so the advice rests mainly on how the drug is handled by the body and on clinical experience.
claims.qualifications: State as a named limitation, not a reason to ignore the risk.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: This is the uncertainty statement.

numbers.meaning: Sande 2016 systematic review, cancer patients with renal impairment

claims.claim: Among 18,343 surgical patients (mean age 52) in two US hospitals, 35.7% used no opioids in the 24 hours before discharge, and 45.6% of those were still prescribed opioids to take home.
claims.supporting_passage: "Among the 18 343 patients (10 069 women and 8274 men; mean age, 52.2 years) who underwent 21 452 surgical procedures, there was wide variation in the amount of opioids prescribed at hospital discharge given a postoperative patient's 24-hour predischarge opioid use. A total of 6548 patients (35.7%) used no opioids in the 24 hours prior to hospital discharge; however, 2988 of these patients (45.6%) were prescribed opioids at hospital discharge, suggesting potential overprescription."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult and paediatric postoperative inpatients (mean age 52.2), two US hospitals, 2014 to 2016 / 24-hour pre-discharge opioid use / amount prescribed at discharge / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of over 18,000 surgical patients (average age 52), about 1 in 3 took no opioid in the last 24 hours before going home, yet almost half of that group were still given an opioid prescription to take home.
claims.qualifications: Must state: surgical patients, average age 52, US hospitals; not older medical inpatients. 'Potential overprescription' is the authors' label; some may have needed pain relief at home.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C10-13-d.

claims.claim: In general surgical patients, opioid use at home after discharge was best predicted by the number of opioid doses taken the day before discharge.
claims.supporting_passage: "For patients discharged after POD 1, in multivariate analysis, the number of opioid pills used at home was associated with the number taken the day before discharge (p < 0.0001) and patient age (p = 0.006), but not the type of surgery. Forty-one percent of patients took no opioids the day before discharge, 33% took 1 to 3, and 26% took more than 4 pills. Eighty-five percent of patients' home opioid requirements would be satisfied using the following guideline: if no opioid pills are taken the day before discharge, no prescription is needed; if 1 to 3 opioid pills are taken the day before discharge, then a prescription for 15 opioid pills is given at discharge; and if 4 or more pills are taken the day before discharge, then a prescription for 30 opioid pills is given at discharge. If these guidelines were used, the number of opioid pills prescribed would decrease by 40%." ... "For patients admitted after surgical procedures, post-discharge opioid use is best predicted by usage the day before discharge."
claims.pico_timeframe: 333 general surgical inpatients discharged home, one US centre; chronic opioid users excluded / doses the day before discharge / home opioid use measured by questionnaire and phone
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of general surgical patients, the number of opioid doses taken the day before discharge was the best guide to how much they used at home. A simple rule based on that count would have met the needs of 85 in 100 patients and cut the tablets prescribed by 40%.
claims.qualifications: Single US centre, 333 surgical patients, not older-person specific. 85 in 100 means about 15 in 100 would have needed more: present 'none used' as a prompt to ask about pain at home, not an automatic no.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C10-13-d.
