claims.claim: A count of the last 24 hours is a rough guide: in a plastic surgery cohort, a 24-hour model predicted home opioid use much less well than a model using the whole inpatient course.
claims.supporting_passage: "The POP model had the strongest association (R2 = 0.899; P < 0.0001) between model output and postdischarge opioid consumption when compared to a procedure-based (R2 = 0.226; P = 0.025) or a 24-hour (R2 = 0.152; P = 0.007) model."
claims.pico_timeframe: 116 plastic and reconstructive surgery inpatients with stays of 2 to 8 days / personalised model vs 24-hour model vs procedure-based model / home opioid use reported at 4 weeks
claims.safe_wording: The 24-hour count is a starting point, not a formula: look at the trend over the whole stay and ask the person what activity at home will involve.
claims.qualifications: Small single-centre study; the 'look at the trend' advice is a judgement informed by it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Conflicts in part with Hill 2018, which found day-before use the best predictor among the factors it tested.

claims.claim: In older adults, opioid use is linked with falls, fall injuries and fractures.
claims.supporting_passage: "Thirty studies, providing 34 relevant effect sizes, met the inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis. Overall, opioid use was significantly associated with falls, fall injuries, and fractures, with effect sizes ranging from 0.15 to 0.71. In meta-regressions, no selected factors explained heterogeneity." ... "While heterogeneity is present, results suggest an increased risk of falls, fall injuries, and fractures among older adults who used opioids."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults / opioid use / non-use / falls, fall injuries, fractures / observational studies
claims.safe_wording: In older people, opioid use is linked with more falls and fractures.
claims.qualifications: Observational; association, not proof of cause; do not quote the pooled effect sizes (log scale). An unneeded take-home supply adds risk without benefit is a judgement, not a measured finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Substantial unexplained heterogeneity.

claims.claim: The evidence comes from surgical patients (mean age 52 in the largest study); applying the counting habit to older medical inpatients is a judgement.
claims.supporting_passage: Chen 2018: "Among the 18 343 patients (10 069 women and 8274 men; mean age, 52.2 years) who underwent 21 452 surgical procedures..." Hill 2018: "We studied 333 inpatients discharged to home after bariatric, benign foregut, liver, pancreas, ventral hernia, and colon surgery."
claims.pico_timeframe: Surgical inpatients
claims.safe_wording: These studies were in surgical patients, mostly younger than the people on a geriatric ward; using the count for older medical patients is sensible practice, not something these studies tested.
claims.qualifications: Required caveat in every version.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No study of older medical inpatients found.

claims.claim: In a UK randomised trial of 608 adults on strong opioids for chronic non-cancer pain, a supported group programme helped far more people stop opioids (29% vs 7% at 12 months) and pain interference with daily life was no worse than with usual care.
claims.supporting_passage: Sandhu 2023: "Of 608 participants randomized (mean age, 61 years; 362 female [60%]; median daily morphine equivalent dose, 46 mg [IQR, 25 to 79]), 440 (72%) completed 12-month follow-up. There was no statistically significant difference in PROMIS-PI-SF-8a scores between the 2 groups at 12-month follow-up (-4.1 in the intervention and -3.17 in the usual care groups; between-group difference: mean difference, -0.52 [95% CI, -1.94 to 0.89]; P = .15). At 12 months, opioid discontinuation occurred in 65 of 225 participants (29%) in the intervention group and 15 of 208 participants (7%) in the usual care group (odds ratio, 5.55 [95% CI, 2.80 to 10.99]; absolute difference, 21.7% [95% CI, 14.8% to 28.6%]; P < .001)." Sandhu 2026 (HTA): "The findings only apply to people willing to consider opioid reduction and may not apply to a more complex secondary care population. The results may not be applicable to people using very high opioid doses." ... "The I-WOTCH intervention helps substantially more people stop opioids than best usual care without adversely affecting pain interference."
claims.location: Sandhu 2023 abstract, Results; Sandhu 2026 abstract, Limitations and Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: 608 adults (mean age 61) on strong opioids for chronic non-malignant pain, 191 English general practices / 3 group days plus nurse support for tapering over 12 months / usual care (booklet and relaxation CD) / pain interference (PROMIS) and self-reported stopping / 12 months
claims.safe_wording: In a UK trial in general practice, people on strong painkillers for long-term pain who got group sessions and nurse support to reduce them were much more likely to have stopped a year later (29 in 100, against 7 in 100 with usual care). Pain getting in the way of daily life was no worse than in the usual-care group.
claims.qualifications: Mean age 61: few very old or frail people. Participants were willing to consider reduction; opioid use self-reported. 'No worse' = no clear difference (the trial did not show pain improved). Absolute figures first.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Serious adverse events were somewhat more common with the intervention (claim C10-24-b).

numbers.meaning: Adults randomised, English primary care
Trial population
Stopped opioids at 12 months, intervention vs usual care; absolute difference 21.7 percentage points
Between-group difference in pain interference score at 12 months (no clear difference; MCID 3.5)

claims.claim: In the same trial, serious adverse events were 8% with the programme vs 5% with usual care, and 1% of the programme group needed extra care for possible withdrawal symptoms.
claims.supporting_passage: "Serious adverse events occurred in 8% (25/305) of the participants in the intervention group and 5% (16/303) of the participants in the usual care group. The most common serious adverse events were gastrointestinal (2% in the intervention group and 0% in the usual care group) and locomotor/musculoskeletal (2% in the intervention group and 1% in the usual care group). Four people (1%) in the intervention group received additional medical care for possible or probable symptoms of opioid withdrawal (shortness of breath, hot flushes, fever and pain, small intestinal bleed, and an overdose suicide attempt)."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C10-24-a
claims.safe_wording: Reducing was not free of risk even with support: serious health problems were reported in 8 in 100 people in the programme and 5 in 100 with usual care.
claims.qualifications: Not all serious adverse events were due to reduction; no significance test is given in the abstract for this difference.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None beyond the above.

numbers.meaning: Serious adverse events, intervention vs usual care, 12 months
Intervention group needing extra medical care for possible or probable withdrawal symptoms

claims.claim: A systematic review of 67 studies found very low quality evidence that pain, function and quality of life may improve after long-term opioid dose reduction.
claims.supporting_passage: "Sixty-seven studies (11 randomized trials and 56 observational studies) examining 8 intervention categories, including interdisciplinary pain programs, buprenorphine-assisted dose reduction, and behavioral interventions, were found. Study quality was good for 3 studies, fair for 13 studies, and poor for 51 studies." ... "Among 40 studies examining patient outcomes after dose reduction (very low overall quality of evidence), improvement was reported in pain severity (8 of 8 fair-quality studies), function (5 of 5 fair-quality studies), and quality of life (3 of 3 fair-quality studies)." ... "Very low quality evidence suggests that several types of interventions may be effective to reduce or discontinue LTOT and that pain, function, and quality of life may improve with opioid dose reduction."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults on long-term opioids for chronic pain / dose reduction or discontinuation strategies / various / pain, function, quality of life, withdrawal, adverse events / variable
claims.safe_wording: Older, weaker studies of people who reduced long-term opioids more often reported that pain and daily function improved than worsened, but most of those studies were small, uncontrolled and poor quality.
claims.qualifications: Say clearly that the studies were weak. Many involved intensive pain programmes, so improvement may come from the programme rather than the lower dose. Use I-WOTCH (C10-24-a) as the lead evidence.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: I-WOTCH (the best trial) found no difference in pain interference, i.e. not worse but not better.

numbers.meaning: Frank 2017 systematic review

claims.claim: In a large US cohort of people on stable higher-dose long-term opioids, tapering was linked with more emergency or hospital visits for overdose or withdrawal and for mental health crisis, and faster reductions were linked with higher risk (corrected figures).
claims.supporting_passage: Corrected abstract (Scite record of the corrected article): "Posttapering patient periods were associated with an adjusted incidence rate of 6.3 overdose events per 100 person-years compared with 4.9 events per 100 person-years in non-tapered periods (adjusted incidence rate difference, 1.4 per 100 person-years [95% CI, 0.7-2.1]; aIRR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.15-1.43]). Tapering was associated with an adjusted incidence rate of 7.4 mental health crisis events per 100 person-years compared with 4.3 events per 100 person-years among nontapered periods (adjusted incidence rate difference, 3.1 per 100 person-years [95% CI, 2.1-4.1]; aIRR, 1.74 [95% CI, 1.50-2.01]). Increasing maximum monthly dose reduction velocity by 10% was associated with an aIRR of 1.05 for overdose (95% CI, 1.03-1.08) and of 1.14 for mental health crisis (95% CI, 1.11-1.17)." Erratum letter (Fenton 2022, 10.1001/jama.2022.0231): "After reanalyzing the data with corrected programming codes, the results showed that dose tapering remained significantly associated with both overdose and mental health crises, although the incidence rate ratios were reduced from 1.68 (95% CI, 1.53-1.85) to 1.28 (95% CI, 1.15-1.43) for overdose and from 2.28 (95% CI, 1.96-2.65) to 1.74 (95% CI, 1.50-2.01) for mental health crisis." Original abstract: "Although these findings raise questions about potential harms of tapering, interpretation is limited by the observational study design."
claims.location: Corrected abstract, Results (via Scite); erratum letter JAMA 2022;327(7):687
claims.pico_timeframe: 113,618 US adults on stable doses of 50 MME/day or more for 12 months (mean age about 58) / tapering of 15% or more / no tapering / ED or hospital encounters for overdose or withdrawal, and for mental health crisis / up to 12 months
claims.safe_wording: Cutting down can carry risk if it is rushed or imposed. In US insurance records, periods after a dose reduction had about 6 emergency visits for overdose or withdrawal per 100 people a year, against about 5 without reduction, and about 7 mental health crises per 100 a year against about 4. Faster reductions were linked with higher risk.
claims.qualifications: USE ONLY THE CORRECTED FIGURES; the PubMed abstract still shows the original (9.3 vs 5.5; 7.6 vs 3.3; aIRR 1.68 and 2.28), which were withdrawn by the authors. Observational; association, not proof that tapering caused the events; people who are tapered may differ. US population, mean age about 58, higher-dose users. The overdose outcome includes withdrawal encounters. Tapering was not separated into voluntary and imposed.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: I-WOTCH (randomised, supported, voluntary) found few withdrawal problems (1%); the contrast suggests support and pace may be important, but that is inference.

numbers.meaning: US adults on stable higher-dose long-term opioids (OptumLabs claims, 2008 to 2019)
Corrected adjusted rates of overdose or withdrawal encounters after tapering vs not tapering; difference 1.4 per 100 person-years
Corrected adjusted rates of mental health crisis encounters after tapering vs not; difference 3.1 per 100 person-years
Corrected relative increase in overdose and mental health crisis for each 10% increase in maximum monthly reduction speed

claims.claim: In the SPACE trial of chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain, opioids were not better than non-opioid medicines for pain-related function over 12 months and caused more side effects.
claims.supporting_passage: "Among 240 randomized patients (mean age, 58.3 years; women, 32 [13.0%]), 234 (97.5%) completed the trial. Groups did not significantly differ on pain-related function over 12 months (overall P = .58); mean 12-month BPI interference was 3.4 for the opioid group and 3.3 for the nonopioid group (difference, 0.1 [95% CI, -0.5 to 0.7]). Pain intensity was significantly better in the nonopioid group over 12 months (overall P = .03)" ... "Adverse medication-related symptoms were significantly more common in the opioid group over 12 months (overall P = .03)"
claims.pico_timeframe: 240 US veterans (mean age 58.3; 13% women) with chronic back or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain / opioid treat-to-target / non-opioid treat-to-target / pain-related function / 12 months
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial in people starting treatment for long-term back, hip or knee pain, opioids did not improve daily function more than paracetamol, anti-inflammatories and other non-opioid medicines over a year, and caused more side effects.
claims.qualifications: This trial was about starting opioids, not reducing them; participants were mostly middle-aged men. Use as background only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

Mean 12-month pain interference score (0 to 10), opioid vs non-opioid

claims.claim: UK guidance recommends gradual, agreed tapering with review, at a specified rate (for example 10% every 1 to 2 weeks).
claims.supporting_passage: Not found in opened sources. Faculty of Pain Medicine Opioids Aware and NICE NG193 pages could not be opened from this environment and no copy was found in Drive. CDC 2022 guideline (PMID 36327391) abstract opened: it contains no tapering rate; full text not read.
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Do not state a tapering rate or cite UK guidance on rate. Say 'slowly, at a pace agreed with the person and reviewed regularly'; this is supported by I-WOTCH's supported approach and Agnoli's link between faster reduction and harm.
claims.qualifications: Remove '[N to verify] weeks' from the visual.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: n/a

claims.claim: In adults with leg pain, having no pain when seated and symptoms that improve on bending forward are the most useful single history features pointing to the clinical syndrome of lumbar spinal stenosis.
claims.supporting_passage: Four studies evaluating 741 patients were identified. [...] The most useful symptoms for increasing the likelihood of the clinical syndrome of LSS were having no pain when seated (LR, 7.4; 95% CI, 1.9-30), improvement of symptoms when bending forward (LR, 6.4; 95% CI, 4.1-9.9), the presence of bilateral buttock or leg pain (LR, 6.3; 95% CI, 3.1-13), and neurogenic claudication (LR, 3.7; 95% CI, 2.9-4.8). Absence of neurogenic claudication (LR, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.17-0.31) decreased the likelihood of the diagnosis. A wide-based gait (LR, 13; 95% CI, 1.9-95) and abnormal Romberg test result (LR, 4.2; 95% CI, 1.4-13) increased the likelihood of the clinical syndrome of LSS. [...] Absence of pain when seated and improvement of symptoms when bending forward are the most useful individual findings.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults (mostly older; highest-quality study mean age 65) with lower limb pain in spine and primary care clinics / history and examination findings / expert diagnosis with imaging confirmation / diagnostic accuracy (likelihood ratios) / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a review of 4 studies (741 people with leg pain), two answers were the strongest single pointers towards spinal stenosis (narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back): no pain when sitting, and symptoms that ease on bending forward. Leg pain on walking that goes away when the person sits, or leans forward on a shopping trolley, points towards the spine.
claims.qualifications: Keep likelihood ratios out of lay text or describe them as 'strong pointers'; never 'X times more likely'. Estimates come mostly from specialist clinics and may be less accurate in primary care. Confidence interval for 'no pain when seated' is wide (1.9 to 30). No single feature confirms the diagnosis; it needs imaging as well.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Nadeau 2013 (C10-22-d) found that individual symptom attributes were only weakly valid for telling neurogenic from vascular claudication head to head; combinations of symptoms were more useful. The two studies compare against different alternatives (Suri: all other causes of leg pain; Nadeau: vascular claudication only).

numbers.meaning: size of the diagnostic accuracy review
no pain when seated; positive likelihood ratio for LSS syndrome
improvement of symptoms when bending forward
bilateral buttock or leg pain
wide-based gait on examination (very imprecise)
absence of neurogenic claudication makes LSS less likely
age over 70 raises the likelihood

claims.claim: Worked example: if about 15 in 100 older adults with leg pain in primary care have the syndrome, symptoms easing on bending forward raises the probability to about 53 in 100 (73 in 100 if the starting figure is 30 in 100).
claims.supporting_passage: Assuming a primary care clinic prevalence of 15% and using only the finding of symptom improvement with bending forward, the probability of the clinical syndrome of LSS increases to 53%. However, if the clinic prevalence of the syndrome of LSS is 30%, the posttest probability would be 73%.
claims.pico_timeframe: Hypothetical primary care prevalence (15% or 30%) / symptom improvement with bending forward / post-test probability / illustrative calculation
claims.safe_wording: The authors' own worked example: if 15 in 100 people with this kind of leg pain have spinal stenosis, relief on bending forward raises the chance to about 53 in 100. That is a strong pointer, not a diagnosis.
claims.qualifications: The 15% and 30% starting figures are the authors' assumptions, not measured prevalence. Optional; useful for practitioners, not needed for the core post.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None beyond C10-22-a.

numbers.meaning: assumed pre-test probability to post-test probability with symptom relief on bending forward
same calculation with a higher assumed starting probability

claims.claim: Leg pain from the circulation (vascular claudication) is typically not eased by changes in posture such as bending forward, tends to come on after a more consistent walking distance, and when the clinical picture is uncertain it can be checked with ankle brachial pressure (ABI) or vascular imaging.
claims.supporting_passage: Vascular intermittent claudication due to peripheral arterial disease in particular is often considered when leg pain occurs with walking. Unlike neurogenic claudication, vascular claudication is typically not improved by changes in posture such as lumbar flexion.The discomfort of vascular claudication may be more consistently reproducible with a specific distance and time of ambulation than neurogenic claudication.When the diagnosis is uncertain by clinical evaluation, it can be confirmed by diagnostic testing including ankle brachial indices (ABIs), duplex ultrasound, computed tomographic angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography.
claims.location: Full text, Differential Diagnosis of the Clinical Syndrome of LSS
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with walking-related leg pain / clinical features of vascular vs neurogenic claudication / descriptive clinical guidance (review text, referenced)
claims.safe_wording: Leg pain from narrowed arteries is usually not helped by bending forward, and it tends to come on after about the same walking distance each time. If the history leaves doubt, checking foot pulses and ankle blood pressure (ABI) helps sort it out.
claims.qualifications: This is descriptive text in the review (citing other sources), not a pooled accuracy estimate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Nadeau 2013 found pain relievers and pain location individually only weakly discriminating; the difference is a tendency, not a rule.

claims.claim: In patients with claudication, calf symptoms that ease on standing still strongly suggest a circulation cause, while buttock or thigh symptoms that start on standing alone, ease on sitting and are helped by leaning on a shopping trolley strongly suggest spinal stenosis; single features on their own are weak.
claims.supporting_passage: We studied 53 patients. The most sensitive symptom attribute to rule out LSS was the absence of "triggering of pain with standing alone" (sensitivity 0.97, NLR 0.050). Pain alleviators and symptom location data showed a weak clinical significance for LSS and PVD. Constellation of symptoms yielded the strongest associations: patients with a positive shopping cart sign whose symptoms were located above the knees, triggered with standing alone and relieved with sitting had a strong likelihood of neurogenic claudication (PLR 13). Patients with symptoms in the calf that were relieved with standing alone had a strong likelihood of vascular claudication (PLR 20.0). [...] The classic symptom attributes used to differentiate neurogenic from vascular claudication are at best weakly valid independently. However, certain constellation of symptoms are much more indicative of etiology.
claims.pico_timeframe: 53 patients with diagnosed LSS or peripheral vascular disease reporting claudication, Canada / 14 symptom questions / neurogenic vs vascular diagnosis / likelihood ratios / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a small study of 53 people with walking-related leg pain, calf pain that eased when the person simply stood still pointed strongly to the circulation. Pain above the knee that came on just from standing, eased on sitting and was helped by leaning on a shopping trolley pointed strongly to the spine. Any one of these features alone was a weak guide.
claims.qualifications: Small single-centre study; likelihood ratios imprecise. Participants already had one diagnosis or the other; people with both conditions are not addressed. Keep figures out of lay posts; 'strong pointer' is the safe phrase.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Suri 2010 found 'no pain when seated' and 'eases on bending forward' useful on their own for LSS against all other causes; Nadeau found alleviators weak individually when comparing directly with vascular claudication. State that the combination of features helps most.

numbers.meaning: study size
calf symptoms relieved by standing still: positive likelihood ratio for vascular claudication
shopping cart sign plus above-knee symptoms, triggered by standing alone, relieved by sitting: positive likelihood ratio for neurogenic claudication
pain not triggered by standing alone makes LSS unlikely

claims.claim: Spinal stenosis and peripheral arterial disease often coexist in older people, so the history points towards a cause but does not exclude the other; pulses or ankle brachial pressure should still be checked.
claims.supporting_passage: Suri 2010: "The differential diagnosis of the clinical syndrome of LSS is complicated by the frequent coexistence of many of the above-described conditions in older adults." Uesugi 2012: "570 patients diagnosed with LSS using a clinical diagnostic support tool and MRI at 64 facilities were enrolled. [...] The LSSPAD group comprised 38 patients (6.7 %); 20 (3.5 %) had pre-diagnosised PAD while 18 (3.2 %) had undetected PAD. The clinical characteristics of these patients were advanced age, diabetes, and a history of ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disorder. [...] Pain in buttocks and legs improved less in the LSSPAD group than in the LSS group (p < 0.05). [...] clinicians should consider the coexistence of PAD in LSS patients."
claims.location: Suri: full text, Differential Diagnosis; Uesugi: Abstract, Results and Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: Uesugi: 570 Japanese orthopaedic patients with LSS / ABI measured / coexisting PAD / prevalence and 3-month outcome
claims.safe_wording: The two causes can occur together. In a Japanese study of 570 people with spinal stenosis, about 7 in 100 also had narrowed leg arteries, and in about half of those (3 in 100 overall) the artery disease had not been picked up before. So even when the story sounds like the spine, check the foot pulses or ankle blood pressure.
claims.qualifications: Prevalence comes from Japanese specialist clinics and may differ in UK primary care. Coexisting PAD was more common with older age, diabetes and heart or stroke history.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found against coexistence; the size of the overlap varies by setting.

numbers.meaning: patients with LSS enrolled at 64 facilities (Japan)
had coexisting PAD (about 7 in 100)
had PAD that was previously undetected (about 3 in 100)

claims.claim: The diagnosis of spinal stenosis needs the typical clinical picture confirmed with cross-sectional imaging; narrowing on MRI is common in older people without symptoms, so a scan alone does not make the diagnosis. Hip osteoarthritis is among the other causes to consider.
claims.supporting_passage: Suri 2010: "The diagnosis of the clinical syndrome of LSS requires the appropriate clinical picture and radiographic findings." and "The prevalence of radiographic LSS using qualitative criteria in asymptomatic older adults 55 years or older has been estimated at 21% to 30% for moderate stenosis and 6% to 7% for severe stenosis.These data make it clear that incidental radiographic LSS on spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is common in asymptomatic patients." and "Lower extremity pain can also be caused by other spinal and extraspinal musculoskeletal diagnoses, including lumbosacral radicular pain due to nerve root impingement, [...] lumbar vertebral compression fractures, and hip osteoarthritis." Katz 2022: "The diagnosis can generally be made based on a clinical history of back and lower extremity pain that is provoked by lumbar extension, relieved by lumbar flexion, and confirmed with cross-sectional imaging, such as computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)."
claims.location: Suri: Abstract Conclusions and full text (Radiographic and Anatomic LSS; Differential Diagnosis); Katz: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with back and leg pain / clinical history plus CT or MRI / diagnosis
claims.safe_wording: The history makes spinal stenosis likely; a scan confirms it. Because many older people have some narrowing on a scan without any symptoms, the scan only means something alongside the story.
claims.qualifications: The 21% to 30% asymptomatic figures are background data cited in Suri's introduction, not that review's own finding; if used, attribute them as 'studies of people without symptoms'. Do not quote Katz's prevalence figure (inconsistent in the abstract).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: moderate radiographic stenosis in asymptomatic adults aged 55 or over (background studies cited by Suri)
severe radiographic stenosis in the same asymptomatic group

claims.claim: In the PRECISE trial, pregabalin did not reduce sciatica leg pain more than placebo at 8 weeks or at 1 year, did not improve any secondary outcome, and caused more adverse events, dizziness most often.
claims.supporting_passage: Mathieson 2017: "A total of 209 patients underwent randomization, of whom 108 received pregabalin and 101 received placebo; after randomization, 2 patients in the pregabalin group were determined to be ineligible and were excluded from the analyses. At week 8, the mean unadjusted leg-pain intensity score was 3.7 in the pregabalin group and 3.1 in the placebo group (adjusted mean difference, 0.5; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.2 to 1.2; P=0.19). At week 52, the mean unadjusted leg-pain intensity score was 3.4 in the pregabalin group and 3.0 in the placebo group (adjusted mean difference, 0.3; 95% CI, -0.5 to 1.0; P=0.46). No significant between-group differences were observed with respect to any secondary outcome at either week 8 or week 52. A total of 227 adverse events were reported in the pregabalin group and 124 in the placebo group. Dizziness was more common in the pregabalin group than in the placebo group." Enke 2018, Figure 3 (any adverse event): "Mathieson et al.: 68/106 (pregabalin) vs. 43/101 (placebo); RR 1.5 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.0)"
claims.location: Mathieson: Abstract, Results; Enke: Figure 3 (read via Undermind)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with sciatica, Sydney / pregabalin up to 600 mg/day for up to 8 weeks / matching placebo / leg pain intensity 0 to 10, disability, adverse events / 8 and 52 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In a placebo-controlled trial of 207 adults with sciatica, leg pain at 8 weeks averaged 3.7 out of 10 with pregabalin and 3.1 with a dummy capsule, and the trial showed no clear difference at 8 weeks or at 1 year. About 64 in 100 people on pregabalin had at least one side effect, against about 43 in 100 on the dummy capsule; dizziness was the most common.
claims.qualifications: Say 'did not show a clear difference', not 'no effect'; the confidence interval (-0.2 to 1.2 points) runs from a slight benefit to slight harm and does not favour pregabalin. 227 vs 124 are adverse EVENTS, not people; use the per-person figures (68 of 106 vs 43 of 101) for people.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with meta-analyses (C10-26-c). Some other neuropathic pain conditions do respond to pregabalin, so keep the claim to sciatica.

numbers.meaning: trial size (106 pregabalin, 101 placebo analysed)
mean unadjusted leg pain at week 8, pregabalin vs placebo
adjusted mean difference at week 8 (positive = more pain with pregabalin); not significant
mean leg pain at week 52
number of adverse events reported (events, not people)
people with any adverse event, pregabalin vs placebo; about 21 extra people per 100 (derived)

claims.claim: PRECISE participants were adults of working age on average (mean ages 52 and 55); the trial took adults aged 18 or older and excluded people with estimated creatinine clearance below 60 ml/min, so many older people were not eligible.
claims.supporting_passage: Enke 2018, Table 1: "207 participants with acute (7 d to < 3 mo) or chronic (≥ 3 mo) sciatica. Mean age ± SD: pregabalin group 52.4 ± 17.2 yr; placebo group 55.2 ± 16.0 yr." PRECISE protocol: "pain duration of current episode of at least 1 week and up to 1 year; age 18 years or older" and "contraindications to pregabalin (known allergy to pregabalin or significant renal impairment. Pregabalin is predominantly renally excreted, so patients with an estimated creatinine clearance of <60 ml/minute will be excluded)"

claims.pico_timeframe: PRECISE trial population / eligibility and baseline age

claims.qualifications: The last clause ('nothing suggests it would work better') is a reasoned inference, not a finding; mark as judgement if used. Applying the result to older people rests on the absence of benefit plus the known side-effect profile.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: mean age, pregabalin and placebo groups

claims.claim: Systematic reviews found gabapentinoids ineffective for low back pain and lumbar radicular pain (sciatica) compared with placebo, with a higher risk of adverse effects, most often drowsiness, dizziness and nausea.
claims.supporting_passage: Enke 2018: "Nine trials compared topiramate, gabapentin or pregabalin to placebo in 859 unique participants. Fourteen of 15 comparisons found anticonvulsants were not effective to reduce pain or disability in low back pain or lumbar radicular pain; for example, there was high-quality evidence of no effect of gabapentinoids versus placebo on chronic low back pain in the short term (pooled mean difference [MD] −0.0, 95% confidence interval [CI] −0.8 to 0.7) or for lumbar radicular pain in the immediate term (pooled MD −0.1, 95% CI −0.7 to 0.5). The lack of efficacy is accompanied by increased risk of adverse events from use of gabapentinoids, for which the level of evidence is high." Full text: "Pooled results indicate high-quality evidence that gabapentinoids were associated with an increased risk of adverse events compared with placebo (pooled risk ratio [RR] 1.4, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.7, 6 studies)." and "The most common adverse events reported in participants taking a gabapentinoid were drowsiness or somnolence, dizziness and nausea". Shanthanna 2017: "Compared with placebo, the following adverse events were more commonly reported with GB: dizziness-(RR = 1.99, 95% CI [1.17 to 3.37], I2 = 49); fatigue (RR = 1.85, 95% CI [1.12 to 3.05], I2 = 0); difficulties with mentation (RR = 3.34, 95% CI [1.54 to 7.25], I2 = 0); and visual disturbances (RR = 5.72, 95% CI [1.94 to 16.91], I2 = 0)."
claims.location: Enke: Abstract and Results, Adverse events (full text via Undermind); Shanthanna: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with low back pain or sciatica / gabapentin or pregabalin / placebo / pain, disability, adverse events / short to intermediate term
claims.safe_wording: Reviews that pooled the trials found that gabapentin and pregabalin did not ease back pain or sciatica more than a dummy tablet, and people taking them had more side effects, most often drowsiness, dizziness and nausea.
claims.qualifications: Mostly working-age trial populations. Shanthanna is chronic low back pain (not sciatica specifically) with very low to moderate quality evidence for side effects. Use relative risks only with absolute figures, or not at all for the public.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Enke graded efficacy evidence moderate to high quality. No review found benefit for sciatica.

numbers.meaning: Enke review size
pooled pain difference (0 to 10 scale), gabapentinoids vs placebo, lumbar radicular pain, immediate term
relative risk of any adverse event with gabapentinoids vs placebo
Shanthanna: number needed to harm for dizziness with gabapentin vs placebo in chronic low back pain

claims.claim: NICE NG59 recommends not offering gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for managing sciatica.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine extract only (nice.org.uk blocked): "Do not offer gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for managing sciatica as there is no overall evidence of benefit and there is evidence of harm." (reported as recommendation 1.2.16, 2020 update). Enke 2018 (opened): "Regarding sciatica, the 2016 UK guideline recommends following neuropathic pain guidelines, which endorse the use of gabapentinoids. However, the recommendation of gabapentinoids for sciatica should be reviewed in light of emerging evidence."
claims.pico_timeframe: People 16 and over with sciatica, England / gabapentinoids / guideline recommendation
claims.safe_wording: Do not state NICE's current position unless the NICE NG59 page is opened and the wording confirmed. If it is confirmed, the post may say: 'NICE advises against gabapentin and pregabalin for sciatica.' Without that check, say: 'The trial evidence does not support starting them for sciatica.'
claims.qualifications: Search extract is not sufficient for an essential claim. The opened source (Enke 2018) records that the 2016 version of NG59 pointed to neuropathic pain guidance endorsing gabapentinoids; the change came in a 2020 update that could not be opened here. The recommendation concerns sciatica, not all nerve pain.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Khorami 2021 (searches to 2019) found guideline recommendations on anticonvulsants for sciatica 'highly inconsistent' internationally.

claims.claim: For sciatica, guidelines consistently recommend explanation and education and commonly recommend physical activity; recommendations on medicines are inconsistent.
claims.supporting_passage: "The consistent recommendation for 'should do' is: educational care [,,,,] and the common recommendation for 'should do' is physical activity [,,,,,,,]. Exercise/physical therapies [,,,,,] is consistently recommended as 'could do'." and "For all the other medications, such as paracetamol, Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, anticonvulsants, muscle relaxants, antidepressants, corticosteroids and antibiotics, the recommendations are highly inconsistent." and "Referral to a specialist is recommended when conservative therapy fails or when steppage gait is present."
claims.pico_timeframe: 23 international guidelines on lumbosacral radicular pain / recommendations / consistency across guidelines / searches to August 2019
claims.safe_wording: Guidelines agree on explaining the condition and helping the person stay active, with referral if things don't improve or there is foot weakness (foot drop).
claims.qualifications: Review predates the 2020 NICE update; it is about adults generally, not older people specifically.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Drug recommendations differ between guidelines.

numbers.meaning: number reviewed, 10 countries

claims.claim: In older people, dizziness and drowsiness from gabapentinoids raise the risk of falls.
claims.supporting_passage: Chaitoff 2025: "Our analytic cohort included 57 086 older adults with a diagnosis of interest initiating treatment with gabapentin (= 52 152) or duloxetine (= 4934). [...] At 6-month follow-up, incident gabapentin users had lower hazard of falls (hazard ratio, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.43 to 0.64]), but there was no difference in the hazards of experiencing severe falls. [...] Claims may contain fewer frail adults and undercount falls. Compared with incident use of duloxetine, incident use of gabapentin was not associated with increased fall-related visits." Oh 2024: "gabapentin initiation was significantly associated with increased odds of new falls at the index + 2 visit (odds ratio [95% confidence interval] 2.5 [1.3, 4.6])."
claims.pico_timeframe: Chaitoff: adults 65+ starting gabapentin vs duloxetine, 6 months; Oh: older adults with cognitive impairment starting gabapentin vs non-users, 1 to 2 years
claims.safe_wording: Do not claim that gabapentinoids have been shown to raise falls risk in older people. Safe: 'Dizziness and drowsiness are the commonest side effects; for someone who is already unsteady, that is a reason not to start a medicine that has not been shown to help.' (judgement)
claims.qualifications: Observational evidence conflicts. The link from dizziness to falls is plausible but the direct evidence is mixed; present the falls point as judgement, not finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Chaitoff 2025 (large, active comparator) found no increase in fall-related visits vs duloxetine; Oh 2024 (smaller, people with cognitive impairment, non-user comparator) found higher odds of new falls.

numbers.meaning: Chaitoff: fall-related visits, gabapentin vs duloxetine starters, 6 months (relative; comparator drug also raises falls risk)
Oh: odds of new falls about 2 years after starting gabapentin vs non-users, people with cognitive impairment

claims.claim: A 2012 systematic review found an unfavourable long-term pain outcome (moderate to severe pain, or pain not relieved) in about 10% to 34% of people after knee replacement and about 20% in the best-quality studies; definitions varied and the authors did not pool.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Total hip or knee replacement is highly successful when judged by prosthesis-related outcomes. However, some people experience long-term pain." and "The proportion of people with an unfavourable long-term pain outcome in studies ranged from about 7% to 23% after hip and 10% to 34% after knee replacement. In the best quality studies, an unfavourable pain outcome was reported in 9% or more of patients after hip and about 20% of patients after knee replacement." Methods: "Favourable outcome includes people with no pain or mild pain at follow-up, while unfavourable outcome includes those with moderate-to-severe pain or for whom surgery had not relieved pain." Discussion: "Although we have interpreted pain outcomes as favourable, unfavourable or uncertain, we do not believe that the data justify combination to provide summary values." and "While acknowledging probable underestimates of the extent of pain after surgery reported in the literature, we should recognise the effectiveness of replacement for many."
claims.location: Abstract; Methods, Data synthesis; Discussion (full text via Undermind)
claims.pico_timeframe: Consecutive unselected patients with primary hip or knee replacement for osteoarthritis / pain in operated joint / 3 months to 5 years
claims.safe_wording: Background only. An earlier review (2012) put the figure at about 1 in 5 after knee replacement in the best studies. Prefer the 2025 update (C10-30-b) for current numbers, and do not give both figures unless the difference is explained.
claims.qualifications: Superseded for current figures. The 'prosthesis-related outcomes' sentence is the authors' framing in the abstract background, not a result.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The 2025 update (Cheng) gives lower pooled long-term figures for knee replacement (about 13 in 100 at 1 year).

numbers.meaning: range of unfavourable long-term pain after knee replacement across 11 cohorts (not pooled)
knee replacement, best-quality studies
hip replacement range; best-quality studies

claims.claim: Current best estimate: after knee replacement, about 22 in 100 people report unfavourable pain at 3 months, falling to about 13 to 15 in 100 at 1 to 2 years; about 14 in 100 after hip replacement at 6 to 12 months. Confidence is low and the figures are probably underestimates.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "For TKR, 68 studies with 89 time points, including 598 498 patients, were included. Multivariate meta-analysis showed a general decrease in pain proportions over time: 21.9% (95% CrI 15.6% to 29.4%) at 3 months, 14.1% (10.9% to 17.9%) at 6 months, 12.6% (9.9% to 15.9%) at 12 months and 14.6% (9.5% to 22.4%) at 24 months. Considerable heterogeneity, unrelated to examined moderators, was indicated by substantial prediction intervals in the univariate models. Substantial loss to follow-up and risk of bias led to low confidence in the results. For THR, only 11 studies were included, so it was not possible to describe the trend. Univariate meta-analysis estimated 13.8% (8.5% to 20.1%) and 13.7% (4.8% to 31.0%) of patients experiencing long-term pain 6 and 12 months after THR". Methods: "We adopted the term 'unfavourable pain' from the previous review, which serves as a collective label to include the various descriptions used by study authors—such as persistent pain, worsening pain, or residual pain—rather than as an indicator of dissatisfaction." Strengths and limitations: "These prevalence rates are likely underestimated due to loss to follow-up and the high risk of bias in the included studies." Results: "Patients in 52 studies with data had a mean age of 69.6 (SD 9.4) years, and 63% (58 to 69) were women."
claims.location: Abstract; Methods, Outcome; Strengths and limitations; Results (full text via Undermind)
claims.pico_timeframe: People having total knee replacement (mean age 69.6) or hip replacement / unfavourable pain in the operated joint (study-specific definitions) / 3, 6, 12 and 24 months
claims.safe_wording: Knee replacement relieves pain for most people, but not all. In a 2025 review of 68 studies (nearly 600,000 people, average age about 70), about 13 in 100 still had troublesome knee pain a year after the operation. At 3 months the figure was about 22 in 100. The authors think these numbers are probably too low, because people with poor results are often missing from follow-up.
claims.qualifications: Say 'troublesome' or 'persistent' pain, defined differently across studies; not 'severe' pain. Low confidence (authors' wording). Across individual studies the 12-month figure ranged from 3.3% to 43.3%. Do not also quote the 2012 'about 1 in 5' without explaining that it is an older, smaller evidence base.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Beswick 2012 (about 20% in best-quality knee studies) is higher; the difference probably reflects different definitions and studies. Satisfaction data (Bourne 2010) give a similar order: about 1 in 5 not satisfied.

numbers.meaning: knee replacement evidence base
knee: unfavourable pain at 3 months (about 22 in 100)
knee: at 6 months
knee: at 12 months (about 13 in 100, roughly 1 in 8)
knee: at 24 months (sparse data)
hip replacement: at 6 and 12 months
mean age of knee replacement patients (52 studies)
range across individual knee studies at 12 months

claims.claim: Most people are satisfied after knee replacement, but about 1 in 5 are not; satisfaction with pain relief varies by activity, and unmet expectations are the strongest predictor of dissatisfaction.
claims.supporting_passage: "We performed a cross-sectional study of patient satisfaction after 1703 primary TKAs performed in the province of Ontario. Our data confirmed that approximately one in five (19%) primary TKA patients were not satisfied with the outcome. Satisfaction with pain relief varied from 72-86% and with function from 70-84% for specific activities of daily living. The strongest predictors of patient dissatisfaction after primary TKA were expectations not met (10.7x greater risk), a low 1-year WOMAC (2.5x greater risk), preoperative pain at rest (2.4x greater risk) and a postoperative complication requiring hospital readmission (1.9x greater risk)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 1,703 primary knee replacements, Ontario / patient satisfaction survey / cross-sectional, at least 1 year after surgery
claims.safe_wording: About 4 in 5 people in a Canadian survey were satisfied with their knee replacement. Satisfaction with pain relief ranged from about 7 in 10 to 9 in 10, depending on the activity. People whose expectations were not met were the most likely to be dissatisfied, which is a reason to ask about likely pain before the operation.
claims.qualifications: Satisfaction is a different outcome from pain. Do not quote the '10.7x greater risk' figure. Older implants and one Canadian province.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent in direction with Beswick 2012 and Cheng 2025.

numbers.meaning: primary knee replacements surveyed
not satisfied with the outcome (about 1 in 5)
satisfied with pain relief, range across specific activities

claims.claim: NICE recommends core non-surgical treatment for osteoarthritis and referral for joint replacement when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical management has not helped.
claims.supporting_passage: Not verified: NICE NG226 and NG157 pages could not be opened; the BMJ summary of NG226 (Wood 2023, PMID 36693668) has no abstract and no accessible PDF.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Omit NICE referral criteria. The post can still end with questions to ask the surgeon ('What are my chances of still having pain afterwards? What else could I try first?'); questions make no factual claim.
claims.qualifications: Not essential for the revised angle.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not assessed.

claims.claim: In population studies, knee X-ray changes and knee pain match poorly: 15% to 76% of people with knee pain had X-ray osteoarthritis, and 15% to 81% of people with X-ray osteoarthritis had pain, depending on definitions.
claims.supporting_passage: "The proportion of those with knee pain found to have radiographic osteoarthritis ranged from 15-76%, and in those with radiographic knee OA the proportion with pain ranged from 15% - 81%. Considerable variation occurred with x ray view, pain definition, OA grading and demographic factors" and "Radiographic knee osteoarthritis is likewise an imprecise guide to the likelihood that knee pain or disability will be present. Both associations are affected by the definition of pain used and the nature of the study group. The results of knee x rays should not be used in isolation when assessing individual patients with knee pain."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in population studies with knee X-rays and pain assessment / radiographic OA vs knee pain / cross-sectional prevalence
claims.safe_wording: Studies of the general population find that many people with arthritis changes on a knee X-ray have little or no pain, and many people with knee pain have X-rays that look fairly normal. The authors concluded that a knee X-ray should not be used on its own to judge a person's knee pain.
claims.qualifications: Ranges are very wide and depend on definitions; avoid presenting a single figure. Use 'a poor guide', not 'no guide' (see C10-16-b).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Neogi 2009 shows a strong within-person link between X-ray severity and pain (C10-16-b).

numbers.meaning: people with knee pain who had radiographic OA, range across population studies
people with radiographic knee OA who had pain, range across population studies

claims.claim: On average, worse X-ray changes do go with more pain: comparing a person's two knees, the knee with more severe X-ray osteoarthritis was far more likely to be the painful one.
claims.supporting_passage: "696 people from MOST and 336 people from Framingham were included. Kellgren and Lawrence grades were strongly associated with frequent knee pain-for example, for Kellgren and Lawrence grade 4 v grade 0 the odds ratio for pain was 151 (95% confidence interval 43 to 526) in MOST and 73 (16 to 331) in Framingham (both P<0.001 for trend). [...] Joint space narrowing was more strongly associated with each pain measure than were osteophytes." and "Using a method that minimises between person confounding, this study found that radiographic osteoarthritis and individual radiographic features of osteoarthritis were strongly associated with knee pain."
claims.pico_timeframe: People in two US cohorts whose knees differed in pain / Kellgren and Lawrence grade of each knee / the other knee of the same person / frequent knee pain / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: The X-ray is not meaningless. When researchers compared each person's two knees, the knee with worse X-ray changes was much more often the painful one. So the X-ray is a poor guide to how much a particular person will hurt or what they can do, not no guide at all.
claims.qualifications: Do not quote the odds ratios for the public and never turn them into 'times more likely'. Within-person design removes differences between people (such as mood or pain sensitivity), which is part of why X-rays match pain poorly across people.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with Bedson if both are stated: strong link within a person, weak match between people.

numbers.meaning: participants from MOST and Framingham
odds of frequent pain, KL grade 4 vs grade 0 knee within the same person (MOST; Framingham); very imprecise; do not convert

claims.claim: Specialist guidance says imaging is not needed to diagnose osteoarthritis in people with typical symptoms; imaging helps when the presentation is atypical or another diagnosis is suspected, or with unexpected rapid worsening, and plain X-ray is the first choice when imaging is needed.
claims.supporting_passage: "17 011 references were identified from which 390 studies were included in the SLR. Seven recommendations were produced, covering the lack of need for diagnostic imaging in patients with typical symptoms; the role of imaging in differential diagnosis; the lack of benefit in monitoring when no therapeutic modification is related, though consideration is required when unexpected clinical deterioration occurs; CR as the first-choice imaging modality; consideration of how to correctly acquire images and the role of imaging in guiding local injections."
claims.pico_timeframe: People with knee, hip, hand or foot osteoarthritis / imaging / clinical diagnosis and monitoring / guideline recommendations
claims.safe_wording: European rheumatology guidance (EULAR, 2017) says an X-ray is not needed to diagnose osteoarthritis when the symptoms are typical. Imaging helps when something is unusual, when another cause is possible, or when the knee gets worse unexpectedly.
claims.qualifications: Exact recommendation wording not seen (abstract summary only). Surgical planning is not named in the abstract; if the post mentions it, say 'for example before surgery' only as general practice, or omit.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: NICE NG226 appears to make a similar recommendation (search extract only, C10-16-d).

numbers.meaning: evidence base and output of the EULAR task force

claims.claim: NICE NG226 recommends diagnosing osteoarthritis clinically without imaging in people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting no longer than 30 minutes.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine extract only (nice.org.uk blocked): "Diagnose osteoarthritis clinically without imaging in people who are 45 or over and have activity-related joint pain and have either no morning joint-related stiffness or morning stiffness that lasts no longer than 30 minutes." and "NICE recommends not to routinely use imaging to diagnose osteoarthritis unless there are atypical features or features that suggest an alternative or additional diagnosis."
claims.pico_timeframe: People 45 and over with joint pain, England / clinical diagnosis without imaging / guideline
claims.safe_wording: Use only after opening the NICE NG226 page. Otherwise attribute the point to EULAR (C10-16-c) and omit the age 45 and 30-minute criteria.
claims.qualifications: Search extract is not sufficient for an essential claim.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.
