claims.claim: People told their knee is 'bone on bone' often come to believe that loading the knee will damage it and that exercise and physiotherapy will make it worse, and some then set aside exercise-based treatment.
claims.supporting_passage: "Thirty-seven patients were approached and 27 participated. Participants were 48% female; mean age was 67 years." and "All participants believed that their knee OA was "bone on bone" (identity beliefs) and most (> 14 participants) believed it was caused by "wear and tear" (causal beliefs). Most (> 14 participants) believed that loading the knee could further damage their "vulnerable" joint (consequence beliefs) and all believed that their pain would deteriorate over time (timeline beliefs). Many (>20 participants) believed that physiotherapy and exercise interventions would increase pain and could not replace lost knee cartilage." and "Once the participants in this study had been "diagnosed" with "bone-on-bone" changes, many disregarded exercise-based interventions which they believed would damage their joint, in favor of alternative and experimental treatments, which they believed would regenerate lost knee cartilage."
claims.pico_timeframe: 27 people with end-stage knee OA on a knee replacement waiting list, one Australian hospital / beliefs about OA / qualitative interviews
claims.safe_wording: In interviews with 27 people waiting for a knee replacement in Australia, all described their knee as 'bone on bone'. Many believed exercise or physiotherapy would make it worse or damage the joint, and many had set exercise aside.
claims.qualifications: Qualitative, small, one hospital, people already listed for surgery: describes beliefs, not how common they are, and does not show that the X-ray description caused the avoidance. Avoid causal wording ('the X-ray made them stop').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: qualitative sample
believed physiotherapy and exercise would increase pain

claims.claim: After surgery, pain on movement is usually much worse than pain at rest, yet many trials measure only one kind of pain or do not say which.
claims.supporting_passage: "Only 39% of trials measured MEP and 52% failed to identify pain outcome as pain at rest (PAR) or MEP. Temporal trending did not suggest that MEP measurement is becoming more frequent. Trials measuring both MEP and PAR suggest that MEP is 95-226% more intense than PAR in the first 3 postoperative days. Among trials measuring MEP, 38% did not specify the physical maneuver used to assess MEP. Five of 7 meta-analyses reviewed (71%) did not distinguish between PAR and MEP [...] This is an important problem because MEP is usually more severe than PAR; MEP exerts a more direct adverse impact on postsurgical functional recovery and several current and novel pain treatments differentially affect MEP vs PAR."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in postsurgical analgesic trials (thoracotomy, knee arthroplasty, hysterectomy) / movement-evoked pain vs pain at rest / first 3 postoperative days / review of trial methods
claims.safe_wording: After an operation, pain when moving is usually much worse than pain lying still. In surgical trials that measured both, pain on movement scored roughly 2 to 3 times higher in the first 3 days. Yet only about 4 in 10 trials measured pain on movement at all.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is from postsurgical trials (including knee replacement), not older people or ward practice specifically. '2 to 3 times' is derived from '95 to 226% more intense' (1.95 to 3.26 times) and refers to average scores in trials that measured both; if in doubt, say 'much worse'. Fractures are not specifically covered.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting evidence found on the direction; magnitude varies by operation and movement tested.

numbers.meaning: postsurgical trials that measured movement-evoked pain
trials that did not say whether pain was at rest or on movement
movement-evoked vs rest pain in the first 3 postoperative days, in trials measuring both (about 2 to 3.3 times the rest score)
meta-analyses that did not distinguish the two

claims.claim: Pain on movement is the measure researchers now prioritise because it better reflects functional recovery.
claims.supporting_passage: Srikandarajah 2011: "MEP exerts a more direct adverse impact on postsurgical functional recovery". He 2025/2026: "We prioritized pain during movement over pain at rest, as it better reflects functional recovery."
claims.pico_timeframe: Postsurgical pain research / choice of pain outcome / expert rationale
claims.safe_wording: Pain researchers now often put pain on movement first, because it is the pain that gets in the way of recovery.
claims.qualifications: These are authors' statements of rationale, not measured comparisons of the two scores against function. Avoid 'proves' or 'shows' language.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Corbett 2019 notes that validation studies linking movement-evoked pain to function are still needed.

numbers.meaning: He network meta-analysis size (knee and hip replacement)

claims.claim: In older adults with chronic low back pain, more pain after standard movement tasks was linked with worse disability and physical function.
claims.supporting_passage: "226 older adults with chronic LBP. [...] LBP intensity was collected before and after the repeated chair rise test, stair climbing test, and 6-minute walk test [...] Greater aggregated posttest MeP was independently associated with worse disability (b = 0.593, t = 2.913, P = .004), self-efficacy (b = -0.870, t = -3.110, P = .002), and physical function (b = -0.017, t = -2.007, P = .039). MeP change scores were not associated with any outcome (all P > .050)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 226 older adults with chronic low back pain, US laboratory / pain after chair rise, stairs and 6-minute walk / adjusted regression / disability, confidence, physical performance / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a study of 226 older adults with long-term back pain, those who had more pain after standing up from a chair, climbing stairs and walking also had more disability and did less well on tests of physical function.
claims.qualifications: Cross-sectional association; does not show that movement pain causes disability. One way of scoring movement pain (the change from before to after) showed no link. Effect sizes small.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No study found here compared resting and movement scores head to head against function in older people.

numbers.meaning: older adults with chronic low back pain

claims.claim: The most commonly used pain measures record pain at rest or recalled pain, which does not capture pain during movement; measuring movement-evoked pain has been slow to reach clinical care.
claims.supporting_passage: "With musculoskeletal pain, the primary driver is often pain experienced during physical activity, commonly referred to as movement-evoked pain []. Yet, the most common used pain measures assess either spontaneous pain or pain recalled through the lens of questionnaires () []. Assessment of spontaneous pain, that does not involve physical activity, cannot discern pain related to movement." and "Burgeoning research supports movement-evoked pain measurement [;;], yet it remains slow to translate to clinical care []."
claims.location: Full text, Introduction (empty brackets are stripped reference markers in the rendered PMC text)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with persistent musculoskeletal pain / pain measurement practice / narrative review
claims.safe_wording: A pain score taken while someone lies still does not tell you how much it hurts to stand, turn or walk. Asking about pain during those movements gives the missing information.
claims.qualifications: Narrative expert review; the point is logical as much as empirical.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: UK national guidelines on assessing pain in older people ask for assessment of how pain affects function and activities, and for observation of pain behaviour during movement or care in people who can't self-report reliably.
claims.supporting_passage: Section 15, United Kingdom (p i14): "Where pain is present, a detailed clinical assessment of the multidimensional aspects of pain should be undertaken including: • Sensory dimension: the nature, location and intensity of pain • Affective dimension: the emotional component and response to pain • Impact: on functioning at the level of activities and participation." and "In people with very severe impairment, and in situations where procedures might cause pain, an observational assessment of pain behaviour is additionally required." Glossary (p i4 to i5): "Checklist of Non-verbal Pain Indicators (CNPI) A summation score of pain behaviours at rest and on movement"; "Mobilization Observation Behaviour Intensity Dementia (MOBID) An observational tool for use in early morning by carers to assess pain behaviours on five movements". Section 10 (p i10): "Re-wording your question to elicit the presence of pain such as 'Do you hurt anywhere?' or 'What is stopping you from doing what you want to do?' can substantiate the presence or absence of pain."
claims.location: Full text (PDF via Undermind): Section 15 UK subsection, p i14; Glossary, p i4 to i5; Section 10, p i10
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people in UK care settings / pain assessment / guideline
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance on assessing pain in older people asks how pain affects what the person can do, and for people who can't easily describe their pain, to watch them during movement or care. A practical question it suggests: 'What is stopping you from doing what you want to do?'
claims.qualifications: The guidance does not explicitly require a separate 'pain on movement' score for every patient; recording pain at rest and on standing is the post's recommendation (judgement) built on this guidance and C10-21-a. Some UK text is the 2018 document's summary of earlier UK guidance.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Acute pain guidance (ANZCA Acute Pain Management: Scientific Evidence 2020) recommends assessing pain with movement and function.
claims.supporting_passage: Not searched or opened in this batch.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Omit the ANZCA reference.
claims.qualifications: Not essential; UK guidance and Srikandarajah cover the point.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not assessed.

claims.claim: Compared with placebo, quinine reduces the number of cramps modestly: about 2 to 3 fewer cramps over two weeks from about 9 on placebo (about a quarter fewer), on low-quality evidence.
claims.supporting_passage: Cochrane 2015, Effects of interventions: "Quinine resulted in a significant decrease in cramp number (-2.45 cramps, 95% CI -3.54 to -1.36, random-effects), equivalent to a 28% (95% CI 15% to 40%) reduction over placebo (see Analysis 1.2, Figure 2). It is worth noting the persistent heterogeneity (I2 = 71%) associated with this result." Summary of findings table: "The mean number of cramps over 2 weeks in the control groups was 8.8 cramps"; "The mean number of cramps over 2 weeks in the intervention groups was 2.45 lower (1.36 to 3.54 lower)" [952 participants, 13 studies, GRADE low]. Cramp days: "The remaining seven trials (n = 842) showed that quinine significantly reduced cramp days compared to placebo (-1.15 days, 95% CI -1.93 to -0.38, random-effects) (see Analysis 1.6). This represents a 20% (95% CI 6% to 33%) reduction in cramp days". Abstract: "There is low quality evidence that quinine (200 mg to 500 mg daily) significantly reduces cramp number and cramp days and moderate quality evidence that quinine reduces cramp intensity." Man-Son-Hing 1998, Abstract: "When individual patient data from all crossover studies were pooled, persons had 3.60 (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.15, 5.05) fewer cramps in a 4-week period when taking quinine compared with placebo." Table 3: placebo "17.08 (15.40, 18.76)" cramps per 4-week period (n = 409).
claims.location: Cochrane: Results (Effects of interventions, quinine versus placebo), Summary of findings table 1, Abstract. Man-Son-Hing: Abstract, Results, Table 3.
claims.pico_timeframe: People with muscle cramps (mostly idiopathic night cramps; trial mean ages 44 to 76) / quinine 200 to 500 mg daily / placebo / number of cramps, cramp days, intensity / two-week treatment period (trials up to 60 days)
claims.safe_wording: In pooled trials, people on a dummy tablet had about 9 cramps in two weeks. People on quinine had about 2 to 3 fewer, so roughly 6 or 7 instead of 9. That is about a quarter fewer cramps, and the evidence is low quality. Cramps were only slightly less painful.
claims.qualifications: Give the absolute figures first; the 28% is relative. Say the evidence is low quality. Trials were short (up to 60 days) and included some middle-aged adults, not only older people. 'About 6 or 7' is derived by subtracting 2.45 from 8.8. The intensity effect was small (0.12 points on a 3-point scale, from 1.2).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: High heterogeneity (I2 71%). Man-Son-Hing 1998 showed that published trials overstated the benefit (8.83 fewer cramps per 4 weeks in published trials vs 3.60 when unpublished data were added). The Cochrane review states there is no evidence to judge the best dose or duration.

numbers.meaning: mean cramps over 2 weeks in placebo groups (Cochrane SoF; 13 trials, 952 participants)
absolute mean difference in cramps over 2 weeks, quinine vs placebo
relative reduction in cramp number vs placebo (2.45 of 8.8)
absolute and relative reduction in days with cramps over 2 weeks (7 trials, n = 842)
cramp intensity, quinine vs placebo (7 trials, n = 666)
Man-Son-Hing 1998: mean cramps per 4 weeks on placebo and absolute reduction on quinine, pooled crossover trials (n = 409)

claims.claim: In trials, minor side effects (mainly stomach upset) were slightly more common with quinine; the trials were too small and short to measure rare serious harms.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "A significantly greater number of people suffered minor adverse events on quinine than placebo (risk difference (RD) 3%, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0% to 6%), mainly gastrointestinal symptoms. Overdoses of quinine have been reported elsewhere to cause potentially fatal adverse effects, but in the included trials there was no significant difference in major adverse events compared with placebo (RD 0%, 95% CI -1% to 2%). One participant suffered from thrombocytopenia (0.12% risk) on quinine." Authors' conclusions: "There is moderate quality evidence that with use up to 60 days, the incidence of serious adverse events is not significantly greater than for placebo in the identified trials, but because serious adverse events can be rarely fatal, in some countries prescription of quinine is severely restricted." ... "Because serious adverse events are not common, large population studies are required to more accurately inform incidence."
claims.pico_timeframe: Trial participants with cramps / quinine / placebo / minor and major adverse events / up to 60 days
claims.safe_wording: In the trials, about 3 more people in every 100 had minor side effects on quinine than on a dummy tablet, mostly stomach upset. The trials lasted up to about two months and were too small to measure rare serious harms.
claims.qualifications: The 3 in 100 is an absolute risk difference (95% CI 0 to 6). 'No significant difference in major adverse events' in short trials must not be read as 'safe'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None that changes the reading.

numbers.meaning: absolute risk difference for minor adverse events, quinine minus placebo
absolute risk difference for major adverse events in trials up to 60 days
thrombocytopenia on quinine across included trials

claims.claim: Quinine can rarely cause serious harm, including immune reactions that destroy platelets (thrombocytopenia), heart rhythm problems especially in overdose, and death in overdose; dose-related side effects are a particular concern in older people.
claims.supporting_passage: Cochrane 2015, Background: "Quinine may have potentially serious adverse effects including fatal hypersensitivity reactions, particularly quinine-induced thrombocytopenia (Barr 1990) which can occur idiosyncratically from the ingestion of even minimal amounts of quinine, such as are present in commercial tonic waters (Schneemann 2006). Other hypersensitivity reactions include angio-oedema, disseminated intravascular coagulation, pancytopenia (Maguire 1993) and haemolytic uraemic syndrome (McDonald 1997)." ... "Quinine can interfere with the conduction pathways in the heart giving rise to arrhythmias, especially in overdosage (White 2007). Acute intoxication (ingestion of 4 to 12 g quinine) can cause convulsions followed by coma; death from respiratory arrest often results with doses exceeding 8 g." Plain language summary: "Quinine can cause serious, even fatal adverse events, especially in overdosage." Discussion: "A case-control study in the USA estimated that quinine-induced thrombocytopenia occurs in 26 of every 1 million users (Kaufman 1993)." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "However, the degree of benefit from quinine is modest and the risks include rare but serious immune-mediated reactions and, especially in older people, dose-related side effects."
claims.location: Cochrane: Background (Description of the intervention), Plain language summary, Discussion (Adverse events due to quinine). Rabbitt: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Quinine users (therapeutic use and overdose) / serious adverse reactions / background and case-report literature summarised by the reviews
claims.safe_wording: Quinine can rarely cause serious reactions. These include a sudden fall in platelets, the blood cells that help clotting, and heart rhythm problems, especially after too many tablets. An overdose of quinine can kill. A review in Age and Ageing notes that older people are more prone to its dose-related side effects.
claims.qualifications: These harms come from case reports, regulatory data and a case-control study summarised in the Cochrane background and discussion, not from the review's own trial results. If the 26 per million figure is used, attribute it to a US case-control study (Kaufman 1993) cited by the Cochrane review, and do not present it as a Cochrane finding. Do not quote the MHRA's list of harms (not opened).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: True incidence of serious harm at usual doses is uncertain; the review calls for large population studies.

numbers.meaning: estimated incidence of quinine-induced thrombocytopenia from a US case-control study (Kaufman 1993) cited in the Cochrane discussion; background figure, not the review's finding

claims.claim: Guidance restricts quinine for cramps to severe symptoms, as a trial with regular review; UK advice reported in the Cochrane review allows up to 4 weeks to see an effect and a pause every 3 months to check benefit; the MHRA issued a quinine safety update in June 2010.
claims.supporting_passage: Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "Quinine treatment should be restricted to those with severe symptoms, should be subject to regular review and requires discussion of the risks and benefits with patients." Cochrane 2015, Discussion: "The British National Formulary (BNF) advises that it may take up to four weeks for the effect on cramp to become apparent and that if there is improvement, then quinine should be taken continuously with close monitoring for adverse events (BNF 2010). The BNF also advises interruption of treatment every three months for review of benefit." Man-Son-Hing 1998, Discussion: "If this fails and the patient's quality of life is significantly affected, then a trial of quinine (of at least 4 weeks) may be warranted. As with all potentially hazardous medications, physicians prescribing quinine need to closely monitor the benefits and risks in individual patients." Acheampong 2013, Abstract: "To ascertain the effects of the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency's (MHRA) safety update in June 2010 on the volume of prescribing of quinine and on indices of quinine toxicity."
claims.location: Rabbitt: Abstract. Cochrane: Discussion (Other considerations). Man-Son-Hing: Discussion. Acheampong: Abstract (Aims).
claims.pico_timeframe: People with night cramps considered for quinine / prescribing guidance / review of benefit at about 4 weeks and every 3 months
claims.safe_wording: Specialists in older people's medicine advise keeping quinine for severe cramps, reviewing it regularly and talking through benefits and risks (Age and Ageing review, 2016). UK prescribing advice reported in the Cochrane review said the effect can take up to 4 weeks to show, and treatment should be paused every 3 months to check it is still helping. The UK medicines regulator issued safety advice on quinine for cramps in 2010.
claims.qualifications: The MHRA 2010 Drug Safety Update was not opened: do not quote its wording (for example 'not for routine use' or 'stop after 4 weeks if no benefit') as MHRA text. The BNF advice is the 2010 edition as reported by Cochrane; the current BNF was not opened, so say 'UK prescribing advice' rather than quoting the current BNF.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Cochrane: 'There is no evidence to judge optimal dosage or duration of quinine treatment.'

numbers.meaning: time for effect to become apparent (BNF 2010 as reported by Cochrane); trial of at least 4 weeks (Man-Son-Hing)
interruption of treatment to review benefit (BNF 2010 as reported by Cochrane)
date of MHRA quinine safety update

claims.claim: MHRA (June 2010): quinine not for routine use for nocturnal leg cramps; consider only when cramps severely disrupt sleep, are very painful or frequent, other causes are ruled out and non-drug measures have failed; review after 4 weeks.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine summary only (not an opened document): "The update stated that quinine should not be used routinely for nocturnal leg cramps." ... "treatment with quinine should only be considered when cramps cause severe disruption of sleep, and should only be used when cramps are very painful or frequent, other treatable causes of cramp are ruled out and symptoms are not alleviated by non-drug measures, such as passive stretching exercises." ... "Treatment should be reviewed after 4 weeks to see whether there is any benefit and monitor for toxicity."
claims.location: WebSearch result summary (GPonline, MIMS pages not opened)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK prescribing of quinine for nocturnal leg cramps / regulatory advice / 2010
claims.safe_wording: Do not attribute this wording to the MHRA in the post. Use the wording in C10-03-d instead.
claims.qualifications: search_extract only; not sufficient for an essential claim. Consistent with the opened sources (Rabbitt 2016, Cochrane 2015, Man-Son-Hing 1998).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None known; simply unverified.

numbers.meaning: review point reported for the MHRA advice (search extract only)

claims.claim: After the 2010 MHRA advice, quinine prescribing in England stopped growing but remained common; areas with comprehensive prescribing reviews saw much larger reductions.
claims.supporting_passage: "Total prescribing continued to increase, but annual growth in quinine prescribing in England declined from 6.0 to -0.6% following the MHRA update [difference -0.04 (95% confidence interval -0.07 to -0.01) quinine prescriptions per 100 patients per quarter, P = 0.0111]. Much larger reductions were observed in Primary Care Trusts that introduced comprehensive prescribing reviews." ... "The MHRA advice was followed by limited reductions in the growth in quinine prescribing and in indicators of quinine overdose and toxicity. Quinine prescribing, however, remains common, and further efforts are needed to reduce availability and use."
claims.pico_timeframe: Primary care prescribing in England / before vs after MHRA June 2010 update / quinine prescribing volume and poisons enquiries / 2007/8 to 2011/12
claims.safe_wording: After the 2010 UK safety advice, quinine prescribing in England stopped rising but stayed common, at least to 2012. Areas that ran thorough prescribing reviews saw much larger falls.
claims.qualifications: Data end in 2012; current prescribing levels were not checked. Ecological before-and-after data: the review programmes are linked with larger falls, not proven to cause them. This contradicts the draft opening line that quinine 'is no longer a routine prescription in the UK'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No more recent UK prescribing data were opened.

numbers.meaning: annual growth in quinine prescribing in England before vs after the June 2010 MHRA update

claims.claim: In a UK primary care trial, advising people on long-term quinine to try stopping it led more of them to stop, without a clear difference in cramps at 12 weeks.
claims.supporting_passage: "One hundred and ninety-one patients prescribed quinine for night cramps were randomised to one of four groups defined by two 'advice' factors: undertake exercises and stop quinine." ... "At 12 weeks there was no significant difference in number of cramps in the previous 4 weeks (exercise = 1.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -3.01 to 6.90; quinine cessation = 3.45, 95% CI = -1.52 to 8.41) nor symptom burden or severity of cramps. However, after 12 weeks 26.5% (95% CI = 13.3% to 39.7%) more patients who had been advised to stop quinine treatment reported taking no quinine tablets in the previous week (odds ratio [OR] = 3.32, 95% CI = 1.37 to 8.06)" ... "Advising those on long-term repeat prescriptions to try stopping quinine temporarily will result in no major problems for patients, and allow a significant number to stop medication."
claims.pico_timeframe: 191 people on repeat quinine for night cramps, 28 English general practices / advice to stop quinine / no such advice / quinine use and cramp frequency / 12 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In a trial in 28 English general practices, people on long-term quinine were randomly given advice to try stopping it, or not. At 12 weeks, about 1 in 4 more of those advised to stop were taking none, and the trial did not show a clear difference in how many cramps people had.
claims.qualifications: The cramp comparison had wide confidence intervals and cannot rule out some rise in cramps for some people. Say 'did not show a clear difference', not 'no effect'. 26.5% is a difference in percentage points. Do not use the 3.45 figure (direction of the difference is not clear from the abstract).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small trial from 2005; outcome relied on recalled cramp counts.

numbers.meaning: patients randomised
more people taking no quinine in the previous week at 12 weeks, advised to stop vs not

claims.claim: Stretching before bed is a low-risk option, but evidence that it reduces night cramps is limited and mixed.
claims.supporting_passage: Hawke 2021, Abstract: "A combination of daily calf and hamstring stretching for six weeks may reduce the severity of night-time lower limb muscle cramps (measured on a 10 cm visual analogue scale (VAS) where 0 = no pain and 10 cm = worst pain imaginable) in people aged 55 years and older, compared to no intervention (mean difference (MD) -1.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) -1.74 to -0.86; 1 RCT, 80 participants; low-certainty evidence). The certainty of evidence was very low for cramp frequency" ... "Calf stretching alone for 12 weeks may make little to no difference to the frequency of night-time lower limb muscle cramps in people aged 60 years and older" ... "No participant in these three studies reported adverse events. The evidence for adverse events was of moderate certainty as the studies were too small to detect uncommon events." Coppin 2005, Conclusions: "Calf-stretching exercises are not effective in reducing the frequency or severity of night cramps." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "There is conflicting evidence regarding the efficacy of prophylactic stretching exercises in preventing cramps."
claims.location: Hawke: Abstract (Main results, Authors' conclusions). Coppin: Abstract (Conclusions). Rabbitt: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults aged 50 and over with night cramps / calf or calf plus hamstring stretching / no intervention or sham stretching / cramp frequency and severity / 6 to 12 weeks
claims.safe_wording: Evidence on stretching is limited and mixed. In one small trial in people aged 55 and over, calf and hamstring stretches before bed for six weeks may have made cramps less painful; whether they came less often is very uncertain. In another, calf stretches alone made little or no difference. No one in these trials reported harm, so stretching is reasonable to try, but it is not a proven treatment.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's claim that stretching 'reduced the frequency and severity' (Hallegraeff 2012 alone) overstates the evidence; present stretching as low-risk to try. Do not use the Hallegraeff '1.2 cramps per night' figure (very low certainty).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Hallegraeff 2012 (positive, 80 people not on quinine) vs Coppin 2005 (negative, people on quinine); Cochrane grades certainty very low to low.

numbers.value: 1.3 cm lower on a 10 cm pain scale (95% CI 0.86 to 1.74)
numbers.meaning: cramp severity, calf plus hamstring stretching vs nothing, 6 weeks, 1 trial of 80 people aged over 55 (low certainty)

claims.claim: Some medicines are linked with night cramps, particularly thiazide-type and potassium-sparing diuretics and long-acting beta-agonist inhalers.
claims.supporting_passage: Garrison 2012, Abstract: "Adjusted sequence ratios (95% CIs) for the 3 drug classes were 1.47 (1.33-1.63 [P < .001]) for diuretics, 1.16 (1.04-1.29 [P = .004]) for statins, and 2.42 (2.02-2.89 [P < .001]) for LABAs. For diuretic subclasses, adjusted sequence ratios (95% CIs) were 2.12 (1.61-2.78 [P < .001]) for potassium sparing, 1.48 (1.29-1.68 [P < .001]) for thiazidelike, and 1.20 (1.00-1.44 [P = .07]) for loop." ... "Cramp treatment was substantially more likely in the year following introduction of LABAs, potassium-sparing diuretics, or thiazidelike diuretics, and 60.3% of quinine users (individuals experiencing cramp) received at least 1 of these medications during a 13-year period. In contrast, statin and loop diuretic associations were small." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "Recent evidence suggests that diuretic and long-acting beta-agonist therapy predispose to leg cramps."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults aged 50 and over, British Columbia / starting diuretics, statins or LABAs / quinine starts in year before vs year after / 2000 to 2008
claims.safe_wording: Some medicines are linked with night cramps. In a large Canadian study of adults aged 50 and over, new treatment for cramps was more common in the year after starting some water tablets (thiazide-type and potassium-sparing diuretics) or long-acting inhalers for the lungs. The link with statins and loop diuretics was small. This kind of study shows a link, not proof that the medicine caused the cramps.
claims.qualifications: Observational; quinine starts are a proxy for cramps. Do not convert sequence ratios into 'X times more likely'. Never suggest stopping a diuretic or inhaler without advice; the action is to ask a doctor or pharmacist.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Canadian prescribing 2000 to 2008; UK practice may differ.

numbers.meaning: adjusted sequence ratios for LABAs, potassium-sparing and thiazide-like diuretics (ratio of quinine starts in year after vs year before starting the drug)
adjusted sequence ratios for statins and loop diuretics (small associations)
quinine users who received at least one of LABA, potassium-sparing or thiazide-like diuretic over 13 years

claims.claim: Co-codamol (codeine with paracetamol) and co-dydramol (dihydrocodeine with paracetamol) contain paracetamol; co-codamol 8/500 is sold in UK pharmacies without prescription.

A total of 14 subjects had overdosed on prescribed compound analgesics, namely dextropropoxyphene/paracetamol (co-proxamol, n = 7) and dihydrocodeine tartrate/paracetamol (co-dydramol, n = 7)."
claims.location: Methods (Definitions); Results (Repeated supratherapeutic overdoses and pain)
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition of product composition (UK, as described in 2012)
claims.safe_wording: Co-codamol is codeine plus paracetamol. Co-dydramol is dihydrocodeine plus paracetamol. The lowest-strength co-codamol can be bought in UK pharmacies without a prescription.
claims.qualifications: OTC status is as described in 2012; not rechecked against current UK rules. Do not name brands.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Some cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol.

Wolf 2012, Table 3 secondary products shown in the double-dipping scenarios include "Brand Name Combination Cold & Cough (650 mg/dose)" [acetaminophen dose].

claims.claim: The usual maximum daily dose of paracetamol for adults is 4 g in 24 hours.
claims.supporting_passage: Reid 2022, Introduction: "Although paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity at standard therapeutic doses (up to 4 g/d) is rare, cases have been reported." Craig 2012, Methods (Definitions): "a staggered overdose described ingestion of two or more supratherapeutic paracetamol doses over a time interval of greater than 8 h resulting in a cumulative dose of >4 g day-1." Wolf 2012, Abstract: "23.8 % of participants demonstrated they would overdose on a single over-the-counter acetaminophen product by exceeding a dose of four grams in a 24-hour period".
claims.location: Reid: Introduction. Craig: Methods. Wolf: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults / standard therapeutic paracetamol dosing / 24 hours
claims.safe_wording: For most adults the usual maximum is 4 g of paracetamol in 24 hours. With 500 mg tablets, that is 8 tablets a day, counting every product that contains paracetamol.
claims.qualifications: The BNF and product labels were not opened; the 4 g standard is taken from published papers. '8 tablets' is derived arithmetic (4 g divided by 500 mg). Lower maximums may apply to some people (see C10-09-f).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C10-09-f on low body weight and frailty.

claims.claim: Taking two paracetamol-containing products at once is a recognised route to accidental excess: in a US study nearly half of adults said they would take two such products together, and about 1 in 5 accidental paracetamol overdose calls to an Australian poisons centre involved more than one product.
claims.supporting_passage: Wolf 2012, Abstract: "In addition, 45.6 % of adults demonstrated they would overdose by 'double-dipping' with two acetaminophen-containing products." Table 4, Double-dipping with 2 products by age: "18-30 37.1; 31-45 44.1; 46-60 52.8; 61-80 40.0" (P = 0.05). Discussion: "Clearly, our study is limited by the fact that the assessments of individuals' misunderstanding and misuse of OTC acetaminophen products reflects hypothetical and not actual health behaviors." Chidiac 2024, Results 3.1: "Multiple paracetamol-containing products (which may include more than one brand of the same category) were taken in 2816 (19.6%) exposures"; Abstract: "The in-depth analysis of exposures recorded during 2021 revealed 1899 exposures (median age 46 years, 63.4% female) with 26.8% requiring hospitalisation." ... "6% of exposures developed hepatotoxicity." Table 1: "Elderly >=75 years: Entire cohort: 1733 (12.1%)".
claims.location: Wolf: Abstract, Table 4, Discussion. Chidiac: Abstract, Results 3.1, Table 1.
claims.pico_timeframe: Wolf: 500 US primary care adults aged 18 to 80 / simulated choice to take two acetaminophen products together / single interview. Chidiac: 14,380 unintentional paracetamol dosing-error calls, people aged 12 and over, New South Wales, 2017 to 2023.
claims.safe_wording: Doubling up is easy to do. In a US study, nearly half of 500 adults, shown real shop products, said it would be safe to take two paracetamol-containing products together; among those aged 61 to 80 it was 4 in 10. At an Australian poisons centre, about 1 in 5 calls about accidentally taking too much paracetamol involved more than one paracetamol product.

Chidiac counts calls, not confirmed harm; hospitalisation and liver-injury figures apply to all ages in 2021, not older people specifically. Neither study is UK-based. Do not say accidental excess 'in older people is often' a counting problem: no source gives that proportion for older people.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No UK or older-people-specific data on how often double-dosing happens were found.

numbers.meaning: of 500 US adults aged 18 to 80, demonstrated they would exceed the maximum by taking two acetaminophen products (simulated task)
same outcome among participants aged 61 to 80 (Wolf Table 4; group size not reported)
Australian poisons centre dosing-error calls involving more than one paracetamol product, 2017 to 2023
of those calls concerned people aged 75 or over
2021 calls (all ages, n = 1899) needing hospital care; exposures developing liver injury

claims.claim: In a Scottish liver unit series of adults with severe paracetamol liver injury, about 1 in 4 had taken too much over several doses rather than at once, and pain relief was the commonest reason among them.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Between 1992 and 2008, 663 patients were admitted with paracetamol-induced severe liver injury, of whom 161 (24.3%) had taken a staggered overdose. Staggered overdose patients were significantly older and more likely to abuse alcohol than single time point overdose patients. Relief of pain (58.2%) was the commonest rationale for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion." ... "had higher mortality rates compared with single time point overdoses (37.3% vs. 27.8%, P= 0.025), although this overdose pattern did not independently predict death." Results: "Staggered overdose subjects were significantly older (median 39 (29-46) years) compared with single overdose patients (32 (24-43) years, P < 0.001)" ... "Information regarding the reasons for overdose was available for 134/161 (83.2%) of staggered overdoses. The most common (58.2%) rationale for overdose was for relief of pain" ... "A total of 46/134 (34.3%) of staggered overdoses were taken deliberately as a suicide attempt." Table 1: "Age (years): 34 (26-44)".
claims.location: Abstract; Results (Single time point vs staggered overdoses; Repeated supratherapeutic overdoses and pain); Tables 1 and 2
claims.pico_timeframe: 663 adults (median age 34) with severe paracetamol liver injury, Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit / staggered vs single time point overdose / reasons, outcomes / 1992 to 2008
claims.safe_wording: In a Scottish liver unit, 663 adults were admitted with severe liver damage from paracetamol between 1992 and 2008. About 1 in 4 had taken too much over several doses rather than all at once. Where the reason was known, the most common was trying to relieve pain (78 of 134). Most people in this series were young or middle-aged adults.
claims.qualifications: State that this was a series of adults of all ages (median 34; staggered group median 39), not older people; do not use 'older' from the abstract. A third of the staggered group were suicide attempts and many misused alcohol. Do not imply that doubling up commonly causes liver failure in older people. Mortality difference was not independent of other factors; do not present it as caused by the staggered pattern.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Single specialist unit, referral bias toward the most severe cases; data from 1992 to 2008.

numbers.meaning: adults admitted with severe paracetamol liver injury, 1992 to 2008
staggered overdoses among 663
pain relief as the reason, among staggered overdoses with a recorded reason
staggered overdoses that were suicide attempts
age of staggered vs single overdose patients
mortality, staggered vs single overdose (not independently predictive)

claims.claim: For people who are frail or weigh under 50 kg, a lower daily paracetamol maximum is often advised, though the safest dose has not been established; full adult doses are common in this group.
claims.supporting_passage: Reid 2022, Abstract: "Paracetamol doses administered in hospital, and doses prescribed on discharge, were compared against consensus guidelines that recommended <=60 mg/kg/d for older people weighing <50 kg, and <=3000 mg/d for frail older people." ... "In total, 240 admissions (n = 229 patients, mean age 84.7 years) were analysed. During 150 (62.5%) admissions, higher than recommended paracetamol doses were prescribed. On 138 (57.5%) occasions, patients were prescribed paracetamol on discharge, and 112/138 (81.2%) doses were higher than recommended." Introduction: "For example, England's Healthcare Safety Investigation Branch, an organisation responsible for the investigating patient safety concerns, is conducting an investigation titled Unintentional overdose of paracetamol in adults with low body weight. This was prompted by reports of paracetamol overdose in patients with low body weight at therapeutic doses." Discussion: "Although there is limited evidence that the standard maximum therapeutic dose (4 g/d) leads to significant rates of liver injury in frail and low-weight older people, we believe that reduced doses should be considered for 3 reasons." Caparrotta 2018, Abstract: "The safe (and still effective) oral dose of paracetamol in patients weighing less than 50 kg has not been established." ... "There is no patient group that is unequivocally at elevated risk of paracetamol-induced liver toxicity."
claims.location: Reid: Abstract, Introduction, Discussion. Caparrotta: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Reid: 229 inpatients aged 70 or over (mean 84.7) who were frail or under 50 kg, Melbourne, 2018 / paracetamol dose vs consensus guideline / hospital stay and discharge. Caparrotta: literature on risk factors for paracetamol liver injury.
claims.safe_wording: If you weigh under 50 kg (about 7 stone 12 lb) or are frail, ask a pharmacist or doctor whether a lower daily maximum is right for you. Some guidelines advise a lower dose for people in this group, although research has not established the safest dose. In one Australian study of frail or low-weight hospital patients aged 70 and over, about 8 in 10 discharge prescriptions were above those guideline doses.
claims.qualifications: Do not quote or cite the BNF: its exact wording for adults under 50 kg was not opened. The consensus guidelines in Reid are Australian. England's HSIB investigation is reported via Reid, not opened. Evidence that 4 g a day harms low-weight older people is limited (Reid; Caparrotta), so frame lower doses as a precaution, not as proven necessary. '7 stone 12 lb' is a unit conversion of 50 kg.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Caparrotta 2018: no group is unequivocally at higher risk; safe dose under 50 kg not established.

claims.supporting_passage: No passage opened. UK pack labelling, the BNF and MHRA pages could not be opened from this environment.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not state what pack labels say. Advise readers to check the ingredients of every product and ask a pharmacist.
claims.qualifications: Unverified; leave out.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Chidiac 2024 notes that labelling changes in Canada did not reduce hospital admissions for accidental overdose.

claims.claim: In randomised trials in people aged 60 and over with insomnia, sleeping tablets increased self-reported total sleep time by an average of about 25 minutes a night and reduced night-time awakenings by 0.63 compared with placebo.
claims.supporting_passage: "24 studies (involving 2417 participants) with extractable data met inclusion and exclusion criteria. Sleep quality improved (effect size 0.14, P < 0.05), total sleep time increased (mean 25.2 minutes, P < 0.001), and the number of night time awakenings decreased (0.63, P < 0.001) with sedative use compared with placebo." Methods: "total sleep time (total amount of time participants perceive that they have slept, measured in minutes)... Ratings were made by patients and not an observer." Inclusion: "Interventions were pharmacological treatments for insomnia for at least five consecutive nights."
claims.location: Abstract (Results); Methods, Outcome measures and Inclusion criteria (pages 1 to 2 of PDF)
claims.pico_timeframe: People aged 60+ with insomnia, free of psychiatric disorders / any sedative hypnotic (mostly benzodiazepines and Z-drugs) / placebo / self-reported total sleep time and awakenings / trials of at least 5 nights (Table 1: 5 nights to 9 weeks); trials published 1966 to 2003
claims.safe_wording: In short trials in people aged 60 and over, sleeping tablets added about 25 minutes of sleep a night on average, as reported by the people taking them, and about one fewer waking every two nights (0.63 fewer wakings a night).
claims.qualifications: Average, self-reported, short-term (trials lasted from 5 nights to 9 weeks); older drugs (trials to 2003); 'wakings' figure is per night. Say 'in short trials', not 'long term'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Possible publication bias: after trim-and-fill correction the estimated gain was 15 minutes (see C11-16-b). Earlier meta-analyses in mixed-age adults found larger gains (40 to 48 minutes), cited in Glass's discussion.

numbers.meaning: mean increase in self-reported total sleep time per night, sedative versus placebo, pooled across trials of at least 5 nights
mean reduction in number of night-time awakenings per night versus placebo
trials with extractable data
minimum age for inclusion
range of treatment duration in included trials (Table 1)

claims.claim: After correcting for possible publication bias, the estimated gain in total sleep time was smaller, about 15 minutes.
claims.supporting_passage: "Funnel plot analyses indicated a possible publication bias on outcomes of sleep quality and total sleep time favouring positive results (rs = 0.78, P ≤ 0.05). The mean effect size did not change after “trim and fill” to correct estimates of effect size, and the result was still significant in favour of sedatives (d = 0.14, P ≤ 0.05 for sleep quality; mean increase in total sleep time = 15 minutes, P ≤ 0.05)."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-16-a
claims.safe_wording: The true average gain may be smaller still: allowing for unpublished negative trials, the authors' corrected estimate was about 15 minutes.
claims.qualifications: Practitioner detail; optional for public posts. If used, say it is an adjusted estimate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors' wording that the 'mean effect size did not change' refers to sleep quality; the total sleep time estimate fell to 15 minutes.

numbers.meaning: publication-bias-adjusted (trim and fill) mean increase in total sleep time

claims.claim: About 13 people needed to take a sleeping tablet for one extra person to report better sleep quality, while about 6 needed to take one for one extra person to have an adverse event.
claims.supporting_passage: "On the basis of four studies (1072 participants), the number of patients who would need to be treated with a sedative (zaleplon, brotizolam or nitrazepam, or loprazolam) for one to have an improvement in sleep quality is 13 (95% confidence interval 6.7 to 62.9)." "On the basis of all adverse events reported in 16 studies (2220 participants), the number needed to harm for sedative hypnotics compared with placebo is 6 (4.7 to 7.1)." Discussion: "The number needed to treat for improved sleep quality was 13 and the number needed to harm for any adverse event was 6. This ratio indicates that an adverse event is more than twice as likely as enhanced quality of sleep. This ratio can be used as a rough indicator only, as more than double the number of participants contributed to the “harm” data than to the “effectiveness” data (2220 v 1072). The effectiveness estimate is less precise (the confidence interval is wider)."
claims.location: Results, Quality of sleep (page 2) and Adverse events (page 3); Discussion, Numbers needed to treat versus numbers needed to harm (page 4) of the PDF; confirmed by Scite full-text snippets
claims.pico_timeframe: NNT: 4 trials, 1,072 participants, zaleplon, brotizolam or nitrazepam, or loprazolam, any improvement in self-rated sleep quality. NNH: 16 trials, 2,220 participants, any adverse event. Short-term trials.
claims.safe_wording: In these trials, for every 13 people who took a sleeping tablet, about 1 more reported better sleep than with a dummy pill. For every 6 who took one, about 1 more had a side effect, most often drowsiness or tiredness, headache, nightmares or stomach upset. The authors describe this comparison as a rough guide.
claims.qualifications: The two figures come from different sets of trials and outcomes; the NNT is imprecise (could be anywhere from about 7 to 63). Icon arrays must be labelled 'about 1 in 13' and 'about 1 in 6', 'extra compared with a dummy pill', 'short trials', and must not imply the same people.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Wide confidence interval for NNT. NNH counts any adverse event, including minor ones.

numbers.meaning: number needed to treat for one extra person to report improved sleep quality versus placebo; 4 trials, 1,072 participants
number needed to harm for one extra person with any adverse event versus placebo; 16 trials, 2,220 participants

claims.claim: Memory and thinking problems (memory loss, confusion, disorientation) and daytime tiredness were reported more often with sleeping tablets than with placebo; falls-type events were not clearly shown in this analysis.
claims.supporting_passage: "Adverse events were more common with sedatives than with placebo: adverse cognitive events were 4.78 times more common (95% confidence interval 1.47 to 15.47, P < 0.01); adverse psychomotor events were 2.61 times more common (1.12 to 6.09, P > 0.05), and reports of daytime fatigue were 3.82 times more common (1.88 to 7.80, P < 0.001) in people using any sedative compared with placebo." Methods: "cognitive adverse events (memory loss, confusion, disorientation); psychomotor-type adverse events (reports of dizziness, loss of balance, or falls)". Results: "The most common adverse events were drowsiness or fatigue, headache, nightmares, and nausea or gastrointestinal disturbances."

claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-16-a; odds ratios, sedative versus placebo
claims.safe_wording: Memory problems, confusion and daytime tiredness were more common with the tablets than with a dummy pill.
claims.qualifications: Do not turn the odds ratios (4.78, 3.82) into 'times more likely' or absolute risks. Do not list 'unsteadiness' or falls as a finding of this paper: psychomotor events were reported as P>0.05 (with an inconsistent confidence interval). For falls and fractures use Beers (C11-16-f) and Berry (C11-16-e).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Wide confidence interval for cognitive events (1.47 to 15.47). Dependence and withdrawal were not assessed in the included trials.

numbers.meaning: odds of cognitive adverse events, sedative versus placebo (do not use in public posts)

claims.claim: In US nursing home residents, use of Z-drug sleeping tablets was linked with hip fracture, more strongly in new users.

claims.pico_timeframe: 15,528 long-stay US nursing home residents aged 50+ with hip fracture (mean age 81) / zolpidem, eszopiclone or zaleplon dispensed in the 0 to 29 days before fracture / same person's earlier control periods / hip fracture / 2007 to 2008
claims.safe_wording: In US care homes, hip fractures were more likely to happen in periods when residents had been taking a Z-drug sleeping tablet, especially when the tablet was newly started. This links the tablets with fractures; it does not prove they caused them.
claims.qualifications: Association, not causation; US Z-drugs (not zopiclone); care home residents only. Do not state 'X times more likely'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Time-varying confounding possible (illness prompting both prescription and fall).

claims.claim: The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria advise avoiding benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults.
claims.supporting_passage: Table 2 (page 22): Benzodiazepines, rationale "In general, all benzodiazepines increase the risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle crashes in older adults." Recommendation "Avoid"; Quality of evidence "Moderate"; Strength "Strong". Nonbenzodiazepine benzodiazepine receptor agonist hypnotics (“Z-drugs”) Eszopiclone, Zaleplon, Zolpidem: "have adverse events similar to those of benzodiazepines in older adults (e.g., delirium, falls, fractures, increased emergency room visits/hospitalizations, motor vehicle crashes); minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration." Recommendation "Avoid"; Quality of evidence "Moderate"; Strength "Strong". Discussion: "“Avoid” is not defined as an absolute contraindication unless specified in the medication’s label."

claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 65 and over, all care settings except hospice and end of life; US
claims.safe_wording: The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria advise avoiding benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping tablets in people aged 65 and over, noting falls, fractures and confusion, and only small gains in sleep.
claims.qualifications: US guideline; 'avoid' means avoid except in unusual circumstances, with shared decision-making; list excludes zopiclone only because it is not marketed in the US. Do not mention delirium as a topic in the post (collection excludes delirium).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The European Insomnia Guideline 2023 allows benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists for short-term use (4 weeks or less) when CBT-I is not sufficiently effective (C11-16-g).

claims.claim: Major guidelines recommend CBT for insomnia as the first treatment for chronic insomnia at any adult age, with sleeping tablets reserved for short-term use if CBT-I is not enough.
claims.supporting_passage: European guideline: "Cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia is recommended as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (including patients with comorbidities), either applied in-person or digitally (A). When cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia is not sufficiently effective, a pharmacological intervention can be offered (A). Benzodiazepines (A), benzodiazepine receptor agonists (A), daridorexant (A) and low-dose sedating antidepressants (B) can be used for the short-term treatment of insomnia (≤ 4 weeks)." ACP: "ACP recommends that all adult patients receive cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. (Grade: strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with chronic insomnia disorder, any age
claims.safe_wording: European and American guidelines recommend CBT for insomnia (a structured talking and sleep-scheduling treatment) as the first treatment for long-term insomnia at any adult age. If it is not enough, a sleeping tablet can be discussed for short-term use.
claims.qualifications: Say 'long-term insomnia' (chronic insomnia disorder). The position that a short course may be reasonable after discussion is consistent with both guidelines. Do not claim NICE wording (not opened).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the first-line recommendation. Access to CBT-I in practice is limited (not sourced here).

claims.claim: In hospital, patients sleep less than at home, and the most reported sleep disturbers are noise from other patients, medical devices, pain and toilet visits.

"A total of 1344 patients (70.4%) reported having been awakened by external causes, which in 718 (35.8%) concerned hospital staff." "The most reported sleep-disturbing factors were noise of other patients, medical devices, pain, and toilet visits."

claims.safe_wording: In a survey of 2,005 adults in 39 Dutch hospitals (median age 68), patients reported sleeping 83 minutes less than at home. Noise from other patients, medical equipment, pain and needing the toilet were the disturbances they reported most.

claims.claim: In people over 60, sedative hypnotics give small sleep gains with more memory and thinking side effects and daytime tiredness than placebo.

The increased risk of adverse events is statistically significant and potentially clinically relevant in older people at risk of falls and cognitive impairment. In people over 60, the benefits of these drugs may not justify the increased risk, particularly if the patient has additional risk factors for cognitive or psychomotor adverse events."

claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-16-a (trials mostly in community and some geriatric inpatients; not specifically single-night inpatient prescribing)

claims.claim: Corticosteroids can disturb sleep, and giving them as a single morning dose may reduce this.
claims.supporting_passage: "GC use can lead to a wide range of psychiatric and cognitive disturbances, including memory impairment, agitation, anxiety, fear, hypomania, insomnia, irritability, lethargy, mood lability, and even psychosis." "GC therapy may also be associated with sleep disturbances and unpleasant dreams [72]; the risk of these events can potentially be decreased by modifying the timing of GC administration (e.g., a single morning dose) and/or night-time administration of drugs with sedative effects." Table 10: "Administer as single daily dose (given in the morning), if possible"
claims.location: Adverse events, Adults, Psychiatric and cognitive disturbances (page 7); Table 10 (page 14) of the PDF, via Undermind read_pdfs
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults on systemic glucocorticoids; expert recommendation, no trial of timing cited beyond a 1993 BMJ letter
claims.safe_wording: Steroid tablets such as prednisolone can disturb sleep. Expert guidance advises a single morning dose where possible, which may reduce this.
claims.qualifications: Expert advice, not trial evidence; do not claim frequency. Split or evening dosing is sometimes clinically intended; the post should say 'check whether the evening dose is needed', not 'always move it'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No numerical frequency of steroid-related insomnia given in this source.

claims.claim: Donepezil can cause insomnia and vivid dreams or nightmares, and moving the dose to the morning may help.
claims.supporting_passage: Jackson 2004: "Although insomnia and other sleep disorders have been reported following administration of donepezil, lengthening the time period before increasing the dose of donepezil from 5 to 10 mg day(-1) or switching to morning dosing can reduce these events to the levels of placebo-treated patients." Moderie 2021: "Medications should also be reviewed, and time of administration should be optimized (diuretics and stimulating medications in the morning, sedating medications in the evening). Importantly, cholinesterase inhibitors (especially donepezil) may trigger insomnia. Switching to morning dosing or to an alternative drug may help." Singer 2005: "We observed a clear-cut relationship between the occurrence of nightmares and an evening dose of donepezil in eight patients with DAT. None of these patients reported nightmares when donepezil was taken in the morning."
claims.location: Abstracts (Jackson: review; Moderie: English abstract of French review; Singer: English abstract of German case series)
claims.pico_timeframe: People with Alzheimer disease or other dementias taking donepezil; review-level and case-series evidence
claims.safe_wording: Donepezil can cause sleeplessness and vivid dreams. Reviews suggest that taking it in the morning instead may help; this is worth raising with the prescriber the next day.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is from reviews and a case series of 8, not a randomised trial of timing. Frame as a question for the day team, not an overnight change.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The UK product information is understood to advise evening dosing (judge's note; SPC not openable here), so morning dosing is a clinical adjustment rather than the default instruction. Do not state what the SPC says.

numbers.meaning: patients in the case series (nightmares with evening but not morning dosing)

claims.claim: A loop diuretic given at teatime or in the evening increases urine output during the night (candidate wording).
claims.supporting_passage: Oelke 2017: "The timing of diuretics is an important consideration, and they should be taken mid-late afternoon, dependent on the specific serum half-life." Reynard 1998: "a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of an afternoon dose of the diuretic frusemide, used to establish an early evening diuresis and so diminish nocturnal voiding frequency and voided volume in elderly men" ... "40 mg of frusemide or placebo, taken 6 h before their usual bedtime" ... "there was a significant reduction in night-time frequency (-0.5 and 0) and percentage night-time voided volume (-18% and 0%) in those taking frusemide compared with placebo." Getaneh 2025: "Limitation of fluid intake, especially in the evening; addressing timing of diuretic intake; and sleep hygiene are recommended." Moderie 2021: "time of administration should be optimized (diuretics and stimulating medications in the morning, sedating medications in the evening)".
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with nocturia (reviews); Reynard: 49 men over 50 with LUTS and nocturnal polyuria, furosemide 40 mg 6 hours before bed versus placebo
claims.safe_wording: Check when any diuretic ('water tablet') is given. Guidance on night-time urination advises taking it earlier in the day, no later than mid to late afternoon, rather than in the evening.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's example of a teatime loop diuretic as a culprit is not supported: in a small trial, furosemide taken about 6 hours before bed (roughly teatime) reduced night-time urination in men with nocturnal polyuria. Only a late-evening or bedtime dose should be named as a possible cause, and even that is expert advice rather than a measured finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Reviews differ on the best time (morning versus mid to late afternoon). No source found that measures night-time urine after an evening loop diuretic in older inpatients.

claims.claim: Mailed education alone, without pharmacist involvement, did not reduce use of sedatives in later US trials.
claims.supporting_passage: Singh 2024: "Patients were randomized to 1 of 3 arms: (1) a mailing of educational materials specific to the medication targeted for deprescribing to both the patient and their prescribing clinician; (2) a mailing to the prescribing clinician only; or (3) a usual care arm." ... "The cumulative incidence of being dispensed a medication targeted for deprescribing was 76.7% (95% CI, 75.4-78.0) in the patient and prescriber mailing group, 77.9% (95% CI, 76.5-79.1) in the prescriber mailing only group, and 77.5% (95% CI, 76.2-78.8) in the usual care group." ... claims.safe_wording: The same idea by post alone has not always worked. In a US trial of 12,787 people with dementia, mailing information to them and their prescribers did not reduce use of the targeted medicines, including sedatives.
claims.qualifications: Singh combined three drug classes and people with dementia; Mak's control arm also got a risk brochure, so it tested extra CBT-I information, not brochure versus nothing. Present as 'the setting and follow-through seem to count', not as disproof of the Quebec trials.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Differences in population (dementia, veterans), delivery (mail only, no pharmacist enrolment) and health system may explain the difference; not tested directly.

numbers.meaning: still dispensed the targeted medicine at 6 months, patient-and-prescriber mailing versus usual care (Singh)
people with dementia in Singh trial
veterans in Mak pilot

claims.claim: Prolonged-release melatonin can be used for short-term treatment of insomnia in people aged 55 and over (up to 3 months in the European guideline); fast-release melatonin is not recommended.

Antihistaminergic drugs, antipsychotics, fast-release melatonin, ramelteon and phytotherapeutics are not recommended for insomnia treatment (A)." claims.safe_wording: The European insomnia guideline says prescribed slow-release melatonin can be used for up to 3 months in people aged 55 and over with insomnia. It does not recommend ordinary fast-release melatonin for insomnia.
claims.qualifications: Use this in place of the candidate's UK licence wording. Grade B for prolonged-release melatonin (moderate strength).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Benefit is modest (C11-24-e).

numbers.meaning: minimum age for prolonged-release melatonin use in the guideline and European approval
maximum usual duration in the European guideline

claims.claim: In the UK, prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg (Circadin) is licensed for short-term treatment of primary insomnia in people aged 55 and over for up to 13 weeks, and melatonin is prescription-only.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine extract only (emc SmPC and PIL results): "Circadin is indicated as monotherapy for the short-term treatment of primary insomnia characterised by poor quality of sleep in patients who are aged 55 or over." "The recommended dose is 2 mg once daily, 1-2 hours before bedtime and after food, and this dosage may be continued for up to thirteen weeks." Search summary also stated the medicine can only be obtained with a prescription in the UK.
claims.location: Search-engine extract; official page not opened
claims.pico_timeframe: UK licensed product
claims.safe_wording: Do not use as an essential claim. If a UK licence detail is wanted, recheck the emc SmPC directly first; otherwise use C11-24-a.
claims.qualifications: Access is search_extract only, which the evidence standard does not accept for an essential claim. The judge's suggested line 'melatonin is prescription-only in the UK' is not verified from an opened source.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None known, but unverified.
