claims.claim: In people with Alzheimer's disease and sleep problems, melatonin up to 10 mg may make little or no difference to sleep over 8 to 10 weeks.
claims.supporting_passage: "We found low-certainty evidence that melatonin doses up to 10 mg may have little or no effect on any major sleep outcome over eight to 10 weeks in people with AD and sleep disturbances. We could synthesise data for two of our primary sleep outcomes: total nocturnal sleep time (TNST) (MD 10.68 minutes, 95% CI -16.22 to 37.59; 2 studies, n = 184)" ... "There were no serious adverse effects of melatonin reported." Conclusions: "We found no evidence for beneficial effects of melatonin (up to 10 mg) or a melatonin receptor agonist. There was evidence of some beneficial effects on sleep outcomes from trazodone and orexin antagonists and no evidence of harmful effects in these small trials"
claims.location: Abstract, Main results and Authors' conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: People with Alzheimer disease (mostly moderate to severe) and sleep disturbance / melatonin up to 10 mg / placebo / actigraphy-measured sleep / 8 to 10 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In trials in people with Alzheimer's disease and poor sleep, melatonin (up to 10 mg) may make little or no difference to sleep over 8 to 10 weeks. The evidence is limited, and no serious side effects were reported.
claims.qualifications: Low-certainty evidence, small trials. Say 'may make little or no difference', not 'does not work'. Do not imply nothing helps: the same review found some benefit for trazodone (low certainty) and orexin antagonists (moderate certainty).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The confidence interval for total night sleep runs from 16 minutes less to 38 minutes more.

numbers.meaning: difference in total night-time sleep, melatonin versus placebo, 2 studies, 184 people; not clearly different from zero
trial duration
melatonin doses tested

claims.claim: Melatonin supplements bought without prescription have been found to contain amounts very different from the label.
claims.supporting_passage: Cohen 2023: "The 30 unique brands entered into the database in 2021 were purchased online." ... "25 products were analyzed. One product did not contain detectable levels of melatonin but did contain 31.3 mg of CBD." ... "In products that contained melatonin, the actual quantity of melatonin ranged from 74% to 347% of the labeled quantity. Twenty-two of 25 products (88%) were inaccurately labeled, and only 3 products (12%) contained a quantity of melatonin that was within ±10% of the declared quantity." Erland 2017: "Melatonin content was found to range from -83% to +478% of the labelled content. Additionally, lot-to-lot variable within a particular product varied by as much as 465%." ... "Melatonin content did not meet label within a 10% margin of the label claim in more than 71% of supplements and an additional 26% were found to contain serotonin."
claims.location: Cohen: Methods and Results (Scite full-text excerpts); Erland: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: US melatonin gummies bought online (2022) and Canadian melatonin supplements (natural health products)
claims.safe_wording: When melatonin supplements sold in the US and Canada were tested, most did not contain what the label said. In one US study, 22 of 25 gummy products were wrongly labelled, with actual amounts from about three quarters to more than three times the stated dose; one contained none.
claims.qualifications: North American supplements, not UK prescribed products. Do not claim this about products sold in UK shops (not tested). 'Bought online' is accurate for the US study.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small samples; products change over time.

numbers.meaning: US gummy products inaccurately labelled (outside plus or minus 10%)
range of actual melatonin as a percentage of label, US gummies containing melatonin
range of melatonin content relative to label, Canadian supplements
Canadian supplements not within 10% of label

claims.claim: In people with primary sleep disorders, melatonin modestly shortened the time to fall asleep and slightly increased total sleep.
claims.supporting_passage: "Nineteen studies involving 1683 subjects were included in this meta-analysis. Melatonin demonstrated significant efficacy in reducing sleep latency (weighted mean difference (WMD) = 7.06 minutes [95% CI 4.37 to 9.75], Z = 5.15, p<0.001) and increasing total sleep time (WMD = 8.25 minutes [95% CI 1.74 to 14.75], Z = 2.48, p = 0.013)." ... "The effects of melatonin on sleep are modest but do not appear to dissipate with continued melatonin use."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults and children with primary sleep disorders / melatonin (various doses and products) / placebo / sleep latency, total sleep time / various durations
claims.safe_wording: In people with insomnia and other primary sleep problems, melatonin helped people fall asleep about 7 minutes sooner and sleep about 8 minutes longer than a dummy pill, on average.
claims.qualifications: Mixed ages including children; not older-specific; average effects.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None major.

numbers.meaning: average reduction in time to fall asleep versus placebo
average increase in total sleep time versus placebo

claims.claim: In a US cohort of new users (mean age 70), low sodium was diagnosed at 146 per 1,000 person-years with desmopressin versus 11 per 1,000 with oxybutynin.
claims.supporting_passage: "We identified 3,137 adults who were newly prescribed desmopressin and matched them to 3,137 adults who were newly prescribed oxybutynin. Mean age was 70, 55% were male, 13% filled a prescription for a diuretic during the baseline time period, and the mean baseline sodium prior to receiving either study drug was 140 mmol/L (normal: 135-145). The rate of hyponatremia was 146 per 1,000 person-years for adults prescribed desmopressin compared to 11 per 1,000 person-years for adults prescribed oxybutynin, corresponding to a 13-fold higher rate (HR 13.19; 95% CI 6.69, 26.01; p < 0.01)." ... "Important limitations of our study include unmeasured confounding (for example, over-the-counter medication use, dietary intake), missing data (i.e., only 20% of patients had a baseline serum sodium), and a lack of data on the newer formulation of desmopressin." Methods: "we assessed hyponatremia as the primary position diagnosis ICD9 or ICD10 code (inpatient or outpatient) following prescription of desmopressin or oxybutynin."
claims.location: Abstract; Methods, Study outcomes (page 4 of PDF, via Undermind read_pdfs)
claims.pico_timeframe: US adults over 50 (mean age 70) newly prescribed the older desmopressin formulation, propensity-matched / versus new oxybutynin users / coded hyponatraemia diagnosis / 2006 to 2017
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of about 3,100 people newly prescribed desmopressin (average age 70), low sodium was diagnosed at a rate of about 146 per 1,000 people per year, against about 11 per 1,000 per year in similar people starting oxybutynin, another bladder medicine.
claims.qualifications: Older formulation of desmopressin, not the newer low-dose products; association in observational data; outcome is a coded diagnosis; only about 20% had a baseline sodium. 'Per 1,000 person-years' can be glossed as 'per 1,000 people treated for a year'. The 13-fold figure is a hazard ratio: prefer the two rates.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A Korean cohort of men with BPH found no significant difference after matching (C11-29-g). Clinical-trial rates are lower, which the authors attribute partly to close sodium monitoring in trials.

numbers.meaning: rate of coded hyponatraemia diagnosis, new desmopressin users
same, new oxybutynin users
relative rate (practitioner detail only)
matched new users
mean age
proportion with a baseline sodium result

claims.claim: The 2023 Beers Criteria advise avoiding desmopressin for nocturia or nocturnal polyuria.
claims.supporting_passage: Table 2 (page 24), Genitourinary, Desmopressin: Rationale "High risk of hyponatremia; safer alternative treatments for nocturia (including non- pharmacologic)." Recommendation "Avoid for treatment of nocturia or nocturnal polyuria." Quality of evidence "Moderate". Strength of recommendation "Strong".
claims.location: Table 2, page 24 of the published PDF (via Undermind read_pdfs)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 65 and over; US
claims.safe_wording: The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria advise avoiding desmopressin for night-time urination in people aged 65 and over, because of the high risk of low sodium and the availability of safer options, including non-drug ones.
claims.qualifications: US guideline; 'avoid' is not an absolute contraindication.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Urology reviews (Oelke 2017, Ebell 2014) regard low-dose desmopressin with monitoring as an option in selected patients.

claims.claim: A review of nocturia in frail older adults concluded that desmopressin is not recommended in frail people because of the risk of low sodium.
claims.supporting_passage: "No studies specific to the frail older adult support the use of pharmacotherapy." ... "Desmopressin may be effective in the older adult, but a high risk of hyponatremia raises concerns for its safety, and therefore it is not recommended in the frail."
claims.pico_timeframe: Frail older adults with nocturia; narrative review
claims.safe_wording: A review of night-time urination in frail older people concluded desmopressin is not recommended for them because of the risk of low sodium, and noted that no drug studies have been done specifically in frail people.
claims.qualifications: Narrative review, expert conclusion.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: If desmopressin is used, sodium should be checked before starting and early after starting, especially from age 65.
claims.supporting_passage: Juul 2017: "A sodium monitoring plan is proposed whereby baseline sodium must be ≥135 mmol/L (especially important in the elderly), with additional monitoring at week 1 and month 1 for those at elevated risk because they are aged ≥65 years or receiving concomitant medication associated with hyponatraemia." Rembratt 2006: "Age was the best single predictor. Elderly patients (>or=65 years of age) with a baseline serum sodium concentration below normal range were at high risk (75%)." ... "Treatment of nocturia in elderly patients with desmopressin should only be undertaken together with careful monitoring of the serum sodium concentration. Patients with a baseline serum sodium concentration below normal range should not be treated." Ebell 2014: "a lower initial dose of 25 to 50 mcg is appropriate in elderly patients. All patients should be monitored for hyponatremia."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in desmopressin trials for nocturia (pooled analyses; systematic review)
claims.safe_wording: If desmopressin is used, published schemes advise checking sodium before starting (and not starting if it is low), then again at about 1 week and 1 month in people aged 65 or over or taking other medicines that lower sodium, using the lowest dose.
claims.qualifications: Monitoring schemes come from manufacturer-authored analyses and a systematic review, not from the UK product information (not opened). Say 'published schemes advise', not 'the licence requires'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The Juul scheme was tested only by retrospective application.

numbers.meaning: minimum baseline sodium in the Juul scheme
additional sodium checks for people aged 65+ or on sodium-lowering medicines
risk of hyponatraemia in people 65+ with low baseline sodium (Rembratt pooled trials)

claims.claim: Desmopressin gives a modest benefit for nocturia.
claims.supporting_passage: "A dose of 100 mcg provided just more than an hour of additional sleep before the first void compared with placebo as well as 0.72 fewer voids per night. Higher doses provided no significant increase in benefit. Hyponatremia (RR 5.1) and headache (RR 4.3) were the most common adverse effects." ... "Desmopressin appears to offer a modest benefit for treating nocturia in generally healthy adults with adequate safety."
claims.pico_timeframe: Generally healthy adults with nocturia / desmopressin / placebo / nocturnal voids, time to first void / 10 RCTs, 2,191 patients
claims.safe_wording: In trials in generally healthy adults, desmopressin reduced night-time trips to the toilet by less than one a night on average (0.72 fewer at 100 micrograms) and gave just over an hour more sleep before the first trip.
claims.qualifications: Generally healthy adults, several trials excluded non-responders in a run-in; benefit in frail older people untested.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on direction.

numbers.meaning: fewer nocturnal voids per night versus placebo at 100 micrograms
extra time asleep before first void versus placebo at 100 micrograms
relative risk of hyponatraemia versus placebo (practitioner detail)

claims.claim: Low sodium is also common with the newer low-dose tablet: in Japanese men (mean age 75) it occurred in 13% over up to a year.
claims.supporting_passage: "The mean age of the total population was 75.0 ± 9.6 years. A total of 351 adverse drug reactions (ADRs) were reported in 259 patients, including 11 serious ADRs in 7 patients (0.7%). The most common ADR was hyponatremia, which occurred in 140 patients (13.3%)." ... "Patients aged ≥ 75 years, those with underlying medical conditions, and those with abnormal clinical laboratory values, such as reduced renal function or a baseline serum sodium level of < 140 mmol/L, should be closely monitored for the development of hyponatremia during desmopressin treatment for nocturia due to NP."
claims.pico_timeframe: 1,049 Japanese men starting desmopressin orally disintegrating tablets for nocturnal polyuria / no comparator / up to 52 weeks
claims.safe_wording: Newer low-dose tablets still carry the risk: in a Japanese survey of 1,049 men with an average age of 75, about 13 in 100 developed low sodium within a year.
claims.qualifications: Manufacturer-run survey without a comparison group; men only; Japan. Most cases were without reported severe symptoms (no confusion, seizures, stupor or coma recorded among the 19 with symptoms).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Definition of hyponatraemia not given in the abstract.

numbers.meaning: men with hyponatraemia as an adverse drug reaction over up to 52 weeks

claims.claim: Not every study finds a higher risk: a Korean cohort of men with enlarged prostate found no significant increase after matching.
claims.supporting_passage: "After propensity score matching, desmopressin use was not significantly associated with an increased risk of hyponatremia (hazard ratio 1.273, 95% confidence interval 0.988-1.640; p=0.062). Significant predictors of hyponatremia included advanced age, chronic heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, and renal disease." ... "clinicians should implement routine monitoring protocols, including serum sodium checks, particularly in high-risk populations"
claims.pico_timeframe: 33,533 Korean men with BPH, desmopressin versus alpha-blocker or combination, 2011 to 2020
claims.safe_wording: Practitioner posts may add that a large Korean study in men with enlarged prostate did not find a clear increase after matching, while still advising sodium checks in high-risk people.
claims.qualifications: Men only; comparator alpha-blockers; formulation not stated in abstract; upper confidence limit allows a 64% increase.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Conflicts in size with Fralick 2019; different populations and outcome definitions.

numbers.meaning: hyponatraemia, desmopressin versus comparison after matching; not statistically significant

claims.claim: In a randomised trial of 327 adults aged 60 and over with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, six 20 to 30 minute telephone sessions of CBT for insomnia over 8 weeks reduced insomnia severity more than education only, and at 12 months 56% versus 26% were in remission.
claims.supporting_passage: "This is a randomized clinical trial of 327 participants 60 years and older who were recruited statewide through Kaiser Permanente Washington from September 2016 to December 2018." ... "Six 20- to 30-minute telephone sessions provided over 8 weeks. Participants submitted daily diaries and received group-specific educational materials. The CBT-I instruction included sleep restriction, stimulus control, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring, and homework. The EOC group received information about sleep and OA." ... "Of the 327 participants, the mean (SD) age was 70.2 (6.8) years, and 244 (74.6%) were women. In the 282 participants with follow-up ISI data, the total 2-month posttreatment ISI scores decreased 8.1 points in the CBT-I group and 4.8 points in the EOC group, an adjusted mean between-group difference of -3.5 points (95% CI, -4.4 to -2.6 points; P < .001). Results were sustained at 12-month follow-up (adjusted mean difference, -3.0 points; 95% CI, -4.1 to -2.0 points; P < .001). At 12-month follow-up, 67 of 119 (56.3%) participants receiving CBT-I remained in remission (ISI score, ≤7) compared with 33 of 128 (25.8%) participants receiving EOC."
claims.location: Abstract: Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 60+ (mean 70.2) with moderate to severe insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, one US health plan / telephone CBT-I, 6 sessions over 8 weeks / education-only control (sleep and OA information) / Insomnia Severity Index; remission ISI 7 or less / 2 months and 12 months
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial of 327 people aged 60 and over who had both insomnia and arthritis pain, six phone sessions of CBT for insomnia (20 to 30 minutes each, over 8 weeks) improved sleep more than information about sleep and arthritis. A year later, 56 in 100 in the phone CBT group had no clinically significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 in the information group.
claims.qualifications: Everyone in the trial had osteoarthritis pain; one US health plan. The remission figures use the people with 12-month data (119 and 128), not all 327. Remission means a score of 7 or less on the Insomnia Severity Index. Pain improved after treatment but the difference was not sustained at 12 months.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The comparator was education only. The trial did not compare telephone with app-based or face-to-face CBT-I, so the post must not imply the phone works better than an app. The abstract does not say whether the control group also had phone contact.

numbers.meaning: people randomised, aged 60 and over
mean age in years

numbers.value: 6 sessions of 20 to 30 minutes over 8 weeks
numbers.meaning: telephone CBT-I dose
fall in Insomnia Severity Index at 2 months, CBT-I vs education (282 with follow-up data); adjusted difference 3.5 points
adjusted between-group difference in Insomnia Severity Index at 12 months
in remission (ISI 7 or less) at 12 months, CBT-I vs education; absolute difference about 30 percentage points; natural frequency about 56 vs 26 in 100

claims.claim: Telephone CBT-I needs only a phone for the sessions and was designed as an access route for people who lack ready access to insomnia treatment.
claims.supporting_passage: "Scalable delivery models of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), an effective treatment, are needed for widespread implementation, particularly in rural and underserved populations lacking ready access to insomnia treatment." ... Key Points, Meaning: "Telephone CBT-I may improve access to an individualized and effective treatment for chronic insomnia among older persons with osteoarthritis pain, including those in rural and medically underserved areas."
claims.location: Abstract (Importance) and Key Points (Meaning), via PMC
claims.pico_timeframe: As for C11-09-a; the access claim is the authors' interpretation, not a measured outcome
claims.safe_wording: The therapy sessions in this trial were delivered by telephone. The researchers present phone delivery as a way to reach older people in rural and underserved areas who lack ready access to insomnia treatment.
claims.qualifications: The trial did not measure access or compare uptake between formats. Participants also kept daily sleep diaries and received written materials; how the diaries were returned is not stated in the abstract, so do not say 'nothing but a phone is needed'. Say 'the sessions were by phone'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether telephone CBT-I reaches people who are offline was not tested; it is a reasonable inference, which the post should present as the argument, not as a finding.

claims.claim: CBT for insomnia is the recommended first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults (ACP and AASM guidelines).
claims.supporting_passage: ACP 2016, Abstract: "ACP recommends that all adult patients receive cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. (Grade: strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence)." | AASM 2021, Abstract: "1. We recommend that clinicians use multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (STRONG)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with chronic insomnia disorder (all adult ages) / CBT-I / other treatments / global and sleep outcomes / guideline recommendation
claims.safe_wording: US guidelines from the American College of Physicians and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend CBT for insomnia as the first treatment for long-term insomnia in adults.
claims.qualifications: Both are US guidelines covering adults of all ages. UK (NICE) guidance was not openable from this environment, so do not cite NICE.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

claims.claim: A substantial share of older people in the UK do not use the internet.
claims.supporting_passage: Discussion: "In contrast, comparable ELSA estimates (i.e., proportion of users of any frequency, aged 60 +) suggest that in England, this remained constant at 79% before and during the pandemic." | Results: "Weighted estimates from the nationally representative English Longitudinal Study of Ageing suggest that the prevalence of daily Internet use among adults aged 50 + in England increased from 52·9% in 2012/2013 (Wave 6), to 71·8% in 2018/2019 (Wave 9), and finally to 73·9% in June/July 2020" | "This discrepancy increased with age, with those aged 85 + being 17 percentage points less likely (or 22·1% relative to the June/July 2020 average) than those aged 50–64 to use the Internet daily." | Abstract: "Daily use in June/July 2020 was negatively related to age, neighbourhood deprivation, and loneliness, and positively related to partnership status, education, employment, income, and organisation membership." | Discussion: "It is also worth noting that older adults in care homes have been excluded by design. There could be an under-representation of infrequent or non-users in our sample, in which case, the rates of Internet use would be lower than estimated."
claims.location: Results (Daily Internet use; Factors predicting use); Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 50+ (and 60+ subset) in private households in England, ELSA / internet use / by age, deprivation, loneliness / self-reported use / 2018/19 and June/July 2020
claims.safe_wording: In England in 2020, about 1 in 5 people aged 60 and over living in their own homes did not use the internet. Daily use was lower in the oldest age groups, in more deprived areas and among lonelier people.
claims.qualifications: England only (not the whole UK); 2020 data; care home residents excluded, and the authors say non-users may be under-represented, so the real figure is probably higher. The 85+ gap (17 percentage points) is adjusted for other factors and past use.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The Ofcom figure the candidate suggested was not openable and is not used. Internet use among older people has been rising over time, so a 2020 figure may overstate current non-use slightly; say 'in 2020'.

numbers.meaning: adults aged 60+ in England who used the internet at any frequency, before and during the pandemic (2018/19 and June/July 2020); so about 21 in 100 did not
adults aged 50+ in England using the internet daily, June/July 2020
adjusted difference in likelihood of daily internet use, people aged 85+ vs 50 to 64, June/July 2020

claims.claim: NICE recommends a digital CBT-I programme (Sleepio, MTG70) as an option in primary care.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not assessed
claims.safe_wording: Do not state this. The NICE page could not be opened and no PubMed-indexed source stating it was found.
claims.qualifications: Non-essential; drop from the post.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Unverified.

claims.claim: In the UK, CBT for insomnia components can be delivered without an app: in an English trial, general practice nurses delivered sleep restriction therapy in four sessions.
claims.supporting_passage: "Adults with insomnia disorder were recruited from 35 general practices across England and randomly assigned (1:1) using a web-based randomisation programme to either four sessions of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy plus a sleep hygiene booklet or a sleep hygiene booklet only." ... "Brief nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy in primary care reduces insomnia symptoms, is likely to be cost-effective, and has the potential to be widely implemented as a first-line treatment for insomnia disorder."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with insomnia disorder (mean age 55.4, range 19 to 88), 35 English practices / 4 nurse-delivered sleep restriction sessions plus booklet / booklet only / Insomnia Severity Index / 6 months
claims.safe_wording: An English trial showed that practice nurses can deliver a core part of CBT for insomnia, called sleep restriction therapy, in four sessions in general practice. It is a practical, non-digital route to ask about.
claims.qualifications: This is trial evidence of feasibility and benefit, not proof that the service is routinely available. The post may suggest asking the GP practice whether CBT for insomnia can be given by phone or in person; it must not state that the NHS routinely offers it. The HABIT population was mostly middle-aged (mean 55).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether HABIT sessions were face to face or by phone was not verified from the abstract; do not say they were by phone.

numbers.meaning: general practices in England
nurse-delivered sessions

claims.claim: The AASM suggests that clinicians not use sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy for chronic insomnia, and recommends multicomponent CBT-I; stimulus control, sleep restriction and relaxation are suggested as single components.
claims.supporting_passage: "1. We recommend that clinicians use multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (STRONG). 2. We suggest that clinicians use multicomponent brief therapies for insomnia for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL). 3. We suggest that clinicians use stimulus control as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL). 4. We suggest that clinicians use sleep restriction therapy as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL). 5. We suggest that clinicians use relaxation therapy as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL). 6. We suggest that clinicians not use sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with chronic insomnia disorder / behavioural and psychological treatments / GRADE-based recommendations
claims.safe_wording: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises against using sleep hygiene advice on its own to treat long-term insomnia. It recommends full CBT for insomnia, and suggests stimulus control, sleep restriction or relaxation therapy as single treatments.
claims.qualifications: The advice against sleep hygiene alone is a conditional recommendation ('we suggest ... not'), as are the single-component recommendations; only multicomponent CBT-I is a strong recommendation. Covers adults of all ages. Sleep hygiene can remain part of a multicomponent treatment.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

claims.claim: In the HABIT trial in English general practice, four nurse-delivered sleep restriction sessions plus a sleep hygiene booklet reduced insomnia severity at 6 months more than the booklet alone, and were likely cost-effective.
claims.supporting_passage: "We did a pragmatic, superiority, open-label, randomised controlled trial of sleep restriction therapy versus sleep hygiene. Adults with insomnia disorder were recruited from 35 general practices across England and randomly assigned (1:1) using a web-based randomisation programme to either four sessions of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy plus a sleep hygiene booklet or a sleep hygiene booklet only." ... "we randomly assigned 642 participants to sleep restriction therapy (n=321) or sleep hygiene (n=321). Mean age was 55·4 years (range 19-88)" ... "At 6 months, mean ISI score was 10·9 (SD 5·5) for sleep restriction therapy and 13·9 (5·2) for sleep hygiene (adjusted mean difference -3·05, 95% CI -3·83 to -2·28; p<0·0001; Cohen's d -0·74)" ... "The incremental cost per QALY gained was £2076, giving a 95·3% probability that treatment was cost-effective at a cost-effectiveness threshold of £20 000."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 19 to 88 (mean 55.4) with insomnia disorder, 35 English general practices / 4 nurse sessions of sleep restriction + booklet / sleep hygiene booklet only / Insomnia Severity Index (0 to 28) / 6 months (also 3 and 12)
claims.safe_wording: In a large English general practice trial, the comparison group received a sleep hygiene booklet. claims.claim: In older adults with chronic insomnia, brief behavioural treatment produced a response in 67% versus 25% with printed educational material (RCT).
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 79 older adults (mean age, 71.7 years; 54 women [70%]) with chronic insomnia and common comorbidities were recruited from the community and 1 primary care clinic. Participants were randomly assigned to either BBTI, consisting of individualized behavioral instructions delivered in 2 intervention sessions and 2 telephone calls, or IC, consisting of printed educational material. Both interventions were delivered by a nurse clinician. The primary outcome was categorically defined treatment response at 4 weeks" ... "Categorically defined response (67% [n = 26] vs 25% [n = 10]; χ(2) = 13.8) (P < .001) and the proportion of participants without insomnia (55% [n = 21] vs 13% [n = 5]; χ(2) = 15.5) (P < .001) were significantly higher for BBTI than for IC. The number needed to treat was 2.4 for each outcome." ... "Improvements were maintained at 6 months."
claims.pico_timeframe: 79 older adults (mean 71.7) with chronic insomnia and comorbidities, Pittsburgh / brief behavioural treatment (2 sessions + 2 phone calls, nurse-delivered) / printed educational material / treatment response and no insomnia / 4 weeks (maintained at 6 months)
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of 79 older adults (average age 72) with long-term insomnia, about 2 in 3 improved after two nurse sessions and two phone calls of behavioural treatment, against 1 in 4 of those given printed information. The benefit was still there at 6 months.
claims.qualifications: Small single-centre US trial; the primary outcome was at 4 weeks. The printed information control is comparable to a leaflet but not identical to a sleep hygiene leaflet. Use 'about 2 in 3 vs 1 in 4' rather than n values, as group denominators are not stated in the abstract.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting evidence identified; small sample means the size of effect is uncertain.

claims.claim: CBT for insomnia is the recommended initial treatment for chronic insomnia in adults.

claims.safe_wording: The American College of Physicians recommends CBT for insomnia as the first treatment for long-term insomnia in adults.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

claims.claim: Incident or recurrent major depression occurred in 12.2% of the CBT-I group and 25.9% of the sleep education group over follow-up (HR 0.51).
claims.supporting_passage: "Incident or recurrent major depression occurred in 19 participants (12.2%) in the CBT-I group and in 35 participants (25.9%) in the SET group, with an overall benefit (hazard ratio, 0.51; 95%, CI 0.29-0.88; P = .02) consistent across subgroups." ... "The findings of this randomized clinical trial indicate that treatment of insomnia with CBT-I has an overall benefit in the prevention of incident and recurrent major depression in older adults with insomnia disorder."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-28-a; outcome time to first major depressive episode; follow-up up to 36 months
claims.safe_wording: Over up to 3 years of follow-up, 12 in 100 people who had CBT for insomnia developed major depression, compared with 26 in 100 who had sleep education. The risk of depression over time was about half as high with CBT.
claims.qualifications: The 12 vs 26 in 100 are crude proportions of everyone randomised (19/156 and 35/135), not adjusted for unequal follow-up; the primary analysis was the hazard ratio of 0.51 (confidence interval 0.29 to 0.88, so the true reduction could be smaller or larger). Label icon arrays 'up to 3 years' and 'people randomised'. Do not use the 82.6% figure for CBT-I remitters: that compares a subgroup defined after randomisation and is not a randomised comparison.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: One trial, not yet replicated in the sources read. Sustained insomnia remission was modest in both groups (26.3% vs 19.3%).

claims.supporting_passage: "The trial protocol was modified to extend follow-up from 24 to 36 months, with follow-up completion in July 2018." ... "7 [2.4%] Asian, 32 [11.0%] Black, 3 [1.0%] Pacific Islander, 241 [82.8%] White, 6 [2.1%] multiracial, and 2 [0.7%] unknown" ... "A total of 140 participants (89.7%) completed CBT-I and 130 (96.3%) participants completed SET (χ2 = 4.9, P = .03), with 114 (73.1%) completing 24 months of follow-up in the CBT-I group and 117 (86.7%) in the SET group (χ2 = 8.4, P = .004). After protocol modification, 92 (59.0%) of the CBT-I participants and 86 (63.7%) of the SET participants agreed to extended follow-up (χ2 = 0.7, P = .41), with 81 (51.9%) of the CBT-I participants and 77 (57.0%) of the SET group completing 36 months of follow-up"

claims.safe_wording: Read it with care: it was one trial at one site, more than 8 in 10 participants were White, and more people dropped out of follow-up in the CBT group (73 in 100 completed 2 years, against 87 in 100 with sleep education). Only just over half completed 3 years.
claims.qualifications: Uneven drop-out could bias the result in either direction. Single site; excluded people with recent major health events, so frailer older people are under-represented.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of 65 studies (3,577 people aged 5 to 102) found that in adults total sleep time, sleep efficiency and deep sleep fell and time awake after sleep onset rose with age, but only sleep efficiency continued to fall significantly after 60; age effects were modified, sometimes diminished, by how well participants were screened for illness, medicines and sleep disorders.
claims.supporting_passage: "65 studies representing 3,577 subjects aged 5 years to 102 years." ... "In adults, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, percentage of slow-wave sleep, percentage of REM sleep, and REM latency all significantly decreased with age, while sleep latency, percentage of stage 1 sleep, percentage of stage 2 sleep, and wake after sleep onset significantly increased with age. However, only sleep efficiency continued to significantly decrease after 60 years of age. The magnitudes of the effect sizes noted changed depending on whether or not studied participants were screened for mental disorders, organic diseases, use of drug or alcohol, obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, or other sleep disorders." ... "effect sizes for the different sleep parameters were greatly modified by the quality of subject screening, diminishing or even masking age associations with different sleep parameters."
claims.pico_timeframe: Healthy non-clinical people aged 5 to 102 / age / cross-sectional comparison across studies / polysomnography or actigraphy sleep measures / studies 1960 to 2003
claims.safe_wording: In healthy adults, sleep gets somewhat shorter, lighter and more broken with age. An older review of sleep studies found that after 60 only sleep efficiency (the share of time in bed spent asleep) kept falling clearly, and that age effects looked smaller when studies screened out illness, medicines and sleep disorders.
claims.qualifications: Do not paraphrase as 'most change has happened by 60': the abstract says only one measure continued to fall significantly after 60, which is not the same thing. Studies were mostly small and published 1960 to 2003.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Boulos 2019 (larger, modern scoring) modelled a steady decline per decade across adulthood (see C11-14-b), so whether change levels off after 60 is uncertain.

numbers.meaning: size of the meta-analysis
age range in years
age after which only sleep efficiency continued to fall significantly

claims.claim: In healthy adults, measured sleep changes gradually with age: for each decade, total sleep time falls by about 10 minutes and time awake after sleep onset rises by about 10 minutes.
claims.supporting_passage: "Of 3712 articles, 169 studies, comprising 5273 participants, were eligible for inclusion." ... "For each decade of age, total sleep time decreased by 10·1 min (95% CI 7·5 to 12·8), sleep efficiency decreased by 2·1% (1·5 to 2·6), wake after sleep onset increased by 9·7 min (6·9 to 12·4), sleep onset latency increased by 1·1 min (0·3 to 1·9), arousal index increased by 2·1 events per h (1·5 to 2·6), percentage of N1 sleep increased by 0·5% (0·1 to 0·8), apnea-hypopnea index increased by 1·2 events per h (0·9 to 1·4)" ... "Changes with age in the percentage of N2 sleep (0·0%, 95% CI -0·1 to 0·1), N3 sleep (-0·1%, -0·1 to 0·0), and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (0·0%, -0·1 to 0·0) were not significant."
claims.pico_timeframe: Healthy adult controls in sleep-laboratory studies (excluding people with conditions or treatments affecting sleep) / age per decade / meta-regression / polysomnography parameters / studies 2007 to 2016
claims.safe_wording: In healthy adults, a large review of overnight sleep studies found that each extra decade of age brought about 10 minutes less sleep and about 10 minutes more time awake during the night. That is a gradual, modest change, not a collapse of sleep.
claims.qualifications: Laboratory sleep of healthy volunteers; averages, not individual limits. Linear per-decade model; it does not show whether change speeds up or levels off in late life. Illustration: 40 years (for example 40 to 80) would be about 40 minutes less sleep on average, but only present this as arithmetic on the per-decade estimate if used at all.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Partly differs from Ohayon 2004 (only sleep efficiency kept falling after 60); both agree the change in healthy people is modest.

numbers.meaning: size of the meta-analysis (healthy adults)
fall in total sleep time per decade of age
rise in time awake after first falling asleep per decade of age
fall in sleep efficiency per decade of age (percentage points of time in bed spent asleep)

claims.claim: The US National Sleep Foundation recommends 7 to 8 hours for older adults, against 7 to 9 hours for younger adults and adults.
claims.supporting_passage: "For teenagers, 8 to 10 hours was considered appropriate, 7 to 9 hours for young adults and adults, and 7 to 8 hours of sleep for older adults." ... "The recommendations reported here represent guidelines for healthy individuals and those not suffering from a sleep disorder. Sleep durations outside the recommended range may be appropriate, but deviating far from the normal range is rare."
claims.pico_timeframe: Healthy people without sleep disorders / expert consensus on appropriate sleep duration by age group
claims.safe_wording: An expert panel for the US National Sleep Foundation suggests 7 to 8 hours a night for older adults, against 7 to 9 hours for younger adults. So the saying that older people need less sleep is only slightly true: the recommended range drops by an hour at the top end, not at the bottom.
claims.qualifications: Consensus opinion, not measured need. The abstract does not state the age at which 'older adults' starts; do not write '65 and over' unless it is checked in the full text.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

numbers.meaning: recommended nightly sleep for older adults (consensus)
recommended nightly sleep for young adults and adults (consensus)

claims.claim: Sleep complaints in older people are common and are associated with health problems such as depression, pain, respiratory symptoms, disability and medicines.
claims.supporting_passage: Foley 1995: "The frequencies of five common sleep complaints--trouble falling asleep, waking up, awaking too early, needing to nap and not feeling rested--were assessed in over 9,000 participants aged 65 years and older" ... "Less than 20% of the participants in each community rarely or never had any complaints, whereas over half reported at least one of these complaints as occurring most of the time. Between 23% and 34% had symptoms of insomnia" ... "In multivariate analyses, sleep complaints were associated with an increasing number of respiratory symptoms, physical disabilities, nonprescription medications, depressive symptoms and poorer self-perceived health. Sleep disturbances, particularly among older persons, oftentimes may be secondary to coexisting diseases." | Foley 2004: "Depression, heart disease, bodily pain and memory problems were associated with more prevalent symptoms of insomnia. Other conditions such as obesity, arthritis, diabetes, lung diseases, stroke and osteoporosis were associated with other sleep-related problems such as breathing pauses, snoring, daytime sleepiness, restless legs or insufficient sleep (<6 h nightly)." ... "These results suggest that the sleep complaints common in older adults are often secondary to their comorbidities and not to aging per se."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling US adults 65+ (Foley 1995) and 55 to 84 (Foley 2004) / chronic conditions, mood, medicines / self-reported sleep complaints / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: Sleep complaints are common in later life, and in large US surveys they were linked with low mood, pain, heart and lung problems, disability and some medicines. The researchers concluded that much of the poor sleep seen in older adults goes with these conditions rather than with age itself.
claims.qualifications: Cross-sectional associations: they do not prove the conditions cause the poor sleep (the link can run both ways). US data from the 1980s and 2003.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

numbers.meaning: people aged 65+ in Foley 1995
range across three communities with insomnia symptoms (Foley 1995)
adults aged 55 to 84 in the 2003 survey (Foley 2004)

claims.claim: New insomnia in later life mostly occurs alongside identifiable health or life factors: in a 3-year cohort of people aged 65 and over, only 7% of new cases occurred without associated risk factors, and nearly half of chronic insomnia remitted.
claims.supporting_passage: "Nearly 15% of the 4,956 participants without symptoms of insomnia at baseline reported chronic difficulty falling asleep or early morning arousal at follow-up, suggesting an annual incidence rate of approximately 5%. Incident insomnia was associated with depressed mood, respiratory symptoms, fair to poor perceived health, and physical disability." ... "Other factors associated with an increased risk of insomnia included use of prescribed sedatives, and widowhood. Only 7% of the incident cases of insomnia occurred in the absence of associated risk factors. Of the nearly 2,000 survivors with chronic insomnia at baseline, almost half no longer reported symptoms upon follow-up" ... "Because the vast majority of incident cases of insomnia were among persons with one or more of these risk factors, these data do not support a model of incident insomnia caused by the aging process per se."
claims.pico_timeframe: 6,899 US community residents aged 65+ / depressed mood, respiratory symptoms, poor health, disability, sedatives, widowhood / people without these / new self-reported insomnia / 3 years (1980s)
claims.safe_wording: In a large US study of people aged 65 and over followed for 3 years, only about 7 in 100 new cases of insomnia happened in people without a linked problem such as low mood, breathing symptoms, poor health, disability, sleeping tablet use or bereavement. Almost half of those with long-standing insomnia had improved 3 years later.
claims.qualifications: Observational and old (1980s US data); self-reported insomnia. The factors are linked with insomnia, not proven causes. Sedative use may be a response to insomnia rather than a cause.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting evidence identified; the finding is consistent with Foley 1995 and 2004.

numbers.meaning: people aged 65+ in the cohort
people without insomnia at baseline who had it 3 years later (about 5% a year)
of new insomnia cases that occurred without any associated risk factor

claims.claim: Needing to pass urine at night (nocturia) is linked with insomnia in older adults.
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 5396 older adults were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled estimate of the OR was 1.958 (95% CI: 1.609-2.384) for nocturia in patients with insomnia based on 7 studies in a random effects model" ... "The overall odds for nocturia in older adults is higher in patients with insomnia than those without and is associated with worse sleep outcomes." ... "A limiting factor of our analysis was the scarcity of available data, potentially causing an important selection bias."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults in 7 pooled studies / insomnia / no insomnia / nocturia (odds) / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: Getting up at night to pass urine is more common in older adults who have insomnia, and the two often go together, so it is worth asking about.
claims.qualifications: Association only; the direction is unclear (waking may prompt voiding, or the bladder may wake the person). Do not convert the odds ratio into 'twice as likely'. Small evidence base.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors note scarce data and possible selection bias.

numbers.meaning: older adults in the pooled analysis

claims.claim: In healthy adults most age-related change in measured sleep has happened by about 60.
claims.supporting_passage: Ohayon 2004: "However, only sleep efficiency continued to significantly decrease after 60 years of age." | Boulos 2019: "For each decade of age, total sleep time decreased by 10·1 min (95% CI 7·5 to 12·8), sleep efficiency decreased by 2·1% (1·5 to 2·6), wake after sleep onset increased by 9·7 min (6·9 to 12·4)"
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-14-a and C11-14-b
claims.safe_wording: Do not say 'most change has happened by 60'. Say instead that in healthy people sleep changes gradually with age, by about 10 minutes less sleep per decade, so a large or sudden change is not explained by age alone.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's paraphrase overstates Ohayon, and the more recent Boulos meta-analysis models a steady decline across adulthood.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Two meta-analyses use different methods and eras; the plateau after 60 is uncertain.

claims.claim: In 1,280 people with polysomnography-confirmed idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder (mean age 66, 82.5% men), the rate of developing an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, and 73.5% had converted after 12 years.
claims.supporting_passage: "Idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is a powerful early sign of Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy." ... "We combined prospective follow-up data from 24 centres of the International RBD Study Group. At baseline, patients with polysomnographically-confirmed iRBD without parkinsonism or dementia underwent sleep, motor, cognitive, autonomic and special sensory testing." ... "Overall, 1280 patients were recruited. The average age was 66.3 ± 8.4 and 82.5% were male. Average follow-up was 4.6 years (range = 1-19 years). The overall conversion rate from iRBD to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with 73.5% converting after 12-year follow-up."
claims.pico_timeframe: People with polysomnography-confirmed idiopathic RBD at 24 specialist centres, no parkinsonism or dementia at baseline / prospective follow-up / Kaplan-Meier risk of parkinsonism or dementia (PD, DLB, MSA) / mean 4.6 years, up to 19
claims.safe_wording: Among 1,280 people whose dream enactment was confirmed as REM sleep behaviour disorder in specialist sleep centres, about 6 in 100 a year went on to develop Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or a related condition. By 12 years the estimate was about 3 in 4.
claims.qualifications: Specialist-centre patients with sleep-study confirmation, mostly men; the 12-year figure is a Kaplan-Meier estimate (average follow-up was 4.6 years). It is not a personal prognosis for everyone who acts out dreams; people reporting dream enactment in the community are much less likely to have confirmed RBD (see C11-21-f). Conversion outcomes include Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Individual risk varies widely; the paper lists predictors (motor, smell, cognition and others). A sleep study is needed to confirm RBD.

numbers.meaning: people with confirmed idiopathic RBD, 24 centres
mean age in years
men
average follow-up (range 1 to 19)
rate of developing an overt neurodegenerative syndrome
estimated proportion converted by 12 years (Kaplan-Meier)

claims.claim: REM sleep behaviour disorder is a core clinical feature in the consensus diagnostic criteria for dementia with Lewy bodies.
claims.supporting_passage: "RBD is now included as a core clinical feature because it occurs frequently in autopsy-confirmed cases compared with non-DLB (76% vs 4%). It often begins many years before other symptoms, may become less vigorous or even quiescent over time, and should be screened for using a scale that allows for patient or bed partner report." ... "If the PSG shows REM sleep without atonia in a person with dementia and a history of RBD, there is a ≥90% likelihood of a synucleinopathy,sufficient to justify a probable DLB diagnosis even in the absence of any other core feature or biomarker"
claims.location: Full text: Core clinical features, REM sleep behavior disorder; Indicative biomarkers
claims.pico_timeframe: People with dementia being assessed for DLB / RBD history / autopsy-confirmed DLB vs non-DLB / consensus criteria
claims.safe_wording: Acting out dreams (REM sleep behaviour disorder) is one of the four core features used to diagnose dementia with Lewy bodies. It often starts many years before other symptoms.
claims.qualifications: The 76% vs 4% compares autopsy-confirmed DLB with other dementias; it is not the chance that someone who acts out dreams has DLB.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

numbers.meaning: RBD frequency in autopsy-confirmed DLB vs non-DLB cases
likelihood of a synucleinopathy when a sleep study shows REM sleep without atonia in a person with dementia and an RBD history

claims.claim: RBD is often reported by the bed partner; conditions that mimic it (such as severe obstructive sleep apnoea) must be excluded, and doubt should prompt referral to a sleep clinic or polysomnography.
claims.supporting_passage: "RBD is a parasomnia manifested by recurrent dream enactment behavior that includes movements mimicking dream content and associated with an absence of normal REM sleep atonia. It is particularly likely if dreams involve a chasing or attacking theme, and if the patient or bed partner has sustained injuries from limb movements." ... "should be screened for using a scale that allows for patient or bed partner report.Conditions mimicking RBD are common in people with dementia, e.g., confusional awakenings, severe obstructive sleep apnea, and periodic limb movements, all of which must be excluded by careful supplementary questioning to avoid a false-positive diagnosis. If there is any doubt whether a sleep disturbance is due to RBD, referral to a specialist sleep clinic should be made, or polysomnography (PSG) requested."
claims.location: Full text: Core clinical features, REM sleep behavior disorder
claims.pico_timeframe: People being assessed for DLB; consensus guidance
claims.safe_wording: Ask the bed partner as well as the person: dreams with a chasing or attacking theme and injuries from movements in sleep make REM sleep behaviour disorder more likely. Other problems can look similar, including severe sleep apnoea, so if there is doubt, refer for a sleep study.
claims.qualifications: Written for DLB assessment; the principle (partner history, exclude mimics, sleep study if doubt) applies generally. Access to sleep studies varies; do not imply everyone will get one quickly.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Injuries to the person or bed partner occur, and bedroom safety measures are recommended.
claims.supporting_passage: AASM 2023, Good Practice Statement: "It is critically important to help patients maintain a safe sleeping environment to prevent potentially injurious nocturnal behaviors. In particular, the removal of bedside weapons, or objects that could inflict injury if thrown or wielded against a bed partner, is of paramount importance. Sharp furniture like nightstands should be moved away or their edges and headboard should be padded. To reduce the risk of injurious falls, a soft carpet, rug, or mat should be placed next to the bed. Patients with severe, uncontrolled RBD should be recommended to sleep separately from their partners, or at the minimum, to place a pillow between themselves and their partners." | McKeith 2017: "if the patient or bed partner has sustained injuries from limb movements"
claims.location: AASM abstract (Good Practice Statement); McKeith full text
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RBD / bedroom safety / expert consensus
claims.safe_wording: US sleep specialists advise making the bedroom safe: remove objects that could hurt someone, move or pad sharp furniture and the headboard, put a soft rug or mat beside the bed, and, if episodes are severe, sleep apart or put a pillow between partners.
claims.qualifications: Good practice statement based on expert consensus, not trial evidence.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Antidepressants can bring on or worsen REM sleep behaviour disorder, so medicines should be reviewed; but antidepressant-associated RBD can still be a sign of early neurodegeneration.
claims.supporting_passage: AASM 2023: "Adult patients with drug-induced RBD" ... "9. * The AASM suggests that clinicians use drug discontinuation (vs drug continuation) for the treatment of drug-induced RBD in adults. (CONDITIONAL)" | Haba-Rubio 2018: "Compared with RBD- participants, RBD+ took more frequently antidepressants and antipsychotics (23.8% vs. 5.4%, p = .005; 14.3% vs. 1.5%, p = .004, respectively)" | Postuma 2013: "Compared to matched controls, RBD patients taking antidepressants demonstrated significant abnormalities of 12/14 neurodegenerative markers tested" ... "However, on prospective follow-up, RBD patients taking antidepressants had a lower risk of developing neurodegenerative disease than those without antidepressant use (5-year risk = 22% vs. 59%, RR = 0.22, 95%CI = 0.06, 0.74)." ... "Development of RBD with antidepressants can be an early signal of an underlying neurodegenerative disease."
claims.location: Abstracts: AASM recommendations; HypnoLaus Results; Postuma 2013 Results and Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RBD (AASM); general population 1,997 (HypnoLaus, cross-sectional); 100 specialist-centre iRBD patients, 27 on antidepressants (Postuma 2013, prospective)
claims.safe_wording: Some medicines, including antidepressants, are linked with acting out dreams, and sleep specialists suggest stopping the drug where it is thought to be the cause. But in one specialist cohort, people whose symptoms came with antidepressants still showed early signs of Parkinson-type disease, so a medicines review should not end the assessment.
claims.qualifications: The link in the general population is an association (people with RBD took antidepressants more often). The specific classes (for example serotonergic drugs) were not verified from the text read; say 'some antidepressants'. Do not use the 'up to 6% of users' figure, which is background in the Postuma 2013 abstract. Stopping an antidepressant needs its own risk-benefit decision.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Postuma 2013 is small and single-centre; 5-year risk was lower with antidepressant-associated RBD (22% vs 59%) but not zero.

numbers.meaning: antidepressant use in people with vs without confirmed RBD, general population (HypnoLaus)
5-year risk of neurodegenerative disease, RBD with vs without antidepressant use, specialist cohort of 100

claims.claim: Dream enactment reported in the community often turns out not to be RBD on a sleep study, so the specialist-centre conversion figures cannot be applied to everyone who acts out dreams.
claims.supporting_passage: "Full polysomnographic data from 1,997 participants (age = 59 ± 11.1 years, 53.6% women) participating in a population-based study (HypnoLaus, Lausanne, Switzerland) were collected." ... "Three hundred sixty-eight participants endorsed dream-enactment behavior on either of the two MUPS questions, and 21 fulfilled polysomnographic criteria for RBD, resulting in an estimated prevalence of 1.06% (95% CI = 0.61-1.50), with no difference between men and women."
claims.pico_timeframe: General population adults (mean age 59), Lausanne / questionnaire dream-enactment report / home polysomnography / RBD diagnosis / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a Swiss population study, 368 of about 2,000 adults said they acted out dreams, but only 21 had REM sleep behaviour disorder on a sleep study. About 1 in 100 adults had it. A report of dream enactment is a reason to assess, not a diagnosis.
claims.qualifications: One city; mean age 59, so younger than many geriatric patients. Screening was by two questionnaire items. 21 of 368 is roughly 1 in 18, but present the raw numbers rather than a derived ratio unless needed.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

numbers.meaning: adults with home polysomnography
reported dream-enactment behaviour on a questionnaire
met polysomnography criteria for RBD
estimated prevalence of RBD in this population

claims.claim: Discussing what RBD may mean (risk disclosure) is valued by patients and professionals, but individual prognosis is uncertain.
claims.supporting_passage: "For healthcare professionals, the main obstacles include uncertainty in formulating individualized prognoses, ethical challenges linked to the principle of beneficence and concerns about the possible emotional impact of disclosure. From the patients' viewpoint, there is a clear need for comprehensive and robust information about their condition, even though obtaining accurate and trustworthy sources can be difficult. Risk disclosure is considered essential by both patients and professionals, but a systematic step-by-step approach has yet to be implemented for people with iRBD on progression to neurodegenerative diseases."
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients with isolated RBD and professionals; 8 studies; attitudes to risk disclosure
claims.safe_wording: A recent review found that both patients and professionals see discussing future risk as essential, while professionals find it hard to give an individual prognosis. The conversation needs time, honesty about uncertainty, and follow-up.
claims.qualifications: Small scoping review (8 articles). The recommendation to have a careful, supported conversation is an ethical judgement and should be written as one ('we should').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

claims.claim: In a sleep laboratory study of 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with mild to moderately severe hearing loss, tested in deep sleep, the standard high-pitched (3100 Hz) smoke alarm at 75 dBA woke 56%, while a lower-pitched 520 Hz square-wave signal at the same level woke 92%.
claims.supporting_passage: Three auditory signals, a bed shaker, a pillow shaker, and strobe lights were presented to 38 adults (aged 18 to 80 yr) with mild to moderately severe hearing loss of 25 to 70 dB (in both ears), during slow-wave sleep (deep sleep). ... The third auditory signal was the current 3100-Hz smoke alarm. All auditory signals were tested below, at, and above the decibel level prescribed by the applicable standard for bedrooms (75 dBA). ... The most effective signal was a 520-Hz square wave auditory signal, waking 92% at 75 dBA, compared with 56% waking to the 75 dBA high-pitched alarm.
claims.pico_timeframe: 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with hearing loss 25 to 70 dB / 520 Hz square wave, bed and pillow shakers, strobe / standard 3100 Hz alarm / woken (EEG) during slow-wave sleep / laboratory nights (number not given in abstract)
claims.safe_wording: In a sleep laboratory study of 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with mild to moderately severe hearing loss, a standard high-pitched smoke alarm woke about 56 in 100 of them from deep sleep. A lower-pitched alarm sound at the same loudness woke about 92 in 100.
claims.qualifications: Say who was studied: adults of all ages (18 to 80), not only older people; laboratory, deep sleep only; small sample. The abstract does not state whether hearing aids were worn; frame the post conditionally ('if you take your hearing aids out at night') rather than claiming participants had removed them. Do not tell readers to buy a 520 Hz alarm: UK availability was not checked.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting study found. The authors' conclusion that low-frequency signals work better in several other groups (including older adults) refers to their other work, which was not opened here.

numbers.meaning: participants, aged 18 to 80, hearing loss 25 to 70 dB in both ears
proportion woken by the standard 3100 Hz alarm at 75 dBA, deep sleep
proportion woken by the 520 Hz square-wave signal at 75 dBA, deep sleep
loudness set by the applicable bedroom standard

claims.claim: In the same study, bed and pillow shakers woke 80 to 84% at the intensity as purchased, while strobe lights woke only 27% even at an intensity above the US standard.
claims.supporting_passage: In the case of bed and pillow shakers intensities below, at, and above the level as purchased were tested. For strobe lights three levels were used, all of which were above the applicable standard. ... Bed and pillow shakers awoke 80 to 84% at the intensity level as purchased. The strobe lights awoke only 27% at an intensity above the US standard. ... Strobe lights, even at high intensities, are ineffective in reliably waking people with mild to moderate hearing loss.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-13-a
claims.safe_wording: A vibrating pad under the pillow or mattress woke about 80 to 84 in 100 of the same people. A flashing strobe light woke about 27 in 100, even when brighter than the US standard.
claims.qualifications: Same population and laboratory caveats as C11-13-a. The shakers were tested 'as purchased', so they were commercial products at the time (2009). Use this to say: if you are offered an alarm kit for hearing loss, check it includes a vibrating pad and not only a flashing light.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: proportion woken by bed or pillow shakers at the intensity as purchased
proportion woken by strobe lights at an intensity above the US standard

claims.claim: UK fire and rescue services offer free home fire safety visits (England: all services offer them).
claims.supporting_passage: James and Clark 2025: "All English fire services offer 'Home Fire Safety Visits', designed to help those vulnerable to fire identify and reduce risk at home however, only four specify that people living with dementia are eligible." Hampton 2025: "The UK Fire and Rescue Service (FRS) routinely deliver Home Fire Safety Visits (HFSVs) in people's homes. HFSVs offer support with fire safety and a range of health-related issues." Cockayne 2025: "Fire and rescue services in England routinely carry out Home Fire Safety Visits which aim to reduce risk of fire, support independent living and improve quality of life."
claims.pico_timeframe: English fire and rescue service websites (James and Clark); UK service staff (Hampton); England (Cockayne); 2024 to 2025
claims.safe_wording: Fire and rescue services in the UK carry out home fire safety visits; in England every service offers them. You can ask for one and say that you are hard of hearing.
claims.qualifications: The papers do not state that visits are free or describe what alarms are fitted for people with hearing loss; that comes only from search extracts (C11-13-d). Eligibility and what is offered vary by service. Scotland's service was not verified separately from the UK-level statement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether these visits reduce fires, injuries or falls is unproven: the FIREFLI trial randomised only 63 of a planned 1156 and concluded 'The evidence for the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of Home Fire Safety Visits remains inconclusive.'

claims.claim: UK fire and rescue services can provide, often free, smoke alarm kits for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, with a flashing light and a vibrating pad.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine page titles only: 'Deaf Awareness Week: rasing awarness of free hard- of- hearing smoke alarms' (Avon Fire and Rescue Service); 'Flashing and vibrating smoke alarms providing peace of mind for deaf people' (Kent Fire and Rescue Service); 'Sensory Smoke Alarms' (Essex County Fire and Rescue Service); 'Fire safety for People with Hearing Difficulties' (Lancashire Fire and Rescue Service).
claims.location: WebSearch result titles and summary (pages not opened)
claims.pico_timeframe: Individual English fire and rescue services; current web pages
claims.safe_wording: Do not state as fact. Phrase as a question to ask: 'Ask whether they can fit an alarm with a vibrating pad for someone who is hard of hearing.'
claims.qualifications: search_extract only; not sufficient for an essential claim. Provision and eligibility vary by service.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Some fire service kits combine a strobe and a vibrating pad; the Bruck study suggests the pad, not the strobe, is the part most likely to wake someone.

claims.claim: Low-frequency (520 Hz) smoke alarms are available to buy in the UK.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not mention buying a 520 Hz or low-frequency alarm.
claims.qualifications: Availability in the UK was not checked (official and retail pages could not be opened).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable.

claims.claim: The 2025 AASM guideline says all patients with clinically significant restless legs should have iron studies (ferritin and transferrin saturation), and that iron should be given if ferritin is 75 ng/mL or less or transferrin saturation is below 20% (and only intravenously if ferritin is 75 to 100 ng/mL); these thresholds are consensus that has not been empirically tested.
claims.supporting_passage: "In all patients with clinically significant RLS, clinicians should regularly test serum iron studies including ferritin and transferrin saturation (calculated from iron and total iron binding capacity). Testing should ideally be administered in the morning avoiding all iron-containing supplements and foods at least 24 hours prior to blood draw. ... Consensus guidelines, which have not been empirically tested, suggest that supplementation of iron in adults with RLS should be instituted with oral or IV iron if serum ferritin ≤ 75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation < 20%, and only with IV iron if serum ferritin is between 75 and 100 ng/mL. ... These iron supplementation guidelines are different than for the general population."
claims.location: Abstract, Good Practice Statement 1 (also page 140 of PDF)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with clinically significant restless legs syndrome; US guideline, 2025
claims.safe_wording: A 2025 US sleep medicine guideline (AASM) advises checking ferritin and transferrin saturation in everyone with troublesome restless legs, and offering iron if ferritin is 75 or below or transferrin saturation is under 20%. It says these cut-offs come from expert consensus and have not been tested directly.
claims.qualifications: Label it as a 2025 US guideline. AASM reports ferritin in ng/mL; UK laboratories report micrograms per litre, which is numerically the same unit (1 ng/mL = 1 microgram/L). Test in the morning, off iron for 24 hours. Between 75 and 100, the guideline suggests intravenous iron only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Thresholds are consensus, 'not been empirically tested'. UK guidance was not opened (see C11-22-g).

numbers.meaning: ferritin at or below which oral or IV iron is suggested in adults with RLS (consensus)
transferrin saturation below which iron is suggested
ferritin range where only IV iron is suggested
avoid iron-containing supplements and foods before the morning blood test

claims.claim: Normal iron results do not rule out benefit from iron in restless legs: the iron thresholds differ from those used in the general population.
claims.supporting_passage: Discussion (page 148): "In the general population, iron administration is generally recommended for those with evidence of iron deficiency as determined by serum iron studies. In RLS, however, it is likely brain iron deficiency, particularly in specific brain regions, is involved in its pathophysiology. Therefore, there are patients with normal serum iron studies who benefit from iron administration, which is borne out by the clinical trials." Good Practice Statement: "These iron supplementation guidelines are different than for the general population."
claims.location: Discussion, page 148 (Undermind read_pdfs); Abstract, Good Practice Statement
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RLS; US guideline, 2025
claims.safe_wording: In restless legs, a ferritin that is normal by the usual standard can still be low enough for iron to help. The US guideline says some people with normal iron results benefit from iron, and it uses a higher cut-off (75) than for iron deficiency in general.
claims.qualifications: Do not state specific laboratory reference ranges (not sourced). The guideline's reasoning about brain iron is a proposed mechanism ('it is likely').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The cut-offs themselves are untested consensus.

numbers.meaning: ferritin cut-off (ng/mL, same as micrograms/L) in the AASM good practice statement

claims.claim: The first step in managing restless legs is addressing aggravating factors: alcohol, caffeine, antihistaminergic, serotonergic and antidopaminergic medicines, and untreated obstructive sleep apnoea.
claims.supporting_passage: "The first step in the management of RLS should be addressing exacerbating factors, such as alcohol, caffeine, antihistaminergic, serotonergic, antidopaminergic medications, and untreated obstructive sleep apnea." Future Directions (page 150): "RLS is often comorbid with mood, anxiety, and pain disorders, which present challenges to treatment because the most common treatments—serotonergic reuptake inhibitors—often worsen RLS."
claims.location: Abstract, Good Practice Statement 2; Future Directions, page 150
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RLS; US guideline, 2025
claims.safe_wording: Before adding a medicine for restless legs, look for things that make it worse: alcohol, caffeine, sedating antihistamines, many antidepressants (serotonergic ones), medicines that block dopamine (such as some anti-sickness drugs and antipsychotics), and untreated sleep apnoea.
claims.qualifications: Good practice statement (expert consensus). Examples of drug classes in brackets are the post's plain-English glosses of the guideline's categories; keep them as examples, not a complete list.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: The AASM now recommends gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil and pregabalin (strong, moderate certainty) and suggests against the standard use of levodopa, pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine (conditional), mainly because of augmentation, a treatment-induced worsening of restless legs over months to years.
claims.supporting_passage: "2. In adults with RLS, the AASM recommends the use of gabapentin over no gabapentin (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). 3. In adults with RLS, the AASM recommends the use of pregabalin over no pregabalin (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence)." "12. In adults with RLS, the AASM suggests against the standard use of pramipexole (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). Remarks: pramipexole may be used to treat RLS in patients who place a higher value on the reduction of restless legs symptoms with short-term use and a lower value on adverse effects with long-term use (particularly augmentation)." Introduction (page 139): "Augmentation clinically describes a gradual worsening of RLS symptom intensity and duration, which occurs over months to years of exposure to dopaminergic agents." "Augmentation manifests as 1 or more of the following: earlier symptom onset than prior to dopaminergic treatment (eg, from nighttime to daytime), reduced latency to symptom onset with sedentary activities, and/or extension to other areas of the body." Discussion (page 148): "Thus, in balancing the risks of augmentation against the clinical benefits of dopamine agonists or levodopa, this CPG suggests against their use as standard treatments in adults with RLS."
claims.location: Abstract, Recommendations 1 to 3 and 11 to 14 with remarks; Introduction page 139; Discussion page 148
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RLS; US guideline, 2025
claims.safe_wording: The 2025 US guideline now puts gabapentin and pregabalin first among medicines, and advises against using pramipexole, ropinirole or rotigotine as standard treatment. The reason is augmentation: over months to years these drugs can make restless legs start earlier in the day, come on faster at rest and spread to other parts of the body.
claims.qualifications: The recommendations against dopamine agonists are conditional; the guideline allows them where short-term relief is valued over long-term risk. The guideline also strongly recommends IV ferric carboxymaltose when iron status is appropriate, and conditionally suggests opioids.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Dopamine agonists do work in the short term ('There is no argument that dopamine agonists have demonstrated short-term efficacy in clinical trials'). The guideline's text quotes US national data (2017 to 2018) that 60% of medication-treated people were still prescribed dopamine agonists; this figure was read only through Undermind and is US-specific.

claims.claim: Gabapentinoids cause somnolence and dizziness; in older people, the Beers Criteria advise dose reduction when creatinine clearance is below 60 mL/min, avoiding combination with opioids, and avoiding three or more CNS-active drugs (including gabapentinoids) because of falls and fracture risk; for people with a history of falls, antiepileptics are to be avoided except for seizures and mood disorders.
claims.supporting_passage: AASM (Recommendations 1 to 3): "Adverse effects included somnolence and dizziness." "Patients who are at a high risk of side effects with this class of medications may choose other treatment options." Discussion (page 148): "This class of medications can have adverse effects, including dizziness and somnolence, which may influence shared decision-making for prescribers and patients." Beers 2023 Table 6 (page 34): Gabapentin, CrCl <60, "CNS adverse effects", "Reduce dose", Moderate, Strong; Pregabalin, same. Table 5 (page 31): Opioids + Gabapentin, Pregabalin: "Increased risk of severe sedation-related adverse events, including respiratory depression and death." "Avoid; exceptions are when transitioning from opioid therapy to gabapentin or pregabalin, or when using gabapentinoids to reduce opioid dose, although caution should be used in all circumstances." Table 5: "Antiepileptics (including gabapentinoids)" ... "Any combination of ≥3 of these CNS-active drugs": "Increased risk of falls and of fracture"; "Avoid concurrent use of ≥3 CNS-active drugs". Table 3 (page 27), History of falls or fractures: Antiepileptics ... "May cause ataxia, impaired psychomotor function, syncope, or additional falls." Recommendation: "Avoid unless safer alternatives are not available. Antiepileptics: avoid except for seizures and mood disorders."
claims.location: AASM recommendation text pages 140 to 143 and Discussion page 148 (Undermind read_pdfs); Beers 2023 Tables 3, 5, 6, pages 27, 31, 34 (Undermind read_pdfs)
claims.pico_timeframe: AASM: adults with RLS, trials; Beers: adults 65 and over, US
claims.safe_wording: Gabapentin and pregabalin commonly cause sleepiness and dizziness. In older people, the Beers Criteria advise a lower dose when kidney function is reduced, avoiding them alongside opioids, and avoiding three or more drugs that act on the brain together because of falls and fractures. For someone who has already fallen, weigh this carefully before starting them.
claims.qualifications: The AASM guideline itself does not mention falls or older adults; the falls link comes from Beers. Beers Table 3 names 'Antiepileptics' (Table 5 states that antiepileptics include gabapentinoids); do not say Beers bans gabapentinoids for restless legs. Beers is a US list; 'avoid' is not an absolute contraindication.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Tension between AASM (gabapentinoids recommended) and Beers (antiepileptics to be avoided after falls except for seizures or mood disorders) should be stated as a trade-off, not resolved.

numbers.meaning: kidney function at which Beers advises reducing gabapentin and pregabalin dose
number of concurrent CNS-active drugs Beers advises avoiding

claims.claim: UK guidance (NICE CKS) may still list dopamine agonists and may differ from the US guideline.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine summary (pages not opened): "The NICE CKS guidance recommends gabapentinoids as first-line treatment, with a statement that due to the high incidence of augmentation and the risk of impulse control disorders, dopamine agonists should not be first-line treatment." "Iron replacement therapy is recommended if serum ferritin is below 75 micrograms/L".
claims.pico_timeframe: UK primary care guidance; date not established
