of US women aged 45+ with accidental bowel leakage in the past year had ever talked to a physician about it (Brown 2013)

claims.claim: Many people prefer the words 'accidental bowel leakage' or 'accidents', and guidance tells health professionals to ask about it directly.
claims.supporting_passage: Brown 2012: "Among 938 respondents with FI, 71.1% (667) preferred the term 'accidental bowel leakage' (ABL) over faecal or bowel incontinence." Assmann (UEG): "When FI is suspected, health care professionals should take it upon themselves to ask the patient whether they suffer from FI, rather than waiting for the patient to mention this problem." "Direct questioning rather than talking around the issue should be aimed for when talking about FI." "Asking the patient about their unwanted loss of faeces should be done in a sensitive manner, cultural preferences for wording should be taken into account (e.g. ‘accidents’, ‘unwanted loss of faeces’, etc.)."
claims.location: Brown 2012: Abstract; Assmann 2022: full text, Diagnosis, History taking
claims.pico_timeframe: US women 45+ with leakage (internet survey 2009-10); European guideline for all adults with FI (expert opinion)
claims.safe_wording: In a US survey of women aged 45 and over with leakage, 7 in 10 preferred the words 'accidental bowel leakage' to 'faecal incontinence'. European guidance tells doctors and nurses to ask about bowel leakage directly, rather than wait for you to raise it, and to use words like 'accidents'.
claims.qualifications: The asking-directly advice is expert opinion (the guideline says its diagnosis recommendations are mainly expert opinion). The word-preference finding is from US women only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None identified.

numbers.meaning: of US women aged 45+ with bowel leakage preferred the term 'accidental bowel leakage'

claims.claim: Common, checkable causes include loose stools, constipation with overflow, damage to the anal sphincter (for example from childbirth or surgery) and faecal impaction; leakage is also linked with urinary incontinence, multiple chronic illnesses and neurological conditions.
claims.supporting_passage: Assmann (UEG): "Bowel habit should be thoroughly assessed to ensure diarrhoea and overflow constipation are not the cause for the unwanted loss of faeces." "The patient should be asked about any possible underlying reason for the presence of FI and about their obstetric history (in women)." "Inspection and physical examination of the anorectal region should be performed to exclude other anorectal pathology, to assess for previous perianal surgery/trauma and faecal impaction and to evaluate anal state/tone at rest and during voluntary effort." "Any patient group with FI with any type of neurological disease and/or cognitive impairment, whether mild or severe (e.g., Dementia, Parkinson, Spinal Cord Injury, Stroke etc.) were included in this section." Whitehead: "Independent risk factors in women are advancing age, loose or watery stools, more than 21 stools per week, multiple chronic illnesses, and urinary incontinence. Independent risk factors in men are age, loose or watery stools, poor self-rated health, and urinary incontinence." "Chronic diarrhea is a strong modifiable risk factor that may form the basis for prevention and treatment." Brown 2012: "Bowel disorders, urinary incontinence, stroke, age 55-64, diabetes mellitus and prior vaginal delivery were associated with an increased odds of FI"
claims.location: Assmann 2022: full text, Diagnosis (History taking; Physical examination) and Special situations; Whitehead 2009: Abstract; Brown 2012: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with FI (guideline assessment); US adults 20+ (risk factors, cross-sectional, adjusted associations); US women 45+
claims.safe_wording: A GP or nurse will ask about your usual bowel pattern, because loose stools and constipation with leakage around hard stool are common causes that can be treated. Women are asked about childbirth, and anyone about past surgery near the back passage. A gentle examination checks the muscle and looks for hard stool. Leakage is also more common in people with bladder leakage and in people with conditions such as stroke.
claims.qualifications: Risk factors from surveys are associations, not proven causes; use 'linked with' for them. Do not list medicines as a cause: no opened source states it (NICE CG49 was not opened). 'Neurological conditions' comes from the guideline's description of a population group, plus the stroke association in Brown 2012.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None that changes the reading.

claims.claim: First-line treatments include diet and fibre advice, a toilet routine, fibre supplements or anti-diarrhoea medicine such as loperamide, pelvic floor exercises, and pads and skin care; many people improve with these simple steps, and further treatments exist if they do not work.
claims.supporting_passage: "First line treatment includes lifestyle adjustments, dietary advice (fibre and water intake, possibly reduction of caffeine and FODMAP intake), basic behavioural advice (toilet routine/bowel training), stool bulking agents and/or anti‐diarrheal medication, pelvic floor muscle exercises, absorbent products for containment and possibly skin care products to treat irritation of the skin around the anus." "Fibre supplementation, especially Psyllium helps reduce FI episodes." "Anti‐diarrheal medication has a positive impact on diarrheal and/or FI symptoms." "Loperamide is not significantly better in reducing FI complaints compared to Psyllium." "Constipation was the most common adverse event for loperamide use (29.1%)" "No significant differences were found between any of the groups in mean number of FI episodes per week (= 0.51 KW), severity of FI (St. Mark's) (= 0.54 KW) or quality of life (QoL) (numerical data not available) after 1 year follow‐up, however both groups improved in all outcomes compared to baseline" "An education pamphlet regarding FI may be effective in treatment of FI. Results should be interpreted with caution." "Biofeedback may not be superior to education only." "In patients where initial first line treatment has not resulted in acceptable symptom reduction additional diagnostic test could be considered prior to starting second line treatment."
claims.location: Assmann 2022: full text, First line treatment for faecal incontinence (Introduction, evidence summaries); Diagnostic tests prior to second line treatment
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with FI / first-line conservative measures / placebo, education or each other / FI episodes, severity, QoL / trials of weeks to 1 year
claims.safe_wording: First steps a GP or nurse can offer: advice on food, fibre and drinks; a regular toilet routine; a fibre supplement, or a medicine that firms up loose stools such as loperamide; pelvic floor exercises; and pads and skin care. Many people improve with these simple steps. If they don't help enough, there are further tests and treatments.
claims.qualifications: Evidence for each first step is modest: psyllium fibre reduced leakage compared with placebo; loperamide worked about as well as psyllium and can cause constipation (about 3 in 10 in one trial); in trials, education and advice alone did about as well as pelvic floor exercises or biofeedback. Do not say pelvic floor exercises are proven better than advice.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The Norton 2003 trial had no untreated control group, so improvement with education alone may partly reflect natural change.

numbers.meaning: constipation as an adverse event with loperamide in the Markland 2015 crossover trial of 80 people, as reported in the guideline

claims.claim: The TOPSY trial randomised 340 women using a vaginal pessary for prolapse at 21 UK NHS centres to self-management (30-minute teaching session, leaflet, phone call at 2 weeks, helpline) or usual clinic-based care (clinic changes about every 6 months).

claims.claim: In a cluster randomised trial of 2152 residents in 14 US nursing homes, the Mouth Care Without a Battle programme did not significantly reduce pneumonia over two years (0.67 vs 0.72 per 1000 resident-days); pneumonia was non-significantly higher in programme homes in year two; a post hoc first-year analysis found a reduction.
claims.supporting_passage: "This pragmatic cluster randomized trial observing 2152 NH residents for up to 2 years was conducted from September 2014 to May 2017. ... The study included 14 NHs from regions of North Carolina that evidenced proportionately high rehospitalization rates for pneumonia and long-term care residents." ... "During the 2-year study period, the incidence rate of pneumonia per 1000 resident-days was 0.67 and 0.72 in the intervention and control NHs, respectively. Neither the primary (unadjusted) nor secondary (covariate-adjusted) analyses found a significant reduction in pneumonia due to Mouth Care Without a Battle during 2 years (unadjusted incidence rate ratio, 0.90; upper bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 1.24; P = .27; adjusted incidence rate ratio, 0.92; upper bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 1.27; P = .30). In the second year, the rate of pneumonia was nonsignificantly higher in intervention NHs. Adjusted post hoc analyses limited to the first year found a significant reduction in pneumonia incidence in intervention NHs (IRR, 0.69; upper bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 0.94; P = .03)." ... "The lack of significant results in the second year may be associated with sustainability. Improving mouth care in US NHs may require the presence and support of dedicated oral care aides."
claims.location: Abstract: Design, Setting and Participants; Results; Conclusions and Relevance
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 2152 residents, 14 North Carolina nursing homes with high pneumonia rehospitalisation; I: Mouth Care Without a Battle (staff training programme); C: standard mouth care; O: pneumonia incidence from medical records (primary), hospitalisation and mortality (secondary); T: up to 2 years
claims.safe_wording: A mouth care training programme was tested in 14 US nursing homes with 2,152 residents. Over two years it did not show a clear fall in pneumonia: 0.67 cases per 1,000 days residents spent in the homes, against 0.72 without the programme. A later look at the first year alone found fewer pneumonias, but that analysis was not planned in advance, and in the second year pneumonia was slightly (not significantly) more common in the programme homes.
claims.qualifications: Say 'did not show a clear fall', not 'had no effect'. Give the post hoc first-year signal with its status (not planned). The authors link the fade in year two to difficulty keeping the programme going, which supports 'sustaining mouth care is hard', not 'mouth care does not work'. Homes were chosen for high pneumonia rehospitalisation rates.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Post hoc first-year reduction (IRR 0.69) and earlier Japanese trials (Yoneyama 2002) point the other way. The trial tested a staff training programme in routine conditions, not the effect of a clean mouth itself.

claims.claim: In 524 community-living people aged 85 and over (453 denture wearers), about 4 in 10 denture wearers slept in their dentures; overnight wearing was independently associated with a higher risk of hospitalisation for or death from pneumonia over 3 years.
claims.supporting_passage: "At baseline, 524 randomly selected seniors (228 men and 296 women; mean age, 87.8 years) were examined for oral health status and oral hygiene behaviors as well as medical assessment, including blood chemistry analysis, and followed up annually until first hospitalization for or death from pneumonia. During a 3-year follow-up period, 48 events associated with pneumonia (20 deaths and 28 acute hospitalizations) were identified. Among 453 denture wearers, 186 (40.8%) who wore their dentures during sleep were at higher risk for pneumonia than those who removed their dentures at night (log rank P = 0.021). In a multivariate Cox model, both perceived swallowing difficulties and overnight denture wearing were independently associated with an approximately 2.3-fold higher risk of the incidence of pneumonia (for perceived swallowing difficulties, hazard ratio [HR], 2.31; and 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.11-4.82; and for denture wearing during sleep, HR, 2.38; and 95% CI, 1.25-4.56)"

claims.safe_wording: In a Japanese study of 524 people aged 85 and over living at home, about 4 in 10 denture wearers slept with their dentures in. Over three years, they were more likely to be admitted to hospital with pneumonia, or to die of it, than those who took their dentures out, even after the researchers allowed for other health differences they measured. This link does not prove that sleeping in dentures causes pneumonia.

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Lim 2024 meta-analysis (6 non-randomised studies) found no conclusive evidence that wearing removable dentures at all is a risk factor for pneumonia; it did not isolate overnight wear. No trial has tested overnight removal against pneumonia.

Refusals did not stop, and over three weeks the trial did not show a clear difference in mouth health.
claims.qualifications: Say 'more often' or (practitioners) 'twice the odds'; never 'twice as likely' (the authors' own discussion uses that phrase, but the analysis gives odds). Results are per mouth care session, so 'more residents accepted' is not accurate; use 'mouth care was accepted more often'. Primary outcomes were not met; the positive findings are secondary. Care was given by trained research staff, not the homes' own staff; people with swallowing difficulty were excluded; three weeks only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Real-world effect when delivered by care home staff is untested in this trial (authors planned a staff implementation study). Assent and completion percentages by group are in tables not returned by the tool.

numbers.meaning: residents randomised (55 experimental, 46 control); 100 analysed
US nursing homes
odds of assenting to, and of completing, mouth care per session, experimental vs control; relative; not 'twice as likely'
extra average increase in mouth care duration in the experimental group (baseline about 2.6 minutes)
small, non-significant differences in resistance intensity and oral health score
intervention period after a 1-week observation period

claims.claim: MOUTh techniques include approaching at eye level, working at a sink and mirror, avoiding elderspeak, cueing with gestures and short commands, bridging (the person holds a toothbrush), chaining (start the task and let the person finish), distraction, hand-over-hand guidance and 'rescue' by a second carer.
claims.supporting_passage: Jablonski 2018 full text, Methods 2.3: "These strategies included: establishing rapport by approaching the resident at or below eye level with a pleasant and calm demeanor; providing mouth care in front of a sink and in front of a mirror (to access procedural or implicit memories); avoiding elderspeak, a type of sing-song “baby talk”; chaining, which involved starting the mouth care and having the older adult finish the task; cueing by using gestures, pantomimes, and short, 1-step commands; distraction; bridging, where the older adult was asked to hold a toothbrush during mouth care; rescue, where a second experimental mouth care provider replaced the first experimental mouth care provider if care-resistant behaviors were escalating; and hand-over-hand, which involved either the older adult placing his or hand over that of the experimental mouth care provider, or the experimental mouth care provider gently guiding the older adult’s hands.The experimental mouth care providers were expected to select strategies on a trial and error basis." Jablonski 2011: "Nurses can safely and effectively provide mouth care to persons with dementia who resist care by using personalized combinations of 15 threat reduction strategies."
claims.location: Jablonski 2018 full text, Methods 2.3 Intervention description; Jablonski 2011 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Description of the intervention as delivered in the trial
claims.safe_wording: The techniques included: coming to the person at or below eye level, calmly; doing mouth care at a sink in front of a mirror; giving the person a toothbrush to hold; starting the brushing and letting them carry on; using gestures and short, one-step instructions; gently guiding their hand; and, if things escalate, letting a different carer take over. Carers tried different techniques to find what worked for each person.
claims.qualifications: The trial tested the package, not each technique separately; do not claim any single technique is proven. Using these in a comic is fine if labelled illustrative.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

numbers.meaning: threat-reduction strategies described in the 2011 practice paper (the 2018 trial lists nine named strategies)

claims.claim: The trial authors concluded that managing refusal may be more realistic than eliminating it.
claims.supporting_passage: "The data suggest that this intervention facilitates mouth care among persons with dementia. The management of refusal behaviour may be a clinically more realistic approach than reducing or eradicating refusals."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C13-26-a
claims.safe_wording: The researchers concluded that the aim is to get mouth care done despite some refusal, not to make refusal disappear.
claims.qualifications: Authors' interpretation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Resisting mouth care is often a response to feeling threatened.
claims.supporting_passage: "Care-resistant behavior is a fear-evoked response to nurses' unintentionally threatening behavior during mouth care."
claims.pico_timeframe: Theoretical framework (threat perception), not a measured finding
claims.safe_wording: The approach is built on the idea that pushing a toothbrush away is often fear: having someone put something in your mouth can feel like a threat if you are unable to follow what is happening.
claims.qualifications: This is the authors' theoretical basis, not a trial result; present it as the idea behind the approach. Word it so no carer is blamed (values concern: the source's 'unintentionally threatening behavior' should not become criticism of care workers).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None tested directly.

claims.claim: NICE guidance on care of dying adults (NG31) advises supporting people to drink if they wish and are able, offering frequent mouth and lip care, encouraging family to help if they wish, and assessing and discussing clinically assisted hydration person by person.
claims.supporting_passage: "Support the dying person to drink if they wish to and are able to. Check for any difficulties, such as swallowing problems or risk of aspiration. Discuss the risks and benefits of continuing to drink with the dying person and those involved in the dying person's care." "Encourage people important to the dying person to help with mouth and lip care or giving drinks, if they wish to. Provide any necessary aids and give them advice on giving drinks safely." "Assess, preferably daily, the dying person's hydration status, and review the possible need for starting or continuing clinically assisted hydration, respecting the person's wishes and preferences." "Offer frequent care of the mouth and lips to the dying person, and include the management of dry mouth in their care plan, if needed." "Consider a therapeutic trial of clinically assisted hydration if the person has or is at risk of distressing symptoms or signs that could be associated with dehydration, such as thirst or delirium, and if oral hydration is inadequate." "...review the risks and benefits of continuing clinically assisted hydration with the person and those important to them continue if there are signs of clinical benefit and reduce or stop if there are signs of possible harm to the dying person, such as fluid overload, or if they no longer want it." "The evidence for clinically assisted hydration varied from moderate to very low quality."
claims.location: Clin Med 2016 concise guideline, Box 1 Recommendations (Maintaining hydration) and commentary; full-text excerpts via Scite
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in the last days of life, UK, all settings; guideline published 2015
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance from NICE on the last days of life says: help the person drink if they want to and can; offer frequent care of the mouth and lips; and encourage family to help with mouth care or drinks if they wish, with advice on doing it safely. It says fluids by drip or under the skin should be considered and reviewed for each person, for example if they have distressing thirst and are unable to drink enough, and stopped if they cause harm or the person no longer wants them.
claims.qualifications: NG31 dates from 2015; whether it has been updated could not be checked (NICE site not reachable). The guidance does not say assisted hydration is never appropriate; the post must keep the 'therapeutic trial' option. Mention that 'delirium' appears in the recommendation only if quoting; delirium is not the post's topic.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: NICE rates the evidence on clinically assisted hydration as moderate to very low quality.

numbers.meaning: NICE: monitor people on clinically assisted hydration at least this often for benefit or harm (practitioner detail)

claims.claim: In 32 terminally ill patients in a comfort care unit, most had no hunger or thirst or only at first, and in all patients hunger, thirst and dry mouth could be relieved, usually with small amounts of food and fluid, ice chips and lip lubrication, using far less fluid than needed to prevent dehydration.
claims.supporting_passage: "Ten-bed comfort care unit in a 471-bed long-term care facility." "Mentally aware, competent patients with terminal illnesses monitored from time of admission to time of death while residing in the comfort care unit." "Of the 32 patients monitored during the 12 months of study, 20 patients (63%) never experienced any hunger, while 11 patients (34%) had symptoms only initially. Similarly, 20 patients (62%) experienced either no thirst or thirst only initially during their terminal illness. In all patients, symptoms of hunger, thirst, and dry mouth could be alleviated, usually with small amounts of food, fluids, and/or by the application of ice chips and lubrication to the lips." "In this series, patients terminally ill with cancer generally did not experience hunger and those who did needed only small amounts of food for alleviation. Complaints of thirst and dry mouth were relieved with mouth care and sips of liquids far less than that needed to prevent dehydration."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 32 mentally aware, competent terminally ill patients (described as terminally ill with cancer) in a US comfort care unit; no comparator; O: hunger, thirst, dry mouth and what relieved them; T: admission to death, 12-month study, early 1990s
claims.safe_wording: In a small US study of 32 people dying in a comfort care unit, described by the authors as terminally ill with cancer, thirst and a dry mouth were relieved in every case, usually by mouth care, ice chips, moistening the lips and sips of drink. The amounts were far smaller than would be needed to prevent dehydration.
claims.qualifications: Small (32), old (1994), single unit, no comparison group, people able to report symptoms, almost all on opioids. Say it is one small study; do not generalise to all dying older people. 'Usually' belongs to the relief method, not to 'in every case'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No direct comparison with assisted hydration in this study. Evidence in people dying with dementia or frailty is lacking (see C13-11-d).

numbers.meaning: patients followed from admission to death
had no thirst, or thirst only at first
never hungry; hungry only at first
hunger, thirst and dry mouth could be relieved
received opioids for pain or breathlessness

claims.claim: In a hospice RCT of 129 people with advanced cancer, 1 litre a day of parenteral fluid did not improve dehydration symptoms, quality of life or survival compared with 100 mL.
claims.supporting_passage: "We randomly assigned 129 patients with cancer from six hospices to receive parenteral hydration (normal saline 1 L per day) or placebo (normal saline 100 mL per day) daily over 4 hours. The primary outcome was change in the sum of four dehydration symptoms (fatigue, myoclonus, sedation and hallucinations, 0 = best and 40 = worst possible) between day 4 and baseline." ... "We found no significant differences between the two groups for change in the sum of four dehydration symptoms (-3.3 v -2.8, P = .77)" ... "Overall survival did not differ between the two groups (median, 21 v 15 days, P = .83)." "Hydration at 1 L per day did not improve symptoms, quality of life, or survival compared with placebo."
claims.location: Abstract: Patients and Methods; Results; Conclusion
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 129 adults with advanced cancer in 6 US hospices; I: 1 L/day saline over 4 hours; C: 100 mL/day; O: fatigue, myoclonus, sedation, hallucinations (primary), symptom scales, quality of life, survival; T: day 4 and day 7
claims.safe_wording: In a trial in six US hospices, 129 people with advanced cancer were given either a litre of fluid a day under the skin or into a vein, or a token 100 mL. The larger amount did not show a clear improvement in symptoms, quality of life or survival.
claims.qualifications: Cancer only. Many were not in their last days (median survival 15 to 21 days). The trial's 'dehydration symptoms' were fatigue, twitching, drowsiness and hallucinations, not thirst or dry mouth, so it does not show that drips fail to relieve thirst. Say 'did not show a clear improvement', not 'no effect'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The 2023 Cochrane review found one other trial (200 participants) suggesting longer survival with hydration vs standard care, at very low certainty (C13-11-d).

numbers.meaning: hospice patients with advanced cancer randomised (63 hydration, 66 placebo)
saline per day over 4 hours
survival, hydration vs placebo, not significantly different

claims.claim: Evidence on clinically assisted hydration near death comes almost entirely from people with cancer and is very low certainty; it does not transfer to dementia or other non-cancer conditions.
claims.supporting_passage: "We identified one new study (200 participants), for a total of four studies included in this update (422 participants). All participants had a diagnosis of advanced cancer." ... "We are uncertain whether MAH improves survival (HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.59; 1 study, 200 participants, very low-certainty evidence)." ... "In adults receiving palliative care in the end stage of their illness, there remains insufficient evidence to determine whether MAH improves QoL or prolongs survival, compared with placebo or standard care. Given that all participants were inpatients with advanced cancer at end of life, our findings are not transferable to adults receiving palliative care in other settings, for non-cancer, dementia or neurodegenerative diseases, or for those with an extended prognosis. Clinicians will need to make decisions based on the perceived benefits and harms of MAH for each individual's circumstances, without the benefit of high-quality evidence to guide them."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: adults receiving palliative care, all with advanced cancer (4 RCTs, 422 participants); I: medically assisted hydration; C: placebo or standard care; O: quality of life, survival, adverse events; T: days to weeks
claims.safe_wording: The trials on drips near the end of life were all in people with cancer, and a 2023 Cochrane review found too little evidence to say whether they improve comfort or prolong life. The reviewers say the results do not apply to people dying with dementia or other conditions, so the decision has to be made for each person.
claims.qualifications: An evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit. Keep the post from implying drips are never right.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: One trial (200 participants) vs standard care suggested longer survival with hydration (HR 0.36) but very low certainty, and adverse events were more common (RR 11.62, very low certainty).

numbers.meaning: all adults with advanced cancer
survival, hydration vs standard care, 1 trial, 200 participants, very low certainty; do not use in public posts

claims.claim: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies in people aged 60 and over, bladder (urological) medicines, antidepressants and psycholeptics were associated with dry mouth in intervention studies, and the number of medicines was associated with dry mouth in observational studies; risk was greatest for drugs for urinary incontinence.
claims.supporting_passage: "Older people (aged ≥60) who participated in intervention or observational studies investigating drug use as an exposure and xerostomia or salivary gland hypofunction as adverse drug outcomes." ... "Of 1,544 potentially relevant studies, 52 were deemed eligible for inclusion in the final review and 26 in metaanalyses. The majority of studies were of moderate methodological quality. In the intervention studies, urological medications (odds ratio (OR) = 5.91, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 4.04-8.63; I = 62%), antidepressants (OR = 4.74, 95% CI = 2.69-8.32, I = 21%), and psycholeptics (OR = 2.59, 95% CI = 1.79-3.95, I = 0%) were significantly associated with dry mouth. In the observational studies, numbers of medications and several medication classes were significantly associated with xerostomia and salivary gland hypofunction." "Medication use was significantly associated with xerostomia and salivary gland hypofunction in older adults. The risk of dry mouth was greatest for drugs used for urinary incontinence."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: people aged 60+; E: specific drug classes or number of medicines; C: placebo/comparator (intervention studies) or non-users (observational); O: xerostomia or reduced saliva flow; literature 1990 to 2016
claims.safe_wording: A review of 52 studies in people aged 60 and over found dry mouth was linked with several kinds of medicine. The link was strongest for bladder medicines taken for leaking urine, and antidepressants were also linked. The more medicines people took, the more often they had a dry mouth.
claims.qualifications: Use 'linked with' (the review reports associations, per the editor's guidance). No absolute rates are available: do not give numbers to the public, and never turn the odds ratios into 'X times more likely'. Name at most one or two drug types in plain words; 'psycholeptics' is a WHO drug-classification group, and any plain gloss of it comes from that classification, not from the abstract.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneity for urological drugs (I2 62%); most studies moderate quality.

numbers.meaning: included in review
odds of dry mouth with urological drugs, antidepressants, psycholeptics vs comparison in intervention studies; relative; practitioners only

claims.claim: Saliva protects teeth, and a dry mouth increases the risk of tooth decay; it also makes chewing, swallowing, taste and denture wearing harder.
claims.supporting_passage: Plemons 2014: "Chronic xerostomia significantly increases the risk of experiencing dental caries, demineralization, tooth sensitivity, candidiasis and other oral diseases that may affect quality of life negatively." Müller 2023 (Abstract): "These conditions negatively affect oral functions, such as chewing, swallowing, speech, and taste. Additionally, the lack of lubrication of the oral mucosa frequently leads to super-infections with candida. Denture retention and comfort may also be compromised. The risk of dental caries and erosion of natural teeth increases since saliva, which is essential for repairing initial lesions in tooth structures, is insufficient." Müller 2023 (Introduction): "Saliva plays a vital role in maintaining the health of hard and soft tissues in the oral cavity. It helps remove food debris, neutralize acids, and protect against bacterial infections, thereby preventing dental caries, periodontal disease, and mucositis"
claims.location: Plemons 2014 Abstract; Müller 2023 Abstract and Introduction (full text)
claims.pico_timeframe: Professional guidance and narrative review; background physiology
claims.safe_wording: Saliva washes the mouth, neutralises acid and helps repair early damage to teeth. When the mouth is dry, tooth decay becomes more likely, and chewing, swallowing, tasting food and keeping dentures in place can all get harder.
claims.qualifications: Dental professional guidance (US) and a narrative review; widely agreed, not a new finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None material.

claims.claim: Sucking sugary sweets to relieve dryness increases decay risk; sugar-free gum or lozenges and sips of water are preferred.
claims.supporting_passage: Müller 2023: "Sucking lozenges should not be too acidic or contain sugar, as the latter increases the risk of caries and tooth loss." "Salivation can also be stimulated by sucking on sweets, although sour drops may cause dental erosion and are therefore less suitable than aromatic lozenges or liquorice. Care should also be taken to ensure that they contain no sugar to prevent the development of tooth decay." "it is unfortunate that all chewing gums presently accessible on the market adhere to denture acrylic, thus rendering the act of chewing exceptionally arduous." "Hence, the derived recommendations listed inandare non-exhaustive and not based on scientific evidence". Plemons 2014: "It also should focus on various palliative and preventive measures, including pharmacological treatment with salivary stimulants, topical fluoride interventions and the use of sugar-free chewing gum to relieve dry-mouth symptoms and improve the patient's quality of life."
claims.location: Müller 2023 full text, sections 9 and 10; Plemons 2014 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Expert recommendations; not trial evidence
claims.safe_wording: Dental advice for a dry mouth is to take frequent sips of water and, if you still have your own teeth, to use sugar-free gum or sugar-free lozenges. Sucking sugary sweets for relief raises the risk of tooth decay.
claims.qualifications: Expert advice, not trial evidence (Müller et al. say their dietary recommendations are not evidence-based). Gum sticks to dentures, so suggest it for people with their own teeth. Saliva sprays: Müller mentions artificial saliva after discussion with a dentist or doctor; keep 'ask which saliva spray or gel suits you'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: An umbrella review (Conte 2025, seen only in Consensus search, not opened) rated most reviews of dry mouth treatments low quality; relief from substitutes is short-lived.

claims.claim: If a medicine may be causing dry mouth, it is reasonable to ask a GP or pharmacist to review it.
claims.supporting_passage: Müller 2023: "The European Society of Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) guideline in geriatrics acknowledges this risk [,]. In cases of malnutrition or risk of malnutrition, this guideline provides guidance for nutritional support and recommends strategies such as reducing or replacing medications that contribute to xerostomia." Plemons 2014: "A systematic approach to xerostomia management can facilitate interdisciplinary patient care, including collaboration with physicians regarding systemic conditions and medication use."
claims.location: Müller 2023 full text, section 8; Plemons 2014 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Guidance statements (ESPEN via secondary report; ADA)
claims.safe_wording: If your mouth is often dry, ask your GP or pharmacist whether any of your medicines could be the cause, whether each one is still needed, and whether there is an alternative. Do not stop a medicine on your own.
claims.qualifications: ESPEN recommendation is reported second-hand by Müller 2023 and applies to people with or at risk of malnutrition; the ADA summary recommends collaboration on medication use. 'Do not stop a medicine on your own' is standard safety advice, not from these sources.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial shows that deprescribing relieves dry mouth in older people; not searched further.

claims.claim: In a study of nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease in long-term care, mean food intake was 25% higher and mean liquid intake 84% higher with high-contrast red tableware than with white tableware, and 8 of 9 men increased their intake.
claims.supporting_passage: Participants were nine men with advanced AD. ... Data were collected for 30 days (10 days per condition) for two meals per day. White tableware was used for the baseline and post-intervention conditions, and high-contrast red tableware for the intervention condition. ... Mean percent increase was 25% for food and 84% for liquid for the high-contrast intervention (red) versus baseline (white) condition, with 8 of 9 participants exhibiting increased intake. [Gaffney 2026, Limitations:] Dunne et al. [] attempted to measure acuity colour discrimination and visual contrast; however, none of the participants could complete the assessments.
claims.location: Dunne 2004 Abstract (Methods, Results); Gaffney 2026 full text section 4.2
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 9 men, advanced Alzheimer's disease, long-term care, USA. I: high-contrast red tableware (10 days). C: white tableware before and after (10 days each). O: grams of food, ounces of liquid at lunch and supper. T: 30 days.
claims.safe_wording: In a 2004 study, nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease living in long-term care ate about a quarter more food and drank much more (84% more on average) during 10 days with high-contrast red plates and cups than during 10 days with white ones. Eight of the nine ate or drank more.
claims.qualifications: Nine men only; no randomisation (white, then red, then white, the same men throughout); 10 days per condition; relative increases in average intake, not absolute amounts; no weight or health outcomes. Do not call it 'the best-known study' (not verifiable); say it is the study that tested red tableware, or 'a 2004 study of nine men'. Do not say 'one facility' (not confirmed in the abstract); say 'in long-term care'. PubMed labels it an RCT, but the design is before-during-after.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C13-33-d (Donnelly: blue plates did not clearly increase intake). Vision was not measurable in any participant, so the mechanism is inferred.

numbers.meaning: participants, all men with advanced Alzheimer's disease
per condition (white, red, white); 30 days in total, two meals a day
mean relative increase in food intake (grams), red versus white baseline
mean relative increase in liquid intake (ounces), red versus white baseline
participants whose intake increased

claims.claim: In a follow-up a year later, high-contrast blue tableware also increased intake, while low-contrast red and low-contrast blue did not, which points to contrast rather than the colour red.
claims.supporting_passage: In a follow-up study 1 year later, other contrast conditions were examined (high-contrast blue, low-contrast red and low-contrast blue). ... In the follow-up study, the high-contrast intervention (blue) resulted in significant increases in food and liquid intake; the low-contrast red and low-contrast blue interventions were ineffectual. [Gaffney 2026:] In a follow-up study a year later, they used high-contrast blue tableware with low-contrast (pastel) red and low-contrast blue tableware [].
claims.location: Dunne 2004 Abstract (Methods, Results); Gaffney 2026 full text section 3.5
claims.pico_timeframe: Same research group and setting, 1 year later; high-contrast blue versus low-contrast (pastel) red and low-contrast blue tableware; food and liquid intake.
claims.safe_wording: A year later the same team tried other plates. Strongly contrasting blue plates also increased eating and drinking; pale red and pale blue plates did not. That points to contrast between food and plate, not to redness.
claims.qualifications: Same small study; the abstract does not give the number of participants in the follow-up or confirm they were the same men. Say 'points to', not 'shows'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Donnelly (in Gaffney 2026) found no significant improvement with blue versus white dishware when meals included low-contrast foods; Gaffney notes 'no strong consensus on which specific colours or tableware types are most effective'.

numbers.meaning: interval between the original study and the follow-up

claims.claim: A 2026 systematic review found only four small studies of visual contrast at meals (64 participants in all), none randomised, and judged the evidence limited, low quality and inconclusive; it is not established that high-contrast tableware improves nutrition.
claims.supporting_passage: Of 2901 records screened, four studies (five reports) met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 64 participants. ... Limited and low-quality evidence suggests a possible effect of modifying the dining environment to improve visual contrast for enhancing dietary intake in older adults, with visual contrast sensitivity, particularly those with dementia. However, the evidence gap is large and remains inconclusive. [Full text:] A total of 64 participants were included across the studies; sample sizes were small, ranging from 9 to 25. ... The studies consisted of mixed methods (= 1) and non-randomised quantitative designs (= 4). ... with the longest test period lasting 30 days. ... MMAT scores ranged from 40 to 60%. ... this review has identified a clear evidence gap instead of establishing the effectiveness of visual contrast interventions. ... Although the studies included in this review have demonstrated increases in food intakes, it remains unclear whether these translate to meaningful outcomes in the long term, such as reduced prevalence of malnutrition, reduced unintentional weight loss, or optimised nutritional status among older adults in long-term aged care.
claims.location: Gaffney 2026 Abstract; full text sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4 and 4.3
claims.pico_timeframe: P: adults 65+ (in practice, long-term care residents with dementia). I: visual contrast (tableware, tablecloths, lighting). C: usual tableware or baseline. O: food or fluid intake; weight/malnutrition not reported. T: longest 30 days. Search to March 2025.
claims.safe_wording: A 2026 review of all the studies it could find on contrast at mealtimes found four, with 64 people in total, the largest with 25. None was randomised and none lasted more than a month. The reviewers called the evidence limited, low quality and inconclusive, and none of the studies showed whether contrast plates prevent weight loss or malnutrition.
claims.qualifications: An evidence gap is not evidence of no effect: most studies reported more eating, though statistical significance varied. Do not say contrast plates 'don't work'. 'Harmless' or 'no downside' is not established by any source here; if used, frame as judgement (for example 'cheap to try').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The review's authors see 'a possible effect' and call a 25% increase clinically important despite n=9; the uncertainty is about size and durability, not direction alone.

numbers.meaning: all studies meeting inclusion criteria to March 2025
participants across all four studies
range of study sizes
longest test period in any included study
MMAT quality scores (higher is better, maximum 100%)

claims.claim: Another study of blue versus white dishware in people with dementia did not show a clear increase in food intake.
claims.supporting_passage: In comparison, Donnelly et al. [] reported that the average number of participant observations was 19 ± 2 meals and found that only less than a third (28%) of participants increased intake by at least 10% during the intervention periods when blue tableware was used. ... Donnelly et al. [] challenged this, finding no significant improvement in food intake with blue dishware compared to white in meals containing low-contrast foods, like mashed potato and white rice, indicating that colour alone may not be sufficient to improve dietary intake.
claims.pico_timeframe: Donnelly et al. (as reported in the review; primary paper not opened): 18 people with dementia, crossover blue versus white dishware, menu with more low-contrast foods; food intake.
claims.safe_wording: A later study of blue plates in 18 people with dementia did not find a clear increase in eating; fewer than a third ate at least a tenth more.
claims.qualifications: Reported via the systematic review; the Donnelly primary paper was not opened. Use as the result that went the other way, stated as plainly as the Dunne headline.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small study; not statistically significant, which is not proof of no effect.

numbers.meaning: participants in Donnelly who increased intake by at least 10% with blue tableware
participants with dementia in Donnelly (per Gaffney: 'Donnelly had double the participants (= 18, five males)')

claims.claim: More broadly, systematic reviews have not established any specific mealtime environment change, or form of eating assistance, as effective for people with dementia.
claims.supporting_passage: [Herke 2018:] We included nine studies, investigating 1502 people. ... The overall quality of evidence was mainly low to very low. ... Due to the quantity and quality of the evidence currently available, we cannot identify any specific environmental or behavioural modifications for improving food and fluid intake in people with dementia. [Abdelhamid 2016:] Forty-three controlled interventions were included, disappointingly none were judged at low risk of bias. ... Eating assistance studies provided inconsistent evidence ... We found no definitive evidence on effectiveness, or lack of effectiveness, of specific interventions but studies were small and short term.
claims.location: Herke 2018 Abstract (Main results, Authors' conclusions); Abdelhamid 2016 Abstract (Results, Conclusions)
claims.pico_timeframe: People with dementia or cognitive impairment, all settings; environmental, behavioural and direct eating-support interventions; food and fluid intake and nutritional status.
claims.safe_wording: Reviews of mealtime changes for people with dementia have not found any single change that is proven to help people eat more, including help with eating, because the studies are small and short.
claims.qualifications: This cuts both ways: the post's position that plates should not replace help with eating must be stated as judgement ('We should not count a plate in place of a person'), not as a finding that eating assistance is proven in dementia. Simmons 2008 (C13-36-c/d; 41 to 43% had dementia) is the nearest trial evidence that one-to-one help increases intake in nursing home residents.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Herke searched to January 2018 and included RCTs only.

numbers.meaning: Herke 2018 Cochrane review
controlled interventions in Abdelhamid 2016; none at low risk of bias

claims.claim: Of 40 well older people (over 65) tested on packs routinely used in NSW hospitals, 39% could not open cheese portions and 10% could not open water bottles; tetra packs, water bottles, cereal, fruit cups, desserts, biscuits and cheese portions were the hardest.
claims.supporting_passage: The aim of this paper was to assess the ability of well older people living in the community to open food and beverage items routinely used in NSW hospitals ... A sample of 40 older people in good health aged over 65 years from 3 community settings participated in the study. ... Tetra packs, water bottles, cereal, fruit cups, desserts, biscuits and cheese portions appeared to be the most difficult food products to open. Ten percent of the sample could not open the water bottles and 39% could not open cheese portions.
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 40 healthy community-dwelling people over 65, NSW, Australia. Exposure: packs used in NSW hospitals. O: observed success at opening, time, grip and pinch strength. Single testing session.
claims.safe_wording: In an Australian study, about 4 in 10 healthy people over 65 could not open a hospital cheese portion, and 1 in 10 could not open a bottle of water. They were well volunteers, not patients.
claims.qualifications: Well volunteers living at home, not inpatients (people who are ill are likely to find it harder, but that is inference). Australian hospital packaging; UK packs may differ and no UK study was found in this search.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; results consistent with Bell 2013 inpatient data.

claims.claim: Opening hospital packs lying in a hospital bed needed more pinch strength and finger dexterity than sitting in a chair; the authors conclude that sitting to eat helps with opening packs.
claims.supporting_passage: the present laboratory study examined the differences between participants opening a selection of products in a hospital bed and a chair. ... in a sample of well older community dwelling adults (n = 34). ... Honey sachets, cheese portions, foil sealed thickened pudding and tetra packs were the most difficult packs to open, with 15% of cheese portions unable to be opened in either the bed or chair posture. Although grip strength was consistent for each posture, pinch grips and dexterity were adversely affected by the bed posture. Lying in a hospital bed required greater pinch strength and dexterity to open packs. ... The present study demonstrates that eating in a seated posture is also advantageous for opening the food and beverage packs used in the NSW hospital food service and supports the notion that patients should sit to eat in hospital.

claims.qualifications: The abstract does not report how many more packs were opened sitting than lying; do not claim a success-rate difference. Avoid the '15%' figure, whose denominator (cheese portions attempted, per posture or combined) is unclear. The line 'eating in a seated position when in hospital has been shown to improve intake' is the authors' background statement, not this study's finding; do not use it as a finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small laboratory study in well volunteers.

numbers.meaning: healthy community-dwelling older adults tested in both bed and chair

claims.claim: The packaging studies are Australian (New South Wales) and mostly in well volunteers; packaging in UK hospitals may differ; recording unopened food as 'not accessible' rather than 'refused' is a judgement.
claims.supporting_passage: The aim of this paper was to assess the ability of well older people living in the community to open food and beverage items routinely used in NSW hospitals [Bell 2016]. ... Participants (140 mostly elderly inpatients and 64 staff members) were recruited from four local public hospitals. [Bell 2013; study conducted in the Illawarra region of NSW, Australia]
claims.pico_timeframe: Setting limitation for all three packaging studies.
claims.safe_wording: These studies were done in Australia, mostly with healthy volunteers. Packs in UK hospitals may differ, but the same kinds of portion packs are common.
claims.qualifications: The final clause ('same kinds of portion packs are common') is not sourced; omit it or mark it as observation. The action (open the packets, help the person sit up, record unopened food as not accessible) is a judgement and should read as advice, not as a trial finding; no study here tested whether opening packets increases intake.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No UK study of pack opening by older inpatients was found in a PubMed search in this batch.

claims.claim: In 74 residents of three US nursing homes given a two-day, six-meal trial of one-to-one feeding assistance, half significantly increased their food and fluid intake at meals.

Total percentage (0% to 100%) of food and fluid consumed during mealtime was estimated across 3 days during usual NH care and 2 days during the intervention. ... One half (50%) of the participants significantly increased their oral food and fluid intake during mealtime.
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 74 residents, 3 US nursing homes. I: one-to-one feeding assistance for 2 days (6 meals). C: 3 days of usual care in the same residents. O: estimated percent of food and fluid consumed. T: 5 days.
claims.safe_wording: In a 2001 US study of 74 nursing home residents, half ate and drank significantly more at meals during two days of one-to-one help.
claims.qualifications: Keep 'significantly'; the other half did not show a significant increase. Two days only, no control group, no weight outcome, US 2001.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Abdelhamid 2016 found eating assistance studies in dementia gave inconsistent evidence.

claims.claim: The one-to-one help took an average of 38 minutes per resident per meal, compared with 9 minutes of help given by nursing home staff in usual care; the help was given by research staff.
claims.supporting_passage: [Simmons 2001:] The intervention required significantly more staff time to implement (average of 38 minutes per resident/meal vs 9 minutes rendered by NH staff). ... These data suggest that it will almost certainly be necessary to both increase staffing levels and to organize staff better to produce higher quality feeding assistance during mealtimes. [Simmons 2008, Introduction, describing the group's earlier two-day studies:] These feeding assistance interventions required a significant increase in staff time from an average of less than 10 minutes to 35 minutes per resident per meal and one minute or less to 12 minutes per resident per snack. In these studies, research staff implemented the interventions for only a two-day period to determine the immediate effect of the interventions on residents’ oral food and fluid intake.

claims.pico_timeframe: As C13-36-a. Timed observation of assistance per resident per meal under usual care and under the intervention.
claims.safe_wording: The help took an average of 38 minutes per resident per meal. In usual care, nursing home staff gave about 9 minutes. The help in the study was given by the research team, not the home's own staff.
claims.qualifications: The research-staff point comes from the same authors' 2008 paper describing their earlier two-day studies (the 2001 PDF could not be opened); the 2001 abstract itself contrasts the 38 minutes with '9 minutes rendered by NH staff'. The 2008 introduction pools the earlier studies as 'less than 10 minutes to 35 minutes'; use the 2001 abstract figures (38 and 9) when citing the 2001 study, and do not mix the two.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the direction; exact minutes vary between studies (35, 38, 42).

claims.claim: In a later controlled trial (2008) in four US nursing homes, mealtime help given by trained research staff took an average of 42 minutes per person per meal, against about 5 minutes of help in usual care.
claims.supporting_passage: [Abstract:] Seventy-six long-stay NH residents at risk for unintentional weight loss. ... Research staff provided feeding assistance twice per day during or between meals, 5 days per week for 24 weeks. ... The average amount of staff time required to provide the interventions was 42 minutes per person per meal and 13 minutes per person per between-meal snack, versus usual care, during which residents received, on average, 5 minutes of assistance per person per meal and less than 1 minute per person per snack. [Results:] Research staff spent an average of 42.19 (± 19.05) minutes per person per meal providing mealtime assistance. Most often (87% of care episodes), assistance was provided one-to-one; ... The average amount of NH staff time spent providing assistance to eat during meals to residents in the control group showed no significant change during the initial 24-week or crossover phases (average < 10 minutes per person per meal at each measurement point for all meals).

claims.safe_wording: A later US trial found the same thing. Trained research staff took an average of 42 minutes per person to help with a meal, mostly one-to-one. In usual care, residents got about 5 minutes of help per meal.
claims.qualifications: The 42 minutes comes from the 19 residents who received mealtime help. Usual care: the abstract gives 5 minutes on average; results say under 10 minutes at every measurement; use 'about 5 minutes' or 'under 10 minutes', not both as separate figures. US, 2008, one region.

claims.claim: In the 2008 trial homes, day-shift staffing was 6 to 11 residents per nurse aide, and the authors state that most US nursing homes lack the nurse aide staffing to give feeding assistance to all residents who need it.
claims.supporting_passage: [Simmons 2008 Methods:] Nurse-aide level staff-to-resident ratios across the four NHs, as reported by the directors-of-nursing, ranged from 6 to 11 residents per nurse aide on the 7am to 3pm shift and 11 to 15 residents per nurse aide on the 3pm to 11pm shift. [Discussion:] Given that most U.S. NHs do not have adequate nurse aide staffing to provide feeding assistance for all residents in need, it may be more feasible in daily care practice to group residents at risk for unintentional weight loss for snack delivery at least twice daily. ... Finally, the interventions were provided by research staff. It is unknown if indigenous NH staff could maintain these interventions with sufficient consistency in daily care practice to have the same effects on residents’ oral intake, weight and BMI status.

claims.claim: In five Dutch nursing homes, 178 residents without dementia (mean age 77) were cluster randomised by ward to family style meals or usual pre-plated service for six months.

During six months the intervention group took their meals family style and the control group received the usual individual pre-plated service. [Full text, Methods:] In most Dutch nursing homes two types of care are available: psychogeriatric care for residents with dementia or chronic somatic care for patients with conditions such as stroke or Parkinson’s disease. ... [Full text, Methods:] The questionnaire consists of 50 statements, scored on a dichotomous scale (yes or no). Each subscale and the total questionnaire could be computed to a range of 0 to 100 ... A high score represents a high quality of life. [Results:] The difference in changes in quality of life between both groups was significant (6.1 units, 95% confidence interval 2.1 to 10.3 units; table 3). The intervention group remained stable (0.4, − 1.8 to 2.5) whereas the control group declined ( − 5.0, − 9.4 to − 0.6). ... Mean body weight remained relatively stable in the intervention group (0.5 kg, − 0.3 to 1.2 kg) but decreased significantly in the control group ( − 1.1, − 1.9 to − 0.2). Changes in body weight between control and intervention groups were significantly different (1.5, 0.6 to 2.4). ... For the public, avoid '6.1 units'; if used for practitioners, say '6 points on a 0 to 100 scale'. claims.claim: Family style mealtimes in the trial were a package: tablecloths and proper crockery, cooked food served in dishes on the table with choice, most residents serving themselves, staff sitting and chatting at each table, and no interruptions during meals.
claims.supporting_passage: [Table 1, Family style mealtimes:] Table dressing: Tablecloth; drinking glasses (no plastic cups); normal plates; full cutlery; napkins; subtle flower arrangements. Food services: Cooked meal served in dishes on table; menu choice between two types of vegetables, meat, and staple foods; no ready to eat sandwiches during breakfast or supper. Staff protocol: Staff sit down at tables and chat with residents; minimum of one nurse or nutrition assistant or volunteer per table; drugs handed out before start of meal; no change of staff during mealtimes ... Residents’ protocol: Balanced seating of residents (typically six per table); residents decide when food is served; most residents serve themselves, with some help from nurse or table companion; mealtimes begin when everybody is seated ... Mealtime protocol: No other activities (for example, cleaning, visits from doctor); dining room closed for visitors and healthcare providers (except where observation by healthcare giver is necessary or visitors help residents) ...
claims.location: Nijs 2006 full text, Methods (The intervention) and Table 1
claims.pico_timeframe: Description of the intervention delivered for 6 months.
claims.safe_wording: Family style meant more than shared dishes. Tables had cloths, glasses and proper plates. Food came in dishes and most residents served themselves. A member of staff sat and chatted at every table, and nothing else happened in the dining room during the meal.
claims.qualifications: The trial cannot say which part helped; do not credit self-service alone. The candidate's opening ('served themselves from shared dishes') must mention that staff sat at the table. Table 1 also lists a moment for reflection or prayer before eating; house style bans religious references, so leave it out rather than misdescribe it (the list above is a faithful partial description).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: residents per table, with at least one staff member or volunteer per table

claims.claim: For people with dementia, family style meals are listed as promising in a systematic review, but the evidence is small and not definitive.
claims.supporting_passage: [Bunn 2016:] We included 56 interventions (reported in 51 studies). Studies were small and there were no clearly effective, or clearly ineffective, interventions. Promising interventions included: eating meals with care-givers, family style meals, soothing mealtime music, constantly accessible snacks and longer mealtimes, ... We found no definitive evidence on effectiveness, or lack of effectiveness, of specific interventions but studies were small and short term. [Nijs 2006, Discussion:] Earlier research showed that residents with dementia benefit from these kinds of interventions. Although we excluded this important group, we think that our principal conclusion may be extended to all nursing home residents.
claims.location: Bunn 2016 Abstract (Results, Conclusions); Nijs 2006 full text, Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: People with cognitive impairment or dementia, all settings; indirect interventions including family style meals; food and drink intake.
claims.safe_wording: For people with dementia, a review of the studies lists family style meals as promising, but the studies are small and short, so the benefit is not proven.
claims.qualifications: Nijs's view that the result may extend to all residents is the authors' opinion, not a finding. Do not say family style meals 'work' in dementia.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Herke 2018 Cochrane (RCTs only) could not identify any specific environmental or behavioural modification for food intake in dementia.

numbers.meaning: Bunn 2016 indirect-interventions review

claims.claim: A 2021 Cochrane review found no randomised trials of tube feeding in severe dementia, only 14 non-randomised studies; studies of PEG tubes found no evidence that they help people live longer (low-certainty evidence).
claims.supporting_passage: "We found no eligible RCTs. We included fourteen controlled, non-randomised studies. All the included studies compared outcomes between groups of people who had been assigned to enteral tube feeding or oral feeding by prior decision of a healthcare professional. Some studies controlled for a range of confounding factors, but there were high or very high risks of bias due to confounding in all studies, and high or critical risks of selection bias in some studies. Four studies with 36,816 participants assessed the effect of PEG feeding on survival time. None found any evidence of effects on survival time (low-certainty evidence). Three of four studies using mixed or unspecified enteral tube feeding methods in 310 participants (227 enteral tube feeding, 83 no enteral tube feeding) found them to be associated with longer survival time. The fourth study (1386 participants: 135 enteral tube feeding, 1251 no enteral tube feeding) found no evidence of an effect. The certainty of this body of evidence is very low." Plain language summary: "We included 14 studies that included 49,714 participants. Of these, 6203 were tube-fed and 43,511 were not." ... "PEG may make no difference to how long people live (4 studies, 36,816 people)" ... "Studies of people with either PEG or nasogastric tubes showed tube feeding may increase the length of time people live (4 studies, 1696 people)"
claims.location: Abstract, Main results; Plain language summary, What did we find
claims.pico_timeframe: P: adults with severe dementia and poor intake; I: PEG, nasogastric or mixed enteral tube feeding; C: no tube (standard or enhanced oral care); O: survival time; T: varied by study; all observational (allocation by clinician decision)
claims.safe_wording: A Cochrane review in 2021 found no randomised trials of feeding tubes for people with severe dementia. In 14 observational studies, PEG tubes (a tube into the stomach through the skin) were not shown to help people live longer. The evidence is of low certainty, and a few small studies of other tube types pointed the other way.
claims.qualifications: Say 'not shown to help people live longer' or 'no evidence that', not 'does not prolong life'. All studies were observational, so sicker or different people may have received tubes. Mention that a few small studies of mixed tube types found longer survival (very low certainty) if the post discusses survival in any detail.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Three of four small studies of mixed or unspecified tube methods (310 people) found longer survival; certainty very low. Palecek 2010 notes some studies found PEG survival in dementia similar to other diagnoses. No randomised evidence exists and the review authors think randomised trials would be ethically very difficult.

controlled non-randomised studies included

claims.claim: In one large study (4,421 people), PEG feeding was linked with a higher risk of pressure ulcers; this is the only finding the Cochrane review rated as moderate certainty.
claims.supporting_passage: "One study of PEG feeding (4421 participants: 1585 PEG, 2836 no enteral tube feeding) found PEG feeding increased the risk of pressure ulcers (moderate-certainty evidence). Two of three studies reported an increase in the number of pressure ulcers in those receiving mixed or unspecified enteral tube feeding (234 participants: 88 enteral tube feeding, 146 no enteral tube feeding). The third study found no effect (very-low certainty evidence)." Plain language summary: "PEG ... leads to a small increase in the chance of developing pressure sores (1 study, 4421 people)." ... "We have moderate confidence in our finding that pressure ulcers were more common in people who were fed with a PEG tube. However, we have little to very little confidence for our other findings."
claims.location: Abstract, Main results; Plain language summary, Main results and limitations
claims.pico_timeframe: P: people with severe dementia; I: PEG feeding (1585); C: no tube feeding (2836); O: pressure ulcers; observational, single study
claims.safe_wording: In the largest study (4,421 people), pressure sores were more common in people fed through a PEG tube. The review rated this finding as moderate certainty and described the increase as small.
claims.qualifications: One observational study; the review calls the increase 'small' in plain language, so do not dramatise it. The absolute rates are not in the abstract; do not give numbers per 100.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: For mixed tube types, 2 of 3 small studies found more pressure ulcers and 1 found no effect (very low certainty).

numbers.meaning: participants in the single PEG pressure ulcer study (1,585 PEG, 2,836 no tube)
GRADE rating for this finding only

claims.claim: The balance of evidence suggested more pneumonia with tube feeding (Davies 2021).
claims.supporting_passage: Davies 2021: "Five studies reported a variety of harm-related outcomes with inconsistent results. The balance of evidence suggested increased risk of pneumonia with enteral tube feeding." AGS 2014: "Careful hand feeding should be offered because hand feeding has been shown to be as good as tube feeding for the outcomes of death, aspiration pneumonia, functional status, and comfort."
claims.location: Davies 2021 Abstract, Main results; AGS 2014 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Five observational studies with inconsistent harm outcomes; certainty for pneumonia not given in the abstract
claims.safe_wording: Feeding tubes have not been shown to prevent pneumonia from food or drink going down the wrong way. Some studies suggest pneumonia may be more common with a tube, but the results were inconsistent.
claims.qualifications: The review gives no certainty grade for pneumonia in the abstract and says harm results were inconsistent. Do not headline pneumonia as a proven harm or give it equal weight with the pressure ulcer finding. The safer claim is 'not shown to prevent aspiration pneumonia' (AGS).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Harm outcomes inconsistent across five studies. The Cochrane authors' conclusion also contains the ambiguous phrase 'and no indication of harm' alongside the pressure ulcer finding; avoid broad statements about harm beyond pressure sores.

numbers.meaning: studies reporting harm outcomes, with inconsistent results

claims.claim: No study has shown that tube feeding makes people with severe dementia more comfortable or improves quality of life: none measured quality of life, and the one study of pain and comfort found no difference.
claims.supporting_passage: "None of the included studies assessed quality of life. Only one study, using mixed methods of enteral tube feeding, reported on pain and comfort, finding no difference between groups. In the same study, a higher proportion of carers reported very heavy burden in the enteral tube feeding group compared to no enteral tube feeding." Authors' conclusions: "We found no evidence that tube feeding improves survival; improves quality of life; reduces pain; reduces mortality; decreases behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia; leads to better nourishment; improves family or carer outcomes such as depression, anxiety, carer burden, or satisfaction with care; and no indication of harm."
claims.location: Abstract, Main results and Authors' conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: Observational studies; quality of life not measured; pain and comfort in one mixed-methods study
claims.safe_wording: No study has shown that a feeding tube makes a person with severe dementia more comfortable. Quality of life was never measured, and the one study that looked at pain and comfort found no difference.
claims.qualifications: This is mostly an evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit. Say 'has not been shown', not 'does not'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Very little data; one study only for comfort.

numbers.meaning: studies that measured quality of life
study that reported pain and comfort (no difference)

claims.claim: The American Geriatrics Society does not recommend feeding tubes for older adults with advanced dementia, recommends careful hand feeding, and says tube feeding is a treatment that can be accepted or declined according to the person's wishes.
claims.supporting_passage: "When eating difficulties arise, feeding tubes are not recommended for older adults with advanced dementia. Careful hand feeding should be offered because hand feeding has been shown to be as good as tube feeding for the outcomes of death, aspiration pneumonia, functional status, and comfort. Moreover, tube feeding is associated with agitation, greater use of physical and chemical restraints, healthcare use due to tube-related complications, and development of new pressure ulcers. Efforts to enhance oral feeding by altering the environment and creating patient-centered approaches to feeding should be part of usual care for older adults with advanced dementia. Tube feeding is a medical therapy that an individual's surrogate decision-maker can decline or accept in accordance with advance directives, previously stated wishes, or what it is thought the individual would want."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with advanced dementia and eating difficulties; US position statement, 2014
claims.safe_wording: The American Geriatrics Society advises against feeding tubes for older people with advanced dementia and recommends careful hand feeding. It says a feeding tube is a medical treatment that can be accepted or declined in line with what the person wanted.
claims.qualifications: US society, 2014. Its comparative statements ('as good as') rest on observational studies. Tube feeding is 'associated with' agitation and restraint: keep the association wording.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with ESPEN 2024 and (by search extract) NICE NG97.

claims.claim: The 2024 ESPEN dementia guideline says tube or drip feeding and hydration are temporary options in mild or moderate dementia, but not in severe dementia or the last phase of life.
claims.supporting_passage: "Oral nutrition may be supported by eliminating potential causes of malnutrition and dehydration, and adequate social and nursing support (including assistance, utensils, training and oral care)." ... "Enteral and parenteral nutrition and hydration are temporary options in patients with mild or moderate dementia, but not in severe dementia or in the terminal phase of life." ... "Due to a lack of appropriate studies, most recommendations are good practice points."

claims.safe_wording: European nutrition guidance (ESPEN, 2024) says tube feeding can be a temporary option in mild or moderate dementia, but not in severe dementia or near the end of life. It recommends supporting eating with help, suitable utensils, staff training and mouth care.
claims.qualifications: Most ESPEN dementia recommendations are good practice points (expert consensus), because trials are lacking.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; consistent with AGS 2014.

numbers.meaning: year of the ESPEN dementia guideline update

claims.claim: NICE NG97 advises: do not routinely use enteral feeding in people living with severe dementia, unless indicated for a potentially reversible comorbidity.
claims.supporting_passage: WebSearch extract (nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/recommendations): "Do not routinely use enteral feeding in people living with severe dementia, unless indicated for a potentially reversible comorbidity."
