claims.claim: A 2010 meta-analysis of 148 studies (308,849 participants) found people with stronger social relationships had higher odds of survival (OR 1.50); strongest for complex measures of social integration, weakest for living alone.
claims.supporting_passage: "Across 148 studies (308,849 participants), the random effects weighted average effect size was OR = 1.50 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.59), indicating a 50% increased likelihood of survival for participants with stronger social relationships. This finding remained consistent across age, sex, initial health status, cause of death, and follow-up period. Significant differences were found across the type of social measurement evaluated (p<0.001); the association was strongest for complex measures of social integration (OR = 1.91; 95% CI 1.63 to 2.23) and lowest for binary indicators of residential status (living alone versus with others) (OR = 1.19; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.44)." Full text (Results): "Participants were followed for an average of 7.5 years"
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in 148 mostly North American and Western European cohorts / stronger vs weaker social relationships (many different measures) / survival (all-cause mortality) / mean follow-up 7.5 years
claims.safe_wording: A 2010 review pooled 148 studies of about 309,000 people, followed for 7.5 years on average. People with stronger social relationships were more likely to be alive at the end of follow-up. The link was strongest when studies used measures combining several kinds of social ties, and weakest (not clearly different from no link) for simply living alone.
claims.qualifications: Association from observational studies; the authors state causality is not easily established. OR 1.50 is an odds ratio for survival; do not convert it to '50% more likely to survive' or to an absolute difference. 'Social relationships' here is a composite of many measures, not loneliness.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Later reviews that isolate loneliness find a smaller association (see C17-15-d and C17-15-f).

numbers.meaning: studies pooled
participants
odds of survival, stronger vs weaker social relationships; relative, pooled across measures
complex measures of social integration
living alone vs with others; confidence interval includes no effect
average follow-up

claims.claim: The 2010 paper compared its effect size in a figure with other risk factors, including smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes a day, and described the effect as comparable with quitting smoking.
claims.supporting_passage: Figure 6 bar label (as printed): "Smoking < 15 cigarettes daily". Figure 6 caption: "Comparison of odds (lnOR) of decreased mortality across several conditions associated with mortality. Note: Effect size of zero indicates no effect. The effect sizes were estimated from meta analyses: ; A = Shavelle, Paculdo, Strauss, and Kush, 2008 [205]; ..." Conclusion: "The magnitude of this effect is comparable with quitting smoking and it exceeds many well-known risk factors for mortality (e.g., obesity, physical inactivity)."
claims.location: Figure 6 (bar labels and caption, read from the PDF via Undermind); Discussion/Conclusion (also in PMC full text)
claims.pico_timeframe: Cross-study comparison: pooled social relationships effect (this meta-analysis) set beside effect sizes from other meta-analyses (smoking <15 a day from Shavelle 2008; also alcohol, vaccination, cardiac rehabilitation, physical activity, BMI, antihypertensives, air pollution)
claims.safe_wording: A chart in the 2010 review set the size of this link beside other risk factors, including smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes a day. The authors wrote that the effect was 'comparable with quitting smoking'. The chart compared numbers from different reviews of different people; it was not a head-to-head test.
claims.qualifications: The comparator is 'fewer than 15' a day, not 15. The social relationships figure pooled marriage, networks, support, integration and other measures, not loneliness. The paper does not itself state the popular line 'loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day'; that the popular line derives from this chart was not confirmed from an opened source, so the post should say the comparison 'appears in' the 2010 review rather than that the slogan 'comes from' it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The US Surgeon General's 2023 advisory is widely reported to repeat the comparison, but it could not be opened (search result only; not used).

numbers.meaning: cigarettes a day in the smoking comparator bar (Figure 6)
bars in Figure 6: 3 social relationship estimates and 9 other risk factors or treatments

claims.claim: Most results pooled in the 2010 review measured social networks, marriage, support or integration rather than loneliness; loneliness contributed only 8 effect sizes.
claims.supporting_passage: Introduction: "three major components of social relationships are consistently evaluated: (a) the degree of integration in social networks, (b) the social interactions that are intended to be supportive (i.e., received social support), and (c) the beliefs and perceptions of support availability held by the individual (i.e., perceived social support)." Results: "...which resulted in a total of 230 unique effect sizes across 116 studies" (structural measures); "We extracted 87 unique effect sizes that were specific to measures of functional social relationships within 72 studies"; "We extracted 64 unique effect sizes that evaluated combined structural and functional measures of social relationships within 61 studies." Table 2 lists 'Perception of loneliness: Feelings of isolation, disconnectedness, and not belonging' as one functional measure; Table 4, 'Loneliness (inversed)': k = 8, OR = 1.45 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.94).
claims.location: Introduction; Results (metaregression sections, PMC full text); Tables 2 and 4 (read from PDF via Undermind)
claims.pico_timeframe: Measures of social relationships across 148 studies; loneliness a sub-category of functional measures
claims.safe_wording: Most of the studies measured things like marriage, the size of people's social networks, the support they had and how involved they were with others. Loneliness itself was measured in only 8 of the several hundred results in the review.
claims.qualifications: k = 8 are effect sizes, not necessarily 8 separate studies. Within those 8, lower loneliness was linked with better survival (OR 1.45), so the review does not show loneliness is unimportant; it shows the headline figure is mostly about other social measures.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None for the counting point.

numbers.meaning: loneliness effect sizes in the 2010 review (Table 4)
survival odds for less vs more lonely, 2010 review, 8 effect sizes

claims.claim: A 2015 meta-analysis found loneliness associated with higher odds of death in adjusted studies (OR 1.26), similar to social isolation (1.29) and living alone (1.32).

Results also differ across participant age, with social deficits being more predictive of death in samples with an average age younger than 65 years."

claims.claim: In ELSA (about 6,500 people aged 52 and over), loneliness was not independently associated with mortality after adjustment for demographic factors and baseline health, while social isolation was.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "We found that mortality was higher among more socially isolated and more lonely participants. However, after adjusting statistically for demographic factors and baseline health, social isolation remained significantly associated with mortality (hazard ratio 1.26, 95% confidence interval, 1.08-1.48 for the top quintile of isolation), but loneliness did not (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% confidence interval, 0.78-1.09)." Discussion: "These results do not imply that loneliness is not important but rather indicate that the experience of loneliness may be characteristic of people who already have major health and mobility problems." and "Reducing both social isolation and loneliness are important for quality of life and well-being, but efforts to reduce isolation would be likely to have greater benefits in terms of mortality."

claims.safe_wording: In a study of about 6,500 people aged 52 and over in England, followed for about 7 years, lonely people were more likely to die at first. Nakou 2025: "Of 11,964 identified studies, 86 met the inclusion criteria. claims.claim: The association is observational; proposed explanations include grief-related stress, loss of support and of a partner who encouraged healthy behaviour and medicine-taking, material resources, and shared risks.
claims.supporting_passage: Moon 2011, Discussion: "marriage could provide additional social and emotional support, which may act as a buffer against harmful effects of various psychosocial stress. The guardian role theory suggests that spouses monitor each other, encouraging healthy behaviors of the partner, such as compliance with medical regimens, as well as discouraging unhealthy and risky ones" and "A final hypothesis is that grief associated with the loss of a loved one increases mortality risk directly via psychoneuroimmune pathways. This is especially plausible given that widowhood effect is markedly stronger in the months immediately following the spouse's death than in the years following." Limitations: "Most prior studies have inadequately controlled for socioeconomic confounders ... thus leading to uncertainty about whether the widowhood effect is causal." Elwert 2008: "Increased mortality following the death of a spouse (the 'widowhood effect') may be due to (1) causation, (2) bias from spousal similarity (homogamy), or (3) bias from shared environmental exposures." "These results strengthen the causal interpretation of the widowhood effect by suggesting that the widowhood effect is not due to homogamy bias to any substantial degree." Stroebe 2007: "bereavement is associated with excess risk of mortality, particularly in the early weeks and months after loss." "Although grief is not a disease and most people adjust without professional psychological intervention"
claims.location: Moon: Discussion (read via Undermind); Elwert: Abstract; Stroebe: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Observational cohorts; proposed mechanisms (hypotheses)
claims.safe_wording: Nobody knows exactly why the risk rises. Suggested reasons include the stress of grief, losing emotional support, and losing the partner who encouraged healthy habits and taking medicines. One large study found the pattern was not explained by spouses simply sharing the same risks, which makes a real effect of the loss more likely, but it is still not proven. Most bereaved people adjust without professional help.
claims.qualifications: Loss of practical care (cooking, medicines, money, driving) is a plausible hypothesis, closest to the 'guardian role' idea; it is not a measured finding. Label it as a hypothesis.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Residual confounding (authors); causality uncertain.

claims.safe_wording: In a UK study, men whose wives died ate less fruit and fewer vegetables, and less variety, over the next few years than men who stayed married. This was not seen in widowed women.
claims.qualifications: Observational; fruit and vegetables only; not a whole-diet or nutrition outcome; cohort includes middle-aged people.

claims.claim: In a meta-analysis of randomised trials, discharge planning that integrated family carers was linked with fewer readmissions at 90 and 180 days.
claims.supporting_passage: Discharge planning interventions with caregiver integration were associated with a 25% fewer readmissions at 90 days (relative risk (RR) = 0.75, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.62-0.91) and 24% fewer readmissions at 180 days (RR = 0.76, 95% CI = 0.64-0.90).
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with informal caregivers discharged to community / multicomponent discharge planning including the carer, begun before discharge / usual care / readmission / 90 and 180 days
claims.safe_wording: A review of randomised trials found that discharge plans that brought family carers in were linked with about a quarter fewer readmissions over the next 3 to 6 months (a relative reduction).
claims.qualifications: Relative, not absolute; interventions were multicomponent so the carer part cannot be isolated; pooled from 6 and 5 trials; trial quality often unclear. Full text re-read 2026-10-08: 11 of 15 studies gave enough detail to calculate readmission rates (6 at 90 days, 5 at 180 days); text gives no pooled arm-level rates. Authors' own 'reduces the risk' conclusion is stronger than the trial quality supports; use 'linked with'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Absolute rates not available in text retrieved, so no 'N in 100' statement. No pooled 30-day result. Cochrane review of discharge planning generally (PMID 35199849, other batch) found a smaller relative reduction (RR 0.89) in readmission at about 3 months.

claims.claim: A systematic review of 13 studies found most barriers minority ethnic carers described were potentially relevant to all carers: not wanting to involve outsiders, not seeing the need, low awareness of services, service availability; specific issues were language barriers and concerns about cultural appropriateness; few studies compared with majority groups.
claims.supporting_passage: Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ... Few studies compared minority ethnic carers' perceptions with majority ethnic groups, making it difficult to identify issues specific to minority groups. Most barriers described were potentially relevant to all carers, irrespective of ethnic group. They included attitudinal barriers such as not wanting to involve outsiders or not seeing the need for services and practical barriers such as low awareness of services and service availability. Issues specific to minority ethnic groups included language barriers and concerns about services' cultural or religious appropriateness.
claims.pico_timeframe: Minority ethnic carers / access to community social care / (few) majority-group comparisons / perceived barriers and satisfaction / studies to July 2013

claims.qualifications: Authors' background statement, not a finding.

claims.claim: Most vs least deprived neighbourhoods: more likely hospital death vs home, acute hospital care in last 3 months, and not receiving specialist palliative care; gradient across quintiles.
claims.supporting_passage: Compared to people living in the least deprived neighbourhoods, people living in the most deprived neighbourhoods were more likely to die in hospital versus home (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.23-1.38, p < 0.001), to receive acute hospital-based care in the last 3 months of life (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.25, p < 0.001), and to not receive specialist palliative care (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.07-1.19, p < 0.001). For every quintile increase in area deprivation, hospital versus home death was more likely (OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.05-1.08, p < 0.001)
claims.pico_timeframe: High-income countries, 112 observational studies / area deprivation / least deprived / place of death, acute care, specialist palliative care / last year of life
claims.safe_wording: A review of studies from high-income countries found people in the poorest neighbourhoods were more likely than those in the richest to die in hospital rather than at home, to have hospital care in their last 3 months, and less likely to get specialist palliative care. The gap grew step by step with deprivation.
claims.qualifications: Describe in words only; observational; modest effects; causes not established; mostly North American studies (53.5%).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneous studies.

numbers.meaning: studies included / used in synthesis

claims.claim: Evidence that anticipatory medicines improve symptom control or prevent admissions is inadequate; professionals believe they help.
claims.supporting_passage: Healthcare professionals believe anticipatory prescribing provides reassurance, effective symptom control, and helps to prevent crisis hospital admissions. The attitudes of patients towards anticipatory prescribing remain unknown. It is a low-cost intervention, but there is inadequate evidence to draw conclusions about its impact on symptom control and comfort or crisis hospital admissions.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults at end of life in community, 34 papers
claims.safe_wording: Professionals believe 'just in case' medicines help, but research has not yet shown whether they improve comfort or prevent hospital admissions.
claims.qualifications: Say "professionals believe"; the review found the evidence inadequate, not evidence of no benefit. Review concerns injectable medicines in the community, searches to May 2017.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Gap in evidence (patients' views unknown, impact on symptoms and admissions not established); not evidence that they do not work.

numbers.meaning: papers synthesised

claims.claim: NICE NG31/QS144 recommend anticipatory prescribing; usual symptom classes covered.
claims.safe_wording: Not verified; NICE pages could not be opened.

claims.claim: On TV dramas most people given CPR survive.
claims.supporting_passage: Diem: There were 60 occurrences of CPR in the 97 television episodes... Seventy-five percent of the patients survived the immediate arrest, and 67 percent appeared to have survived to hospital discharge. Portanova: CPR was depicted 46 times in the 91 episodes, with a survival rate of 69.6%. Among those immediately surviving following CPR, the majority (71.9%) survived to hospital discharge
claims.pico_timeframe: US TV medical dramas 1994-95 and 2010-11
claims.safe_wording: In 1990s US TV dramas, about 2 in 3 people given CPR appeared to survive to leave hospital. In Grey's Anatomy and House (2010-11), about 7 in 10 survived the CPR itself.
claims.qualifications: Compare Diem's 67% (discharge) with the audit; Portanova's 69.6% is immediate survival, not discharge. Diem TV patients were mostly young with trauma.

numbers.meaning: TV patients appearing to survive to discharge, Diem 1996, n=60
immediate survival, Portanova 2015, n=46

claims.claim: UK in-hospital arrest survival to discharge 18.4%; 10.5% for non-shockable rhythms (72.3% of arrests).
claims.supporting_passage: Overall unadjusted survival to hospital discharge was 18.4%. The presenting rhythm was shockable (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) in 16.9% and non-shockable (asystole or pulseless electrical activity) in 72.3%; rates of survival to hospital discharge associated with these rhythms were 49.0% and 10.5%, respectively, but varied substantially across hospitals.
claims.pico_timeframe: 22,628 adults, 144 UK hospitals / team-attended CPR / survival to discharge
claims.safe_wording: In UK hospitals, fewer than 1 in 5 adults given CPR by the hospital team survived to leave hospital. For the most common kind of arrest, about 1 in 10 did.
claims.qualifications: Unadjusted; audit data about a decade old; all ages 16+, so older frailer people likely lower (not shown here).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Frailty claim (Ibitoye) not verified; omit.

numbers.meaning: survival to discharge, all
non-shockable, 72.3% of arrests
shockable, 16.9% of arrests

claims.claim: Anticipatory medicines are often not all used: use after prescription varies by setting.
claims.supporting_passage: Use in nursing homes appears to be less common: one retrospective study reported that 'less than a third' of patients required the administration of prescribed medications, and a qualitative study of nursing home nurses reported that very few dying patients required the administration of prescribed drugs. Much higher proportions of use have been reported at home, ranging from 70%-77%. [Table, home study:] A significant amount of medicines went unused, but 77% of boxes issued had at least one drug used.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults at end of life; community and nursing homes; use of prescribed anticipatory medicines (mostly UK); review of 34 papers, searches to 2017
claims.safe_wording: In studies reviewed, the box was used in most home deaths (about 7 in 10 to 3 in 4 of those studied) but less often in nursing homes (fewer than 1 in 3 patients), and many individual medicines in the box go unused. Having a box does not mean death is close or that every medicine will be given.
claims.qualifications: Few, low-to-medium quality studies; use data are limited (review says literature on use after prescription is limited); the 70%-77% for home is the range reported by the review, not a national figure. 'Boxes' study is a single service evaluation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Rates of use are not the same as benefit.

numbers.meaning: use of prescribed medicines at home, as reported across studies in the review
patients in nursing homes given prescribed medicines, one retrospective study

claims.claim: What families should do with unused anticipatory medicines after the death.
claims.safe_wording: Do not state. Official guidance (NICE, local policy) could not be opened; the Bowers review gives costs of unused medicines, not disposal advice.

claims.claim: A hand-held fan blown at the face reduced breathlessness compared with the fan on the legs.
claims.supporting_passage: Fifty participants were randomized to use a handheld fan for five minutes directed to their face or leg first and then crossed over to the other treatment. ... There was a significant difference in the VAS scores between the two treatments, with a reduction in breathlessness when the fan was directed to the face (P=0.003).
claims.pico_timeframe: 50 adults with advanced disease / fan to face 5 min / fan to legs / breathlessness VAS / immediate
claims.safe_wording: In a small trial of 50 people with advanced illness, five minutes of a hand-held fan blowing on the face eased breathlessness more than the same fan blowing on the legs.
claims.qualifications: Small, short-term (5 minutes) study.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Longer-term benefit not shown by this trial.

numbers.meaning: participants
duration of each exposure

claims.claim: In people without low oxygen levels, oxygen through nasal tubes gave no more relief than room air; both groups improved.
claims.supporting_passage: From baseline to day 6, mean morning breathlessness changed by -0.9 points (95% CI -1.3 to -0.5) in patients assigned to receive oxygen and by -0.7 points (-1.2 to -0.2) in patients assigned to receive room air (p=0.504). ... Since oxygen delivered by a nasal cannula provides no additional symptomatic benefit for relief of refractory dyspnoea in patients with life-limiting illness compared with room air, less burdensome strategies should be considered after brief assessment of the effect of oxygen therapy on the individual patient.
claims.pico_timeframe: 239 outpatients, life-limiting illness, PaO2 >7.3 kPa / oxygen 2 L/min via nasal cannula / room air via same concentrator / breathlessness 0-10 / 7 days
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of 239 people with serious illness whose blood oxygen was not low, oxygen through nasal tubes eased breathlessness no more than room air given through the same tubes; both groups felt a little better.
claims.qualifications: Excluded people with low blood oxygen; outpatients, not dying people; 7 days.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Improvement in both groups may reflect air flow, expectation or natural course; the trial cannot separate these.

numbers.meaning: randomised participants
mean change in morning breathlessness (0-10 scale) day 6, oxygen vs room air, p=0.504

claims.claim: In 32 people near death, oxygen, medical air and no flow made no difference to observed respiratory distress; 91% tolerated the protocol.
claims.supporting_passage: Most (91%) patients tolerated the protocol with no change in respiratory comfort. Three patients (9%) displayed distress and were restored to baseline oxygen ... Repeated-measure analysis of variance revealed no differences in the Respiratory Distress Observation Scale under changing gas and flow conditions. ... The n-of-1 trial of oxygen in clinical practice is appropriate in the face of hypoxemic respiratory distress.
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients near death without baseline distress / oxygen, air, no flow alternated every 10 min / observer-rated distress
claims.safe_wording: In a small study of people close to death who were not in distress, switching between oxygen, air and no flow made no difference to breathing distress for most; 3 of 32 became distressed and went back on oxygen.
claims.qualifications: Small; people not distressed at start; distress rated by observers.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The same study supports trying oxygen for an individual with low oxygen and distress.

numbers.meaning: of 32 patients tolerated with no change
showed distress and returned to oxygen

claims.claim: Oxygen can cause nasal irritation and add cost.
claims.supporting_passage: Campbell (background): "Oxygen may produce nasal irritation and increase the cost of care." Abernethy: "The frequency of side-effects did not differ between groups."
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Oxygen tubing and equipment are a burden for some people; the post should not claim trial-proven extra side-effects.
claims.qualifications: Campbell's statement is background, not a finding. In Abernethy nasal irritation was not more common with oxygen than air through the same tubes.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Abernethy found no difference in side-effects.

claims.claim: The noise is presumed to come from secretions gathering in the airways that the dying person cannot clear.
claims.supporting_passage: Cochrane: "The cause of death rattle remains unproven but is presumed to be due to an accumulation of secretions in the airways. It is therefore managed physically (repositioning and clearing the upper airways of fluid with a mechanical sucker) or pharmacologically (with anticholinergic drugs)." SILENCE: "Death rattle, defined as noisy breathing caused by the presence of mucus in the respiratory tract, is relatively common among dying patients."
claims.pico_timeframe: definition
claims.safe_wording: The rattling sound is thought to come from saliva and mucus collecting in the throat and airways when a dying person can no longer cough or swallow it away.
claims.qualifications: Mechanism presumed, not proven.

claims.claim: The person is thought not to be distressed by the sound.
claims.supporting_passage: The impact of death rattle on patients was less well described, although there was a consensus that death rattle is not distressing to affected patients (but may be distressing to other patients).
claims.pico_timeframe: Scoping review of 14 studies
claims.safe_wording: Experts generally agree the sound is unlikely to distress the dying person, but this has not been measured well.
claims.qualifications: Consensus/inference, not measured.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Further research on patients' experience called for.

claims.claim: Some relatives are distressed by the sound, especially if they think the person is choking or drowning; others are not.
claims.supporting_passage: Wee II: "Seventeen of the 25 bereaved relatives interviewed had heard the sound of death rattle. Ten relatives were distressed by the sound, but seven were not. Some relatives regarded the sound of death rattle as a useful warning sign that death was imminent. ... Relatives were distressed when they thought that the sound of death rattle indicated that the patient might be drowning or choking." Wee I: "almost half of the 12 relatives who had heard the sound of death rattle had been distressed by it. The others were either neutral about the sound or found it a helpful signal of impending death." Fagan 2025: "related distress was common amongst informal carers".
claims.pico_timeframe: Bereaved relatives, UK, interviews
claims.safe_wording: In interview studies, some relatives were upset by the sound, especially when they thought the person was choking or drowning; others were not, and some took it as a sign that death was close.
claims.qualifications: Small qualitative studies; Wee I abstract says 'almost half of the 12' (the 5 of 12 figure is from Wee II's summary of study I).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A Dutch interview study (van Esch 2020) found most relatives distressed and that information alone did not always ease it.

numbers.meaning: relatives who heard the sound and were distressed (Wee II)
Wee I, as reported in Wee II abstract

claims.claim: Repositioning is a recognised way to manage the sound; evidence that any treatment helps an established rattle is lacking.
claims.supporting_passage: It is therefore managed physically (repositioning and clearing the upper airways of fluid with a mechanical sucker) or pharmacologically (with anticholinergic drugs). ... There is currently no evidence to show that any intervention, be it pharmacological or non-pharmacological, is superior to placebo in the treatment of death rattle. ... relatives need time, explanation and reassurance to relieve their fears and concerns.
claims.pico_timeframe: Cochrane review, to 2007
claims.safe_wording: Changing the person's position is a common first step; there is little trial evidence that medicines or other measures quiet the sound once it has started. Relatives need time and explanation.
claims.qualifications: Do not claim repositioning is proven to reduce the sound. Review is from 2008.

claims.claim: A preventive injection of hyoscine butylbromide reduced death rattle from 27% to 13% in Dutch hospices.
claims.supporting_passage: A death rattle occurred in 10 patients (13%) in the scopolamine group compared with 21 patients (27%) in the placebo group (difference, 14%; 95% CI, 2%-27%, P = .02).
claims.pico_timeframe: 157 dying hospice patients / scopolamine butylbromide 20 mg SC four times daily from recognition of dying / placebo / grade 2+ rattle
claims.safe_wording: In a Dutch hospice trial, giving hyoscine butylbromide as soon as dying was recognised, before any rattle, meant about 13 in 100 developed the rattle compared with 27 in 100 on placebo.
claims.qualifications: Prevention, not treatment of an established rattle; hospice setting; restlessness 28% vs 23%.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether prevention is worthwhile is debated (van Esch 2023 controversies article).

numbers.meaning: rattle occurrence, drug vs placebo, absolute difference 14 percentage points

claims.claim: Abrupt stopping of Parkinson's medicines can rarely cause parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, a dangerous condition resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
claims.supporting_passage: Beckers 2025 (full text, Introduction): "In rare cases, acute cessation causes parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome. This potentially life-limiting syndrome is a specific form of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and consists of severe rigidity, autonomic dysfunction (e.g., hyperthermia, tachycardia), rhabdomyolysis and disturbances of consciousness." And: "Acute cessation of levodopa might result in a severe relapse of PD symptoms ... This includes a worsening of motor symptoms, such as akinesia, rigidity or tremor, and also of non-motor symptoms, such as anxiety and pain." End-of-life section: "If a person has sufficient symptom control with palliative treatments, including palliative sedation, one can opt to omit dopaminergic treatment altogether – although sudden cessation carries a risk of parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome." Also: "In the 72 h before death, severe motor symptoms were present in only 6% of persons in one study." Wang 2022 abstract (retained): "...caused by abrupt withdrawal of antiparkinsonian medication."
claims.location: Beckers: Introduction; 'Unplanned cessation ... at the end of life'. Wang: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Case reports and review of 56 cases
claims.safe_wording: Stopping Parkinson's medicines suddenly can bring severe stiffness, pain and anxiety, and in rare cases a dangerous reaction with high fever. At the end of life, some people have good symptom control without them, so the decision is individual: ask what is making the person uncomfortable, and decide on purpose rather than by default.
claims.qualifications: Withdrawal syndrome is rare. Expert review, not trial evidence. Reviewers note that tapering off dopaminergic medicine may be possible with limited harm in some people; terminal stiffness was documented in only 3 of 51 people in the 72 hours before death (Wilson 2024) and 6% in one study cited by Beckers. The post must not say that stopping is always harmful.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Several experts argue dopaminergic medicine can be tapered at the end of life with limited negative consequences; others continue it until death. Frequency of the withdrawal syndrome near death is unknown.

claims.claim: A rotigotine skin patch is commonly used when oral Parkinson's medicines can no longer be swallowed at the end of life; conversion is approximate.
claims.supporting_passage: Hindmarsh: "when oral administration of antiparkinsonian medications is no longer possible in dying patients, it is becoming common place to initiate transdermal rotigotine, despite a paucity of evidence to guide dosing. ... The majority of patients were converted to transdermal rotigotine (90%). Patients converted to a higher than equivalent dose of rotigotine were more likely to be agitated (p < 0.05)" Ibrahim: "25 (30%) patients were prescribed the recommended dose of Rotigotine; 31 (37%) higher and 28 (33%) lower than recommended. ... Inappropriate dosing may precipitate or worsen delirium/hallucinations. Use at end-of-life requires further evaluation." || Beckers 2025: "Based on these studies, transdermal rotigotine is the most widely used non-oral strategy at the end of life. In a UK-based cohort of 51 PwP at the end-of-life, 55% had dopaminergic medication substituted with transdermal rotigotine at death. However, evidence regarding its effectiveness is scarce" and "The equivalency factor from levodopa to transdermal rotigotine is 30:1 and the maximum dose of rotigotine is 16 mg/24 h, corresponding to 480 mg levodopa." and "it can sometimes induce psychotic symptoms or worsen autonomic symptoms" and "as many as 24% of subjects developed a delirium" (in a study of people with advanced PD started on a rotigotine patch). || Hewer 2024 abstract: "83% (n = 52) of PWP were eligible for rotigotine and, of those, 13% (n = 7) received the correct dose, 38% (n = 20) a lower dose, 12% (n = 6) a higher dose and 37% (n = 19) did not receive any. ... Rotigotine dose and admission LEDD were both associated with proxy measures of distress in the last 72 hours of life. This suggests cautious use of rotigotine at EOL." || Kim 2023 abstract: "Although rotigotine patch and apormorphine injections are most frequently recommended, there are no clinical trials in this patient population to support those recommendations."
claims.location: Beckers: 'Unplanned cessation ... at the end of life' and Table 1; Hewer, Kim: Abstracts
claims.pico_timeframe: UK hospital inpatients with Parkinson's, retrospective
claims.safe_wording: When a person with Parkinson's can no longer swallow, a rotigotine skin patch is the most widely used non-oral option near the end of life, but no trials show it works there. Doses are approximate (about 30 mg of levodopa to 1 mg of rotigotine), the patch cannot replace high levodopa doses, and too high a dose is linked with confusion, hallucinations and agitation. In one Australian hospital, only 7 of 52 eligible people got the recommended dose. Agree the dose with pharmacy or the Parkinson's team.
claims.qualifications: Observational and expert-opinion evidence only. Absorption through skin can be reduced by sweating, weight loss and poor circulation. Apomorphine and subcutaneous levodopa are other non-oral routes but need specialist set-up and may be unavailable. Use the conversion ratio only if the practitioner audience is the target and label it approximate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Case reports conflict (two improved, two had insufficient effect). Hindmarsh found lower-than-equivalent doses possibly better tolerated. Rotigotine dose was associated with more benzodiazepine use in the last 72 hours (Hewer).

numbers.meaning: levodopa to rotigotine equivalence factor; maximum rotigotine 16 mg/24 h corresponds to 480 mg levodopa (Beckers)
eligible people given the correct rotigotine dose in the last 72 hours of life, one Australian hospital (Hewer)
patches prescribed at the recommended dose, UK teaching hospital (Ibrahim)
of 100 dying inpatients converted to rotigotine (Hindmarsh)
UK cohort with dopaminergic medicine substituted with rotigotine at death (quoted by Beckers)

claims.claim: Dopamine-blocking medicines (for example metoclopramide and haloperidol) are contraindicated in Parkinson's disease, including near the end of life, and are still prescribed.
claims.supporting_passage: Hewer 2024 abstract: "Contraindicated dopamine antagonists were prescribed for 43% of PWP and administered in 31% of those cases." || Beckers 2025 (full text, surgery section): "certain drugs which are commonly used periprocedurally are contraindicated in PwP (examples include ketamine, metoclopramide and haloperidol)." || Lertxundi 2017 abstract: "...the administration of centrally acting antidopaminergics. ... inappropriate antiemetic administration OR = 2.15 CI 95% (1.36-3.39); and inappropriate antipsychotic administration OR = 1.91 ... Inappropriately omitted doses and both inappropriate antipsychotic and antiemetic administration were associated with a significant 4-day increase in median hospital stay."
claims.location: Hewer: Abstract (Results). Beckers: Surgery section. Lertxundi: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: 1628 PD inpatients, Spain / antidopaminergic drugs / none / mortality, LOS
claims.safe_wording: Metoclopramide and haloperidol block dopamine and are listed as contraindicated in Parkinson's disease. In an Australian audit of people with Parkinson's who died in hospital, 43% were prescribed a contraindicated dopamine blocker and 31% of those prescriptions were given. Check every anti-sickness, calming and sedative medicine on the chart against its dopamine-blocking effect.
claims.qualifications: Beckers names metoclopramide and haloperidol (with ketamine) in a perioperative context, not specifically for the last days of life; the Hewer audit is end-of-life but its abstract does not list the drugs. Do not name safe alternatives or other drugs (for example levomepromazine, prochlorperazine) as unsafe or safe: not verified from an opened source. NICE NG71 and Scottish guideline text could not be opened. Lertxundi is observational and not end-of-life specific.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Beckers notes opioids and benzodiazepines, otherwise best avoided in earlier disease, are the mainstay at the end of life; and for confusion lorazepam or midazolam subcutaneously are suggested. Guideline-level list of dopamine-blocking drugs to avoid not verified.

numbers.meaning: of people with Parkinson's who died at one Australian hospital were prescribed a contraindicated dopamine antagonist (Hewer; denominator about 63 people, check full text before using)
of those prescriptions were administered

claims.claim: About 1 in 10 bereaved adults develop prolonged grief disorder after non-violent loss; higher mean age linked with higher prevalence.
claims.supporting_passage: Meta-analysis revealed a pooled prevalence of PGD of 9.8% (95% CI 6.8-14.0). Moderation analyses showed higher mean age to be associated with higher prevalence of PGD. ... Due to heterogeneity and limited representativeness, the findings should be interpreted cautiously
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults after non-violent bereavement, 14 studies
claims.safe_wording: Studies suggest roughly 1 in 10 adults bereaved by a non-violent death develop grief that stays intense and disabling; it appears more common in older groups.
claims.qualifications: Heterogeneous studies, pre-ICD-11 criteria; age link is across studies.

numbers.meaning: pooled prevalence

claims.claim: In adults 50+, complicated grief treatment gave a response rate of 70.5% vs 32.0% with interpersonal psychotherapy.
claims.supporting_passage: Response rate for CGT (52 individuals [70.5%]) was more than twice that for IPT (24 [32.0%]) (relative risk, 2.20 [95% CI, 1.51-3.22]; P < .001), with the number needed to treat at 2.56. ... Results were not moderated by participant age.
claims.pico_timeframe: 151 adults 50+ (mean 66), New York / 16 sessions CGT / grief-focused IPT / response at 20 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial of 151 people aged 50 and over, about 7 in 10 improved with a grief-specific therapy, compared with about 3 in 10 with a talking therapy proven for depression.
claims.qualifications: One US trial; comparator is an active therapy.

numbers.meaning: response at 20 weeks
participants

claims.claim: ICD-11 includes prolonged grief disorder with a 6-month criterion.
claims.safe_wording: Do not state the ICD-11 duration unless verified; may say it was 'expected to be included in ICD-11' (Lundorff 2017).
claims.qualifications: WHO page not opened.

claims.claim: Guidance sets the as-needed opioid dose at one sixth (or one tenth to one sixth) of the 24-hour dose and advises recalculating when the regular dose changes.
claims.qualifications: Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines, PCF and EAPC text not opened in this batch.

claims.claim: People with more positive self-perceptions of ageing lived 7.5 years longer in one cohort of 660.
claims.supporting_passage: This research found that older individuals with more positive self-perceptions of aging, measured up to 23 years earlier, lived 7.5 years longer than those with less positive self-perceptions of aging. This advantage remained after age, gender, socioeconomic status, loneliness, and functional health were included as covariates. ... The sample consisted of 660 individuals aged 50 and older who participated in a community-based survey, the Ohio Longitudinal Study of Aging and Retirement (OLSAR).
claims.pico_timeframe: 660 Ohio residents aged 50+; exposure: self-perceptions of ageing measured once; comparator: less positive; outcome: survival; up to 23 years
claims.safe_wording: In one US study of 660 people aged 50 and over, those with more positive views of their own ageing lived on average 7.5 years longer, after adjusting for age, sex, income, loneliness and health. This is a link, not proof of cause.
claims.qualifications: Observational; single cohort; adjusted; do not say 'because of'; title's word 'increased' is the authors' causal framing.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Reverse causation (unmeasured illness) and residual confounding possible; later pooled evidence shows a small effect.

numbers.meaning: adjusted survival difference, more vs less positive self-perceptions
participants aged 50+
maximum time since measurement

claims.claim: Meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal studies found a small significant effect, stronger with shorter follow-up and younger samples.
claims.supporting_passage: A systematic search ... resulted in 19 longitudinal studies ... The analyses revealed heterogeneity, with stronger effects for studies with a shorter period of follow-up, for studies of health versus survival, for studies with younger participants ... Subjective aging has a small significant effect on health, health behaviors, and survival.
claims.pico_timeframe: 19 longitudinal studies, mean ages 57-85; subjective ageing; health, behaviours, survival
claims.safe_wording: When 19 long-term studies were pooled, how people view their own ageing had a small link with later health and survival, weaker with longer follow-up.
claims.qualifications: Keep 'small'; effect larger for health than survival.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneity; observational primary studies.

numbers.meaning: longitudinal studies pooled
pooled likelihood ratio; do not translate for public

claims.claim: Association may reflect reverse causation and confounding; the case against ageism is ethical.
claims.supporting_passage: (methods interpretation; no source needed as general point; ethical position marked as judgement)
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Studies like this cannot rule out that people who were already less well viewed ageing more negatively. We should oppose ageist treatment because it is unfair, whatever the survival figure.
claims.qualifications: State as interpretation and judgement, not finding.

claims.claim: Glass 1998 described discordance between hypothetical and enacted function in MacArthur data.
claims.supporting_passage: Failure to attend to this distinction has obscured considerable discordance between what people say they are able to do in standard functional disability assessments, and what they actually do at home. To illustrate this point, data from the MacArthur Studies of Successful Aging comparing the hypothetical to the enacted tenses are presented. These data show a consistent pattern of discordance between these two tenses.
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults, MacArthur Studies; hypothetical vs enacted (and experimental) function
claims.safe_wording: A 1998 paper described three 'tenses' of function: what people say they can do, what they do in a test, and what they actually do at home. In US data, what people said they could do and what they did at home showed 'a consistent pattern of discordance'.
claims.qualifications: No numbers available; do not quantify.

claims.claim: Self-reported and performance-based function agree only moderately in older people.
claims.supporting_passage: Cross-modal agreement was moderate, with by-criterion and frailty-wide Kappa statistics of 0.55-0.60 in all cases. ... Commonly used self-reported disability items cannot be assumed to stand in for performance-based criteria in the PFP. [Owens 2002:] Disagreement between the self-reported and performance-based measure of function was common (slight disagreement, 55.0%; substantial disagreement, 19.3%). Most women (95.4%) overreported their level of function.
claims.pico_timeframe: CHS older adults (n=5888) self-report vs grip/walk tests; post-stroke women (n=620) Barthel vs Physical Performance Test
claims.safe_wording: In a large US study of older adults, self-reported walking and strength difficulty agreed only moderately with measured tests, and one could not simply stand in for the other.
claims.qualifications: Owens is post-stroke women only; do not generalise its percentages.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Direction of disagreement varies by study.

numbers.meaning: moderate agreement, CHS; practitioner post only
of women who disagreed/overall overreported, post-stroke cohort only

claims.claim: WHO ICF distinguishes capacity from performance.
claims.supporting_passage: Not opened (WHO document not accessible from this environment).
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Omit or state without attributing to WHO.

claims.claim: Newcastle 85+: median diseases women 5, men 4; 77.6% rated health compared with others their age good or better.
claims.supporting_passage: Overall, 77.6% (646/832) of participants rated their health compared with others of the same age as good, very good, or excellent. ... Women had significantly higher disease counts (medians: women 5, men 4; P=0.033) ... This large cohort of 85 year olds showed good levels of both self rated health and functional ability despite significant levels of disease and impairment.
claims.pico_timeframe: People aged 85 (born 1921), Newcastle/North Tyneside, including care homes; baseline 2006-07 cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a study of 85-year-olds in Newcastle, the typical woman had 5 recorded diseases and the typical man 4, yet about 3 in 4 (78 in 100) rated their health as good, very good or excellent compared with others their age.
claims.qualifications: Keep 'compared with others their age'; do not say disease lists 'say little' about life; cross-sectional.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Comparative self-ratings may be optimistic.
